#3601. Love Is Blind’s Sarah Says John Accused Her of Cheating Before Escort Drama

Love Is Blind season 11 star Sarah Williams is getting candid about why she really ended her marriage to John Shannon.

“It was quick, [and] I think I felt a lot of shame about myself, like, he would say things that made me feel shame about myself,” Sarah, 34, said on the Wednesday, November 11, episode of “The Viall Files” podcast. “I felt down … I felt like a meeker version of myself. I started being quiet, so even when he would say something that I felt was out of pocket or I disagreed with, I did eventually stop trying to have the conversation because it just didn’t feel worth it to me.”

Sarah and John, 33, were the only couple to get married during the season 11 finale. Their union, however, was short-lived after John admittedly crossed boundaries by exchanging three explicit texts with a stripper, who also worked as an escort. (John confessed during the reunion that he had been emotionally unfaithful but denied having a physical affair.)

As Sarah noted on Nick Viall’s podcast, there were also other reasons for the pair’s divorce.

“[His] behavior was enough for me. I needed to get out. I knew that,” she stated. “I think at first I was like, ‘I can fix this.’ There was a certain point where I was like, ‘What am I doing? Like, this is crazy.’ And then, [in] December [of 2025], he started accusing me of cheating in weird ways.”

Sarah claimed John thought she was having an affair because she kept the front door “ajar” when he left their home in the middle of her workday.

“I’d run down to get a package at some point, and he thought I was cheating on him in the 45 minutes that he was at the gym,” she alleged. “I was like, ‘What is going on?’ And there were a few more moments like that.”

By the time Sarah saw John’s text message chain with alleged “sexually explicit requests” with an unidentified escort, she realized her marriage was over. (Sarah said John briefly messaged the sex worker in February after going on a boys’ trip months before she found out in April.)

“John and I had an open phone policy, but I’ve never been through his phone. I found out because on boy trips, I’m fine with the strip club, like, it’s fine. And we explicitly talked about it,” she said of discovering the messages. “I was like, ‘Yeah, if you go and the guys go, that’s totally OK, just behave [and] don’t be weird about it.’ … [Instead], he lied for no reason because we had talked about it and I was like, ‘No, you can go.’ So then that triggered something in my brain.”

After John’s apparent lie, Sarah decided to look through his phone, where she found the aforementioned texts with the escort.

“I was like, ‘Oh, he lied about the trip. That’s weird.’ And then, it was very laid out for me. It was very easy [to find in his phone],” she said, claiming that John also had an active profile on Tinder with at least one match. “He says [he didn’t use the app further] and nothing physical happened and that, after the texting and stuff, he wanted to come home ‘cause that’s when he realized he liked being married.”

John has not publicly addressed Sarah’s claims about their marriage. Us reached out for comment.

Love Is Blind is currently streaming on Netflix.

Amazon First Reads is a program aimed at Prime members that offers early access to new e-books across many genres, as curated by First Reads editors (one of many Prime Member benefits). Prime members can choose to download one free e-book every month from a rotating list—though some months that number is bumped up to two, usually with a free short novel—and non-members get them for a discounted price. These e-books can be read on any compatible Kindle device or via the free Kindle app.

Go to the First Reads landing page to see the full list of e-books available this month. Once you find a book that seems interesting, click the "Shop Now" button from the First Reads landing page. Make sure you’re not being redirected to the Kindle or Amazon mobile application, because you won't see the free book option there; instead, use your internet browser on your phone or computer.

Make sure you’re not clicking the ”Pre-order for...” button, as that will direct you to pay. Instead, click the “Read for Free” or the "Buy Now with 1-Click" button under the "First Reads" banner on the book's Amazon page (don't worry, you won't be charged). This will send the e-book directly to the Kindle linked to your Amazon account. You can see what it should look like from the screenshot below.

You’ll know you did it right when you see a “Thanks, [your name]!” order summary indicating the e-book is being auto-delivered to the Kindle Cloud Reader.

#3599. Jensen Huang Did: Have an Ill-Advised Affair. He Did Not: Wear Vintage Saint Laurent.

Jensen Huang, the president, cofounder, and CEO of Nvidia is making headlines this week. Not for developments in AI technology—for all the wrong reasons.

On Sunday, Nvidia said it had opened an investigation into Huang regarding his relationship with a woman whom intelligence agencies have said is a Chinese spy. (The Chinese government has denied that the woman is a spy.) That same day, Huang sent an email to the company’s employees apologizing for being unfaithful to his wife and for “hurting” her and their children with the affair. He also apologized to his colleagues and the company’s board and shareholders. “My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility,” he wrote. “I am fully committed to Nvidia and will work to earn back your confidence.” He said he’d cooperate with the investigation opened by Nvidia’s board of directors. “I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security,” he wrote. “I am proud and grateful to be an American.”

The news of Huang’s affair filled X with memes about Chinese spies and mistresses in a variety of configurations. By Monday evening, Huang had reached the fashion world’s stylish netizens: The Instagram account @hidden.ny, an anonymous digital mood board and cultural platform, posted a series of images of Huang in a studded leather jacket. The caption read, “NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang in Hedi Slimane SLP Studded Leather Jacket after admitting to affair with alleged Chinese spy.”

It’s well-known that Huang is a leather-jacket enthusiast, and he is seldom seen in public without one. In July Sotheby’s auctioned one of his pre-worn jackets, this one by Tom Ford. The auction house originally estimated its sale price between $40,000 and $60,000, but it sold for a whooping $960,000.

Despite Huang’s penchant for a black-leather moment, it appears that he was, in fact, not wearing the Saint Laurent jacket as previously shared by Hidden and a variety of other accounts on both Instagram and X. A quick run through an AI image detector debunked Huang’s being a “Slimaniac”—what Slimane’s fervent fans often call themselves—at least in this particular case. SynthID, the detector created by Google DeepMind to identify AI-generated or enhanced media by OpenAI, Google, Kakao, and, of course, Nvidia, detected that the images posted by Hidden and other users online had been generated or edited with OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT. To burst the bubble even further, it appears that the images used as the base for this particular edit weren’t taken following the disclosure of Huang’s affair, but from a trip to South Korea in June. (He was wearing a Dior jacket by Jonathan Anderson then.)

Just last week, a Free Press reporter went viral on X for posting an image she had not disclosed as enhanced by AI as part of her election-night reporting, which was also debunked by VF. It’s not necessarily fun being the AI fashion police, and the stakes of netizens giving Huang the fashion-meme treatment versus a reporter using AI to illustrate a point are not the same. But as the use of AI becomes harder to detect, disclosure has become paramount.

Apologies to the menswear crowd for ruining the fantasy—but did you all really want Huang to be a certified “Hedi boy” after this news? As one comment under the original post read, Huang might be the “first person in history to have negative aura wearing archive Hedi.”

#3598. All the Health and Fitness Products You Didn't Realize You Could Buy With HSA Funds

If you have a flexible spending account (FSA), it's that time of year: Use those funds, or you'll lose them. Luckily, there are plenty of clever ways to spend your remaining FSA funds on qualifying healthcare costs—some that you may never have considered as "qualifying."

For instance, you can use your FSA or HSA funds to get yourself a sweet new fitness tracker or smartwatch (even the latest Fitbit Air). At least, that's what plenty of brands like Whoop, Oura, and even Nike want you to think. Is the process really as straightforward as the marketing suggests? Here's what to know about all the unexpected ways you can spend your FSA funds before the end of the year.

Right off the bat, when it comes to most of these fitness trackers and smartwatches, your HSA/FSA dollars won't be able to cover the entire purchase; instead, you'll save an average of 30% on eligible health purchases.

There is some more fine print, although it’s not as tricky as you might think. For the most part, if a device is necessary for treating or monitoring a specific medical condition—and not just “general wellness”—it could be eligible to purchase with those pre-tax health dollars.

The main “catch” here (as I’ve previously explained) is proving that device is in fact necessary, which requires you to obtain a Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN). Your LMN is basically a doctor's note required to classify certain purchases as qualified medical expenses under IRS guidelines, proving that the device will be used to treat a legitimate medical condition, such as obesity or a heart condition. Let’s take a look at what you can actually expect if you want to get a fitness wearable approved as a medical necessity.

When it comes to securing your LMN, you might not even need to make a doctor's appointment, thanks to third-party players like Truemed. When you browse sites like Coros, Amazfit, and more, you'll see the option to “Pay With Truemed” at checkout. From there, you'll be asked a few questions about your health circumstances, and you’ll be matched with a provider to determine your eligibility. If you qualify, you’ll get an LMN that will allow you to use your HSA or FSA funds to complete your purchase—all without ever having to meet with your primary doctor.

Truemed is one of the most popular payment platforms in this space, with the company claiming on its site that “90% of LMNs are issued within seven hours.” I spoke with Truemed’s co-founder and CEO Justin Mares to find out how it works behind the scenes. After you take that short survey about your health, an independent licensed provider reviews your answers before deciding whether the purchase looks medically necessary. If it doesn't, Truemed won't bother forwarding the request at all. Because Truemed screens your case before it has a chance of getting denied, those approval numbers get to stay mighty high. And the reality is, most Americans will have at least one health marker—like weight or cholesterol levels—that they can self-report to prove that, say, a Fitbit Air is necessary tool for prevention and maintenance.

For the purchases that do go through to a medical professional, approval turns out to be surprisingly straightforward. It comes down to the idea of "standard of care" in general. “If you go into a doctor's office and say your family has a history of high blood pressure,” Mares says, “your doctor probably is not going to ask for lab work before they'll talk to you about it. They simply take you at your word and help you manage the risk.” Proving HSA/FSA eligibility works on that same standard fairly often, according to Mares. You're not submitting a stack of medical records; you're answering a simple intake form about your health history, and a licensed clinician uses that, plus their own judgment, to decide whether a given product is appropriate for you.

Before you get your hopes up too high, FSA/HSA eligibility for wearables is still far from a free-for-all. An LMN only covers you, personally, for a specific product from a specific merchant, and it's usually tied to a specific condition, like cardiovascular risk, pre-diabetes, sleep issues, chronic pain, and so on. Some employers' FSA administrators scrutinize wearable purchases more closely than others, and even a fully compliant LMN doesn't guarantee your plan will approve the claim. Some companies (like Coros, for one) are more transparent about walking customers through the required medical consultation at checkout, while other brands market "HSA/FSA eligible" prominently without explaining that the LMN step is what actually makes that true. Luckily, I’ve saved you some time and rounded up some of the major wearables—and other unexpected items—that you might be able to prove as FSA/HSA eligible.

Screenless recovery trackers like Whoop, Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Oura Ring can usually be justified as HSA/FSA eligible around sleep quality, HRV-based stress monitoring, or recovery tracking tied to a chronic condition. These tend to draw more scrutiny from plan administrators simply because they're marketed as lifestyle products first, so the strength of your intake answers matters more here than it does for something obviously medical, like a blood pressure cuff.

If cardiovascular monitoring, training load tracking, or heart rate accuracy is relevant to a documented health concern, these watches can qualify the same way a basic tracker does. For instance, Coros offers FSA/HSA eligibility for all its watches and heart rate monitors through its partnership with Truemed. Amazfit similarly lets you filter by HSA/FSA eligibility for its smartwatches. Sadly, no Garmin watches are HSA/FSA-eligible. Still, the following Garmin-brand products are eligible for an HSA/FSA purchase:

You can filter by HSA/FSA eligibility and browse all eligible Garmin items here.

Think adjustable dumbbells, rowing machines, and connected bikes. It's the same logic doctors use when they tell a patient with pre-diabetes or high cholesterol to start exercising regularly; if a clinician is willing to attest that structured exercise is part of your treatment plan, equipment that enables that can qualify. For instance, here are some HSA/FSA eligible products from Nike Strength:

The common thread across all of these is that the product itself doesn't determine eligibility—your health history does. A Whoop band might be an easy approval for someone managing a cardiac condition, but it'll get more pushback for someone with no relevant health history at all. If you're curious whether something on your wish list might qualify, it's worth filling out the intake process just to see how creatively you can spend those pre-tax health dollars. However you choose to spend your FSA funds, don’t let that money go to waste.

#3597. Former South Carolina QB Makes Emotional Announcement Amid Cancer Battle

Former University of South Carolina quarterback Stephen Garcia provided a hopeful update amid his battle with stage IV cancer.

“Got some pretty solid news last night. We are completely cancer free,” Garcia, 38, wrote via Instagram on Wednesday, November 11. “Everything has been taken out with negative margins.”

He added, “I can’t express my gratitude towards everyone. The constant checking in, thoughts and prayers, support, and donations! It means the world to me and my family.”

Garcia — who played quarterback for the Gamecocks from 2008 to 2011 — announced he was diagnosed with stage IV colorectal cancer in May.

“It’s been amazing to see the messages of success stories from others as well as people telling me that I’ve inspired them to quarterback their own health,” his post on Wednesday continued. “That’s why I’ve been so open and vocal about this. Going to continue to try to inspire folks and spread the message. Again, thank you everyone and will continue to keep everyone updated!! Love yall!!”

In a video from his hospital bed accompanying his Instagram post, Garcia said his doctor checked his pathology results right in front of him.

“The margins on the lungs are negative,” he said in the video. “The lymph nodes were clear. All of the cancer is completely out of me. Extremely thankful for him and his team.”

Garcia admitted, “I cried like hell yesterday. It’s taking everything in my power not to cry like crazy right now.”

Looking ahead, Garcia vowed to “stay the course” and noted he has at least one more procedure on the horizon to “keep this damn thing out of me.”

“That’s what the hell we’re gonna do,” he said. “We may do a couple rounds of chemo just to zap and clean anything that might be floating around just to make sure this thing is done.”

Garcia concluded, “It’s been a hell of a journey. To go from stage IV and having it all over the place to it being completely out of my body is just unbelievable. I just want to thank you guys for all the thoughts and prayers, constantly checking in, constantly giving me words of encouragement and support. It’s invaluable.”

The former quarterback explained that his wife, Masha, was responsible for him getting checked out after “sporadic stomach pain” led to him making unusually frequent trips to the bathroom.

“It was definitely a shock,” Stephen recalled of his diagnosis during an interview on the Today show in September. “But I think it was just like, ‘What’s next?’ I wasn’t going to sit there and be like, ‘Well, I guess I’m dead.’ It’s like, what are we going to do? What’s the game plan? How are we going to beat this thing?”

Stephen said of his wife, “She probably did save my life.”

Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has announced that id Software is officially working on a new game, believed to be another Doom title. This is happening after Sharma oversaw id Software losing half of its staff to layoffs that were part of the Xbox "reset."

Id Software replied to Sharma's post on Twitter to provide a few more details on the new game, which the team didn't say was a Doom game, but everyone suspects it will be. Sharma cut staff at id Software (and numerous other Xbox studios around the world) earlier this year as part of a "reset" of the Xbox business. Marty Stratton of id Software recently said the studio is "doing great," despite the mass layoffs.

Id Software's latest game was 2025's Doom: The Dark Ages. The game's newest update is coming on November 16, adding the new wave-based Slaughter mode.

#3594. Model Alex Consani on Starring in American Horror Story and Pursuing a Career as an Actress

Alex Consani, a mainstay of the runways and one of the most emblematic supermodels of her generation, was notably absent from the spring-summer 2027 shows in September and October, bar a few exceptions. That’s because the California native, 23, has been busy broadening her horizons: Consani is following in the footsteps of many supers before her—including Cindy Crawford, Gisele Bündchen, and Tyra Banks—and trading the runway for the silver screen to pursue a career as an actress. She’s currently starring in American Horror Story: 13, the latest installment of Ryan Murphy’s stylish horror anthology series. Up next, Consani will appear in Molly Gordon’s Peaked and Janicza Bravo’s Preppy.

On Saturday night, Consani joined Demna and his Gucci crew at the 15th annual LACMA Art + Film Gala, where she says she had to do a “Hannah Montana”–style wardrobe change so that her voluminous gown could make it to the step-and-repeat before changing again to “pump it in a side-slit” in the look she wore on the runway in September. Yesterday, the model and newly minted actress Zoomed in after touching back down in New York to break down her film ambitions.

Alex Consani at the 2026 LACMA Art + Film gala.

José Criales-Unzueta: I’m not going to lie, I miss you on the runway. But you’re busy and otherwise occupied!

Alex Consani: I miss being on the runway. I’ve been busy. I’ve been doing a lot of cool projects. You might not see me on the runway, but you’ll definitely see me on the silver screen.

I mean, American Horror Story, all the episodes just came out. I don’t know if you watched, but that was obviously super fun. I also have two projects that are coming out next year, Preppy and Peaked. I’m just really excited. I’m in this era now where I’m kind of shifting into a different space, and it’s exciting to be able to do it specifically with people that understand that. For fashion and film, there are many places where both come together in such a natural way, and I think the LACMA [gala] really is that.

I worked with Sarah Paulson for American Horror Story, and then I sat next to her at LACMA, and we’re both wearing witchy outfits. Sarah and I were looking at Demna and he was like, “Look at my witches,” [laughs]. I love that the fashion world and the film world come together in such a fun way. I think Demna specifically is really big into characters—it’s not just the clothes, but it’s the woman in the clothes.

Did you always intend to go into acting, or was it something that unfolded as you went into fashion?

It’s something that I’ve always been interested in. And I think, in a way, fashion for me has always been acting. I mean, what I enjoy most about fashion is being able to become the character, being able to ask the designer, who is the woman that’s wearing this? It gives me the most gratification when I’m able to build the world around the clothing. [Acting] came naturally, but obviously it was in the back of my head. When I was a kid, I did classes and stuff. With fashion, the time constraints or the time needed to be in fashion is a lot. So I think it was just difficult. I’m blessed to be at a point in my fashion career and also in the [acting] projects that are coming to me, that it isn’t impossible to do both.

I’m putting work into being a better actress. It’s a really exciting endeavor for me, especially considering all the projects that I’ve done that are coming out. There’s a lot of diversity within the projects. I did American Horror Story, which is obviously a horror TV show, and then I have a comedy movie coming out, and then I also have a period piece coming out. It’s fun to be able to bounce around those. And fashion-wise, fab, honestly, the fashion in the films that I’ve done is quite fun. It’s nice because then I get to give my insight as someone in fashion to all the teams, and it feels like a real collaboration, which is my favorite part of any creative job.

Alex Consani with Sarah Paulson (left) and Leslie Grossman (right) in the sixth episode of American Horror Story: 13.

You and I are from the generations that grew up on Ryan Murphy shows.

Coven, for me, is my favorite American Horror Story season by far. What was it like to join the project? Did you audition? Did you get a call?

I’m signed with a really incredible agency that manages that facet of my career, and they expressed that Ryan had some interest in seeing me. I sent in an audition and it fell into place in that way. I definitely was auditioning and going through that script a lot before I got to filming. It was really important for me to really understand the character. And so when I got there, it was obviously super exciting, but I was also a little bit nervous considering the fact that I’m with some of the most seasoned actors in the industry. It was so gratifying and comforting hearing how supportive these women were. My biggest takeaway from this experience is that the reason that those women and those people in Coven are so acclaimed, on top of being incredibly talented, they’re kind and they’re open arms to anyone that wants and that puts in the effort into the acting industry.

What I find so exciting about it is that it doesn’t feel as exclusive as fashion does, in a way. It opens up the conversation to anyone that’s willing to work for it. Fashion is being the right person in the right place at the right time. I think that acting is being the right person, yes, but putting the right energy and the right time into the job. It was just such an incredible experience. Jessica Lange, Emma Roberts, Sarah Paulson, Gabourey Sidibe… it was fab. It was fab! I have so many iconic memories made on that set that I’m going to have forever. I got so much knowledge from these women. I think that it was just really reassuring to see how kind and open-minded these people were, especially Billie Lourd. She’s an icon of mine, but then I got to work with her, and she was just so open and honest about how she’s felt in her first roles. It’s just really gratifying to hear this stuff.

There’s a long legacy of supermodels trying to crack into the silver screen. A lot of models have done it, some very successfully, some have done it once and then moved on. Do you feel any sort of pressure for this to work?

I think I was really ready to just lock in and have fun, but for me, what I was most excited about was being able to be ugly. I see this a lot in models and actresses, where it becomes difficult when you’re so aware of the camera, and you grow up being so aware of the camera to then unlearn that awareness. It was so exciting to be able to go into a space where I was able to get into the character without there being the perception of others there. Obviously there’s a camera, but it’s not a fashion show where you hear like, yeah, work! [laughs] It was a real experience that I worked on within myself.

I was reading The Artist’s Way, which, not to be all corny, I think I realized that the feeling of gratification and the feeling of completing something is only as good as that feeling. I think that perception, especially now with social media and [giving] a numeric value to art, it’s really important to be able to feel like you did the best you could and that’s enough. I think for me, that was really where it kind of progressed. I was able to lock down away from the facet of just being pretty. I didn’t get the touch-ups before set, I didn’t get the lighting right. I wasn’t asking to see the playback, which, as a model—I know you’ve been on many sets where you see the girls and with every single shot we’re looking at the screen, there’s a mirror behind the photographer— it’s very not that. I do the day, and I don’t know if I did a good job. I felt like I did a good job, and that’s enough for me. I’m excited to see it in seven months when it comes out. But that really took a lot of the pressure away. I was just enjoying the experience and doing my best. I think that that’s the beauty of it and that’s the beautiful difference between fashion and film.

I love a lot of animated characters. I was watching Rio yesterday. Did you know Anne Hathaway is the love interest? That’s my dream. Honestly, I would love to do some really fab, cool animation because I think that in itself is a challenge. It’s nice to be able to build a character with just your voice.

Fundamentally, I would really love to have a role that really personifies someone different for me. I also watched Catwoman yesterday with Halle Berry. I think powerful women roles are obviously exciting for any female actress. Having the opportunity to do that would be incredible. I’m very “divine timing” when it comes to this stuff, so I believe everything will happen and run its course in the way it should. But there’s also a lot of really interesting biopics that I would love to see. Maybe I write them, maybe I act. Who knows?

Consani arriving at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art.

A polaroid of the final glam for the night.

So you want to get into writing too, or have you been writing?

Yeah, I actually have. I have been in the background of my mind thinking about this and maybe moving into that space as well. I think it’s quite exciting. In my whole career, it’s always been if you’re not given the opportunity, you make it yourself. I think of other actresses, and the behind-the-camera work that goes into the shows that they do.

That’s a really good point. A lot of the actors that we grew up with—Nicole Kidman, Reese Witherspoon—have really gone into production, or are part of the writing process. Do you have a dream director to work with? Do you have a bucket list?

Totally. Wes Anderson is a really big one... I love Wes Anderson. I think he’s an incredible director. But on top of that, I just worked with Janicza Bravo, and I’m such a big fan. She’s so incredible with the way that she thinks. Lena Dunham [is another]. There’s so many incredible people, but I think I like the way that each different director works. My favorite part about working with Janicza was just the youth in her perspective. I’ve worked with multi-generations of directors at this point, and to see the difference between how Ryan works versus how Janicza works versus how Molly Gordon works, it’s just quite interesting. There’s a lot of directors that I’m a big fan of, people who are obviously focused on cinematography, but also understand how to have fun.

#3593. Candy Crush Is Celebrating Xbox’s 25th Anniversary With Halo, Fallout, And Doom Crossovers, Including Remixed Music

2026 is the 25th anniversary of Xbox, and it's been a tough year for the brand with mass layoffs, studio closures/divestitures, and game cancellations. But the celebrations are still going ahead, including an event from the Xbox-owned Candy Crush mobile game juggernaut.

Announced today, Candy Crush Saga is marking the Xbox anniversary with a "Game On" season that brings items and elements from Halo, Fallout, Sea of Thieves, Forza, Doom, Banjo-Kazooie, Crash Bandicoot, and Spyro into the game through a virtual pin-collection event. Additionally, the popular and recognizable music from some of those games is coming to Candy Crush in "unmistakable Candy style," developer King said.

The Game On event runs now through December 6. Players earn the themed pins, including Master Chief's iconic helmet, by progressing through Candy Crush's various levels throughout the season. The pins are being released physically, too, and people can enter a contest at the Candy Crush website for a chance to win.

In terms of the updated music, Candy Crush Saga is adding "Candyfied" versions of music from Halo, Fallout, Sea of Thieves, Forza, Doom, and Banjo-Kazooie.

You can check out a neat behind-the-scenes video below to see how composer Federico Truzzi worked with the developers at King to remix the songs with a Candy Crush flavor. The music was recorded by the German Film Orchestra Babelsberg and the Bulgarische Orthodoxe Chor Berlin e.V. choir.

In other Xbox anniversary news, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma released a statement marking the milestone, and referencing how the future of gaming could be focused on AI and vibe-coding. Microsoft also released a new hub called Xbox Playback where you can see your biggest Xbox accomplishments over the past quarter-century.

#3592. ‘Mormon Wives: OC’ Reveals How Much Money Zac Affleck Lost Before Jen Divorce

Before filing for divorce, Jen Affleck revealed how much of their money Zac Affleck lost due to gambling.

Jen, 27, broke down on camera while filming season 1 of The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County, saying, “Someone came to Zac’s parents’ house yesterday and was trying to serve him papers. They were looking for him and he was like, ‘Remember we lived in that home in Arizona? I guess I didn’t pay all the extra charges for us to move out.'”

The reality star was surprised to learn Zac, 30, didn’t handle the payment.

“Zac and I have moved a lot in the past couple of years. We rented a house in Arizona for a year and we ended up moving back to Utah. We literally moved out of that house in Arizona two years ago. So I thought everything was taken care of,” she explained. “Zac was handling the finances during that time. But finding this out has made me question everything.”

Jen went on to describe Zac’s behavior as “really weird,” adding, “It seemed like he just wasn’t being honest.”

“So I went to check our bank and the money is gone. There was over $100,000 in there. He’s done this before multiple times — whether it was through online poker or it was through investing crypto,” she continued. “I said, ‘You’re not allowed to do that anymore.’ Because he’s done this multiple times. I can’t tell you how many times we’ve gone through this in our marriage. Whether it was poker or sports betting, now I’m seeing that he invested a ton of money in Bitcoin without telling me and lost it.”

Jen originally made claims about Zac having issues with gambling when The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives premiered on Hulu in 2024. Zac, for his part, claimed most of the conversations about his finances were misconstrued.

“My medical school tuition — that never happened. I hadn’t even been accepted to medical school when that season was filmed. There wasn’t even a deposit to pay for school because I hadn’t been accepted into a school yet,” he said on “The Viall Files” in 2025. “So a lot of those things that were said by the girls were hurtful and untrue and has led to a lot of backlash on social media, which has been really sad.”

Jen, however, disagreed with Zac’s comment about her not paying for his medical school. The pair didn’t agree while filming the episode and according to Jen on the OC spinoff, Zac only “admitted” to not handling their money well when cameras weren’t rolling.

“He’s like, ‘I f***ed up and you wanted to separate so I didn’t tell you this because I knew if you found out, you would divorce me,'” Jen added in the new Hulu show. “I said, ‘Yeah. I’m done. I’m divorcing you.'”

Jen ultimately filed for divorce days before the spinoff’s Thursday, November 11, premiere. She hinted at plans to end their marriage while filming season 1 of Mormon Wives: OC.

“Luckily, I have my job and I’m making more than enough,” she continued about their alleged money problems.” I said, ‘I want a divorce. I don’t want a separation. I want to move forward this week. I’m filing this week. I’ve given you every chance. I bailed you out so many times. I’ve defended you. I’ve wanted to keep our family together.’ After everything that I’ve tried to do for our family, why?”

Jen, who shares three kids with Zac, told Us that being pregnant with baby No. 4 made her reconsider her situation.

“I had to ask myself very hard questions like, ‘Is this the type of relationship I want this child to look up to?'” she shared earlier this month. “When I realized it was a no, that’s when I realized that I needed to make a change. You’ll see a lot of that unfold in season [1 of the spinoff].”

The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County premieres Thursday, November 12, on Hulu.

#3591. Apple Is About to Release a Touchscreen MacBook Pro (Plus Four More Devices)

Apple has had a busy fall. Head to the company's website, and you'll immediately be greeted by a sea of new products: the foldable iPhone Duo; the iPhone 18 Pro; HomePod mini 2; Apple Watch Series 12; the list goes on. It seems, under new Apple CEO Jon Ternus, the company is ready for a refresh of just about every product it sells. To that point, the company seems far from finished. Just this week, Apple is planning to release five brand new products, each launching on Friday. While four of these are Macs, Apple does have a new iPad in the works, as well. Here's everything new Apple is releasing this week.

Finally. For the first time, the iPad mini is about to ship with an OLED display. Apple's smallest tablet has always come with a standard screen. Despite its price tag, the iPad mini has never come with an OLED display, or even a mini-LED screen, until now. With this new model, there is no backlight. As such, each individual pixel on the iPad's display will be able to shut itself off when displaying dark content. That will benefit the content you watch on this device, as well as the overall contrast of the screen.

Beyond the new OLED panel, the new iPad mini is thinner and lighter than the previous model. It also comes with Apple's newest A20 Pro chip, the same processor the company put in its iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo smartphones. The new device starts at $699 for 128GB of storage, though there are various upgrades, including nano-texture glass (add $100) and cellular (add $150).

Good news: There's a new iMac. Bad news: Not much is different here from the previous model. The biggest change here is the new M6 chip, which Apple says is up to five times faster than the iMac with M4 and up to 12 times faster than the iMac with M1. With that M6 chip, the iMac now supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Other than that, this is the same iMac you may already know: It comes with a 24-inch LED display (no OLED, unfortunately), two or four USB-C ports (depending on the configuration), and a built-in 12MP webcam. If you're looking for a new all-in-one computer, or you've been considering upgrading your older iMac, this is likely a great choice. But if you already have an M-series iMac, it's not such an obvious upgrade. (My M1 iMac may be up to 12 times slower, but it's still plenty fast for me.) Apple didn't change the price here: The M6 iMac still starts at $1,499 for two ports, 16GB of RAM, and 256GB of storage.

Similarly, Apple's newest 14-inch MacBook Pro isn't much different from the previous model—save for the new processor. This model also comes with Apple's M6 chip, which Apple says is up to 13 times faster for AI processing than the M1 MacBook Pro. (Apple seems keen on convincing stubborn M1 users to upgrade this cycle.) Now, the company is offering this model of MacBook Pro in three chipsets, depending on use case: M6 for "entry-level" pro work; M5 Pro for mid-tier pro work; and M5 Max for the most demanding situations.

But, like the M6 iMac, this is the same MacBook Pro Apple sold before. It has a 14-inch mini-LED display with a refresh rate up to 120Hz. It comes with three Thunderbolt 4 (USB-C) ports, an HDMI port, and an SDXC card slot. It, too, has a 12MP webcam for video calls. Apple's newest MacBook Pro starts at $1,999, but you can quickly ramp up that price tag with screen, chip, memory, or storage upgrades.

Apple's most exciting product launch this week is undoubtedly the new touchscreen MacBook Pros. Unlike the M6 MacBook Pro, which only comes in the 14-inch variant, Apple's first touchscreen laptop comes in both 14- and 16-inch options. Apple says this touchscreen lets you scroll, zoom, or draw on the display. That works with basic functions, like web browsing or selecting files, but also with specific workflows, like playing virtual instruments in Logic Pro, or manipulating an object in a 3D modeling app. Like the iPad mini, this laptop comes with an OLED display (Apple calls it PROLED XDR), with up to 1,000 nits of typical brightness and 2,000 nits of HDR brightness. It also brings back the backlit Apple logo, something I've missed on my last two MacBooks.

This MacBook Pro also comes with the iPhone's Dynamic Island for the first time. This replaces the "notch" that other MacBook Pros and MacBook Airs currently ship with. It can function as a basic webcam, but also as a dedicated zone for Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri AI. This machine comes in either M5 Pro or M5 Max variants—no M6 for this model—as Apple seems to be positioning it exclusively for the most taxing situations (particularly AI). The company says the new MacBook Pro has up to 13 more hours of battery life than Intel-based MacBook Pros, and can fast charge up to 50% in 30 minutes. It's essentially a supercharged version of the existing MacBook Pro.

As such, this is Apple's most expensive laptop. The 14-inch M5 Pro version starts at $2,899, while the 16-inch starts at $3,399. However, you can configure these machines to have outrageous price tags. The maxed-out 16-inch MacBook Pro is $14,549, roughly half of which is the 16TB of RAM.

#3590. Six Fitness 'Rules' That Don't Actually Matter

I’ve learned a lot in my many years in the gym, and beginner-me would be shocked and appalled by the things present-me does during workouts. With the benefit of experience, I now do exercises I used to think one should “never” do, and I’ve broken pretty much every other rule besides.

I've already explained a bunch of things you can stop worrying about as a beginner, but I’d like to expand on that list with a few more rules that even intermediate-level exercisers can ditch without consequence.

If you can theoretically do 13 bicep curls with a certain weight, how many curls should you actually do? One common misconception is that if you don’t do all 13, you’re leaving gains on the table. The rule kind of makes sense if you have truly no clue where to start; if you go until you can’t do a single rep more, then at least you know you’re not slacking off.

But the downside is that going to failure for every set of every lift is just going to make you exhausted. On bicep curls, maybe not so much, but once you’re squatting pretty heavy weights, you’re going to feel spent if you do every single set to failure, and that fatigue will get in the way of getting a good workout in consistently. What’s better is to follow a program that advises you on when to hold back and when it’s a good time to really push your limits. You’ll find that most of the time, you stop a set at least 2-3 reps shy of failure, and sometimes even more.

Rest days are a convenient tool for making sure you’re not overworking yourself, but that’s all. Organizations like the American College of Sports Medicine recommend leaving 48 hours between intense strength-training sessions for a given muscle, but if you look at where they get that number, it’s meant to be a general recommendation for beginners and for people who are exercising just to stay healthy. Once you’re talking about athletes or enthusiasts, the ACSM acknowledges that training most days of the week is fine if your program manages fatigue effectively. That may mean alternating between heavier and lighter days, rather than taking complete rest days.

The “10% rule” is a not-terrible guideline for figuring out how quickly to ramp up your training. But like many of these other myths, it’s a suggestion, not a commandment to be strictly obeyed.

As running coach Jason Fitzgerald told Lifehacker, “While the adage is to only increase weekly mileage by 10%, this may be either too conservative or even too aggressive depending on where you start from.” When you’re coming back from a short layoff, you can probably increase mileage a lot faster. Same goes if you’re a beginner and your mileage is overall very low; if you took the rule literally, you wouldn’t be able to increase from zero to any other number.

Meanwhile, serious running programs—once again, a program is a wonderful thing—may give you a bigger increase for a few weeks in a row, then cut back and decrease your mileage temporarily before ramping up again. Or they may keep you at the same mileage for weeks at a time before venturing a larger increase. If you were to stick to the 10% rule, you would miss out on the advantages of programs that work this way.

There are pros and cons to lifting before cardio, and to doing cardio before lifting. It’s more of an “it depends” than a rule. So here are some of the ways to decide which makes sense.

Your lifts tend to suffer when you’re fatigued, and doing them fresh is important to you

Cardio is your top priority, and you want to have more energy for it

Your lifts are the kind of thing that can get done even when you’re fatigued

Or you only intend to do a small amount of cardio before lifting

So a cyclist may prefer to do a strength workout after hopping off the bike, but a powerlifter would probably rather get their conditioning in after finishing squats for the day. Either is fine if you don’t care, or if you prefer to mix it up.

There are a few supplements that can help you in your fitness journey, but none of them are necessary. Creatine is one of the best-known muscle-building supplements. It’s understood to be effective, but here’s the thing: Just because it does something for most people doesn’t mean it does very much. If you decide it’s too expensive or just that you would rather not have another thing to remember to take every day, you’re not missing out on any substantial amount of gains.

Likewise, protein powder is a helpful way to get more protein in your diet, but you don’t need to use a supplement; you can just eat more protein-containing foods.

And finally, pre-workout drinks can give you more energy in the gym (it’s mostly caffeine), but the idea that you need it is a very recent development. Even ten years ago, it wasn’t really a thing. People showed up to the gym with a coffee or a coke or with no caffeine at all in their stomach, and worked out just fine.

Look, people have been exercising successfully for millennia, but all of our apps and devices weren't even a thing until the 2000s. Tracking every minute, every step, or every mile of your routine is not actually necessary. You’re still a runner even if you don’t have an app that knows how many miles you ran. You don’t even have to track your sets and reps in your lifting journal if you don’t want to. Your body is what knows how much work you put in, even if your phone were to get wiped overnight.

#3589. Minnesota Dad, 3 Sons Found Dead in House Fire in Suspected Murder-Suicide

A Minnesota father and his three sons were found dead following a house fire, and authorities now suspect their deaths were the result of a murder-suicide.

The Mower County Sheriff’s Office said that four family members were found dead on Sunday, November 8, after the fire. The victims have since been identified as Levi Christenson and his sons Oliver and Felix, both 14, and Calvin, 7.

Authorities said that Oliver, Felix and Calvin’s deaths were all ruled as homicides by gunshot wound, while Christenson, 38, was determined to have died by suicide.

It’s not currently clear whether authorities believe Christenson had a motive in the killings.

The investigation into the fire remains ongoing, and officials said that “there are several questions that cannot be answered definitively at this point until further analysis is completed and confirmed,” according to People.

It was initially reported that first responders went to the home late on Sunday morning and found smoke coming from the residence.

The Mower County Sheriff’s Office did not immediately respond to Us’ request for comments regarding updates in the case.

Following the tragedy, family friend DeeDee Payne started a GoFundMe to financially help the boys’ mother, Lauren Hosp, during her difficult time.

“No mother should ever have to endure such a heartbreaking loss, and there are simply no words that could ever begin to describe the pain she is facing,” Payne wrote in the fundraiser’s description.

Payne added that “Lauren’s three boys were her entire world, her greatest blessings, and the light of her life.”

“Everything she did was rooted in the love she had for them. She was a truly spectacular mother who loved her boys beyond measure. Her love, dedication, and devotion to them were evident in everything she did,” she added.

Payne also urged those contributing to acknowledge the work of the emergency personnel who responded to the fire.

“These are the individuals who run toward situations that most of us cannot even begin to imagine,” she wrote in an update. “Beneath their uniforms are human beings who feel, hurt, and carry the emotional weight of what they encounter. Our hearts are with each and every one of them as they, too, navigate the aftermath of this heartbreaking day.”

If you or someone you know is struggling or in crisis, help is available. Call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org.

#3588. Warby Parker and Gentle Monster Are Launching Smart Glasses. Does Anyone Want Them?

This is the November 11, 2026 edition of Fit Check, your front row seat to the power players, peacocks, and deep pockets of fashion—and how they influence the rest of the world.

It’s been a meme-worthy news week: the new Met Gala theme launched endless online discourse, Jensen Huang ignited the internet with news of his affair with an alleged Chinese spy, then fashion netizens had a time memeifying him as a Hedi-boy, and Maybelline changed its slogan with some very confusing punctuation.

IRL, Gentle Monster and Warby Parker are getting into the smart glasses space. Like Meta, they’re working hard to get fashion’s co-sign in order to have tastemakers influence everyone else to wear them, though I have yet to find a fashion person happy to wear these without a check involved. And this week, Alex Consani video-called me to discuss her acting ambitions after her debut in American Horror Story: 13. She’s already filmed two movies coming next year.

Mentioned in this issue: Iron Man, Robert Downey Jr., Kylie Jenner, Timothée Chalamet’s security guard, Steven Meisel, Martine Rose discourse, Luca de Meo, Woke 3.0, Hedi Slimane, Slimaniacs, Sarah Paulson, Ryan Murphy, and many more.

Amelia Gray at the Gentle Monster launch dinner.

Last night Warby Parker and Gentle Monster celebrated the launches of their “intelligent eyewear” lines (not to be confused with Meta’s “smart glasses”), both developed with Google and Samsung. Warby Parker hosted a literary activation with Vogue, and Gentle Monster held a “preview experience” and dinner attended by Alex Consani, Anok Yai, Charles Melton, Joaquin Phoenix, and more.

Snap also tapped Robert Downey Jr. to star in videos showcasing its technology, Iron Man–style. Phoenix appeared in Gentle Monster’s launch campaign in a callback to his role in Her, in which he plays a man who falls in love with an AI voiced by Scarlett Johansson. (In 2024, she had a dispute with OpenAI after learning the company had created a voice that sounded similar to hers for its AI, which she had declined to license for ChatGPT. Sam Altman denied any intentional imitation.) Leveraging two movie stars who’ve been the face of this kind of technology in film to bring their products to the masses is a cunning move from Google and Samsung. Yet it’s possible that no co-sign can combat the anxiety around AI and its surrounding gadgets. There is a budding battle in the smart glasses space—but does anyone actually want them?

Martine Rose is officially taking over from Pierpaolo Piccioli at Balenciaga. I still think he could have been right for the brand, but he came at the wrong time. Balenciaga is essentially Kering’s youth vehicle after a decade under Demna, and Piccioli just wasn’t the designer to fulfill that brief. That his collections seemed to try to honor both Demna’s casualwear range and his own couture-like sensibility only muddled the brand’s remit further. But Rose, who worked with Demna on his Balenciaga menswear early on, is a much better fit in this context, and she has the industry’s goodwill—fans have been advocating her ascent to a role like this one for years.

Rose is the first official hire under Luca de Meo’s tenure as Kering’s CEO, and she is walking into a brave new world. De Meo believes Kering has been overly dependent on its creative directors, and is looking to streamline operations with a new strategy dubbed “ReconKering.” If reports are confirmed that Chemena Kamali will head to Saint Laurent and Virginia Burlina to McQueen, four out of five creative directors at Kering will soon be women. Along with Rose and Louise Trotter at Bottega Veneta, these are designers who are better known as prolific workhorses rather than buzzy household names. De Meo is evidently looking to grow beyond the star creative director strategy that defined fashion in the 2010s, with Demna as an exception. What this means for Rose and Balenciaga, and for Saint Laurent and McQueen, which have historically depended on the persona of their creative leads, remains to be seen.

Balenciaga is back in the news this week with the opening of the first of several activations around the 25th anniversary of its Le City bag, arguably the most enduring of It bags after the Birkin. Damien Hirst has hand-painted 25 bags for the occasion, and Nicole Richie is fronting the campaign in a callback to the aughts. This was planned prior to Piccioli’s exit, yet it’s taking place in between creative directors speaks to an undeniable fact that plays right into ReconKering: These brands are bigger than their designers, despite how important these appointments are to industry insiders and fanatics.

A look from Jun Takahashi’s fall-winter 2024 collection for Undercover, which will be included in the upcoming Met Costume Institute exhibition.

In case you missed it: The Met announced on Thursday the replacement exhibition for the John Galliano blockbuster postponed earlier this year. “ExtraORDINARY: Fashion and the Poetics of the Everyday” will focus on how designers have explored familiar, ordinary garments: jeans, T-shirts, workwear, and more. It sounds like both an ode to normcore and to the ingenuity with which designers like Matthieu Blazy, Demna, Jun Takahashi, and more have reimagined the most simple of clothing. Andrew Bolton, the curator in charge of the Costume Institute, told Vogue he “didn’t have a plan B” after Galliano and that he wanted the replacement show to be “challenging and provocative.” The announcement drew both positive and negative reactions. Its main criticism is its simplicity, especially when compared to Galliano’s extravagance. Bolton has a singular way of placing fashion in larger cultural contexts to underscore its historic importance—I’m curious to see what he’ll do when the fashion he’s dealing with already exists in an atmosphere that requires little explanation.

Maybelline has updated its famous slogan, “Maybe she’s born with it. Maybe it’s Maybelline,” which was first introduced in 1991, to a more democratic, inclusive riff: “Maybe. We’re born with it. Maybe. It’s Maybelline.” Confusing punctuation aside, the change feels like it belongs to the late 2010s era of DEI marketing. It’s true that binary pronouns have fallen out of style, particularly at the makeup counter, even if brands shied away from this kind of revamp in the Trump era. But then again, after last week’s blue wave in the midterm elections, maybe Maybelline is just in time.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang waves to the media as he arrives at Gimpo airport in Seoul on June 5, 2026 wearing a Dior jacket. Images from this same outing were modified with AI by fashion netizens.

The news of Jensen Huang’s affair filled X with memes about Chinese spies and mistresses in a variety of configurations. By Monday evening, Huang had reached the fashion world’s stylish netizens: the Instagram account @hidden.ny, an anonymous digital mood board and cultural platform, posted a series of images of Huang in a studded leather jacket. The caption read: “NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang in Hedi Slimane SLP Studded Leather Jacket after admitting to affair with alleged Chinese spy.”

It’s well-known that Huang is a leather jacket enthusiast. But despite Huang’s penchant for a black leather moment, it appears he was not, in fact, wearing the Saint Laurent jacket. A quick run through an AI image detector debunked Huang being a “Slimaniac,” at least in this particular case. SynthID detected that the images posted by Hidden and other users online were generated or edited with OpenAI. To burst the bubble even further, it appears the images used as the base for this edit weren’t taken after the disclosure of Huang’s affair, but during a trip to South Korea in June. Apologies to the menswear crowd for ruining the fantasy.

Amazon has cut the price of its latest Fire TV Stick 4K, dropping it to $24.99 from $59.99 and bringing it to its lowest price ever, according to price trackers. At this price, it's an affordable way to bring 4K streaming to an older television or give a sluggish smart TV a performance upgrade. And because this streaming stick measures just 3.6 inches and draws power directly from your TV's USB port using the included cable, it can sit out of sight behind your screen without taking up another wall outlet.

Despite its small size, it supports 4K streaming over Wi-Fi 6, along with HDR10, HDR10+, and HLG for improved contrast and color on compatible televisions. What you don't get is Dolby Vision or Dolby Atmos audio. If either is important to your home theater setup, the Fire TV Stick 4K Plus, currently $39.99, is worth considering for the extra $15. Otherwise, there's little to complain about when it comes to performance, with PCMag reporting that apps respond almost instantly and 4K streams load quickly with almost no blurry, low-resolution moments.

The redesigned Alexa voice remote is another improvement, with a more comfortable shape, an easier-to-find home button, and dedicated shortcuts for major streaming services. You can also use Alexa to search for shows, launch apps, or control compatible smart home devices. The software experience is less impressive, with advertisements and recommendations dominating the home screen, leaving relatively little room for your actual apps. There's also no support for Apple AirPlay or Google Cast, so sharing content directly from your phone isn't particularly convenient. Still, if you're comfortable with Amazon's interface and don't need the missing Dolby formats, the Fire TV Stick 4K delivers responsive streaming and a useful remote for just $25.

When I think about Karen Gillan’s Ruby Roundhouse, her maroon crop top and green mini cargo shorts immediately come to mind. That costume is iconic now, and Gillan’s sense of humor about it makes it even better. Now, as we prepare for the release of Jumanji: Open World on the 2026 movie schedule and to see the cast say goodbye, the actress has one question about her costume.

With Jumanji: Open World premiering on Christmas (and in the wake of Dunesday), the cast is getting ready for one last ride as the video game characters we know and love. In fact, they’re getting back into costume too, and during a clip posted on the film’s Instagram account, the Doctor Who actress pondered if she’d get to keep hers. Take a look:

A post shared by Jumanji: Open World (@jumanjimovie)

Karen Gillan has gotten weird flak for this costume since the first Jumanji starring her, Dwayne Johnson, Kevin Hart and Jack Black came out. However, there’s a valid and clever reason for the crop top: Ruby (or the person who is in her body during a given game) is not happy about it. And personally, I’ve always interpreted the costume choice as a cheeky commentary on the way women have been portrayed in video games.

Anyway, all these years later, that costume is synonymous with Ruby Roundhouse, and it sounds like Gillan wants to keep it, as you can see from this conversation she had with her co-stars:

Well, I hope Hart gets to keep his backpack, and I hope Gillan gets to put that crop top and those cargo shorts in her closet.

Along with the Guardians of the Galaxy star’s question, the video also included The Rock, obviously, roasting Kevin Hart, and then the actors sharing a group hug. Seriously, it all felt so on-brand for Jumanji.

It also made me very excited for Open World. In the third movie set to star this quartet, their characters are thrust into the real world. Then, it seems they wind up back in the game with a new set of people stuck in their bodies. This time, Alex Wolff’s Spencer is the one in Ruby’s body, while his mother, who is played by Marin Hinkle, ends up being Dwayne Johnson’s Dr. Bravestone. Meanwhile, Kevin Hart’s Mouse is taken over by a child named Tyson, and Jack Black’s Professor Oberon is possessed by Dan Hildebrand’s “kitchen gentleman,” Donatas.

All around, it looks like an action-packed, silly, goofy good time, just like the movies that came before it. And obviously, the characters are still wearing those iconic costumes they’ve been donning since 2017.

Now, to see our last trip to the jungle, you can catch Jumanji: Open World in theaters on December 25.

#3585. Donald Trump Jr. Defends Russell Brand After Rape Conviction, Sentencing

Donald Trump Jr. claimed bias played a role in Russell Brand’s rape and sexual assault conviction.

“When he was, like, married to Katy Perry, he’s one of the most famous actors in the world, no one seemed to have a problem,” Trump, 48, said during the Tuesday, November 10, episode of his show Triggered. “No one seemed to think he was a rapist then. But he finds God, I guess, changes his ways, sees some aspects of conservative life and talks about them.”

Brand, 51, publicly shifted from left-wing political views, endorsing President Donald Trump and his administration in recent years. He also announced his conversion to Christianity in 2024.

“Now he’s going to spend … years in prison for rape when no one had a problem with it in the prior 27 years,” the president’s son added on Tuesday.

Earlier this month, a London jury declared Brand guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault in incidents spanning from 2004 to 2009. He was acquitted of two other counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

Brand, who pleaded not guilty and has denied all wrongdoing, was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison on Monday, November 9.

The conviction and sentence came after a four-week trial exploring sexual assault and rape accusations made by multiple women. Statements from the victims were read in court on Monday, with one claiming she feared she contracted HIV after Brand anally raped her in 2009. Another stated that she felt like “damaged goods” after Brand assaulted her in 2004.

In a recent statement, Metropolitan Police Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy commended the victims for their “bravery” during the trial, noting that the verdict was “first and foremost a testament to the extraordinary courage, resilience and determination of the women who came forward and reported what happened to them.”

“Despite intense media and public scrutiny, they relived deeply personal and traumatic experiences and placed their trust in us,” he continued. “Without their bravery, this outcome would not have been possible.”

After the trial’s conclusion, the Metropolitan Police told Us that Brand is now under investigation for further allegations of rape made by two unidentified women.

“The suspect has previously been interviewed under caution in connection with the allegations,” a spokesperson said. “Files have been submitted to the Crown Prosecution Service in relation to both complainants.”

The statement continued, “Detectives remain in close contact with prosecutors as enquiries continue and further investigative work is carried out. Anyone who wishes to speak to detectives or make a report can contact the investigation team by email at CSOU@met.police.uk.”

If you or someone you know has been sexually assaulted, contact the National Sexual Assault Hotline at 1-800-656-HOPE (4673).

#3584. How To Rob A Bank Producer Explains How The Movie Reinvents The Heist Genre [Exclusive]

It's easy for novices to make the mistake that if you've seen one heist film, you've seen them all. As the genre junkies among us know, it takes a little more effort than most to make these sorts of movies stand out from the crowd. Steven Soderbergh found lightning in a bottle with his "Ocean's Eleven" remake in 2001, while Christopher Nolan added a mind-bending spin with "Inception" less than 10 years later. Classic cinema is rife with examples of how to craft memorable heist movies, from Michael Mann's "Thief" to Sidney Lumet's "Dog Day Afternoon" to Stanley Kubrick's "The Killing."

So when David Leitch came across writer Mark Bianculli's script for "How to Rob a Bank" and chose this as his next directorial effort after "The Fall Guy," it quickly became apparent how this could become a heist flick like nothing we've ever seen before. As the title implies, the unconventional heroes of this story are a group of social media influencers who've become viral sensations — not just for pulling off bank robberies like they were born to do it, but for creating a YouTube channel teaching others how to stick it to the man and perform heists of their own.

Not long ago, I had the chance to talk to the creative team of Leitch and "Violent Night" producer Kelly McCormick (who happens to be Leitch's longtime producing partner at 87North, as well as his wife) during the "How to Rob a Bank" press junket about what drew them to the script. According to McCormick:

"In this case, it's like, 'How do you turn a heist movie on its head — not your daddy's heist movie?' And it's the [idea of] thieves hiding in plain sight, as opposed to not wanting to be seen."

It's a staple of practically every heist story ever told, from "The Italian Job" to "Heat" and everything in between: In order to pull off the perfect caper, our protagonists must cover their tracks, don some clever disguises to maintain a low profile, and escape the scene of the crime without anyone being the wiser. It's definitely not advised for robbers to film themselves while on a job, edit and upload those tutorials to YouTube, and revel in the viral fame that comes with being the most well-known crew the internet has ever seen. It's all about avoiding detection — not seeking it out.

But "How to Rob a Bank" isn't exactly interested in the conventional approach. With Nicholas Hoult's Ryan as the ringleader, this motley group of Robin Hood-like revolutionaries have figured out how to successfully weaponize simmering anti-capitalist sentiments among a generation fed up with living under a broken system. They just happen to do so with a GoPro strapped to their masks and a knack for live-streaming their crimes to an eager audience. According to director David Leitch, this was the main appeal behind taking the screenplay by Mark Bianculli and bringing it to life:

"That's what we saw in it and that's why we really wanted to do this material. It had all of those elements where you could create something fun, but yet also with a bigger message. That was one of the things we haven't gotten to do: maybe have something that has a little bit more of a commentary. There's usually a moral tale [in heist movies], but this has a little bit of ... it's asking you big questions about where we are in the world right now."

Where studios like A24 and Blumhouse deserve credit for establishing themselves as high-minded horror destinations, 87North has cornered the market with the most exciting action films. Upon seeing David Leitch's name attached to any given film, audiences can safely expect more visceral set pieces, an emphasis on practical effects, and a certain, undefinable je ne sais quoi when it comes to mixing and matching genres. After "Atomic Blonde," "Deadpool 2," and "Bullet Train," "How to Rob a Bank" seamlessly fits into Leitch's ongoing interests.

Or, as Kelly McCormick aptly puts it in our conversation, "I believe one of David's pillars is that he always is doing a little bit something different with the genre every time out, and wants to and enjoys changing genres and the subgenres within action and really wanting to tell a lot of different tales." It's one thing to identify that branding, however, and another to actually put it into action. As she went on to explain:

"So then, how can you make that Leitchian? How can you make that atonal? And ['How to Rob a Bank'] had all the things, with regards to the drama versus the social media content and all those kinds of aspects. And then, I think the extra unique part is being able to have a bigger message, more front-and-center than what we do a lot of times out with our commercial propositions."

That "bigger message" may hit particularly hard at a time when working-class struggles remain at the forefront of the national conversation as the rich only get richer. "How to Rob a Bank" hits theaters on November 13, 2026.
