#3583. Chris Harrison on Launching The Vow, His Faith-Based Reality Show, and Leaving The Bachelor

“It really has very little to do with being on The Bachelor,” Chris Harrison, the series’s former host, tells me over breakfast at Manhattan’s Whitby Hotel in mid-October. Harrison orders avocado toast with poached eggs on top, then gently redirects the conversation to The Vow, his new faith-based dating series that premieres November 11 on Fox Nation. “It’s what we noticed, reading articles about this revival of young people going to church more than ever,” he says, turning to his wife and fellow executive producer on the show, Lauren Zima, who is seated beside him. “Here in New York, there are youth nights at the Catholic Church, at the temple, that are selling out thousands of kids. Clearly, this generation is searching for something solid—salvation, foundation.”

The six-episode series airs on the conservative-associated Fox Nation, Harrison says The Vow isn’t meant to have a political slant. “We’re not telling you to believe this or follow this path,” says Harrison. “Good shows look into a niche, this one’s about faith-driven people trying to find love. The hookup culture was a big deal and settling down became a cocktail joke. This generation’s really pushing back the other way.”

Faith-based dating shows aimed at Gen Z audiences have begun to infiltrate the reality TV landscape in recent years, from The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives to Hulu’s Ring by Spring Break, an upcoming series “that drops single Christian college students into a steamy spring break in Cabo, where finding ‘The One’ isn’t a dream…it’s a deadline.” But mixing romance and religion can be tricky business, as evidenced by the indeterminate future of the Mormon Wives and a ready-to-release season of The Bachelorette put on pause following allegations made against Taylor Frankie Paul, who leads both shows.

On The Vow, Jace Cates is a 30-year-old devout Christian mortgage-loan officer from Canby, Oregon that 10 similarly faith-driven women compete to marry. The goal is that, “Jace finds love,” says Harrison. “If it leads to marriage and children, we don’t have enough time for all that to happen on the show, but I want to help try and create the real article on TV. And if we don’t, that has to be real as well because this show is not predicated on the fact that it’s guaranteed to work.” But it’s hard to imagine any contenders stand a chance against Sierra, a virgin who lives 20 minutes away from Jace and attends his same Portland church. Her frontrunner status is cemented with a night-one kiss, the filming of which happened to coincide with Sierra’s 26th birthday. “We cast her before we cast Jace,” says Harrison, which feels as telling a reveal as any about producers’ ability to set themselves up for a successful outcome.

In February, before Fox Nation’s public involvement, Harrison shared a casting call for The Vow on Instagram, seeking single men and women aged 21 and older “who want a traditional, marriage-minded partnership built on commitment and shared values.” The description sparked early backlash on social media, but an initially surprised Harrison says he now understands the reaction. “Because in this day and age, we all have our guard up when we hear something that might be controversial,” he explains. “I’m not going to shy away from the fact that [the show] is about faith-based people saying, ‘I really do want to get married. I really do want to have babies’ Even those that might think it’s polarizing, I hope you watch,” Harrison adds. “You might be pleasantly surprised at how unbiased and uncontroversial it really is.”

The 55-year-old Harrison and Zima, who is 16 years his junior, are themselves “on different stages of faith,” she says as her egg-white frittata arrives. “Not drastically, but a bit. He’s probably more traditionally spiritual than I am.” Harrison was raised by a Jewish mother and grandparents, but grew up in a Protestant household during adolescence in the Bible belt of Dallas, Texas. After getting baptized as a Christian in his twenties, Harrison now says he identifies as “a religious mutt.”

“What matters most in our relationship,” the Chicago-born Zima continues, “[are] our values—family, loyalty, wanting to be good to people—those conversations [about] core things that drive you were what we really wanted people to have on the show.” Seeking “a really diverse spectrum of faith” meant casting Christians who ranged from the recently baptized to a first-generation American from Ghana. And the term “tradwife” means something different to everyone—Audrey aspires to be “a woman who makes her own money” as a penile implant sales rep fromin Wisconsin, while California native Mya is a second-grade teacher who one day wants to “do my husband for a living and have a big family.”

“We are always wanting to bring people together,” Zima continues. “And part of the way you bring people together is conversation—giving them dynamic, interesting, layered things to unpack together.”

The couple is open to devoting future seasons to different religions outside Christianity. “The important thing is finding really good, authentic people who have faith in their heart—whatever that faith is—but then really want to get married,” says Harrison. As “one of the rare few that was there on day one back in 2001 when we were inventing what The Bachelor was,” he adds, “it was rough and raw. We shot tons of silly things that never made air because you’re not exactly sure. So there will be some of that on The Vow. As veteran as I am, we’re still asking people to watch our art and accept it.”

The stakes are high for Harrison, who parted ways with The Bachelor franchise following a controversial Extra interview in February 2021, during which he excused racist behavior from one of the show’s contestants. He later issued an apology acknowledging that “by excusing historical racism, I defended it.” After announcing he would be “stepping aside for a period of time” from the series, Harrison also attempted a poorly received daytime TV mea culpa on Good Morning America that anchor Michael Strahan called “a surface response.,” Harrison promptly announced that he would be “stepping aside for a period of time” from the series. He permanently departed the show in June 2021 and reportedly received a “mid-range eight-figure settlement” from ABC, according to Deadline. A follow-up report by Variety adjusted that figure, revealing he received roughly $10 million. Vanity Fair has reached out to Harrison for comment about the payout.

Harrison’s comeback project has already ruffled feathers at his former workplace. In mid-September, Warner Bros, owner of the Bachelor franchise, sent a cease and desist letter against Harrison and Fox Nation, regarding what they viewed as an IP violation on the teaser for The Vow released on September 16. “Sadly, I wasn’t surprised. It’s par for the course. I don’t know why, because in my opinion, you can’t put a cease and desist on finding love,” says Harrison. “So it was unfortunate that’s where they wanted to go in this breakup. I feel a bit like a lover they can’t let go.”

For better or worse, Harrison and Zima’s real-life love story will forever be linked to his time spent hosting The Bachelor. “Oh, the other show?” Zima quips. “All of that, I look back [at it] as a blessing. And blessings don’t always come wrapped in this cute box under the tree,” Harrison says. “Sometimes it’s a humbling and traumatic experience.”

Zima met Harrison while covering The Bachelor franchise as a red-carpet reporter for Entertainment Tonight before things turned romantic in August 2018. “Obviously, what I loved most about her in the beginning was that she was a great interviewer,” says Harrison.

“This is so weird for me. I have to clock myself as being interviewed right now,” says Zima, who brings a bubbly, over-caffeinated energy to Harrison’s politely warm, but largely stoic presence. “By the way, I’m going to shut up. This is his interview,” she says a few times during breakfast, each of them subtly, but noticeably aware that a fellow journalist is meant to be observing their dynamic. They seem more at ease and physically affectionate as the interview wraps up; indeed, it’s only when my recorder stops that Zima dispenses her juiciest morsel of reality TV gossip—a blind item involving Harrison and a certain Real Housewife.

Zima, who earned thousands of views on weekly recaps of the show, credits Harrison’s level of care for those who came on The Bachelor with “how Bachelor Nation was created,” says Zima. “Speaking as someone who watched and reviewed it before we were ever together—he created that energy. What we have together is such a deep understanding of each other’s fields that really adds a passion and joy to our relationship and takes away what could be, in other scenarios, resentment or confusion about a very demanding job.”

Harrison and Zima were both previously married, and he saw two kids off to college in the early years of their relationship. “Maybe it just took the right person, but when she knocked me upside the head with those feelings that I had, that made me want to stop,” Harrison says of his hosting duties on The Bachelor, which often required extended amounts of international travel. “For the first time, I didn’t want to hop on a plane and go to Asia for the next season.”

Coincidentally, his post-COVID epiphany overlapped with Harrison’s exit from his day job. “I’d been on the road for a long time and I felt like something special was happening here with Lauren,” says Harrison, before asking for a reheat of his tea. “I’m just going to hit the pause button and be selfish, fall in love. It allowed me to fall in love and get married. I don’t think she was going to wait around and pine for me while I was on the road shooting another show.” ABC later enlisted former Bachelor, NFL quarterback, and sports commentator Jesse Palmer to replace Harrison as host.

As they celebrate their third wedding anniversary, the Austin-based couple say they’ve come to a peaceful place about “the other show.” Says Harrison, “What a weird thing that I was hosting this show about love and that it allowed me to find love myself. So how can I begrudge that completely?”

As Hollywood weathered hardships of its own, Harrison was happy to employ some of his former Bachelor colleagues, including casting director Lindsay Liles, executive producer Louis Caric, co-EP Deb Read, and director Michael Shea for The Vow. “It’ll probably end up being one of those silly reality TV show drinking games, drink every time someone says ‘intentional’,” says Zima, “but there’s so much meaning behind it and that’s why it gets repeated so much. When we’re kids we read about fairytales and hope to find our love. This guy’s literally bought a house and is filling his savings account for the family he hopes to have one day.”

The show’s dates are grounded in real life. “It’s not too hard to fall in love on a beach in Bora Bora,” says Zima, borrowing a line from Harrison. And there are no elimination rituals where the show’s lead can “hide behind a flower,” says the host. Instead, breakups happen face-to-face and at any time. “It’s what real relationships require,” Harrison tells the participants in the show’s premiere, the only episode provided in advance of our interview. “And honestly, it’s what a gentleman would do.”

That isn’t the only element of The Vow that directly invokes Harrison’s time on The Bachelor. One of the contestants vying for Jace’s heart is Kylee, a 28-year-old who appeared in a post-Harrison season of The Bachelor and now declares herself “on fire for Jesus” following her recent baptism. “There were others. We had a lot of people reach out to us,” from his former franchise, says Harrison. “Kylie was somebody that we were very thoughtful about.”

The showman in Harrison says “it’s fun to poke the bear” with references to his former gig. “It’s reality TV. I’m a TV host. There’s always a side of you that wants to promote the show.” Plus, it’s easier for Harrison to claim his victory in the breakup, given that The Bachelor franchise hasn’t aired a season of its product since March 2025. “And as far as I know, they’re not going to be on the air anytime soon,” says Harrison with a shrug. “So I would just say worry about cleaning up your own mess. Don’t worry about mine.” Roughly two weeks after our mid-October conversation, and just five days before Harrison’s return to TV, ABC announced the official return of The Bachelor in March 2027. No casting has been confirmed.

The search for love is a sensitive one, even for someone as seasoned as Harrison. “I’m not bitter and angry about The Bachelor because I don’t take for granted that I’ve been to the Super Bowl,” he says with a polished kind of sincerity. “I am opening my heart and bearing my soul to everybody, hoping that we could be together again. I do miss that connection and I hope it’s still there. But it’s a very vulnerable thing to do. That’s why I’m not out banging my chest or beating the drum. I’m a producer like anybody else hoping to produce a great television show. My guard is up,” he admits as our plates get cleared away. “Like I was for 20 years before, I will be in front of everybody taking the bullets, and I told [the participants] I will be standing beside you and [we will] do the best we can.”

Behind the scenes, Harrison and Zima often had to convince their young participants that the show wasn’t part of a larger gimmick. “There’s no gotcha—this is really just about you guys finding love,” Harrison recalled. “It was shocking at how low the bar has been set. I don’t mean dating shows, I just mean dating in general. I told the women, ‘I apologize to you on behalf of all men.’ Maybe too arrogant of me and maybe too lofty of a goal, but my hope is that, of all things, maybe we raise the level of debate of what women deserve and what men need to be.”

Zima remembers what it was like to see Harrison return to his element, getting visibly emotional just before our goodbyes. “That first night in the control room, when I saw him on screen, I teared up like I’m tearing up now,” she says with a slightly embarrassed laugh. Harrison reaches over to grab her hand. “It means the world to me that as his wife, more than seeing him on screen, when people stop him in the street and say, ‘Man, you were the thing I could watch with my grandma every week,’” says Zima, “and please come back and do a show because I miss that connection with my family.’ What a meaningful thing to have done in this life, to bring people together.”

Amazon has knocked $100 off the latest Google Pixel Watch 5 (45mm, LTE), bringing it down to $429.99 from $529.99, its lowest price yet, according to price trackers. If you can do without cellular connectivity, the 45mm wifi model is also down by $100, now selling for a record-low $329.99 (down from $429.99). Plus, either one comes with 90 days of free Amazon Music. PCMag calls the Pixel Watch 5 the best smartwatch for Android users, largely because Gemini is built in so deeply—the assistant works proactively, so it can surface your flight details on the way to the airport or suggest a contact's number while you text about dinner plans, and a new AI-powered Health Coach reviews your workouts with tailored feedback, though some of its fitness advice sits behind a paid subscription.

Helping all of those AI features along is a faster Qualcomm processor that Google says improves the overall performance of this smartwatch by 20%, while RAM increases from 2GB to 3GB and storage doubles to 64GB compared with the Pixel Watch 4. As for its health hardware, Google left it largely untouched, so you still get heart rate and blood oxygen monitoring, ECG readings, skin temperature, GPS, and sleep tracking, with reportedly accurate findings. The catch is that this remains an Android-only watch, requiring Android 12 or newer, and some of the better AI features work best with a newer Pixel phone.

Physically, the Watch 5 doesn’t stray far from its predecessor, keeping the familiar domed display under 3D Corning Gorilla Glass while adding new watch faces that curve around its edges—with the screen reaching up to 3,000 nits and adjusting to ambient light, so it should remain easy to read during a sunny afternoon run or in a dim room. As for its durability, its IP68 and 5ATM ratings mean you can wear it through a workout, at the beach, or in the pool without worrying about dust or water. And charging shouldn’t necessarily be a nightly routine, either, with the watch lasting up to 56.5 hours in testing. Heavier use will cut into that figure, but you should still have a good chance of making it through two full days with enough power left to track your sleep overnight.

#3581. How To Watch Avengers Endgame: Encore At Home

What if you could take the same movie that swept up the entire globe in hype and watch it all over again ... but, this time, with a little extra #brandsynergy? That was the (admittedly cynical) gimmick behind "Avengers Endgame: Encore," the buzzy re-release that ruled the box office again earlier this year and will no doubt do so on the streaming charts in the days and weeks ahead. The blockbuster, at one time considered the capstone to the grand Marvel Cinematic Universe experiment, now comes with a whopping four minutes of new footage meant to tie things together with the upcoming "Avengers: Doomsday." That includes a noticeably altered ending and new post-credits scenes, all of which will serve as a bridge to the multiverse-focused chaos to come.

That means you can expect to get your Infinity Vision on (no, we're still not quite sure what that means) with just a snap of your fingers, now with added scenes and new color grading.

Party like it's 2019, folks, because everything old is (slightly) new again. Back then, we had no inkling of a certain novel virus making its way across the globe, we had not yet had the privilege of seeing Palpatine somehow return in "Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker," and we certainly didn't think the MCU could ever top its grand finale of Earth's Mightiest Heroes assembling against the Mad Titan Thanos. Less than a decade later, Marvel Studios is hoping to keep the hype train going on the road to "Doomsday" with "Avengers Endgame: Encore."

In short, it's a good time to be a Disney fan ... and a Disney stockholder, for that matter. For those looking for an excuse to revel in some nostalgia, "Endgame: Encore" fits the bill. "Avengers: Doomsday" will finally arrive in theaters on December 18, 2026.

Ramayana is one of the most epic projects on the 2026 movie schedule, especially because it tells the famed story that’s been told for thousands of years. But what did it take for its star to embody one of the beloved roles in India? Ranbir Kapoor told us a bit about how he trained to become Lord Rama as the movie continues to take on the global box office.

When CinemaBlend chatted with Kapoor, who is one of India’s biggest stars, about taking on the role of Rama, he detailed what was involved in playing the great hero. In his words:

I did take lots of classes. I joined an archery school in New York for some time, and then when I came back to India, I worked with an Olympic archer. I had this board at my house, and every day I used to practice. But, eventually what became harder on the film set was that I had to imagine the arrow because the arrow was created in CG because they were all powerful weapons.

Whoa, he did it all! Being a great archer is certainly a big part of it since Rama must be able to believably be one of the best there ever was. And the character's skills are really put to the test in the movie when he proves to be the only person who can lift and string Lord Shiva’s bow.

While Kapoor hasn’t named which Olympic archer he worked with on Ramayana, it certainly sounds like he really committed to the role, and having a pro helped him be fully convincing as Rama. It’s reminiscent of Jennifer Lawrence working with Olympic archer Khatuna Lorig to train for The Hunger Games movies.

Though, as he brought up, he wasn’t always drawing back an actual bow due to it often being added by the visual effects department after he had shot the movie. There was a lot of imagination needed on the side of the actors in order for Ramayana to be brought to life. The project, which reportedly cost around $400 million to make, implemented a mix of their own LED volume stages with a bunch of practical sets. Kapoor also told us this about what he learned to play Rama:

Being an actor, doing films enables you to learn new skills with every project. But with Ramayana in particular, I got to learn so much. I got to do different kinds of action, learn archery. I practised yoga for a long time. It's just been quite such an amazing process trying to make this character believable.

Kapoor definitely did an incredible job of playing the hero who is an avatar of the god Vishnu, who is reincarnated to take on the villainous character of Ravana. After hearing this story, I wouldn’t challenge him to an archery match anytime soon – unless you enjoy losing!

Along with this conversation, CinemaBlend also had the chance to speak to Ramayana's director Nitesh Tiwari and producer Namit Malhotra, who clarified the movie’s use of A.I. in order to provide more realistic dubbing for a global audience. Malhotra also told us how his love of Christopher Nolan movies led to Hans Zimmer becoming one half of the composing team.

Ramayana was beaten by Godzilla Minus Zero in its first weekend here in the United States, but it’s doing bigger business internationally. You can check out the results of Kapoor’s intense training by seeing Ramayana yourself in theaters now.

#3579. Dua Lipa Talks About Her Book Club, and Her Favorite Authors Join Her for a Photo

It’s the 41st week of this year, and Dua Lipa has already read 22 books. Next up is Sufiyaan Salam’s novel, Wimmy Road Boyz, a coming of age story about a British Pakistani friend group. But fresh on her mind is Careless People: A Cautionary Tale of Power, Greed, and Lost Idealism by Sarah Wynn-Williams, which Lipa has just finished, logging the accomplishment in the Notes app on her orange iPhone.

“Do you know about it?” she asks me, eager to recommend the whistleblower’s memoir. “She’s getting censored because she started working at Facebook very early on and she dishes it all out.”

PAGE TURNERS Lipa at Albertine Books in October with seven of her hand-selected Service95 book club monthly reads. Shirt by Gucci; jewelry by Bulgari.

It should come as no surprise that Lipa, the internet’s favorite hardworking “vacanza queen,” gets most of her reading done while traveling. “I can read in cars. I don’t get sick. It’s kind of a flex,” she says. When we meet in New York in early October, Lipa has just returned from a trip to Madrid, where she performed with Shakira, doing what she humbly refers to as her “day job,” and Paris, for a Chanel show. No matter the destination, for work or play, Lipa will always toss a book—no e-readers—in her bag. “I love the feeling of a book. I love when all the pages get all fucked up a little bit,” she says.

Dressed in an off-duty uniform of blue jeans, a black Chanel sweater, leather boots, and a black Gucci purse big enough to stash a hardcover or two, Lipa, the 31-year-old British Albanian singer who has emerged as a leading literacy advocate, is gearing up for the London Literature Festival, which she guest-curated this year.

Her reading habit is impressive. Not just because she is a jet-set Grammy Award–winning pop star and half of a newlywed power couple (she and husband Callum Turner famously bonded over finishing the same chapter of Hernan Diaz’s novel, Trust) whose Instagram suggests that she exists in a perpetual state of glamour, but because, according to a recent statistic, more than half of American adults read approximately zero books in a year. “Sad,” Lipa says when I give her this stat.

Since 2021, Lipa has been using her spare time to run Service95—a website, newsletter, book club, and podcast—described as a “cultural concierge.” Through the platform, Lipa offers bespoke recommendations and publishes writing on a wide range of topics from style, travel, and wellness to politics and activism. It’s also where, since Service95’s inception, she has hosted in-depth conversations with authors from around the world and across genres. With dozens of podcast episodes under her belt so far, she’s quickly learned what it’s like to be on the other side of an interview. “I’ve done so many interviews myself and I’ve had to answer the same question over and over again. I’m quite sensitive to the fact that I don’t want to put the author in the same position of having to repeat themselves,” she says. “It’s one of my favorite things that I do. I feel like I get so much out of the conversations.”

Today, at the Villa Albertine, a French cultural institution on the Upper East Side, she’s brought her bookshelf to life, gathering seven of her favorite writers—memoirists, novelists, journalists, a National Book Award and Booker Prize winner—for a class photo. Standing together in one room, beneath a mural of a constellation, the stars align: Douglas Stuart, Brit Bennett, Patti Smith, Roxane Gay, Jennifer Clement, Patrick Radden Keefe, Min Jin Lee, and Lipa, all looking like the English department of your wildest dreams. Sitting next to Smith, the author of Just Kids, Lipa, one of the biggest celebrities in the world, appears to be starstruck. In a rare role reversal, Lipa is the fangirl, whipping out her phone to commemorate the occasion with a group selfie.

Here, her impact in the literary world is undeniable—and so is her range.

Between takes, Smith inquires about how many languages Lipa speaks—English, Albanian, some Spanish, and she’s learning French and Italian, she says. The Just Kids author quips that she only knows how to ask where the “biblioteca” is. “That’s kind of all you need,” jokes Keefe, author of Say Nothing, who tells me he often encounters young readers who were introduced to his work via Service95.

READ THE ROOM Dua Lipa and authors take a selfie at Albertine Books. Lipa’s shoes by Prada; jewelry by Bulgari.

Watching all of these literary titans in conversation with each other, it’s impressive to see them all embrace Lipa as an advocate of their work. “I’m sure that there are lots of other things she could be doing with her time that would be far more profitable than championing books,” says Bennett, author of The Vanishing Half. “It’s amazing that she does this out of a genuine love for reading.”

“It’s fun work. It’s good work,” insists Lipa, who is happy to disprove naysayers who think she just “holidays all the time.” “I’m having a good time, and I get all my work done, and I do what I want to do, and then I go on holiday, and I’m happy with that.” It’s what keeps her motivated: “Sometimes being underestimated gives me extra fire in my belly.”

In 2023, when Lipa launched her book club, which has racked up nearly 1 million Instagram followers, she joined the likes of Oprah Winfrey, Reese Witherspoon, Kaia Gerber, Dakota Johnson, Emma Roberts, and Jenna Bush Hager. But the saturation of the celebrity book club market gave her no hesitation. “If people feel a little bit inclined to just go and pick up a book and read something, we’re all doing our job,” she says. “I don’t care if someone’s going to go to this book club or the next one. As long as they’re reading, I’m happy.”

But Clement, author of Widow Basquiat, considers Service95 to be in a league of its own. “It is not simply curating individual titles; it is curating perspective,” she says. “Almost as if, taken together, the books themselves are forming an arc, a larger story unfolding through the choices.”

Lipa works closely with her book club director, Maria Padget, but selects Service95's monthly reads herself, guided not by what’s trending but instead, as Lee, the author of Pachinko who calls Lipa an “exemplary literary citizen,” puts it, by honoring “her intellectual curiosity,” often highlighting marginalized voices, and not absorbing literature through a strictly Western lens.

“When she looks at her readers, she doesn’t think what would be easiest for you to enjoy, or what would comfort you or challenge you the least,” says Stuart, author of Shuggie Bain. “Instead she signals, go on, you can read this, you should read this; read this challenging book, read this banned book, and see what they want to deny you, see what you can achieve and have access to what would make you more powerful!”

In the face of a burgeoning literacy crisis, global book bans, rampant censorship, and the rise of artificial intelligence, Service95 is a venue for Lipa to educate herself and her readers on global issues—encouraging an open dialogue and discourse. “I don’t shy away from it. I also like the fact that I do it on my own terms,” says Lipa, who calls activism an “important pillar” of Service95.

As a result, she’s spoken to Margaret Atwood about the fight for female reproductive rights and discussed sexual violence and intersectional feminism with Gay, author of Bad Feminist. “The book had already been out for more than a decade, so it was quite a thrill to see her introducing the work to a new audience,” the essayist says. Lipa has also pondered the impacts of AI with Nobel Prize laureate Kazuo Ishiguro and provided required reading on Israel and the war in Gaza. She’s even joined a reading group at a women’s prison in Surrey and opened the Manifesto Library—stocking banned books inside the Livraria Lello in Portugal.

“The whole goal was to get people to take a breather, learn about the thing that’s happening, and not to be afraid to ask questions or not be right all the time,” she says.

Lipa, who admits to using the Opal app, which limits her to an hour a day on social media to post her famous photo dumps, is hopeful Service95 can also serve as an antidote to doomscrolling and AI. “Not only are we declining in reading and not picking up a book, but the fact that you can have these cheat codes that completely bypass the whole point of the learning or the ingesting of information,” she says. “It’s just going to make us stupider as people.”

She credits her mother, Anesa, for her love of reading, reminiscing on their weekends spent at a London bookshop. “I basically would just sit there and read for hours and hours and hours. I loved it,” she says, rattling off the names of authors from her childhood, like Jacqueline Wilson and Malorie Blackman and the Mr. Men and Mary-Kate and Ashley Olsen series. Reading is formative to who she is as an artist; it makes her a better songwriter, as she tells me, but it is also fundamental to who she is as a person. “I feel like we get a better understanding of ourselves, of our friends, of our family members, of the people around us, what they might be going through, what’s happening in their life by just picking up a book,” says Lipa.

When I bring up the recent claim from influencer Alix Earle that she had never read a book (apart from maybe Dr. Seuss), Lipa considers the topic thoughtfully and speaks without passing any judgment, generously suggesting the possibility that maybe, as a public figure, Earle said this as a protective measure, to shield her from further prodding and criticism. “Books are so personal, I think people also get intimidated,” she says. “Books should just be enjoyable. No one’s expecting anything from the person reading it. You don’t have to overanalyze it. It’s just supposed to make you feel something.”

And true to form, she offers a book recommendation: “I love The Girls by Emma Cline. I think that’s a cool gateway drug book.”

For Lipa, it all harkens back to searching for that feeling. She returns to her recent interview with Ishiguro, the Klara and the Sun author, who drew parallels between pop music and literature and their ability to foster connection. “He said the heart has so many rooms, so many things that make us, and AI can’t do that,” she says. “There is something really encouraging about that, that some things can't be replicated. Our real humanness and the love we feel, the loneliness even, it can make us feel even more alive and more human.” Perhaps Lipa’s book club is an act of resistance, but it’s also, to borrow a line from her last album, an act of radical optimism.

#3578. The Out of Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: What Does 'Code Rot' Mean?

A weekly deep dive into the current trends, slang, and viral videos of youth culture in terms that even the squarest can understand.

This week's Out-of-Touch guide takes a look at a phenomena that's probably going to define the lives of generations of young people: Code rot—both actual computer-style code rot, and the more elusive cultural kind. I'm also taking a look at the fake controversy over the "cancellation" of Freddy Krueger, and finally, bringing things home with viral videos of boyfriends dancing.

Expect to hear young people talking about code rot for awhile, maybe for the rest of their lives. It's a concept that's going to affect them more than any previous generation. Code rot, or software rot, describes what happens to a computer program when the hardware and operating system it runs on advance. If older programs aren't updated, they become less stable and glitchy until they eventually become unusable.

The idea of code rot has really caught on in the young people's popular imagination, probably because they're going to spend a lot of their lives dealing with it. They've even taken the idea of code rot into life, and use the phrase to describe anything that is worn out or malfunctioning. If the ice cream machine isn't working at McDonald's, it's code rotted. Bad grades on a report card? Code rot.

Kids are making videos where they demonstrate actual code rot:

or point out physical things that are code rotted, like a cat:

Interestingly, a lot of the online discourse around code rotting concerns the massive video game platform Roblox. Because Roblox games there are made by users, there's often not a lot of incentive for the creators to keep the games current with the platform's changes, so a lot of Gen Z's childhood memories of playing games are sinking into code rot. Here's a video about it:

Another interesting wrinkle is the tone these videos take. Code rot is seen as apocalyptic. While it's mostly hyperbole, I think part of it is the realization that the entire world is code rotted. The old programs that used to run within the "Western Culture" operating system no longer apply and everything is starting to glitch out.

The meaning of "PDF file" depends on the context. If you're at work, it refers to a Portable Document Format file, a format created by Adobe that is famously hard for older people to open. In slang, though, PDF file is algo speak for "pedophile." Because that word is flagged by moderation software online, people say "PDF File" to skirt the censorship.

The run-up to Halloween brought a lot of online discourse about Nightmare on Elm Street villain Freddy Krueger. The supernatural serial murder/PDF File was supposedly cancelled online by overly woke, Gen-Z Tiktokers outraged that he is a child predator. The controversy started with a post from Entertainment Industry Reporter that points out how strange it is that in the '80s and '90s, Freddy Krueger, depicted in 1984's A Nightmare on Elm Street as a child murderer so driven by bloodlust he transcended death, was featured on dolls, board games, and lunchboxes aimed at children. It's a good point, but not a call for "cancellation."

Although the article does say that "Freddy Krueger lunchboxes shouldn’t exist," and that parents "shouldn’t have been buying their kids action figures of a child murderer," this is not a call to action. It's not suggesting cancellation of any kind, and it's hard to even conceive of what cancellation of a fictional character in an old horror franchise would even mean. The article is actually an observation about how merchandising (and low-quality sequels) change the meaning of art. But people online missed the point entirely and invented a scenario where "woke" young people are calling for the cancellations of a fictional villain for doing bad things.

I've been scouring TikTok, looking for even one video where someone is calling for "canceling" Freddy Krueger, and I can't find any, but there are hundreds, maybe thousands of videos like this:

In these videos, people point out how enraging it is that the woke people are calling for Krueger's cancellation and vowing that they won't let it happen. Even though it is not happening. There are even levels to the myths about woke mobs canceling Freddy. Supposedly, younger users were unaware that Krueger is depicted as a "PDF file" as well as a murderer in the 2010 reboot of the franchise, so there are online arguments about whether that's the reason he's being canceled. Even though no one is canceling anything. These anti-woke folks are, ironically, defending a fictional villain from cancellation by creating another fictional villain, the shadowy woke mob that's ruining horror movies. Meanwhile, the real villain is a lack of media literacy. Saying "wow, it's crazy that previous generations made a comedy mascot of such a terrible character and marketed him to children" is not the same as cancellation.

This week's viral videos are of boyfriends dancing. The newest thing on the TikTok is young women sharing video of their boyfriends getting down accompanied by a clip from the song "gay alligations fr. my girlfriend" by TikToker OH MICKEY. Like this:

It's a simple, silly template that maybe doesn't mean a whole lot, but this generation of young men are so messed up when it comes to relationships and masculinity, I'm always happy when a meme becomes popular that indicates that young women want goofy dudes, dudes who know how to dance, and dudes who act silly as boyfriends more than they want red-pilled, manosphere, looksmaxxing types. I don't know if these kinds of messages ever really "break through" to the underground of internet incels, but I like to hope they do, because a lot of young men are not OK.

#3577. One Of 2025's Biggest TV Shows Is Now A Box Office Success As Well

One of the biggest breakout TV shows of 2025 has now found success at the box office. The "Heated Rivalry" Season 1 finale ended last year with a barnburner and the show's popularity has only continued to grow since then. While fans eagerly await Season 2, Regal Cinemas partnered with HBO Max and Crave to bring the first season to theaters. Fans turned up to see Shane and Ilya on the silver screen.

As "Godzilla Minus Zero" ruled the box office with a $30.5 million opening, much further down on the weekend's chart, "Heated Rivalry" pulled in a respectable $1.4 million on just over 1,000 screens, making for a solid $1,409 per-screen average. That's certainly not bad for a show that anyone could stream right now from the comfort of home with the price of a subscription they likely already pay for. But this speaks to the rabid fanbase that has developed around the romantic hockey show.

"Heated Rivalry" focuses on two rival hockey stars at the top of their game who develop feelings for each other, complicating their careers and the sport's expectations. It's based on the book series by Rachel Reid. Hudson Williams and Connor Storrie lead the cast as Shane Hollander and Ilya Rozanov, respectively.

To say that the show took off in a way that surprised people would be a bit of an understatement. It dominated HBO Max's charts and became a downright cultural sensation. So much so that a former NHL player hopes "Heated Rivalry" can change pro hockey culture. It made a real impact.

For Regal, Crave, and all involved, the millions the show makes in its theatrical release is a cherry on top of the sundae. Regal is charging $9.99 for two episode blocks of the series, which fans can watch in order if they choose to go three times to watch all six episodes.

This is just the latest example of an already successful TV show finding success on the big screen. Netflix's "Stranger Things" finale was a huge hit for theaters even if it didn't impact the box office, as those tickets were for "concessions vouchers" and not actual tickets. But lots of people still turned up nonetheless. "Doctor Who" has also had multiple theatrical events for various episodes over the years, sticking in the sci-fi realm.

More recently, an unlikely savior emerged at the box office in 2024, with two very different shows doing meaningful business. "Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba — To the Hashira Training," which is just several episodes of the TV show fashioned into a feature, helped establish anime as a true, blue way to sell a lot of tickets. At the same time, the faith-based series "The Chosen" was finding lots of success by screening episodes in theaters. All together, those episodes have grossed more than $100 million worldwide.

Not every show is a good fit for this sort of thing but the right show at the right time can certainly benefit from catering to more hardcore fans. Meanwhile, "Heated Rivalry" Season 2 is in the works, but that's just the tip of the iceberg. Deadline recently reported that Season 3 is also being filmed, along with a movie. So there's much for fans to look forward to.

Microsoft’s flagship development tool, Visual Studio Professional 2026, reduces much of the friction that used to come with large projects, and it’s on sale for just $29.97 on StackSocial right now, which is far less than what most developers expect to pay for a professional-grade IDE.

Microsoft Visual Studio Professional 2026 is a desktop-only Windows product built as a 64-bit application, designed for people working on real-world codebases. Think multi-project solutions, long build times, and code that’s touched by more than one person. In day-to-day use, the biggest benefit is the context the software provides while you work. Visual Studio 2026 supports C#, C++, .NET, ASP.NET, Blazor, and .NET MAUI, so you can move between desktop, web, and cross-platform projects without switching tools. You also get Hot Reload, which helps reduce rebuild time by letting you edit code in .NET and C++ apps and see changes immediately. And CodeLens adds useful context right inside the editor—who last edited a method, which tests cover it, and whether recent changes broke anything—without forcing you to dig through menus or version history. The software’s AI-powered IntelliCode suggestions also feel more restrained than flashy. They tend to fill in logical patterns based on your existing code. It saves time on repetitive work, but you’ll still want to read what it writes.

Collaboration is another area where this version earns its keep. Live Share allows teammates to jump into a debugging or editing session without cloning the repo or matching environments. That’s useful for code reviews or troubleshooting, but it depends heavily on a stable internet connection. System requirements are also worth noting: While it can technically run on 4GB of RAM, 8GB or more is far more realistic, especially for larger solutions, and storage needs can balloon depending on workloads, reaching well over 100GB in some setups. Also, it doesn’t support 32-bit systems and won’t run on mobile devices or Chromebooks. For developers already working in the Windows ecosystem, this is a solid long-term license. For everyone else, those limitations can be deal breakers.

Microsoft Visual Studio Professional 2026 is a full-featured, 64-bit IDE for Windows designed for developers working on complex, multi-project codebases, and it's on sale right now for a one-time price of $29.97 on StackSocial.

#3575. The Rings Of Power Season 3 Finally Solves A Major Lord Of The Rings Lore Mystery

Spoilers are never late (nor are they early; they arrive precisely when they mean to), so don't read ahead without first watching the Season 3 premiere episodes for "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power."

"The Rings of Power" Season 3 is here, and it finally feels like the series we were promised from the start (i.e. the one that showrunners J. D. Payne and Patrick McKay wanted to make all along). At this point, the introductions are done and the show's characters, lore, and locations have all been established. Most importantly, the very silly mysteries around the identity of certain characters all disappear in the first four episodes of Season 3. Because of this, we now know that Gandalf (Daniel Weyman) and Sauron (Charlie Vickers) are a big part of the story, that the insufferable kid Theo (Tyroe Muhafidin) is actually a Ringwraith, and the truth about Ciarán Hinds' Dark Wizard.

As you might recall, the reveal that Weyman's "The Stranger" is actually Gandalf didn't mean all that much in Season 2, given how Gandalf-coded the character was from the get-go. By comparison, the Dark Wizard has been quite Saruman-coded from the start, be it the color of his beard or the way he calls Gandalf an old friend. Yet, the notion of him being Saruman has never made much sense, given how blatantly evil he is. After all, it's meant to be a huge shock when Saruman aligns with Sauron in "The Lord of the Rings," so the idea that he was known as the "Dark Wizard" for centuries would seem to undermine that.

Thankfully, "The Rings of Power" has now confirmed that the Dark Wizard is really Pallando the Blue Wizard, not Saruman.

While Sauron is very much the focus of "The Rings of Power" Season 3 (something that's been praised in early reactions to the show's latest batch of episodes), Pallando is an important part of the story. Except, Pallando doesn't exactly ally himself with Sauron out of greed, ambition, or evil the way that Saruman does in "The Lord of the Rings" (nor does he seem all that afraid of the Dark Lord). Instead, he's already murdered his fellow Blue Wizard and Istar companion Alatar prior to his first appearance on the series.

Pallando's betrayal, it turns out, was an act so malevolent that it turned the once-green realm of Rhûn into a desolated wasteland. The wizard isn't entirely repentant by the time "The Rings of Power" takes place, but he does acknowledge that it's his fault the region has turned to desert, and he seeks specifically to fix it. Hence, his submission to Sauron and the power of Mordor represents a desperate last attempt at correcting his greatest mistake.

All we know from J.R.R. Tolkien's source material is that the Blue Wizards failed their mission and their fates are unknown when "The Lord of the Rings" begins (although they're presumed dead). In other words, "The Rings of Power" can resolve a major "Lord of the Rings" mystery by revealing what ultimately became of Pallando in particular. This should also make Gandalf's mission in Season 3 all the more interesting, as he might yet have a chance at saving the Blue Wizard. Either way, there's much we've yet to learn about the character.

"The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" is currently streaming on Prime Video.

#3573. In 'The Spot', Claire Danes and Ewan McGregor Unravel Together

Claire Danes was standing in the operating room, dressed in scrubs and a mask, when a surgeon’s assistant gave her the opposite of a pep talk. “You may think you’re badass, but if you think you’re fainting, you’re fainting, and we can’t have that, so just let me know,” she told Danes.

Danes, luckily, did not faint, though she says she was incredibly aware of her breathing as she watched an intricate brain surgery performed by a team of doctors.

The three-time Emmy winner was observing in preparation for her role in The Spot, a new Hulu series in which she plays a successful neurosurgeon who begins to suspect that she may be responsible for the hit-and-run death of a child. As she tries to investigate the horrific possibility, she and her husband (Ewan McGregor) find themselves falling deeper and deeper into a web of suspicion and dark secrets.

“I’ve always thought of it as an exploration of a marriage through the lens of a crime and maybe exploration of a crime through the lens of a marriage,” says Solomon of The Spot.

“I’m fascinated with this notion of what if your worst-case scenario way in the back of your head started to really look like it was true, and how could you dramatize that?” says writer, creator, and showrunner Ed Solomon.

The bold psychological thriller, which Vanity Fair can exclusively reveal will debut on January 13, follows a woman unraveling at the possibility of her worst fears coming true, and a marriage under enormous strain. There’s been a steady stream of whodunit miniseries in the last decade, but here Solomon, whose past work includes writing The Christophers and Now You See Me, has created a highly watchable, page-turning series that’s more of a “did I do it?”

“I never want it to be pretentious,” says Solomon. “I just want it to be fun and entertaining, but also elevated, respectful of the viewer.”

"I had wanted to work with Claire for years and we just had great fun acting and playing together while making this show,” says McGregor.

Danes was initially drawn to the series because of the portrait of the marriage at the heart of it, and Solomon’s particular gift for weaving the tragic into the comic. “It gets really very dark pretty quickly,” she says, “but it’s absurd too.”

She not only watched two brain surgeries in preparation but also shadowed a surgeon on his rounds, being with patients before they went into surgery and while they were recovering with their families. “I felt horrible that there I was in this room with these people who couldn’t be more vulnerable, and there I was, trying to be discreet in the corner,” she says.

But the experience gave her insight into what kind of person her character Lou Shadwick would be: intense, hypervigilant, and high achieving. “There’s a lot of marathon runners in there, and highly, highly focused people,” she says. “And they carry a lot of responsibility, and I think they compartmentalize very effectively.”

Danes had previously worked with Solomon on the 2023 series Full Circle, which was directed by Steven Soderbergh. When Kate Winslet, who was initially attached to play Lou, exited, Danes stepped in. Solomon needed an actress who could portray a mother and surgeon who is obsessed with doing the right thing and being a good person. “To be able to see someone who has a very, very present and active inner life that when you look, you can see well beyond the eyes and you can see someone who can be basically playing many things at one time, which was really important and interesting to me,” he says.

Danes had never worked with McGregor before, though they both had previously worked with Baz Luhrmann (on Romeo + Juliet and Moulin Rouge, respectively) and she thinks they had met briefly around that time. “We were definitely of a certain time, the ’90s,” she says. “So we share a lot of references, but it was just an immediate rapport.”

Lou is doing what many mothers juggling work and family have done: driving home from work, talking on the phone about dinner while also checking an unending flurry of text messages. It’s at that moment when she thinks she might have accidentally hit a child on a bike and not realized it until she heard about it later. “It’s so effective, this circumstance that he’s drawn for us,” she says of Solomon. “It’s entirely relatable, and I think it’s the fear that we all have experienced and hosted many, many times, if not on a daily basis.”

Michael Patrick Thornton as Pete Porphyry

As she tries to piece together what might have happened, a police officer (Daveed Diggs) and a detective (Michael Patrick Thornton) are doing the same, and begin to suspect Lou. Her husband, Damon, gets involved, making more trouble for both of them.

Lou and Damon met in medical school, but Damon dropped out and is now pursuing medical aid work in the shadow of his wife’s illustrious career. “I really like the idea of a man, who is charming and good-looking and therefore used to feeling very much in control when he walks into a room, having a spouse who is quite significantly on the rise,” says Solomon. “What does that do to your sense of ego if you’re a guy like that?”

Lou begins to see signs that she may be the guilty party.

McGregor says he had wanted to work with Danes for a long time, and was drawn as Damon as a character. “I think the character has an amazing arc throughout the story from where he starts to where he ends,” he says. “He has a very deeply hidden, shameful secret that gets uncovered as the story goes on.”

McGregor brings to the role a kind of playfulness. “I’ve always loved a certain quality of Ewan’s where there’s a maturity and a boyishness happening simultaneously,” says Solomon. “The boyish quality within this character is really important and the ability to cover a sense of wound.”

Set in upstate New York, the new series will take viewers on a wild ride following two people who are putting themselves in an increasingly dire situation and web of lies. “She’s a decent person, and so is her husband, really,” says Danes. “And yet, they allow their moral compass to become increasingly compromised.” Solomon hopes that even as the story gets darker and wilder, it will leave viewers with at least one big question they’ll have to grapple with: “I would hope that they’re asking questions, like what would I do if I were in that situation?”

“In Ewan, you can see the fragility in him,” says Solomon of McGregor.

#3570. The Lord Of The Rings: The Rings Of Power Season 3's Two Big Character Deaths Explained

The land of Mordor is where the shadows lie, and this article is where major spoilers lie. Read no further if you haven't watched the Season 3 premiere episodes of "The Rings of Power."

"The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" has one thing in common with the TV phenomenon that was "Game of Thrones" — they're both exercises in enduring misery. After all, the show is all about watching stupid sexy Sauron (Charlie Vickers) make everyone in Middle-earth suffer season after season. And sure, the series is willing to kill beloved characters, but it really excels at killing hordes of people and turning entire kingdoms into desolated volcanic wastelands where the sun never shines.

Things are even worse at the start of Season 3, between Sauron trying to forge the One Ring, Mordor's Ringwraiths spreading across Middle-earth, and a Dark Wizard (Ciarán Hinds) ruling Rhûn. Elsewhere, when it comes to the civil war plaguing Númenor, the realm's only hope is Eärien (Ema Horvath), who was responsible for the King's Men usurping the Númenórean throne in the first place. In fact, Eärien is an unexpected main character early in Season 3, acting as a faithful servant and the head torturer for the usurper Ar-Pharazôn (Trystan Gravelle) while at the same time operating as a double agent for her brother Isildur (Maxim Baldry) and father Elendil (Lloyd Owen) as they try to restore Queen Míriel (Cynthia Addai-Robinson) to power.

Unsurprisingly, things don't go well, as "The Rings of Power" Season 3 kills off two original characters made for the show in its first four episodes. First, Eärien dies in the second episode, followed by the wood elf Arondir (Ismael Cruz Córdova) being tragically betrayed and murdered in Episode 4.

Let's start with Eärien. The character has always felt out of place on "The Rings of Power," with her scenes slowing down the pace and taking away from other, better storylines. Frustratingly, the show simply doesn't have time to cover all the ground it wants to, with the limited number of episodes per season forcing it to jump around too quickly. That being said, Eärien aiding the rise of the King's Men in the secluded and isolated island of Númenor due to her mistakenly believing that following Queen Míriel had gotten Isildur killed was interesting, as was her becoming a double agent once she learned the truth.

Unfortunately, Eärien's double age storyline — her best so far — doesn't last long. By Episode 2, she's already been discovered. So, rather than be subjected to torture and forced to become truly loyal to the King's Men, she dies by suicide by jumping off a balcony.

Likewise, when he was first introduced, Arondir was a great character. Sure, he didn't actually do much, with much of his screen time being dedicated to an attempt at a romance between him and the now-deceased Bronwyn (Nazanin Boniadi). And yet, Ismael Cruz Córdova has always played his role with great gusto, giving Arondir a strong personality that makes him feel like more than just a Legolas knock-off. But that just makes his departure all the more upsetting.

Indeed, Arondir gets little more to do in Season 3 than worry about Bronwyn's annoying son Theo (Tyroe Muhafidin). This all leads to a confrontation in Episode 4 when Sauron orders Theo — now a Ringwraith — to murder the elf. A tragic end, sure, but with little buildup.

With Arondir and Eären's deaths, "The Rings of Power" is quickly getting rid of its original characters. After all, the show had already killed off one of its best brand-new additions in Adar (Sam Hazeldine and Joseph Mawle), while the Harfoots that were so essential in Seasons 1 and 2 are nowhere to be found in Season 3 so far. Granted, Theo's still around, but he's likely to be killed soon as well (due to that whole being a Ringwraith thing). That just leaves Kemen (Leon Wadham), the tiring nepo baby at the center of the Númenor story.

Instead, it's clear "The Rings of Power" is currently more focused on bringing in previously missing characters from J.R.R. Tolkien's source material, like Isildur's brother Anárion (Andrew Richardson) and Middle-earth's own Odysseus, i.e. Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower), who's married to Morfydd Clark's elfish warrior Galadriel. It makes sense for the show's writers to be doing this right now, too, as we're getting closer and closer to the end of the series' reported five-season plan. But that means "The Rings of Power" will also have less and less time to explore any of its original characters from this point on.

Another problem is the show's condensed timeline, as "The Rings of Power" is trying to tell a story that spans thousands of years in Tolkien's literature over a much, much shorter period. That means we still have a lot of major "Lord of the Rings"-related developments to get through, be it Elendil and his sons founding the kingdom of Gondor or Celeborn creating Lothlórien with Galadriel. Will all that and more to cover, there's just no more room for the likes of Arondir the wood elf.

#3568. The Best Ways For Star Trek Fans To Play Magic's New Set: A Guide For Beginner Players

When I sat down at my friendly local game store to participate in a pre-release drafting event for Magic: The Gathering's new "Star Trek" set, several players saw the Enterprise tattoo on my forearm and asked me the same question. If a longtime Magic player wanted to sample "Star Trek," what was the best place for them to start?

Ironically, I was there to ask the Mirror Universe version of that same question: If a longtime "Star Trek" fan wanted to sample the new Magic set, what's the best place for them to start?

I am new to Magic, having only picked up the game a few months ago to prime myself for the new "Trek" release. And one thing Magic and "Star Trek" have in common is that they're both absolutely daunting at first blush. One is a collectible card game with over 30 years of history and dozens of ways to play. The other is a sci-fi universe with nearly 1,000 episodes of television and 13 movies, with dozens of possible entry points.

I can answer one question immediately. "Trek" newbies should start with "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds," with its glossy production values and modern streaming sensibilities, before backtracking and sampling the various other shows and finding the one that connects with their tastes. (This is a sometimes controversial opinion, but I stick by it.)

But the other question involved some legwork, a lot of time spent at a gaming table, a great deal more time sorting through cards, and even a question proposed to the lead designers of the set itself. So, what is the best way for a "Star Trek" fan to sample the new Magic: The Gathering set? Here's what I learned.

One thing I will not do here is explain the rules of Magic: The Gathering, which are intuitive and easy to learn, but challenging to master. There are countless online resources to learn before you try anything I recommend below. I'm writing this piece under the assumption you intend to seek those out on your own.

The best way to truly dive in headfirst is to visit your local gaming shop and participate in a sealed or drafting event. Naturally, this is dependent on your location and whether your local gaming shop is an inviting and safe space (shout out to Mothership Games in Austin, Texas for playing host to my first sealed event). If such a place exists for you, check the calendar and see what's on offer. The good news is that the "Star Trek" set is brand new and there should be plenty of opportunities.

At events like these, players are organized into one-on-one matches and construct their decks from scratch, tearing open booster packs, examine their cards, and trying to build the most effective strategy possible around a 40-card deck. While experienced players will have an edge, they can't bring finely honed and powerful decks from home to immediately wipe the floor with you. Everyone starts at square one. And "Star Trek" fans should take very easily to this format, since the characters you'd expect to be powerful tend to have cards that are powerful. It also leads to some amusing team-ups, like how my winning deck involved an unlikely alliance between Deanna Troi and Gul Dukat.

In a friendly shop with a friendly crowd, this is Magic at its purest: a direct, competitive game where tactics at the table are as important as the strategy behind your deck construction. And the mechanics in the "Trek" set are intuitive and mesh well, meaning that creating a deck that functions as needed is fairly straightforward, and going with your gut choices (i.e., building around characters you like) often leads to strong results.

I can hear your next question: You don't have access to a local shop, or you don't feel comfortable going to one, so what's the best way to play at home? Once again, there are options.

You and a friend (or more) could always buy booster packs, tearing them open and building personal collections and constructing 60-card decks for standard play. However, I would recommend booster packs being the start of your collection, and once you have bought a few, track down single cards to complete your strategy rather than buying more and blindly hoping for strong pulls.

Another option is for you and a friend to buy a pre-release kit, as there are always plenty leftover after the initial week of special event. Use these to construct imperfect but fun starter decks to learn the game, and then grow and expand those decks as you see fit, doubling down on the characters and strategies you're enjoying.

However, the best at-home experience would be to pick up one of the set's Draft Night boxes, which are pricy but offer bang for your buck: enough cards for four friends to craft decks and go head-to-head for an evening, leaving everyone with enough cards to build upon in the future.

However, all of these options require tinkering, and suggest that you'll enjoy the process of building a deck as much as playing one. These options require additional legwork, additional financial investment, and even a bit of luck (although that can be mitigated by buying single cards from reputable online and brick-and-mortar shops). If you want to truly just dive into the game itself and skip the rest of the process, there is another way.

When I had a chance to speak to the key designers behind Magic: The Gathering's "Star Trek" set during a launch event in Los Angeles, I asked if the new set was friendly for "Star Trek" fans with no gaming experience, and if they had a recommendation on where to start.

First, they noted that the set was designed with new players in mind and puts narrative first. A card will generally behave like its counterpart in the "Star Trek" universe, so a fan knows that a Captain Kirk card will be a bit more headstrong and aggressive while Spock will allow for more wily, thoughtful strategy. This means a "Trek" fan should be able to grasp the new cards fairly quickly, using their existing knowledge as a crutch.

Second, they highlighted their recommendation for the best way to sample the game: the "Star Trek" commander decks.

Commander is the most popular format in Magic, where players utilize 100 card decks in four-player games that are slowly paced, socially driven, and generally take an entire evening to play. Think of them as more of a board game experience — or a nerd poker night — than a standard Magic set. Many Magic sets are accompanied by a few pre-constructed commander decks, which players can purchase, open, and play immediately without any prep. The "Star Trek" set has four of them: Federation Fleet, We Are the Borg, Klingon Fury, and Landing Party.

Specifically, the designers recommended the Federation Fleet commander deck as their choice for a "Star Trek" fan hoping to play the game.

Naturally, the next step was to test the designers' suggestion. I rounded up three friends and assigned them each a different Star Trek commander deck, taking Federation Fleet for myself. It's easy to see why this one was recommended: With Picard on the cover and a deck full of '90s "Trek" staples, it's the most popular era of the franchise in one 100-card deck.

Our four-player game took over three hours, and frankly, it was some of the best Magic I've ever played, with all four decks interacting in surprising and wild ways that left everyone at the table screaming and laughing. The "Trek" fans were impressed by the thematic touches, and how the mechanics relate to character personalities and motives, while the Magic players simply relished in the new design elements. I squeaked out a win, but only after the Borg player staged a comeback that essentially wiped out the table. My victory told a story in of itself: Dr. Bashir threw himself at the Borg player, perishing, but in the process, activated his ability to resurrect Ro Laren from the dead, activating her ability and ending the Borg threat once and for all.

After seeing the commander decks in action, I'm inclined to agree with the designers' recommendation. The Borg deck is scary and powerful, but makes them an immediate threat the other players will team up against to defeat. The Klingon deck is pure aggression, which may work against a new player's inherent shyness. The Landing Part deck, with its focus on Original Series characters, is fairly straightforward, but has a lot of moving pieces to consider. The mechanical simplicity of the Federation Fleet deck, and its arsenal of beloved characters, makes it easy to grasp and understand quickly.

Much like with "Star Trek" itself, there are countless ways to get into Magic: The Gathering, and no incorrect way. Ultimately, I agree with the designers: the pre-constructed commander decks, and specifically the Federation Fleet deck, are the best point of entry. Ideally, you'd buy all four and learn with friends for the best possible experience.

But like with "Star Trek" itself, you should be warned: once Magic has sucked you in, be prepared to be sucked in for the long haul.

#3567. Xbox CEO Hints Its Studios Will Heavily Use AI to Make Future Games

While Sharma didn’t say AI directly, the implications are clear

This Sunday marks 25 years of Xbox. To commemorate the occasion, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma wrote a lengthy post on X cataloging Microsoft’s long history with gaming that goes back long before the original Xbox was released on Nov. 15, 2001. However, while the post mostly reads like a typical anniversary blog from a gaming executive, the last chunk implies the company may be going in a new direction with the most controversial technology of the moment: generative AI.

“While modern games demonstrate the heights of human craft in ways unimaginable just decades ago, the cost, resources, and risk required to create them have grown just as dramatically,” Sharma wrote. “As a result, too many ideas never become games, and too many games fall short of what their creators imagined. For decades, this has been the unavoidable tradeoff of ambition. We must change this.” Sharma recently described Microsoft’s gaming division as “not healthy," and declared Xbox was in the middle of a “reset” that has already led to more than a thousand job cuts and the sale of several beloved studios, including Double Fine.

Sharma’s next paragraph provides some insight into how the company may try to turn things around. “Throughout human history, the scale of what we could create was determined by the people, capital, and resources we could command,” Sharma continued. “That relationship is beginning to break. A single person will soon be able to wield capabilities that once required entire nations. A small team will be able to build worlds that today demand hundreds of developers and hundreds of millions of dollars. And our largest studios will be able to pursue ambitions as far beyond today’s games as Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024 is from its first entry in 1982.”

While Sharma was careful never to use the term “AI,” the idea of a “small team” being able to “build worlds that today demand hundreds of developers and hundreds of millions of dollars” only seems feasible in the context of this technology. Modern AAA video games tend to require more developers, not fewer, and as a result, development costs have been rising across the industry.

Since Sharma was appointed the new CEO of Xbox, many have speculated that Microsoft’s gaming division would eventually lean into AI. Before landing her current role, Sharma served as Microsoft’s corporate video president and head of product for its AI platform and then led the company's CoreAI product organization.

Amid ongoing backlash against generative AI over its potential negative impact on labor, artistic expression, and the environment, Sharma has downplayed her previous involvement with this technology. In a blog post from February, she said, “As monetization and AI evolve and influence this future, we will not chase short-term efficiency or flood our ecosystem with soulless AI slop. Games are and always will be art, crafted by humans, and created with the most innovative technology provided by us.”

However, on Oct. 13, she announced Xbox Labs, an experimental division inspired by the recent crush of AI-driven game decompilations, ports, and mods. Despite this group unambiguously dealing in AI-generated code, Sharma managed to avoid using the word AI even once in the post revealing this team.

Sharma’s latest blog is quite similar, describing ongoing changes in the video game industry driven by generative AI without directly naming the technology. While many players rightfully dislike generative AI being used to create games, using AI to write or assist with code has quietly taken over the software industry. Stack Overflow's 2025 year-in-review survey found that 84% of polled software developers were using AI tools in some capacity. While there is still hope that this situation could be reversed through legislation or other means, it seems likely that most large game companies will continue to lean into generative AI until something significant changes.

#3566. How to Try 'Audio Intelligence' on Your Apple Watch Early

It has been a big year for Apple. There's a new CEO, prices have increased across the board, and there's been a seemingly endless rollout of new devices, including two new Apple Watches: the Series 12 and the Ultra 4. All things considered, these watches offer only minor upgrades over the previous models, shipping with new heart rate monitors and the latest S11 processor. But one of the biggest new watch features, "Audio Intelligence," is also the most controversial—and it's rolling out in beta today.

Audio Intelligence is Apple's branding for a new set of features exclusive to the Series 12 and Ultra 4. These features use the new Apple Watches' hardware, along with on-device and cloud-based AI, for tasks like sound and music identification as well as dictation. "Sound Recognition" can alert you to important sounds, like alarms and doorbells, while "Music Recognition" can automatically display songs playing around you—but these aren't the features you'll hear talked about in discussions of Audio Intelligence.

Rather, everyone is up in arms about "Live Rewind" and "Siri Recap." These Audio Intelligence features passively "listen" to your conversations throughout the day, and, using AI, deliver summaries of what was said. When you double-click your Apple Watch's crown to use Live Rewind, you'll get a loose transcript of the last 15 seconds of conversation it overheard, while Siri Recap can show summaries of all your in-person chats throughout the day. You can even configure a schedule for when your watch is "listening" for recaps—e.g., only run during work hours. Apple suggests each is intended to help jog your memory; maybe you use Siri Recap to remember important discussions you had that morning, while Live Rewind is meant for moments where you forget what someone just said. (As opposed to asking them to repeat themselves, I suppose.)

Apple's claims may or may not assuage your fears, but it seems the company is pushing on ahead regardless. Apple is releasing Audio Intelligence as part of iOS 27.3, which launches in beta on Tuesday. If you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4, you can try it out today, assuming you enroll in Apple's latest beta version.

To do so, you'll need to sign up for the Apple Developer program, since iOS 27.3 is rolling out first for devs. This program used to require a $99 fee, but you can skip it now if you opt for the free account. Once you enroll your Apple Account in this program, you can open your iPhone, head to Settings > General > Software Update > Beta Updates, and choose "iOS 27 Developer Beta." Go back one page, then follow the on-screen instructions to download and install iOS 27.3 when it's available.

#3565. Henry Cavill Comments On Superman Return After James Gunn's DC Studios Exit

Henry Cavill was a great Superman who never got a great Superman movie, and that should have been the end of it. But it's now 2026, and we're still talking about whether Cavill will return as the Man of Steel. With James Gunn and Peter Safran "stepping down" as DC Studios co-heads, DC's cinematic future is very much up in the air, and now Cavill is saying he'd always be open to returning as Supes.

During an Inverse interview, the actor was asked if he'd ever play the DC hero again and seemed open to the idea. "Look, there's lots of fantastic storylines," he replied. "There's always a lot of opportunity. As the pigeon sang to Fievel in 'An American Tail,' "never say never." And I buy into that." It's hardly surprising, given that Cavill and his former DC Extended Universe colleague Dwayne Johnson once launched a pretty bizarre attempt to remain in the cinematic universe, most pointedly with 2022's immediately forgettable "Black Adam." At the time, Cavill proudly announced his return as Superman in a social media post following the film's release, but it never actually amounted to anything more than that and left Gunn deeply (and understandably) confused about what was even happening.

Since then, Gunn has introduced us to an all-new Man of Steel in David Corenswet, who made his debut in the charming crowd pleaser that was 2025's "Superman" and is set to return in the 2027 follow-up "Man of Steel." But with Gunn out at DC Studios it remains to be seen where the Corenswet version of the character and his story will go from there. Meanwhile, we've got Cavill telling Inverse he "had such a wonderful time playing Superman in the past" and "would never say never now." It's a bit tiresome, no?

Directly after the extremely perplexing return of Henry Cavill's Superman in "Black Adam," the DCEU collapsed with back to back flops in 2023. Meanwhile, James Gunn was gearing up to launch his DC Universe, which is why the whole situation left him baffled – especially since he was already actively preparing his DC reboot at the time. He wasn't the only one, either. Audiences thought they'd seen the last of the so-called Snyderverse after 2023, but Gunn chose to soft reboot DC with a new cinematic universe that retained elements of the old one. What's more, calls to reinstate the DCEU persist even today.

Now that Gunn and Peter Safran have been removed (er, "stepped down") from DC Studios, it looks as though Skydance CEO David Ellison — who's running the newly-merged Warner Bros. and Paramount — is planning to pretty much dismantle everything Gunn built at DC to prepare for yet another reboot.

Whatever Ellison and his new president and chief creative officer of DC Studios, Jeremy Latcham, have planned for the brand, I think it's safe to say we really don't need more talk of Cavill suiting back up. Had the actor left this character alone following 2017's "Justice League," it might have been a thrill to hear of his possible return a decade later. As it stands, like calls to restore the Snyderverse, this seems to be the discussion that never dies. Perhaps it's that lingering feeling that Cavill never got the movie he deserved, or the fact that Superman remains his best-known character. But for now it would be nice to go a few years without hearing about anything from the Snyderverse era coming back.
