#3548. Beto O’Rourke Says He’d “Do Anything” for James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa—Including Work for Them

After the shocking Democratic victories in Texas last week, it was hard not to look over the shoulders of James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa and see the shadow of Beto O’Rourke, whose losses for Senate in 2018 and governor in 2022 had become cautionary tales of Democratic hopelessness in Texas. And perhaps proof that nice guys couldn’t win. But in the years after those failed runs, O’Rourke never really went away. He launched a voter-registration group called Powered by People, punched out missives on Substack, livestreamed his thoughts, and quietly advised his party from the background.

“Should I have talked to Joe Hagan when he was on my front porch in 2019?” O’Rourke says now, looking back at the cover story I wrote, in which he proclaimed he was “just born to be in it,” a premature declaration that almost immediately sank his prospects. “I’m glad I did. I’m grateful for everything that’s happened, because look where we are. It’s a beautiful new day in America.”

O'Rourke taks the stage during the Fight the Trump Takeover rally at the Texas Capitol in August 2025.

Like Stacey Abrams in Georgia, who lost her own race for governor but used her visibility to build a stronger coalition, O’Rourke can claim some credit for setting the table for Democratic success in Texas. Talarico won his first race, for a Republican-held state House seat, on O’Rourke’s 2018 wave. And as it turns out, O’Rourke himself weighed another Senate run this year. When Talarico asked whether he’d run, O’Rourke said only if Talarico ran for governor instead, eventually stepping aside after concluding that the moment called for “something and someone new.” When he launched his Senate campaign, Talarico said he wanted to replicate O’Rourke’s “energy.”

O’Rourke, meanwhile, became a behind-the-scenes player: Powered by People was one of four partners in the Texas Democrats’ $30 million coordinated campaign, and it says it reached more than 110,000 new and young voters in Texas this cycle. Ken Paxton noticed and tried to put O’Rourke “behind bars” for funding the Democrats who fled the state to block its Donald Trump–backed redistricting.

O’Rourke says the wave cascaded so far down the ballot in Texas that a candidate who tried backing out of her campaign before Election Day ended up winning. “At that point it was too late to take her name off the ballot,” he says. “She didn’t campaign, just won her election. That speaks to the magnitude of the wave, but also to the value of having a fighter on every front. Somebody said to me, ‘A wave’s great, even better if you have a surfboard.’”

Over an hour-long conversation, O’Rourke parses the political revolution in his home state, suggests how Democrats can hold on to their land grab, and, perhaps unsurprisingly, looks ahead to another run for office.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Vanity Fair: The conventional wisdom is that this was a revolt against Trump, and that the candidates and the Democratic strategy were secondary. What’s your read?

Beto O’Rourke: So much of this election was a rejection of Trump and Trumpism: the corruption, the wars, the cruelty. But after 2024, people were anxious that we didn’t have a unifying national leader. [Joe] Biden was not going to be it. Kamala Harris turned out not to be it. President Obama, I think wisely, held back…. Chuck Schumer was persona non grata in any gathering of Democrats. The DNC was in the red.

What it did was allow for candidates in different parts of the country to really establish themselves in their own right and by their own merits, never having to fear being under the shadow of a larger figure. It’s really a blessing. That’s how you get Abdul El-Sayed, James Talarico, Mary Peltola, all these extraordinary candidates who are extraordinarily different from each other. In Texas, for the first time in half a century, Democrats fielded a fighter on every front: 150 state House candidates, 38 congressional candidates, 16 state Senate candidates. You had to have a historically terrible, corrupt president. But you also had to have this historically beaten-down Democratic Party; that the Democrats don’t have a message, they don’t have a leader. That all turned out to be a great thing.

Read Party Animals: A letter from the back rooms, barstools, and bacchanals of Washington, DC—with exclusive reporting, interviews, and analysis.

A year ago you convened Talarico, Colin Allred, and Joaquin Castro to think about a statewide slate. Talarico went his own way. You warned him he’d “want friends on that ticket.” What did you mean?

I just wanted to win, and I put that before anything else. James and I had many conversations before he officially announced. He asked me, “Are you interested? Would you run?” And I told him, “The only condition on which I would run is if you were to run for governor, or somebody else who could draw that kind of attention and resources, and if we had the ticket rounded out by strong contenders for every position on the ballot.”

My advice to him was: “Look, I’ve done this before. No matter how talented you are, no matter how much you can raise, this state is so big, the Republicans are so entrenched, you need a fighter on every front.” And ultimately, that’s what happened. Gina really hit her stride at the right time. Her strength as a candidate a year ago compared to how she finished is worlds apart, and that is a testament to what an exceptional leader she is.

Clearly, it was the right call for James to be there. He is just an extraordinarily talented communicator. He was a phenomenally focused candidate. He was absolutely the right guy for the moment. I also think it was the right call for Jasmine Crockett to run too. I know from being on college campuses how electrifying she is, how many young people she brought into the electorate this time. They stayed in even after Jasmine was defeated in the primary.

The Atlantic reported that you told Hinojosa, “Not one person can win Texas. It has to be two.” Is that what you said?

I definitely spoke to Gina before she made the decision to run, and then after. To be honest with you, I can’t remember if I said “two.” What I said consistently to everybody who was thinking about it—Colin, Joaquin, Gina, Jasmine [Crockett], James—was that you need a fighter on every front and the strongest possible ticket. That was based on the last run I had, in 2022, and even the ’18 run. If Joaquin or Julián Castro had run for governor when I was running for Senate, who knows? Of course, at that time, we didn’t know the size of the wave that was about to crash.

I definitely did. I could have run…. You’d have to ask James, but I think he probably would have supported that if I had. We have an amazing organization in waiting, volunteers who’ve been with me, the ability to raise money. But was that the right thing to do? No. I had been before Texas twice before, and the moment demanded something different and, I would argue, something better.

You can’t discount a politician’s ambition and ego. I had to find a way to get past that. It helped having conversations with my wife. It helped having conversations with our kids. It helped having conversations with people who’d been on these runs with me before. Also, I spent a lot of time traveling Texas. My love language is a town hall meeting, where it’s just a free-for-all and anybody can step to the mic and ask any questions. At the end of that, I really felt this moment called for something and someone new. I don’t know that Texas could have produced a stronger—I was going to say candidate, but really a one-two punch. It was James and Gina. They’re both exceptional individually. Together, they transcended what had happened in politics for as long as I’ve been alive.

Honestly, my own doubt about whether Texas could be won was based on you. We’d seen this story before.

I wouldn’t have done this work as a volunteer for the last four years if I didn’t believe in Texas. I know in my heart and in my bones that we are so much better than the people in power. It’s the obscene abortion ban that has cost the lives of girls and women, the $7.25-an-hour minimum wage, the fact that we’re the least insured state in the country. Four years after Uvalde, and no one in power has done a single thing. It’s insane having Texas Republicans say, if you’re Muslim, regardless of whether you’re an immigrant, you should be deported from this country. That’s just not who we are.

O'Rourke speaks during the Fight the Trump Takeover rally, where 5,000 people attended. Attendees protested proposed redistricting, immigration enforcement, and other Trump-backed legislation and proposed changes.

When I ran for governor, 9 million registered voters didn’t cast a ballot. It’s not because they don’t care; it’s not that they’re lazy. This state makes it harder than any other to participate, so we’ve got to try that much harder. I knew it was a matter of time and effort. The greater the effort, the shorter the time. But did I know it would be 2026? Did I know it would be every statewide office and the state House? Fuck no, man. Nobody knew that.

Ken Paxton called you a “repeat loser” and tried to prosecute your PAC. He lost by 12 points.

We’ve spent more than $600,000; we have Powered by People defending our organization, defending me. He accused me of bribery. He tried to remove the license for Powered by People to do voter-registration work in the state of Texas. He promised to lock me up, to put me behind bars. The 15th Court of Appeals [judges], all of whom were appointed by Greg Abbott, so none of them friends of mine, have ruled against Paxton for attacking somebody for exercising their First Amendment rights. Do I think that I’m going to get that money back? I don’t know.

Couldn’t have happened to a better person.

Did Talarico and Hinojosa acknowledge your role, or did they keep their distance?

You’d have to ask them. I got a really nice message from James on election night, and I had a chance to campaign with Gina in the closing days of the election. That’s not an easy choice for Gina, right? Both of them did an exceptional job of being themselves and not seeming to be beholden to anybody. They invited nobody in from outside of Texas, and we all understood: This is their show. So getting to campaign with Gina here at the University of Texas at El Paso, at the University of Houston, it was really nice to hear her acknowledge the work that so many of us have been doing, especially all these volunteers who’ve been out there, whose names most people will never know.

I’ve known them both for a decade. James and I were on the campaign trail together in 2017 and 2018, when he was running his first race for state House in Williamson County. Somebody just sent me a picture of the two of us at an event in Williamson in 2017. These are really fucking good human beings, and they’re also really good at understanding power and how to win it. It is so rare that those two things come together.

O'Rourke speaks during a "Fighting Oligarchy" event in Houston, Texas on Oct. 20, 2026.

Are Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries the right leaders for this moment?

Chuck Schumer absolutely is not. Early 2025, [Elon] Musk is running wild with DOGE, Trump is steamrolling every center of power. They’re all bending the knee—the Ivy Leagues, the big law firms, the media companies. Hakeem marshaled every Democratic vote in the House but one to stop Trump, DOGE, and Musk, and the deal with Schumer was going to do the same. Then, inexplicably, Schumer bent the knee as well. In that moment, it was absolutely over for me.

Schumer deserves so much credit and praise for his work over the decades. But he doesn’t deserve to be majority leader at this major turning point for the country, not when you have James Talarico, Abdul El-Sayed, or Jon Ossoff. We have an embarrassment of talent in the Senate right now, and we should use it. The age when any American cares what the majority leader reads on the Senate floor is over. I don’t even know what his message is, and that says something.

Hakeem Jeffries hasn’t had the chance to lead as Speaker. We were elected in the same class in 2012, and I’m grateful that he stood strong early in the Trump administration. I wish he could communicate more effectively than he has so far. Maybe there’s a scenario where he’s Speaker, but he taps the far better communicators in his caucus, like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, to do more of that work, and he’s focused on getting the legislative results.

Eleven House Democrats missed the vote to impeach [Pete] Hegseth, enough to have changed the outcome. What happened there?

Eleven is a big number. That certainly invites some conspiracy thinking, or, maybe just as bad, the idea that these folks aren’t up to the job. It’s really important that the Democratic leadership in the House address this directly, explain what happened, and take ownership and responsibility for it.

You’ve said Democrats wasted their power in 2009 and 2021, and that next time they should “drive that car like we stole it.” What happens in the first 100 days?

Right off the bat, you have to make our lives better in a way that we can feel. In Texas, that’s not hard, because we are in such a fucking hole. Raise the minimum wage from $7.25. Expand Medicaid when the federal government’s paying 90 cents on the dollar. Stop this voucher thing that is draining tax dollars from local schools, and pay teachers so they don’t have to work a second or third job.

Nationally, you have to do the same. The response to this from many is that Trump has the power of the pen and will veto that. Make him veto that. I don’t like anything about him, but I don’t know that there’s a more successful political operator than Trump. I don’t think there’s someone who reads power better than he does. Maybe there are deals to be had. Maybe you force the veto, and you set up a clear contrast going into 2028. At a minimum, you have to get caught trying.

The huge issues that Democrats have absolutely failed to lead on, we have to lead on now, so that would include immigration and that would include democracy. Immigration was arguably the issue that voters made their decisions on in 2016 and 2024, and if we continue to hope that it’s just going to solve itself, instead of making tough choices and using political capital on this, then it’s going to be our demise in future elections as well. [On democracy], there’s no democracy to restore or save. There is a democracy you can build anew. Getting corporations out of politics; what just passed in Montana is potentially a wonderful precedent from which we could build. Getting a voting rights act passed again. [Pushing] the popular-vote compact; I think we have enough trifectas now. I’m probably in the minority in the Democratic Party, but I’m a big believer in term limits. People give a speech and are like, “We’ve got to overturn Citizens United,” or, “We’ve got to do away with the Electoral College.” That’s a great applause line, but when is that ever going to happen?

O'Rourke spoke in October 2026 as the fight for the Senate came down to the wire.

The big dig on Democrats is: You talked a great game on immigration, then you won the White House; you had the House and the Senate. You didn’t do anything. You talked a great game about voting rights. You had the trifecta, and you didn’t do anything. Now we have the power. We’d better deliver, or watch out.

I’m surprised I’m not hearing more from you about prosecutions and subpoenas. You spent the last two years warning about fascism and calling for accountability.

That’s got to be part of it too. The law is king in this country; no one’s above it, no one’s below it. We’ve allowed the precedent, through the Epstein crimes, that you can be rich enough and well-connected enough to rape and traffic girls and women with complete impunity. I spent a lot of time with young people doing this voter-registration work, and that is probably the number one thing I hear from them for why they don’t vote: This shit doesn’t work. Ghislaine Maxwell [went to jail], but no man who actually did this has gone to prison or even faced trial.

Then there’s the corruption that flows from the president through his family, through his Cabinet officials, through the oligarchs [with whom] he surrounds himself. If we let this stand, much the way that we let stand his crimes against this country on January 6, 2021, that sets the most dangerous precedent. Look at the Roman Republic. It wasn’t Caesar crossing the Rubicon. It was Sulla turning his armies against Rome, and there was never a consequence or accountability for that, so the precedent was set and Caesar picked that up. [Editor’s note: O’Rourke is an avid fan of the podcast The Rest Is History.] There will be a more capable, powerful demagogue than Trump—he or she may be a Democrat; he or she may be a Republican—who will use that precedent unless that door is closed. I know this is an unpopular thing to talk about within our party, because folks want to turn the page. But that keeps biting us in the ass. Everyone who went to prison for [January 6] was pardoned by this president.

But if you spend the next two years investigating him and prices stay high, Democrats are cooked.

That’s exactly right. That’s why I said you’ve got to deliver for people, and they have to feel it immediately. Democrats are responsible for so many good things that are both slow-working and expressed through the tax code, like the child tax credit, and for which they don’t claim credit. Those things have to change.

I was in the Rio Grande Valley after 2020, doing voter registration, knocking on doors, and talking to this guy who voted for Trump. I said, “You had a front-row seat to kids in cages, to family separation, to this cruelty here. Tell me what’s going on.” And he said, “I hate all that stuff, but voting on those issues when I can’t feed my family and I may lose my home is a luxury. I don’t have that luxury.” We have to learn that lesson. You’ve got to make people’s lives better, and if you do that, you build trust and legitimacy: “Okay, these guys are really helping me. They really reflect my values and my interests. And now that they are pursuing these investigations and this accountability, I trust them, and I know that, regardless of the outcome of these investigations, my life is better because they are in power.”

If Trump felt that he or his family were under real legal threat, is there any world in which investigations become a chip to trade, say, for immigration reform? I realize this is very Trumpy thinking, but you are dealing with Trump.

No. Totally understandable, and it’s a recognition of how politics and power typically work. But part of how we got Trump in the first place was that there weren’t consequences for massive failures or crimes committed: these banks that were bailed out after they had driven so many Americans into poverty and homelessness in 2008 and 2009, these wars the Bush administration launched on false pretenses. They lied to us, they lied to the world, and it took the lives of so many Americans, Iraqis, and Afghans. Never any consequence or accountability.

This corruption has been so flagrant, it’s as though Trump and those closest to him were daring America to hold them accountable. Then there’s the open defiance of the law and the Constitution: killing people on fishing boats in the Caribbean, kidnapping a head of state, launching a war and continuing it in violation of the War Powers Act. When you allow these things to stand, they become the precedent. But if there’s accountability, then that becomes the precedent upon which future leaders will be able to act. Trump may feel he’s fighting for his life, that he’s backed into a corner. He may make it harder for Democrats to do the things that they need to do. But I don’t think we can operate in fear of him.

Some Democrats, like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, argue that the corruption and the high prices are the same story. Do you buy that?

Talarico is masterful at saying that: Their corruption is costing you and your family. So many examples in Texas. Billionaires bought off Governor Greg Abbott and persuaded him to pursue a voucher scheme that took public dollars out of local schools and sent them to private schools, decreased the quality of your school, and raised your local property taxes to make up the difference. Abbott, beholden to corporate interests, opened the door [to data centers], and our electricity prices went up and the quality of our water and air was compromised.

O'Rourke says he doesn't know if there’s an office he can imagine running for in 2028 or 2030.

The biggest one was in 2021, when we had the winter storm. In the energy capital of the world, they couldn’t keep the lights on or the power running, and pipeline operators [and others in the energy industry], among the biggest donors to Greg Abbott, began to price-gouge, bankrupting utilities and causing ratepayers to pay sky-high prices. One of the pipeline operator CEOs wrote Abbott a $1 million check at the end of that winter storm, almost as if to say thank you for not prosecuting them. It’s not corruption in an abstract way; it’s corruption that’s costing you. And yes, that corruption should be prosecuted. It’s not enough to just win the election and throw the bums out. If the bums broke the law, then they have to face the consequences.

If Democrats hold this ground, it would seem to open the door for you again. Is there an office you can imagine running for in 2028 or 2030?

I don’t know, and people would have to answer that question for me. That’s what I’ve been trying to do these last four years, just listen to people and figure out where I can be most useful. I’ve tried to remain agnostic.

I had a conversation earlier in the year with somebody who just won in Texas, and they had been one of the people to encourage me to run for governor in 2022—what the fuck was I thinking, running in Joe Biden’s midterm?—and I asked them, “Did you think I had any chance to win?” And they said, “Oh God, no.” But they knew that we needed somebody to galvanize the state, protect our gains in Harris County, and shore up the wins that we’d [earned] in 2018. Somebody had to carry us through that next stage of the relay.

Just so I’m clear, I would not have run if I didn’t think there was a chance we could win in 2022. It was an incredibly tough environment that got tougher and tougher as the race proceeded. But it did a lot of good, and in some small way it was probably helpful toward what happened in 2026.

When [my wife] Amy and I made the decision in 2016 that we had to do something, I went to everyone: Joaquin and Julián Castro, Clay Jenkins, Michael Sorrell, Wendy Davis. I asked each of them, “Will you run? If you do, I will get behind you.” Ultimately, I was like, “Okay, if you guys aren’t going to do it, I am going to do it. I know this is crazy, and I know all of you are better positioned, I’m going to do it.” So if I feel the way that I felt that time, that I’m the right person for this, then, whatever the odds, I’m going to get out there. But if running could hurt us, if there’s somebody better—and that was a conclusion I drew coming into this cycle—then please step up, and I’ll get out of the way and support you as a volunteer.

The next statewide race in Texas is 2030. One thing I’m thinking about right now is 2028, and the fact that the 40 Electoral College votes in Texas are ours to lose. I want to be part of the team getting Texas ready for that nominee to win our state. I’m happy to follow James and Gina’s lead. They’re our leaders now.

Can you imagine working in a Hinojosa administration?

I will do anything for her, and the same for James. It’s just crazy, hearing that.

What about taking Powered by People to Florida? They could use some help, evidently.

These states of the former Confederacy have worked so hard to make it hard for people, especially young people, to vote. We don’t have Election Day data yet, but through early voting, 60% of our voters, overwhelmingly 18 to 29 years old, voted through early voting. That’s about 33 points ahead of the average for that demographic in Texas. I sure wish our party had put resources behind [Angie] Nixon and [David] Jolly in Florida. We could have won those races. What was [the margin] in the governor’s race? 1.3%. Heartbreaking. If I can be useful there, I’m happy to go.

About a year after my 2019 story came out, I texted you that I hoped there were no hard feelings, and you took responsibility for your own errors. It seems like you’ve been through a process since then.

That’s just life, right? I truly feel so incredibly lucky: getting to serve in Congress, getting to run for the US Senate, being considered for the nomination in 2020, being back out on the trail for governor, and then doing this work with Powered by People. When I get depressed is when I don’t have purpose. Then I’m prone to feel sorry for myself or to wonder what if. I’m a big believer that action is the antidote to despair. So I try not to dwell too much on decisions that I’ve made. Should I have talked to Joe Hagan when he was on my front porch in 2019? I’m glad I did. I’m grateful for everything that’s happened, because look at where we are. It’s a beautiful new day in America.

Joe Rogan suggested on his podcast that Talarico should run for president. Any advice for him?

I am the last guy to give Talarico advice, because he’s just been so freaking smart and amazing. Whether he runs for president, whether he serves out his full term in the Senate, he is one of very few leaders in this country who have met the moment. I trust him to make the best decisions for, first and foremost, the country, for Texas, and then for himself.

Who excites you in the 2028 field? You’ve got Gavin Newsom on the center-left, and AOC and Ro Khanna presenting themselves as heirs to Bernie Sanders.

We could have added another 15 people to that list. There was a lot of gnashing of teeth two years ago: We don’t have a national leader; what is Democrats’ message? That was liberating for all of these candidates, and you’re going to have so many diverse perspectives in 2028. What you did these last 10 years is going to be an important consideration. Gavin Newsom was one of the first national Democrats to recognize what Trump was trying to do by redrawing these congressional maps, starting in Texas, and I was really impressed with how quickly he moved and how strong he was on offense. Pete Buttigieg has been nonstop traveling the country supporting candidates. In the wake of 2024, with this sense of total defeat, a few people just got out there, and AOC was one of them. I like the folks who never stop fighting, who are true to themselves and not susceptible to the prevailing winds. Bernie Sanders is probably the best example of that.

Ro Khanna and I, when we were in Congress together, authored the No PAC Act. We asked our legislative staffs, “Can you find out who last authored a bill like this so we can amend it and improve it and make it our own?” There was no bill. Nobody had ever done that. He’s been so consistently focused on democracy. Greg Casar, he’s from Texas. He’s the chair of the [Congressional] Progressive Caucus and also has been crisscrossing the country. There are a lot of good people out there.

O'Rourke speaks at a campaign rally at the University of Houston on October 20, 2026.

After 2016 and 2024, a lot of women I know concluded that this country won’t elect a woman president. Can a woman be elected?

Absolutely. Gina Hinojosa—here in Texas, the conventional wisdom was that if a Democrat ever wins, it’s got to be a straight white man who fits the following characteristics. And here you have the first Latina from the border. It’s fucking awesome. It’s going to sound corny, but I really believe in this country, and that faith was vindicated last Tuesday. It wasn’t the country being like, “Go Democrats!” It was the country saying, “We can do better, and we’re going to take a chance on folks who may not fit the profile.” I think that holds true for the country in 2028.

You just turned 54. If you never ran again, would you be okay with that?

I think about it sometimes. Is the prize the office—junior senator from the state of Texas, president of the United States of America? Or is the prize a much better world for my kids and this country? I always want that to be the answer, and it is. I just fucking won the lottery in life. Our kids are absolutely thriving; my oldest is about to be 20, middle kid is 18, my youngest just turned 16. I’ve been lucky with Amy and living in El Paso, getting to do this fulfilling work.

But just to be clear: Would I love to serve in office again at some point? Absolutely. The El Paso City Council may have been my most fulfilling time in politics. Loved being in Congress—what a high honor. But if it doesn’t happen, I’m more than okay. I’m the luckiest guy out there. I’m good, no matter what happens.

The Gen-Z comedy, Adults, dropped its sophomore season on FX and Hulu as part of the 2026 TV Schedule back in August, and since then fans have been loudly campaigning for another season. After months of waiting, the series was officially renewed for a Season 3, much to the delight of the fans.

The cast took to Instagram to share the news with their devoted viewers, which included the reveal that the third season will include 16 original episodes, nearly double the length of the first two seasons. As a massive fan of the show and a firm believer that sitcoms need more episodes, I’m thrilled at the news! In fact, I’m so excited I’ve already compiled a list of things I absolutely need the extended season to feature.

Holiday episodes used to be a sitcom staple, but as television seasons started getting shorter and shorter, these episodes started to disappear. I had accepted the fact that I would never get to see my favorite characters celebrate birthdays or the holiday season, but now that might not be the case.

With a 16-episode season comes space for these beloved one-off episodes. Just think of all the hijinks that could ensue from the Adults gang trying to celebrate the holidays. We’ve already seen them struggle to host a sophisticated dinner party in the first season. Now imagine it’s the holiday season and Paul Baker’s family decides to make the trek to New York to spend Christmas with their son and his new husband after his sister lets it slip that he’s married. The shenanigans would be hilarious!

Over the course of the first two seasons, Adults has found time to include some fun guest stars like actor Charlie Cox, actress/model Julia Fox, and sitcom royalty Raven-Symoné. I’m sure the tradition will continue in Season 3, and I have some ideas on whom the creators should reach out to.

Since Adults films in Canada, it makes total sense that the Gen-Z show should approach a breakout Gen-Z actor who also appears on a hit Canadian-produced show. Yes, I’m talking about Heated Rivalry’s Hudson Williams. Williams could play himself and act as an old friend from Paul Baker’s childhood, since he canonically grew up in Canada and has a history of befriending famous people without realizing it.

Another obvious, albeit more difficult to get, choice would be New York’s Mayor Zohran Mamdani. I can totally see Issa finding a way to reach out to the Mayor about some minor inconvenience affecting her city that no one else cares about.

Season 2 ended on a major high note with Paul Baker and Anton finally getting together, but it also shocked fans with a plot twist in the final moments that featured Billie and Samir hooking up. Don’t get me wrong, I can’t wait to see Paul Baker and Anton enter their “relationship era,” but I’m also excited to see what shenanigans Billie and Samir get into now that they’ve crossed such a huge line in their friendship.

On one hand, I’d love Billie and Samir to channel the relationship between Chandler and Monica from Friends and try to keep their hookup and subsequent relationship a secret from the rest of the house. It would be difficult considering how close they all are, but definitely worth it to keep it away from everyone meddling.

However, I could also see them trying to act as if their hookup was casual and something they can continue doing without catching feelings. Neither Billie nor Samir do anything without their whole heart involved, so this would be a recipe for disaster but also great for laughs.

Season 3 has so much room for fun and hijinks with its longer episode order, and I can’t wait to see what the writers come up with. While it’ll be a while before the new season is out, fans can stream the first two seasons with a Hulu subscription now.

#3545. Who Plays Thrain In The Lord Of The Rings: The Rings Of Power Season 3

You shall not pass! This article contains minor spoilers for "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" Season 3, Episodes 1-4.

After two years, "The Rings of Power" is back and as sprawling as ever. In fact, it may be even more so than it already was. Seasons 1 and 2 of the Prime Video series took us all over the map (quite literally, thanks to all those nifty map transitions), from the island kingdom of Númenor far in the West to the volcanic wastes of Mordor in the East. Season 3 expands the borders of Middle-earth even further, taking us to new locations and introducing multiple new characters to keep track of — some of whom seem more trustworthy than others.

Somewhere in the middle of all this is the Dwarf prince known as Thráin, the elder brother of King Durin (Owain Arthur) and a figure referenced with no small amount of suspicion towards the end of Season 2. As viewers quickly find out upon returning to Khazad-dûm, there is a fair bit of internal strife going on within the underground city, and Thráin's arrival only exacerbates the tension in the air. While this is actually an original character created solely for the show, he still requires quite a lot of nuance and complexity to fully bring him to life.

So, who better to do so than character actor Eddie Marsan? Yes, it might be incredibly difficult to tell who's actually playing the stoutly Dwarf underneath that mountain of prosthetics, makeup, and that bushy mane of flaming red hair. But, if you take notice of those piercing eyes and distinctive voice, you just might be able to recognize the talents of a performer you've definitely seen before.

As it turns out, maybe there are some Dwarves that you can only trust as far as you can toss them (with respect to Gimli). While watching Thrain do his mischievous thing throughout the early episodes of "The Rings of Power" this season, you'll likely find yourself wondering what else you've seen Eddie Marsan appear in before. In a quirk of scheduling, his most recent high-profile role was actually in this year's "Clayface," where he portrayed Frank Fitzpatrick. As the shady talent manager to Matt Hagen (Tom Rhys Harries), this is a perfect example of the kind of slippery character Marsan plays so well. Before that, he popped up in three episodes of the Netflix series "Heartstopper" and had supporting roles in three of director Guy Ritchie's most recent movies: "Operation Fortune: Ruse de Guerre," "Wrath of Man," and "The Gentlemen."

You'd have to go back a little further to pinpoint what might be his most well-known role of all, however. He was cast in the 2009 "Sherlock Holmes" film as the famous Inspector Lestrade, a role he would then reprise in the 2011 sequel "A Game of Shadows" (yes, both of which were also directed by Ritchie). Having worked regularly since the 1990s, the English actor can be seen in a prolific amount of titles over the decades. Some notable examples include Martin Scorsese's "Gangs of New York," the Wachowski Sisters' "V for Vendetta," "Mission: Impossible III," "Miami Vice," "The World's End," "Deadpool 2," and far too many more to name.

In short, Marsan is an acting veteran who knew exactly how to breathe life into a newly-arriving figure like Thráin.

New episodes of "The Rings of Power" Season 3 premiere on Prime Video every Wednesday.

#3544. DMZ key and locations in Modern Warfare 4

There are loads of DMZ keys in Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4. Used to open both locked containers and locked doors, keys are your fast-track to getting your hands on some of the best loot the extraction mode has to offer. However, when you receive a key, you're only given a brief description of where to use it, so we're going to outline where you can use every key the game has to offer.

Here are all the keys we've found in Modern Warfare 4's DMZ mode and where to use them, listed in alphabetical order by the name of the key.

Note that this guide is a work-in-progress, so if the key you're looking for isn't listed here, check back soon.

Update (Nov. 12): We've added where to use the Commandant Office key, Field Depot key, and Weapons Mod Workshop key.

The blackmarket weapons locker key can be used in two different locations in Hajin. Look for the blackmarket weapons store, identifiable by its iron wrought gates and red advert on the roof. One of them is in southern Deadtown, while the other is in eastern Hanrin Village. Go to the basement to find two lockers at each location, so if you have a second blackmarket weapons locker key, it's worth bringing with you.

Along with finding it as loot in Hajin, the coin mining den key can also be obtained by completing the "Operating Shopping Hacks" story mission. It opens a door on the third floor of an otherwise unassuming building directly north of the Netshin Tech Complex and east of the gas station found to the west of the NuriGO Mall. Inside, you'll find a number of lootable containers, including plenty of server racks, which are handy for electronic sensors.

The Chang-san Air Base is one of the most fortified areas in all of Hajin, which means you're going to have a constant swarm of enemies on you. To use the commandant office key, head to the eastern side of the second floor of the main building in the air base, and you'll find the locked door here.

Completing the "Operation Silent Ledger" story mission will net you the counting room vault key, but to use it, you'll need to go back into the casino. Our dedicated guide explains exactly where to go, but briefly, you'll want to take an immediate right-hand turn as you enter through the main entrance then go through the brown door in the following corridor. You'll find a bunch of safes, loose cash, and containers inside.

The executive arms auction key can be used inside the DBN Headquarters building, which is the tallest skyscraper inside The Grid. If you choose the "Operation Shopping Hacks" mission, you'll spawn nearby. This place is highly fortified, so there are loads of enemies around, and to find the locked room, you'll need to use the various elevators and ziplines dotted around to go to the very top floor (but not the roof). Here, you'll find the locked door pictured above.

Another door inside the Chang-San Air Base, this room is a little easier to get to. It's on the ground floor in the building immediately on the right-hand side of the main entrance, which also contains ammo and armor caches. It's on the eastern side of the building, in a corridor with lots of shelving units.

The Gangbyeong apartment A key can be used on an apartment block at the northeastern end of Hajin River Heights. The building is next to the compound, and is the one that is perpendicular to the river to the south. If you need to get inside Gangbyeon apartment A without the key, then you can descend into the parking lot below and search for the staircase that will take you up inside the apartment block.

The key for Gangbyeon apartment B can usually be found inside Gangbyeon apartment A, which is quite handy. I found it on top of a table in one of the apartments. Gangbyeon apartment B is the building right next to apartment A, running parallel to the river. The key can be used to get inside either the first floor, the basement, or the roof, and if you have the militia arms depot key, you'll need to get inside apartment B first. Apartment B has several apartments to explore, full of decent loot.

Southeast of Imjin Farmland is where you'll find the mill stronghold, and in the very center of this point of interest is a tower. Enter via the door at the bottom to find a parkour section, where you must clamber from ledge to ledge in order to ascend. At the very top are two doors next to each other, both of which require Gorani's scout overlook key.

Much like the blackmarket weapons locker key, there are two locations for the gun store weapons locker key, and each location has multiple lockers inside. The gun stores can be found in western Cheongun Village and northern Songdo Wharf. Each of them has an arched red brick roof and a sign above the entrance depicting a cartoon character. In the basement, you'll find multiple lockers that the keys can be used on.

The Hanex guard station key is used inside the bank within The Grid, which is the slightly smaller building next to the DBN Headquarters, which is the tallest building there. Go inside and take a zipline to the roof, then go down one floor to find the bank's vault. The locked door inside this room, pictured above, is where you can use the Hanex guard station key.

At the Imjin Mill, southeast of Imjin Farmland, there's a rectangular building on the other side of the barbed wire fence to the road. On the second floor of this building, there's a locked door leading to the Hoesik supply room.

Inside the Imjin Mill, southeast of Imjin Farmland, the foreman's office can be found on the second floor. It's right next to the short walkway with a window that you can jump through if you climb up the crates, and is marked with a sign that says "office" next to the wooden door.

The militia arms depot is located inside Gangbyeon apartment B, which is northeast of Hajin River Heights. Once you've got the key for apartment B, which can usually be found inside apartment A (details on those keys above, including how to get into apartment A without a key), you'll find the locked door for the militia arms depot on the first floor. Inside is an apartment with loads of locked containers and high-tier loot.

You'll receive the Mirae electrical room key upon completing "Operation Critical Extraction," which is the story mission where you must escort a high-value target out of the general hospital. This key unlocks a room in the underground parking lot for the hospital, which can be found by going to the northwestern corner. Enter through a door at the back and follow the signs for parking, which will lead you to a parking lot with purple walls. At the back is a room with iron bars over the windows and "danger" above the door, which can be unlocked with the key.

The police station armory key is one of the most common keys in DMZ, as it opens armories in all five police stations in Hajin. The map above shows all the locations. In each police station, the armory can be found in the basement, where you'll find weapon crates and other locked containers.

In Deadtown, the re-education center is the most notable landmark, as it's the most central building and it has a sprawling underground section. On its south side, you'll see it has a small building attached. The door for this is on the first floor, aka ground level, near the stairs leading down into the basement.

The re-education center annex in Deadtown has a big underground section that connects it with the building to the northwest, and in the center is a long corridor with a series of blue doors. The central one can be opened with the underground propaganda store room key, and while there isn't much to loot in here, you can pull a lever to unlock another locked door nearby.

Another locked door inside the Chang-San Air Base, you can find the weapons mod workshop on the second floor of a building northwest of the main stronghold. The room is on the northern side of the building, next to a cork board and red sign on a white wall, at the top of a staircase.

We're updating this guide with more keys as we find them, so check back soon.

Grey’s Anatomy is currently in its 23rd season on the 2026 TV schedule, which is still hard to comprehend. Given that the fans are still tuning in, though, no matter what that hospital has been through, it makes sense. While Ellen Pompeo loves Grey’s Anatomy fans, who have been keeping the show on the air for over 20 years, there is just one thing that annoys her. And I can’t say I blame her.

Pompeo starred in Grey’s Anatomy as the titular Dr. Meredith Grey since the very beginning, before ultimately departing as a series regular midway through Season 19. She’s remained on as narrator and executive producer, frequently returning to the halls of Grey Sloan Memorial in a guest capacity. Having been a staple on television for over 20 years, you’d imagine that Pompeo runs into a lot of fans. Unfortunately, it’s not always the greatest experience. The actress told Magic Radio that even though she loves the fans, she’s annoyed by one thing that would honestly annoy me, too:

To be honest, I’m so grateful for the show and so grateful for the fans, and I love them. But to be honest, when people call me Meredith, I do get a little bit annoyed. So I do get a little annoyed with that. I love that you love the show, but just call me by my right name. And everybody’s so nice, and they just say, you know, ‘I love you so much.’ And so, how really can I be upset at that?

I get why people would call celebrities by their characters’ names. You see them as their characters on television or in movies, and in the moment, you spot them and call them by their signature role. That being said, fans should probably be saying the celebrity’s name rather than their character’s, and I am someone who is a stickler for that. I would definitely find that annoying, because you’re meeting the actual person, not the fictional character. They’re two different people.

For a show like Grey’s Anatomy that has been on for over two decades, I can get why it’s especially annoying as people have had 20 years to Meredith Grey’s actual name. That being said, Pompeo doesn’t seem to have any ill will towards the loyal Grey’s Anatomy fans. Sure, she’s annoyed when they don’t call her by her name, but she still loves them anyway. Folks may just want to be a bit more aware of what they say when they meet Pompeo or any other celebrity and make sure you’re getting the name right.

The actress is not on Grey’s Anatomy as much anymore, but whenever she does return to the medical drama, you never know what to expect. It’s always hard to see a Grey’s Anatomy star leave the series, but in Pompeo’s case, she’s simply not a series regular anymore, but is still a recurring actor. Of course, you can’t have Grey’s Anatomy without the Dr. Meredith Grey, so it’s not like the show could wipe the slate completely clean.

As of now, it’s hard to tell how long Grey’s Anatomy will remain on the air, but there doesn’t seem to be any end in sight. Meaning fans will have plenty of time to practice their hellos to Pompeo if they ever meet her so that they can get the name right. If anything, there are 23 seasons of Grey’s Anatomy reminding you who is starring in the series, so that’s a great place to start, and they’re all streaming with a Hulu subscription.

Passionate writer. Obsessed with anything and everything entertainment, specifically movies and television. Can get easily attached to fictional characters.

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. A price drop always stands out more when the product in question already has a reputation for delivering above its size, and that’s the case with the Bose SoundLink Plus. It hasn’t been on the market for long, but it’s already earned strong reviews—CNET labeled it “the Goldilocks of Bose Bluetooth speakers.” And right now, ahead of Black Friday, it’s down to $179 from $269, which price trackers show is the lowest it’s ever been.

Bose positions it right in the middle of the SoundLink lineup, and you feel that balance in how it’s built. It’s compact enough to clip onto a backpack using its built-in nylon strap, and tough enough to handle getting knocked around, and sealed against dust and full water submersion with an IP67 rating. Battery life can last up to 20 hours, depending on the volume, which is sufficient for full-day outings. On the connectivity side, there’s Bluetooth 5.4 with AAC and AptX Adaptive support, as well as the ability to keep two devices paired for smoother switching. What you don’t get is a microphone, an aux port, or any voice assistant support, which is worth considering if you prefer wired options or use speakers for calls.

As for its sound profile, it leans into mid- and high-bass, which gives electronic and pop tracks a lively pulse, though at higher volumes, you may notice some compression (which is common in speakers this size). It also doesn’t reach into true low-bass territory, so anyone who wants thumping sub-bass may not get it here, but the punch it does deliver feels clean for its size, notes this PCMag review. And while you won't get the width and separation of a stereo mix since the SoundLink Plus plays audio in mono, its directivity is good—meaning its sound remains clear from different listening positions, so you don't have to sit directly in front of it to get a good experience.

#3540. How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Dominated the Box Office: GKIDS Chief on IMAX’s Impact and the Growing Market for Foreign-Language Movies

“Godzilla Minus Zero” almost pulled of a Godzilla-times-three on its opening weekend, earning $31.6 million in North America to nearly triple the domestic debut of its 2023 predecessor “Godzilla Minus One.” With that Godzilla math, it destroyed the record for the biggest North American debut for a live-action foreign language film.

It was a crowning moment for the speciality distributor GKIDS. Founded in 2008, the label primarily built itself as a distributor of foreign language animated features, most notably with its acquisition of the North American distribution rights to the Studio Ghibli library. As a day-one employee of GKIDS, and its president since 2017, Dave Jesteadt has helped expand the stateside audience for subtitled features. After a 2025 acquisition by Toho, the Japanese film industry giant behind “Godzilla,” the reach of GKIDS is wider than ever with “Minus Zero,” which drew a box office debut that some studio tentpoles this year would envy. Related Stories Sandra Wollner’s ‘Everytime’ Is a Stunning Film About Grief Like You’ve Never Seen Before Democrats Won. When Do Hollywood Crews Get Back to Work?

“Anecdotally, so many people I know are like, ‘I took my dad this movie and he doesn’t go to any subtitle movies,'” Jesteadt told IndieWire. “Godzilla brings us together. If we’re spreading the gospel of foreign cinema, and Godzilla is a vehicle to get people to engage with great films and deep themes, then I’m all for it.”

After a flashy premiere at the New York Film Festival and a historic cume from IMAX and other premium large-format auditoriums, Jesteadt digs into how GKIDS helped “Minus Zero” come to America.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

IndieWire: “Godzilla Minus One” was seen as a breakout success in 2023, with $57 million in North America. What lessons did GKIDS take away from Toho‘s release of “Minus One” in building toward this big opening for “Minus Zero”?

Dave Jesteadt: GKIDS joined the Toho Group in October 2024, but our story of working together on this began before that, back in 2023. GKIDS had “The Boy and the Heron” from Hayao Miyazaki and Studio Ghibli in theaters just a week after “Godzilla Minus One” opened, which was being handled by Toho’s L.A. office at the time. We got to know that team because we had these two films in theaters, sort of competing for similar audience profiles.

In terms of lessons that both sides took, it’s that you can really drive conversation with theaters as a source of celebration and community. When we joined the Toho Group, we took in the team that worked on “Minus One.” We re-released “Shin Godzilla” in 2025 as a test for bringing modern Japanese “Godzilla” films to theaters. Then the planning for “Minus Zero” really began in terms of how we could build and improve on the audience that “Minus One” already found.

Did “Minus Zero” get a bigger marketing spend stateside? How did you consider which people to reach to expand the audience for a Japanese “Godzilla” film?

I can’t give a specific number, but I’d say that we’re very efficient and very mindful of how we can reach the audience in the most direct way possible. For this film, we have the great benefit of our colleagues at Toho International owning and operating Godzilla.com, overseeing merchandise licensing. They have direct communication with the “Godzilla” fan as they exist in America.

But the other goal is to reach, as “Minus One” did, an audience that hadn’t engaged in Japanese “Godzilla” films. We also balanced reaching that core “Godzilla” fan and making sure that they turn out with this desire to continue the story from “Minus One,” reminding people that these films from director Takashi Yamazaki really speak to broader feelings today. They have prestigious bona fides through playing film festivals and great critical reviews. We’re leading with the quality of the film, making people feel that this is a very safe choice — not just if you like spectacle, but that this is going to be one of the best films of the year.

The New York Film Festival premiere played as a flex, especially after a stretch where Hollywood would premiere summer blockbusters at Cannes, draw mediocre reviews, and then have to weather weeks of bad buzz for their expensive tentpoles. With the NYFF premiere, “Minus Zero” was positioned as a prestige object. Is that the aura you were trying to cultivate around it?

I think so. Godzilla has been one of the most famous characters in the world. There’s a big audience that you can potentially address. But the “Minus” franchise takes it into more realistic, human-centered stories. That differentiates it. It is a risk to go to a film festival; I think that has been pretty well-argued. It is a risk anytime you want to share something with the world early before you open, especially when you have such high hopes about how it’s going to go. On the other hand, this was a really important way to demonstrate confidence.

“Minus Zero” opened in more than 3,200 theaters, roughly 1,000 more theaters than “Minus One.” How much did you expand its presence in premium large-format auditoriums?

“Minus Zero” was the first Japanese production filmed for IMAX. That was a central part of the very first announcement and it was a defining part of the marketing campaign. IMAX mentioned it was the highest-indexed opening gross on IMAX screens for an opening weekend in the U.S. We had Godzilla Day on November 3, with IMAX early access screenings globally. So, PLFs definitely played a big presence: Imax, 4DX, Dbox, and others. That’s very unusual for a subtitled foreign film.

It speaks to the expectations for high quality that audiences brought. The PLF story is a way to reinforce production quality. Everyone is saying, “You have to see it in the biggest screen possible with the best sound.” I’ve seen many, many beautiful foreign films. They often end up playing circuits to audiences that are very passionate, but don’t have access to those kind of screens. So it’s a privilege to be able to play a film on the kind of screen that’s typically reserved for the biggest mainstream titles.

How long are you staying in IMAX and PLFs?

It depends on the market. We’re definitely here for the rest of this week. But as “The Odyssey” and other titles have demonstrated, there’s such draw to these moments. It can even create this quest to see something in multiple formats. But as we head into the Thanksgiving frame, the Hollywood competition is obviously huge. We’re realistic about that, even while we’re trying to encourage people to see it as soon and as often as they can.

The reported statistic that more than 70 percent of grosses came from PLFs seems a bit of a double-edged sword to me. It speaks to a high regard for the film among consumers, but it also might indicate that it has a specialized audience that may only want to see the movie in a premium format. Is that a consideration GKIDS takes in, particularly when other titles are taking those auditoriums in the coming weeks?

Obviously, PLFs are time-sensitive. It’s not just about performance, but also about new titles coming in. We’re up against the biggest studios in the world. I’m obviously thrilled that we were able to get so many and I’m thrilled that people saw it that way. I also encourage everyone to just see it in regular theaters too. The way that it was mastered and the way that director Yamazaki made the film is so you won’t have a bad experience in any house watching it. But with any of these core fandoms, there’s a lot of interest in seeing something “the right way.” I’m happy for that, but then the hope is they tell their friends and we continue the growth from there.

You’ve been with GKIDS since its inception and have played a major part in growing the American audience for foreign language cinema. What do you think has changed in the marketplace that has allowed a Japanese “Godzilla” film to now find a much broader audience in the West than it could find before?

There’s no doubt that the quality of the films really helps. “Minus One” was a fantastic film. It won the Oscar for visual effects and became an audience darling. But really, the thing that’s changed the most is that younger generations are much more open to subtitled and foreign cinema than they would have been 10 or 20 years ago. We’ve entered an age of opportunity where what can constitute a hit film is really broadening. That gives me a lot of optimism compared to negative stories about the overall economics of the industry. GKIDS has been bringing subtitled animated movies and anime to audiences for almost 20 years and seeing that audience grow naturally. At first, dubs were essential; now, they’re not.

Though GKIDS isn’t producing these films, I’m curious if, as a distributor, you think that Japanese productions like “Minus Zero” are now being developed and produced with more of a global audience in mind.

The films are still intrinsically Japanese and are basically impossible to separate from the cultural tradition of “Godzilla” in Japan, as well as the overall Japanese film industry. On the other hand, there’s no doubt that the property has the ability to reach a global audience. The popularity with the “Minus” series is really a focus on quality, and how its storytelling is rooted in a time and a place that feels authentically Japanese. Although it deals with a post-war moment in Japanese history, it is incredibly contemporary in terms of the thoughts and preoccupations of a global audience.

So I don’t think there’s necessarily a change in focus. I would say that the audience and the director are in a much more direct conversation. On social media now, everything is auto-translated. You can see real-time active conversation between Japanese fans and viewers commenting about the film with American or Spanish or European audience. Everyone is able to share their thoughts or opinions about some of these themes in a way that brings local perspective to the table. By creating something that feel like it’s created for a specific audience, ironically, you end up making it feel more universal, just because it feels more lived in.

Do you think we are headed to a world where a Japanese “Godzilla” film can outgross a Western “Godzilla” film in North America?

I don’t really think about that. I’m very competitive against a lot of people, but the “Godzilla” franchise has benefited from having a lot of flavors to it. By building that big tent, it ends up being a character that has endured.

“Godzilla Minus Zero” is now in theaters.

#3539. 5 Years Ago Today: Andrew Garfield Gave An Oscar-Worthy Performance In A Netflix Movie

There are, in my estimation, many actors who should have Oscars who don't. Amanda Seyfried should have one (and might be eligible for one in 2027 thanks to one of 2026's most confounding films). Amy Adams' various near-misses have led her to stumble headfirst into awful Oscar bait projects like "Hillbilly Elegy." John Goodman has never even been nominated. When it comes to the best actors who don't have Academy Awards, the list is long ... and Andrew Garfield is definitely on it.

Garfield, who rose to prominence in projects like "Doctor Who" and "Lions for Lambs" before earning international fame and acclaim for his pivotal role in "The Social Network," is genuinely one of the most talented performers of his generation. You could point to any number of his projects and make a case, but I'm going to say that Garfield should have an Oscar for playing "Rent" writer Jonathan Larson in the 2021 movie musical "Tick... Tick... Boom!" (for which he did earn a Best Actor nomination).

Even if you're not a reformed musical theater kid like me, you know about "Rent" — but generally, we need to talk about "Tick... Tick... Boom!" way more. Before "Rent," Larson — who died at the age of 35 in 1996 after suffering from an aortic dissection — penned the mostly-autobiographical "Tick... Tick... Boom!" about his struggles to make it in musical theater, coming on the heels of his failed futuristic musical "Superbia." Initially written as a solo show performed just by Larson on piano, the musical got a full-length treatment thanks to David Auburn after Larson's tragic passing, and "Hamilton" and "In the Heights" scribe Lin-Manuel Miranda adapted it into a film that released on November 12, 2021. Garfield's performance as Larson is electrifying, pitch-perfect, and gripping, and he should have an Oscar for it.

The "plot" of "Tick... Tick... Boom!" is relatively simple — Andrew Garfield plays Jonathan Larson as he works days at the Moondance Diner and spends his free time perfecting that aforementioned musical "Superbia" for an upcoming workshop. Along the way, he grapples with the idea of leaving the arts behind for a more lucrative and stable career — like his best friend Michael (Robin de Jesús), who works for an ad agency — while also stressing about turning 30 years old.

If you're familiar with "Rent," you may not be surprised to learn that the HIV-AIDS crisis plays a role; his friend Freddy (Ben Levi Ross) is HIV-positive, and it's eventually revealed that Michael is as well. As Jonathan tries to manage his personal and professional lives, he crosses paths with his idol Stephen Sondheim (played by Bradley Whitford, though the real Sondheim did lend his voice to an answering machine message before he passed away in 2021) and frets about whether or not "Superbia" has any chance of success.

Usually, the gift of hindsight doesn't really serve an actor, but I think knowing that Larson passed away before "Rent" won a Pulitzer Prize (and Tonys) gives Garfield a great perspective here. His Jonathan is frenetic, a live wire, and lives his life to the fullest; Garfield's passionate performance throughout the film paints a picture of a man who's running out of time, and even though that's obviously expressed through the character's anxieties about turning 30, it's also a poignant representation of an artist whose life was cut tragically short ... and in numbers like "Why," "30/90," and "Louder than Words," Garfield pays perfect homage to Larson's life and legacy.

I think I've been pretty clear about the fact that Andrew Garfield should have an Oscar for "Tick... Tick... Boom!" He should, however, have won his second Oscar for that movie — because Garfield should have an Academy Award for best supporting actor for playing Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin in "The Social Network."

Under careful direction from David Fincher and working with one of Aaron Sorkin's all-time best scripts — which he ultimately betrayed with his dog-brained sequel "The Social Reckoning" — Garfield is extraordinary as Eduardo, best friend to Jesse Eisenberg's Mark Zuckerberg who provides money and support during the initial founding of Facebook. In one timeline, we see Mark and Eduardo as Harvard University students trying to get their social media platform off the ground; in another, we see Eduardo suing Mark after Mark cruelly cuts Eduardo out of the company and brings his shares down drastically on the advice of new partner Sean Parker (a ridiculously well-cast Justin Timberlake).

Garfield should probably have several awards just for the way he delivers the line "Sorry, my Prada's at the cleaners, along with my hoodie and my f***-you flip flops" to Eisenberg's Mark after he discovers his betrayal ... but throughout the entire film, he's uniformly excellent as a man whose closest friend is also the most destructive force in his life. Garfield needs to be taken more seriously as an actor across the board, and an Oscar nomination for "Tick... Tick... Boom!" is a good start. In my opinion, though? He should be swimming in a pool full of trophies every day when he wakes up ... and he should have Oscars for "The Social Network" and "Tick... Tick... Boom!" Because the musical is a Netflix original, you can screen it there and see for yourself.

#3538. How to farm rupees in Zelda Ocarina of Time

Rupee farming in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake looks a bit different than you might be used to if you played the N64 original or any of its later ports. The most common method in older versions of the game — getting some red rupees above the Castle Town drawbridge — doesn't work anymore. However, there are several other quick and straightforward ways to fill your wallet, whatever size it is.

Below, we break down the best ways to farm rupees in Ocarina of Time remake.

Early in the game, your best bet for rupee farming is scooping up bugs in empty bottles and selling them to the Buyer, which is the man in Hyrule Castle Town who's fanatical about creatures in bottles. He's sitting on the ground across from the Shooting Gallery and slapping the ground with his palms. He'll pay 20 rupees per beetle.

Bugs live under rocks and bushes in various parts of Hyrule, but when you're playing as young Link in the past, the best location to get a bunch of bugs is this spot in northeastern Hyrule Field, near Kakariko Village. You'll notice a Song of Storms bloom, but you can ignore that for now, since the Song of Storms is something you'll only learn in the future. (It leads to a cave with a rupee reward, but it's also full of ReDeads — not a great place for kids!)

Bugs live in the plants and shrubs that surround the Song of Storms plant. Destroy the plants with your sword, scoop up as many bugs as you have empty bottles to fill, and trot back to Hyrule Castle Town to sell them. Repeat the process as often as you want. It's a bit slow, given young Link has to travel on foot, but at least Hyrule Castle Town isn't too far away.

You can keep using this method as adult Link. The Buyer is just in Kakariko Village instead of Hyrule Castle Town.

This method of rupee farming is the most lucrative, but it takes some setting up before you can do it. In the adult Link timeline, the Buyer relocates to Kakariko Village with the rest of Hyrule Castle Town's survivors. He still pays for bugs and fish, but after you visit the Ice Cavern, he'll also buy blue fire off you for 40 rupees apiece.

Make sure you have Farore's Wind from the Great Fairy Fountain in Zora Domain, and clear the Forest, Fire, and Water Temples. Then, unlock the Shadow Temple and learn the Nocturne of Shadow from Sheik so you can fast travel back to Kakariko Village at any point.

With that done, head off to the Ice Cavern, and set a Farore's Wind warp point in one of the rooms with blue fire. Now you can fill all five empty bottles, play Nocturne of Shadow to go back to Kakariko Village, sell them to the Buyer, return to the Ice Cavern using Farore's Wind, and repeat the process until your wallet's full to bursting.

This one's also exclusive to adult Link. No shops are left in the Hyrule Castle Town of the future, but there is a new vendor right at the entrance. They do only one thing: buy Poes. Poes are the spirits that attack you at night in Hyrule Field or any time of day in the Kakariko Graveyard. They leave behind a spirit ball when you defeat them, and if you bottle it up, you can sell it to the Poe Collector for 15 rupees. The graveyard has a seemingly endless supply of them, too.

This method is quicker if you have Epona and learned the Prelude of Light from Sheik after clearing the Forest Temple.

Defeating Skull Kids is one of the more challenging rupee farming methods, but it's also the most lucrative. Defeated Skull Kids drop a gold rupee worth 200 rupees. (It's basically the same as the giant orange rupee from the original game, just not giant. And not orange.) They don't seem to respawn following an in-game timer like other enemies, based on our testing. It appears Skull Kid respawns are tied to real-world time, possibly once per day, though we haven't been able to 100% confirm that yet.

Skull Kids only show up as adversaries when you're in the Lost Woods as adult Link, and they attack as soon as you approach. Skull Kids keep their distance and fire darts at Link, and they're immune to Deku nuts. The easiest way to land a hit is by using the Biggoron Sword thanks to its extended reach. If you take too long to defeat a Skull Kid, they'll vanish and then reappear the next time you enter the Lost Woods.

The quickest way to find Skull Kids is by taking a right as soon as you enter the Lost Woods. You'll find two of them there.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is a little bit different than the original game, so if you need guides to help you through, we don’t blame you. We have walkthroughs for all the dungeons, from the Deku Tree to Ganondorf's Castle. We also have guides for the sillier, in-between parts of the game, like when you have to find Richard (the dog) or Cuccos.

For those going for 100% completion, we also have guides on where to find every Piece of Heart, every Gold Skulltula token, and where to plant every Magic Bean.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3537. Eight 'Winter Arc' Rules That Will Actually Deliver Results

There are a lot of terrible social media trends out there aimed at self-improvement, yet even though everybody has been making fun of the "Winter Arc" craze, I actually think it’s a good one. During your Winter Arc, you promise yourself you’ll stick to your fitness and self-care routines during (and despite) the end-of-year chaos. It's a good goal, with one caveat: Make sure you choose rules that will actually improve your life and deliver results.

Think of the “arc” in the sense of a “story arc.” The Winter Arc is a self-improvement journey that unfolds over the last few months of the calendar year. The most hardcore #gymtok-ers will tell you the Winter Arc officially begins on Oct. 1, but others start in early November, or whenever they get around to it. The "when" isn't critical, though—whenever you read this is a fine time to start. The close of the Winter Arc is fixed, however: It ends Jan. 1, just as everybody who is less dedicated than you is waking from their holiday food comas and resolving to get in shape.

You get to choose your own terms for your Winter Arc. The general vibe is one of locking in, committing to your goals, and actually doing the things you’re always saying you’ll do. TikToker @carlyupgraded has said that her own mental image of someone nailing their Winter Arc is “hood up, headphones on, getting ready to go for a run in the rain at 5 a.m.”

It turns out I’ve accidentally been Winter-Arc-ing for years; I just didn’t know it had a catchy name. Why save your gym routine for New Year’s when you’ll have the place to yourself all December? We’re even gifted with an extra hour in the mornings to fill with something productive.

I really love the mindset shift involved. Commonly, people are active in the summer (great time for outdoor fun), may or may not stick with their routines in the fall, and let everything fall apart as the holidays approach. Who has time to go to the gym when you’re planning Thanksgiving, attending holiday parties, studying for final exams, or whatever else the end of the year throws in front of you?

But that’s the exact reason why this time of year is the best to start (or restart) a fitness routine, or really any kind of routine. When you start a routine during a busy time of year, you’ll be forced to make it sustainable. The gym routine you can stick with amid the chaos isn’t going to be one you drop after a few months. You’re already training yourself to work around obstacles as they come up, which is a key component of self-efficacy. And when the chaos clears on Jan. 1, your routine will be even easier to stick to.

Of course, there are ways to lean in too hard: Choosing unsustainable habits, falling for bad diet advice, mistaking not masturbating for some kind of health hack, the usual suspects. There’s also the pitfall of focusing too much on the vibes and too little on what you’re actually going to do or how you’ll benefit.

And then there’s the framing: You were working on yourself all year, but you’re in danger of letting up on the gas, but you’re committed to locking in so that you’re a step ahead of everybody who takes this time to slack off. I really don’t love this tack. Self-improvement is not a competition. There’s a difference between being consistent in your training and healthy eating (good) and seeing the pursuit of health and fitness as something where you always have to work harder because you’re at risk of getting left behind.

I also don’t love how gendered the Winter Arc TikToks tend to be. When you search for Winter Arc content, the first few suggestions include “winter arc for women” and “winter arc for men.” When I first started looking at the Winter Arc trend a few years ago, the women’s versions were more likely to include restrictive dieting or to focus on how the Winter Arc will finally (sigh) snatch your waist. These days, the focus is more on personal goal setting: Lots of the girlies filming their Winter Arc rules are doing so in a notebook and talking about journaling exercises that will help you identify what you need to work on to get to your "best self." Sometimes this is all monetized; training plans and journaling prompts can, of course, be purchased at the link in bio.

I do like that many of the women’s versions emphasize sustainability and setting your own goals rather than copying somebody else's. I don't love the enormity of the mental burden you're supposed to shoulder before even beginning. Should I really have to file an in-depth written report with myself before revamping every area of my life with a 100% commitment to multiple goals?

The men’s versions tend to go off the rails in another direction, with rules like “no girls” or “go ghost.” No distractions! Here, I've seen a shift over the years as well: at first there was overly serious content, followed quickly by satire (yelling at the viewer to get divorced and go work out in the dark). Now the men's videos tend to be more vibes-based, featuring images of pre-dawn workouts and plates full of salad with motivational quotes playing in the background. When the men give their rules, they tend to be simpler than the women's—no journaling exercises—but they often boil down to the same overly strict routines. (And then, of course, they'll offer to sell you a 90-day or 60-day plan.)

If you’re going to do a Winter Arc (or if you’re already doing one), make sure to structure it in a way that benefits you. Choosing 10 overly ambitious goals and setting yourself up for failure is not a healthy way to approach self-improvement, OK? Pick goals that are meaningful, achievable without divine intervention, and trackable with tools you already have at hand (for example, tracking your steps with a Fitbit or your running mileage with a Garmin watch).

It’s also helpful to think of developing yourself over this arc, rather than taking it as a three-month (or two-month) challenge where you have to do everything right all the time. If you currently wake up at 8 a.m. and want to wake up at 5 a.m., you don’t have to set your alarm for 5 a.m. tomorrow. It’s OK to aim for 7:30 a.m., make that a habit, then try for 7:00 a.m., and so on.

With that in mind, here are some "rules" I've seen from creators that I'm actually on board with (so long as you don't overwhelm yourself with them):

Wake up earlier. A great goal, especially if you take advantage of the time change to make things easier on your body.

Get to bed on time. Never a bad idea. Cultivating good sleep habits in general is always worthwhile.

Get your steps in. Be thoughtful about what your target is: 10,000 is not for everybody. Better to choose a number that would be a modest improvement on what you already do.

Exercise X times per week. Pick a number that works for you, and get into it. Be realistic about your goal, and for the best results, be consistent even if you’re sore at first.

Eat healthy. This is a great goal, with the major caveat that there are a lot of ways to eat healthy. You don’t need to cut out sugar or pretend that there’s something evil about seed oils. Do get more protein and veggies.

Be more thoughtful about using social media. I’m not going to tell you to delete all your apps (“except TikTok,” as the TikTokers say). But it’s fair to consider whether you might want to delete a few apps, turn off some notifications, or put your phone on Do Not Disturb for more hours of the day.

Journal or read more. Journaling can be great for working through your feelings or cultivating a creative habit. Reading can be entertainment or a great way to learn. Choose whichever you need most.

Learn a new skill. I’ve mostly seen this one in the men’s TikToks, and I love it. They’re often thinking of “skills” that will help in some kind of entrepreneurship grift they’re about to sell you, but there are tons of skills that will come in handy in life, or that are at least fun to learn. Practice a language, get better at cooking, make some art. Skills are, as I’ve noted, a multi-layered exercise for your brain. And they may come in handy someday.

This year I've slacked off on my fitness routine as I've gotten more involved in other hobbies, but I'm actually looking forward to being more consistent. My winter goals include exercising early in the day when possible and reading 20 minutes each day. (I'm even tracking the second one with a sticker chart.)
