#3536. Clint Eastwood's 2021 Neo-Western Movie Is One Of Netflix's Biggest Streaming Hits

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

A late-era Clint Eastwood Western is one of Netflix's biggest streaming hits. To be more specific, it's a neo-Western, which is to say a more contemporary take on the genre containing Western themes but set in more modern times. The movie in question is "Cry Macho," which won't go down as the best Western ever directed by Eastwood, but it will probably go down as his last. That in itself makes it significant.

"Cry Macho" is currently sitting at the number 10 spot on Netflix's most-watched movie charts, per FlixPatrol. It's sitting just behind Tom Cruise's "The Mummy" from 2017, which isn't exactly remembered fondly but somehow continues to find an audience. In many ways, streaming viewership remains a great mystery.

The movie is based on the book of the same name by N. Richard Nash. It takes place in the late 1970s and focuses on a former rodeo star named Mike Milo (Eastwood) who takes a job from an ex‐boss to bring his young son home, taking him away from his alcoholic mom. Crossing rural Mexico on their back way to Texas, the unlikely pair faces an unexpectedly challenging journey.

Eastwood's "Cry Macho" flopped in theaters five years ago, but there are many reasons for that. The box office was on life support during the pandemic and people weren't heading back to theaters en masse at that time. It also didn't help that Warner Bros. decided to premiere its entire 2021 movie slate on HBO Max and in theaters on the same day. That killed a lot of people's motivation to leave the house, which was already low.

Be that as it may, more than five years later, people appear to be catching up with this one now that it's on a new platform and available to watch from the comfort of home. The film's current popularity speaks volumes about Clint Eastwood's continued draw as an American cinema icon, both as an actor and a director. Westerns, in particular, have been the bread and butter for him dating back to his early days as an actor.

The legendary filmmaker has starred in many classics of the genre, including "The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly" and "Unforgiven," arguably the best movie directed by Eastwood. So even if "Cry Macho" wasn't considered to be among his best works as a director, it still scratches an itch for viewers — especially viewers who have a certain nostalgia for Eastwood wearing a cowboy hat and boots.

/Film called "Cry Macho" an "old-fashioned cowboy drama" in our review from 2021. It was a mixed review overall, which is pretty much how most critics felt about it. What makes the movie significant, above all else, is that it's probably going to serve as Eastwood's swan song within the genre and could quite possibly mark his final on-screen performance. He's well into his 90s and there is a decent chance he's effectively retired at this point.

2024's intense courtroom drama "Juror #2" was expected to be Eastwood's final go-around as a director, which notably didn't feature him as an actor. Bearing that in mind, it's probably worth watching "Cry Macho" for a great many folks, if only as a send-off of sorts to one of the greatest to ever do it in the genre he's mostly closely associated with.

You can also grab "Cry Macho" on 4K, Blu-ray, or DVD on Amazon.

#3535. Sandra Wollner’s ‘Everytime’ Is a Stunning Film About Grief Like You’ve Never Seen Before

Few human emotions are as fathomable as grief. Someone (or something) was here, had meaning and value and presence, and is now gone. There is a hole, a gap, an empty space. The pain that accompanies that void may manifest in different people in different ways, but its very existence is understandable. What makes people happy? What makes them sad? What makes them angry? Grief, well, that’s an easier question with a tougher answer.

For her third feature film, German filmmaker Sandra Wollner tackles the most tangible of dramatic genres — the grief tale — and turns it on its head in a way that our own David Ehrlich called “infinitely beguiling.” Mostly, the film shows how infinitely elastic and malleable this genre is, and the emotions that power it. Related Stories How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Dominated the Box Office: GKIDS Chief on IMAX’s Impact and the Growing Market for Foreign-Language Movies Democrats Won. When Do Hollywood Crews Get Back to Work?

The logline for the Un Certain Regard winner is simple enough: after the death of teenager Jessie (Carla Hüttermann), her mother Ella (Birgit Minichmayr), her little sister Melli (Lotte Shirin Keiling), and her boyfriend Lux (Tristán López) form an unlikely family unit as they attempt to move on. To say much else is spoiler-y in the truest of senses: It would detract from the joy and wonder of watching this story unfold.

That Wollner’s film is doing something different with seemingly well-trod material is obvious from the start, as “Everytime” layers on cut scenes from the video game “Vintage Story” — not “Minecraft,” though Wollner understands why the audience might think it’s the more well-known game — long before the real drama kicks in.

A familiarity with “Vintage Story” is not required to understand her film, Wollner promised during a recent interview with IndieWire. “Maybe if someone hears the dialogue of Melli and Lux, then maybe they would feel they have to know more about it, because they’re talking about how you can basically cut trees to harvest stuff and to get that, but I don’t feel that you have to know anything,” she said.

Wollner herself isn’t even a “hardcore gamer,” but she admires video games for their world-building and how they can encourage exploration. Her early forays into both “Vintage Story” and “Minecraft” tickled that. “It felt like the ‘Backrooms’ phenomenon, but before the ‘Backrooms’ phenomenon,” she said. “You’re walking through infinite worlds that feel so big, but minimalistic in a way. And the sounds; a very ambient sound feels eerie and soothing at the same time. I was just very compelled and inspired by that.”

The idea that Jessie would leave behind her own video game world that Melli could then play in was one of the film’s first seeds. “I thought, it’s a way of a memorial I haven’t seen so far,” she said. “[We have this] whole world of avatars and gaming communities where people meet online and then if someone really goes out, their avatar might live forever in there and create a life on its own in a way. I just found that very intriguing, and this is why I wanted in there.”

While the film is unique in how it handles digital mementos — avatars, literally — Wollner also pays close attention to real-world details that can make grief feel even bigger.

“One of the first scenes [I thought of] was Ella lying down on the couch and hearing how her daughter would come back [into their apartment],” the filmmaker said. “It’s something I think also everybody can relate to, even with a more natural loss and not such a tragic one. For example, when I was a kid, my aunt would always run down the stairs [in the apartment complex where we lived], and I would always hear her in the morning, running down in the morning. The noise was very specific to this person. I didn’t want it to be full on, but to let us think, it couldn’t be Jessie.”

Wollner was also intrigued early on by the “constellation of people” impacted by the loss of one. “The boy, the little girl, and the mother, it’s people I’ve met in my life in several decades, I would say, variations of them, but somehow similar constellations,” she said. “They seemed very clear to me. Three people who, especially the mother and the boy, really tried to do the right thing in a way. But there is a big conflict in there. They are having a weird dependent relationship. She needs him to grieve. He needs her to forgive. Of course, I could have made this conflict much bigger, but I really was interested in ordinary people who just try to do the right thing and just try to go along with that.”

Having her own child added a new dimension to the film, even for Wollner. The filmmaker was editing the film when her daughter was born (her longtime partner is writer and cinematographer Timm Kröger, who also worked on the digital imaging in “Everytime”), an experience that deepened her understanding of her own work.

In the film’s second half, the trio travel to Tenerife, Spain on holiday, a place that baby Jessie (who we’ve seen in home videos) once visited. There, they discover another baby, who looks just like Jessie, playing happily in the same quiet space that baby Jessie once occupied.

“We watched the scene again of baby Jessie sitting there, and we looked at each other,” she said. “I always understood what [that scene] means for me, but there, we really felt it for the first time, being a parent. And I felt, oh, I really nailed it! I mean, that sounds so stupid, but when I had the baby, I think, as many people feel, you still sometimes have the feeling, oh, where does it come from? It’s suddenly here. Suddenly there’s a person there. It’s like with that moment when she walks around the corner, and baby’s sitting there.”

Wollner was also compelled by the way we memorize different places and the unpredictability of memory. The odd little space, located in the far reaches of the resort’s clubhouse, comes to haunt Ella, Melli, and Lux in different ways, forever linked to Jessie and her absence.

“When my dad died, I was with him, and I suddenly had this image of him standing somewhere in this bend on the river and fishing, and it felt so familiar,” the filmmaker said. “This memory intruded on my present. We cannot control when we get a memory. They’re just coming. Sometimes we can make them happen to come. But we never know if maybe the weird place where we saw our baby sitting or the weird moment is the one that haunts us the most. It’s this weird banal little room with this weird banal kitschy toy that is playing this music. And this is the thing that then comes back.”

Those “banal little” details pack immense emotional power. So do turns from Minichmayr and López, who never turn to over-the-top histrionics to convey their grief. Wollner’s choice to set the majority of the film a year after Jessie’s death helped, giving the characters some distance from the immediate stab of loss.

“It was a conscious choice to pick some time after the death [to mostly focus the film on],” she said. “As a writer, we need to know what happened in the time between, and so I wrote that as well, but it honestly felt not depictable. I feel I can only fail to show that. I wasn’t interested in these big emotions. That just felt too overwhelming. And sometimes we are made to believe that grief comes in these neat boxes to check: Now you’re sad, now you’re angry, now you accept. Maybe you can be angry again, then you accept. It’s just this messy thing that you can feel for a very long time.”

Keiling also offers a nuanced performance, built more on a kid’s curiosity than on saddling the young actress with big, showy scenes. There’s no screaming and crying here, no sobbing or yelling. But that doesn’t mean that Keiling wasn’t accessing some major emotions.

“I love to work with kids,” Wollner said. “And even having a kid, I think I still am a kid in a way. For this one, I met Lotte, I had not met another kid, I only met her, I did not do any other castings. I just fell in love and thought, oh, she’s exactly what I thought of Melli could be and even better, so I trusted the script to her.”

Wollner worked with fellow filmmaker Juli Neuhaus, who served as a “kids’ coach” for the younger members of the cast. Wollner and Neuhaus were eager to meet Keiling where she was. The young performer loves to draw, so she would draw the scenes before performing them, to better understand what they were about, which allowed her to access a full spectrum of feeling.

“With Melli, there was no scene where she really had to act her grief,” she said. “I always felt that the film itself, the editing and the framing, the absence, we see her doing her homework, and then we see the same room behind her, but now we know that the sister is not there anymore, I always felt that this will tell us the grief, so she doesn’t need to act it. If she holds her phone and is texting her sister, it will already make us feel the grief. She doesn’t need to feel the heavy weight of that. So, actually for her, it was, I would say, like a very light shoot. Playful. It was really playful.”

Still, for all its sense of fantasy and play, “Everytime” is about a terrible heartbreak. Yet, as ever, Wollner chose to depict Jessie’s sudden, shocking death in a unique way, tracking her fall from a tall building while out with Lux from a great distance away. We can see it. We can do nothing about it. That’s grief, too.

“This was one that really was clear to me in the writing process already, that we’re going to have this lens and that we have this weird perspective of the universe itself looking at it, being so far away and still not able to do something about it, but still witnessing so intimate,” she said.

The actors were on one high-rise building, while Wollner and her crew were on another, about half a mile away. “And we had this insane lens. I had a 3,000-millimeter consumer camera, which is an insane lens,” she said. “It’s really like you don’t want to point it on people. It feels really not OK. But I was sure that I wanted to work with exactly that length or something similar to that, that feels kind of forbidden to be so close and too far away at the same time.”

While the scene is shot as if Jessie and Lux are very close to the edge of the building, the actors were not. (Hüttermann later told Wollner that she still had the feeling she might fall, even with myriad safety measures in place. That’s just how immersive the entire thing felt.) Hüttermann’s actual fall was shot in a studio, and their visual effects supervisor Kariem Saleh combined that footage with the outdoor shots.

Because they needed a certain kind of light, Wollner estimated they had only about five takes to get it right, though she knew they would likely only get one shot with the “perfect” light. Her script also called for the camera to follow a bird after the fall, but she said with a laugh, “Unfortunately, no bird came in exactly that moment.” (They lensed other birds, though, and those also ended up in the final composite shot.)

“We worked so many hours just on the sounds, just to get the right level of there is a little sound, and there is a little tink when she falls down, a little bit,” she said. “Just to realize, given how far away we had to be, how does the sound have to be? We worked the whole time on that, and I never really felt it until I sat at Cannes in the audience. And I heard the gasps for the first time and really it went through my bones. I mean, it’s weird to say that, but I was happy, but I felt the first time that it actually worked.”

Wollner remains very emotionally connected to the film, constantly talking about the way certain scenes make her feel, either while making them or editing them or even seeing them with an audience. Of course, such a deep-feeling filmmaker crafted such a beguiling film, one that invites all sorts of responses and theories. Since Cannes, audiences have been talking about its genuinely thrilling third act and the implications of its final scenes. And while we won’t spoil them here, we had to ask: What did Wollner want her viewers to feel in those moments?

“The feeling that I wanted to have is that [this film that is] grounded or hopefully grounded in the beginning, then suddenly you walk around the corner and you feel still some ground, but it’s such an odd place now and you don’t know,” she said. “I always hoped it doesn’t feel just dreamy, but there is some groundedness to it and that the people still react in a way that made sense for them, the characters, but that you don’t know what room you entered now, some kind of back room. That was clear from the beginning.”

And, as fantastical as it might sound, she’s clear: it’s all real. “I mean, it’s such a cliché to say that, but everything we see at the end is true at the same time,” she said.

A 1-2 Special release, the film is in limited theaters now, with a wide release to come in February 2027.

#3533. The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Will Be A Bigger Box Office Hit Than You Realize

One of the biggest expected hits of the fall season is nearly upon us — and it's going to be even bigger than a lot of people realize. "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" will explore Haymitch Abernathy's origin story, with Woody Harrelson having popularized the character in the original run of "Hunger Games" films. This time, Joseph Zada is playing the younger Haymitch, and it turns out folks are very eager to see how he ended up winning his games in his youth.

Once again directed by franchise shepherd Francis Lawrence, "Sunrise on the Reaping" is currently eyeing a monster box office opening between $105 and $140 million domestically when it arrives next weekend, per Box Office Theory. These estimates have climbed a lot in recent weeks, so I'm personally included to lean on the higher end of projections. Either way, it's going to be a dramatic improvement for the property.

In 2023, "The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" topped the box office, but Lionsgate wasn't partying like it's 2012. It opened to $44.6 million en route to $349 million worldwide. All of "The Hunger Games" movies have been hits at the box office, yet that prequel's grosses were far behind the previous entries, which all opened north of $100 million and made at least $650 million worldwide. This latest prequel is, by all appearances, going to be more in line with those earlier entries.

"Sunrise on the Reaping" takes place more than two decades before the first-ever "Hunger Games" film/book and four decades after "The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes." Its story is focused on the 50th annual Hunger Games, aka the Second Quarter Quell, in which Haymitch famously competed and won before mentoring Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence) in the 74th Hunger Games.

Why is the latest "Hunger Games" prequel expected to perform so much better than its predecessor? For one, author Suzanne Collins' source novel was incredibly well received, telling a story many have been curious about for a long time. For another, Jennifer Lawrence is reprising Katniss for "Sunrise on the Reaping," with Josh Hutcherson and Woody Harrelson coming back as Peeta Mellark and the older Haymitch as well.

While these appearances should be fairly brief, getting the band back together absolutely helps make this more of an event for fans. Similarly, "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" was about the insidious President Snow's origins, whereas casual audiences are probably more interested in learning about Haymich's backstory. Lionsgate spent over/under $200 million to make "Sunrise on the Reaping," which was risky in light of how "Songbirds and Snakes" performed, but it's currently shaping up to be money well spent.

The last time the franchise saw a hit of this size was when 2015's "The Hunger Games: Mockingjay — Part 2" opened to $102 million domestically en route to $653 million in theaters worldwide. If this film opens on the higher end of projections? It could be closer to "Catching Fire" ($158 million opening/$865 million worldwide). Either way, this is going to be the biggest opening of the fall season to date, by far.

Early reactions to "Sunrise on the Reaping" have been largely positive, which also bodes well. And while Thanksgiving will bring in big competition like "Focker In-Law" and Disney's "Hexed," it falls over one of the biggest moviegoing weeks of the year. As such, all these films should be able to co-exist.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" hits theaters on November 20, 2026.

#3531. After ‘Whalefall’ Flops, Can Imagine Entertainment Return to Box Office Glory with ‘How to Rob a Bank’?

“How to Rob a Bank” may benefit from doing just that. With career-low reviews for director David Leitch, the Amazon MGM Studios release has been tracking poorly and now looks unlikely to crack $10 million from 2,810 theaters in its domestic debut.

For the film’s production banner, Imagine Entertainment, it is shaping up to be a second theatrical non-starter after its high-concept survival thriller “Whalefall” — about a scuba diver trapped in the belly of a marine mammal — got beached after its October opening with just a $39 million total worldwide despite solid reviews. Neither “How to Rob a Bank” nor “Whalefall” marks an auspicious wide release homecoming for Imagine, even if Amazon and Disney, respectively, fronted the budget and marketing spend on the films. Related Stories ‘How to Rob a Bank’ Review: David Leitch’s Fun and Poppy YouTube Heist Movie Almost Gets Away with It Ebenezer’s Venmo and ‘How to Rob a Bank’ ATMs: Studios Are Now Promoting Movies by Just Giving Away Money

The two features are Imagine’s first to play across more than 2,000 domestic screens in more than eight years; the last was Lionsgate’s buddy comedy “The Spy Who Dumped Me” in 2018. That’s practically an epoch for Imagine, which was founded by Ron Howard and Brian Grazer and spent its early years asserting itself as a theatrical force with hits like “Kindergarten Cop,” “Liar, Liar,” “The Nutty Professor,” and Howard’s own films, like “Apollo 13” and “How the Grinch Stole Christmas.” A spokesperson for the banner declined to comment for this report.

But Imagine, as with much of the industry, saw its focus on original, often adult-oriented programming hit diminishing returns in the past 20 years. The company’s biggest hit after 2010 was the 2016 Dan Brown adaptation “Inferno,” which, at $220 million global, earned less than half the gross that its 2009 predecessor “Angels & Demons” did.

Around that time, Imagine hitched its wagon to the then-burgeoning streaming industry, expanding its focus on television projects and aggressively branching into the documentary market, as theatrical features fell by the wayside. Packages for narrative features like “Tick, Tick… Boom!” and “The Beanie Bubble” were sold off to streaming services. But with an industrywide reawakening to the benefits of theatrical (which has even drawn in Netflix), along with a waning demand for unscripted programming, Imagine is now at the start of its return to wide-release, big-screen features.

There were some false starts along the way. Notably, Howard’s own 2022 rescue thriller “Thirteen Lives” had originally been set up at MGM before the studio’s acquisition by Amazon, which then executed an extremely limited theatrical release and opted out of reporting box office. The film’s star Viggo Mortensen later slammed the decision. Then there was Howard’s island-set thriller “Eden,” which sold to the mostly digital-focused distributor Vertical after debuting to withering reviews. And Luca Guadagnino’s post-#MeToo morality thriller “After the Hunt” never cracked 1,300 theaters from Amazon MGM after critics ripped it apart at Venice Film Festival. Many of these films carried hefty price tags — “Eden” had a $35 million net budget, while “After the Hunt” cost $80 million to produce.

“How to Rob a Bank,” co-produced by director Leitch’s 87North, faces a significant climb to any theatrical success with a $40 million production budget and intense Thanksgiving season competition incoming. Imagine has a more promising (though less novel) plan to lean further into IP in 2027. Another Amazon MGM release, the legacy sequel comedy “Spaceballs: The New One,” will come in April. And Universal is distributing a Snoop Dogg biopic, which Imagine developed along with the rapper’s own Death Row Pictures. Can Imagine find the same success with Snoop’s story that it did with “8 Mile”?

More original is the Adam Driver military thriller “Alone at Dawn,” directed by Howard himself, which shot in 2025 and is slated for a Christmas 2027 theatrical release from Amazon MGM. Further down the line, Imagine is developing a sequel to “How the Grinch Stole Christmas,” with Jim Carrey tapped to return. The first film was the top-grossing North American release of 2000 and remains a high watermark for Imagine’s commercial success.

Imagine Entertainment’s future of theatrical IP also comes after years of murmurs that the banner was fielding suitors amid its rise in the documentary space, including a Variety report of a 2021 valuation around $800 million and a 2022 report from TheWrap that a $700 million valuation deal with Centricus Asset Management Ltd. had fallen through. But more recently, TheWrap reported on October 1 that majority stakeholder The Raine Group, which came aboard for $100 million in 2016, was in talks to sell its 51 percent ownership to private equity; an Imagine representative issued an emphatic denial of the claim in the piece.

After a boom among independent production banners to start the decade, the business has faced growing instability over recent years, with shrinking valuations and sharp cutbacks in content spending. For decades, Imagine has been one of the industry leaders in the space, but “How to Rob a Bank” and “Whalefall” are the first test of whether it can reassert itself as a theatrical hitmaker. If the poor tracking for “Rob a Bank” pans out, it’ll then look to “Spaceballs” for, as the joke in Mel Brooks’ 1987 goes, “The Search for More Money.”

#3530. Your Android Can Get Hacked Without You Doing Anything at All

You probably know that clicking suspicious links online or opening attachments from strangers in an email or text is a recipe for hacking. It's a dangerous world out there online, so it's always important to be vigilant. However, the danger doesn't always involve something you do. There are ways to hack your devices without requiring any intervention on your part whatsoever—and one such example is likely plaguing your Android device right now.

As reported by The Hacker News, there is a critical Android security flaw that could enable remote code execution on your device. In other words, bad actors could use the flaw to run their own code on your phone, effectively taking over the device for their own gain. The flaw, identified as CVE-2026-58868, isn't universal, but it is widespread: It currently affects Android 14 through Android 17, the latest version of Google's OS. If your phone runs Android 12 or Android 13, it may be unaffected, as Google doesn't identify these versions in its security bulletin, but it doesn't explicitly rule them out, either.

There are two silver linings here, however. One, Google hasn't confirmed any active exploits for this security flaw. While that isn't a guarantee that bad actors have missed this exploit so far, it at least opens that possibility. As such, there may be time for users to patch their devices before hackers truly take advantage of the flaw. Second, Google does have a patch for the flaw. The patch may not be available to you right away, however, as it's up to both the manufacturer of your phone and your carrier to issue these updates. Still, a patch is, at the very least, on its way.

This flaw is perhaps the most important to fix, but it's not the only serious issue. In all, Google's latest bulletin highlights 216 vulnerabilities, and, of those, 23 are "critical." As The Hacker News explains, two other of those critical flaws could also allow remote code execution when exploited.

To see whether the patch is installed on your end, open the Settings app on your phone, tap "About phone" or "About tablet," then choose the Android version on-screen. Look for a date of "2026-11-01" or later. All security patches from Nov. 1 and on will fix this issue. If not, you'll ned to wait for the patch.

#3529. Why The Lord Of The Rings: The Rings Of Power Season 3 Feels Like A Reboot [Exclusive]

Keep it secret, keep it safe ... from spoilers. This article discusses major plot details from Episodes 1-4 of "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" Season 3.

"The world is changed," Cate Blanchett's Galadriel intones in the very first words of "The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring." In the Peter Jackson film, the Elven royal is mourning the passing of the ages. In "The Rings of Power," viewers may feel a similar sense of time slipping by as they tune into the first four episodes released by Prime Video. The Season 3 premiere quickly establishes that, following a five-year time jump, Middle-earth is not the same as before. War rages, certain characters now play very different roles, and things have never felt quite so dire.

"The Rings of Power" may still struggle to live up to the hype, but there's no mistaking that sense of starting over this time around. After a relatively up-and-down journey to this point, was Season 3 meant to be a creative reset for newcomers to jump on board? That was one of my biggest burning questions when I sat down with series co-showrunner Patrick McKay during a recent press junket. While stopping just short of endorsing a complete 180-degree pivot in approach, he admitted this was very much intended to keep viewers on their toes:

"The big thing is, honestly, we want to keep shaking things up. We want to surprise the audience. We want to come at you with a pitch you haven't seen yet. Seasons 1 and 2 kind of roll straight through, linearly. And this time, it felt like a good opportunity to shake things up and drop you in a story in a place you're not expecting."

For those who've watched all four episodes released to this point, it's abundantly clear that "The Rings of Power" isn't messing around this season. Not only has Charlie Vickers' Sauron finally unmasked himself and declared open war upon all free peoples, but the writers themselves have developed a bit of a ruthless streak. Multiple characters are killed off in the early going, neither of whom had much of a place in the ongoing story anymore, while even the Hobbit-like clan of Harfoots from Seasons 1 and 2 are now completely missing in action.

Taken as a whole, it's a promising (if overdue) development for viewers who have struggled with the show's unwieldy ensemble cast and patience-testing armada of subplots. For Patrick McKay, however, this all goes back to the desire to avoid lulling viewers into a predictable pattern of storytelling,  instead coming right out of the gate swinging. After a few table-setting sequences, Season 3 begins with a major battle sequence that confirms how overmatched our heroes really are. Sauron's power has grown, his fearsome proto-Ringwraiths (known as Nazgnagôl) are now in thrall, and, of course, the threat of the One Ring overshadows everything. As McKay told me, this season was the perfect opportunity to take a really big swing:

"That was very much a conscious choice. We wanted to invert the structure of the prior couple seasons. We [previously] built to big events and big battles. And we love those seasons, I'm very proud of them. But we wanted to do something different and we felt like, 'What if we started with a battle? What if we started at the height of the war and then maybe hit the ground running?'

There's a lot to be said for spending years carefully establishing the tone and structure of a mega-budget streaming show ... only to upend the board at its halfway point. As "The Rings of Power" hits its middle act in Season 3 (remember, this was planned to last five full seasons), the timing couldn't be better to kick things into another gear. As the villains of the story gain the upper hand and our heroes race to catch up, the creative team applied a similar mindset to the experience of actually watching this season unfold.

"Look, as viewers, J.D. [Payne], my co-showrunner and I, we love chasing a show," Patrick McKay revealed to me. "When you're in a movie theater, and you can feel an audience keying in and chasing the film, it's always great, and it makes your investment even more powerful." That, as it turns out, helped influence their decision to pull a similar trick with "The Rings of Power."

"If you're entering a story at a point where it's in medias res and you've got to kind of figure it out and [you go], 'Oh wow, Galadriel and Arondir [the Elf character played by Ismael Cruz Córdova] are friends now and, oh my gosh, Barad-dûr has been built and oh, that must be Rivendell and what is this?' It's kind of an exciting way to watch something."

Clearly, the hope is for this chapter of "The Rings of Power" to provide a jolt and give fans reason to stick around. After the four-episode premiere, we have half a season left to see where this goes. Two new episodes drop on Prime Video on November 18, 2026.

#3528. Ghost Rider Star Says He's Down to Return for Marvel's 2028 Reboot

Marvel Studios is bringing back the supernatural hero Ghost Rider in a new movie in 2028, with Ryan Gosling in the lead role. Exactly which version of Ghost Rider Gosling will tackle remains unclear, but one former actor who donned the flaming skull says he's down to ride alongside the rebooted silver screen Spirit of Vengeance if Marvel calls: Agents of SHIELD star Gabriel Luna.

In an interview with Polygon, Luna said, "If they call, I'll do it."

Speaking with Luna for Dexter: Resurrection season 2, Polygon's Jake Kleinman asked The Last of Us and Terminator: Dark Fate actor for his reaction when Marvel announced the new Ghost Rider at this year's San Diego Comic-Con.

"I was excited," Luna said. "I think it’s gonna be pretty awesome. I like [director] Shawn Levy. [...] It’s gonna be really, really exciting."

Luna portrayed the Roberto "Robbie" Reyes version of Ghost Rider in season 4 of Agents of SHIELD, which aired on ABC from 2016–2017. Reyes was the fifth character to be named Ghost Rider in Marvel Comics, and was introduced in the pages of All-New Ghost Rider in 2014. For the past decade, Luna said, he's received plenty of questions about reprising the role.

"First of all, I love and appreciate everybody who loves Robbie and how they keep asking here after 10 years," he said. "Eventually they wore me down. I was like, 'All right, fine. If they call, I’ll do it.' You gotta stay open to all these types of things. And the story is number one. And if there’s a reason for Robbie to ride side by side with Ryan’s Ghost Rider, then there’s a reason to do that. But otherwise, I’m gonna love and enjoy the continuation of one of the most iconic and the greatest characters in Marvel lore."

Luna said he doesn't have any insider info on which version of the character Gosling would play in Ghost Rider — reportedly, it's Johnny Blaze — but has one hopeful take in mind: "I don’t know who he’s gonna play. I kinda hope it’s Danny Ketch. But yeah, I’m gonna be front row when it all goes down," he said.

Gosling will be at least the fourth actor to portray a Ghost Rider in live-action, following Nicolas Cage's role as Johnny Blaze in 2007's Ghost Rider and its 2012 sequel Ghost Rider: Spirit of Vengeance; Sam Elliott as Carter Slade in Ghost Rider; and Luna in Agents of SHIELD. (Incidentally, two other actors on that TV show were also briefly possessed by the Spirit of Vengeance: Clark Gregg and Henry Simmons.)

Marvel Studios' Ghost Rider is slated to arrive in movie theaters on July 28, 2028.

#3527. ‘Ebenezer’ Review: Johnny Depp Is Absolutely Insufferable in a Dull and Dreary Christmas Carol

A Sauvage and jowly overactor in dire need of career rehabilitation could hardly ask for a better part to play than Ebenezer Scrooge. He’s a cruel miser of a man who comes to learn the error of his ways over the course of a ghost story that preys upon Christian precepts of redemption and forgiveness (along with the more secular warm and fuzzies of seeing a bad guy discover the joys of being good). Indeed, what is “cancel culture” if not a shackled delusion that visits self-made pariahs in the dead of night, and what is Charles Dickens’ “A Christmas Carol” if not a plea to believe that even the most odious of souls are still capable of being saved? Related Stories Sandra Wollner’s ‘Everytime’ Is a Stunning Film About Grief Like You’ve Never Seen Before How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Dominated the Box Office: GKIDS Chief on IMAX’s Impact and the Growing Market for Foreign-Language Movies

It’s been reported that Johnny Depp accepted the title role of Ti West’s “Ebenezer” at a fraction of his usual rate, but I suspect that he probably would have done this movie for free. While the embattled star earned more than $250 million for his work on the “Pirates of the Caribbean” franchise, even that psychotic number pales in comparison to the pricelessness of starring in a major studio Christmas movie that allows him to look just left of the camera and say lines like “I’m not the man I was!” and “I was once good, and I know I can be again!” before his character saves a cherubic little boy from certain death and invites a freezing beggar inside for a warm cup of tea. If an old crank like Scrooge can make his way back toward grace, why not the convicted star of “Mortdecai,” and the alleged perpetrator of several even more serious crimes?

Johnny Depp may prefer for that to be framed as a rhetorical question, but his insufferable turn as literature’s most cantankerous moneylender demands an honest answer. For me, that answer is rather straightforward: While Depp has never been the subtlest of actors, his post-Sparrow pivot away from artistic curiosity has distended his talents into such a grotesque caricature of their former charm that “Ebenezer” left me feeling like I may never be able to empathize with his screen presence again.

Scrooge is obviously a scenery-chewer’s dream, but the crescent arc he traces from grinch to Christmas miracle is only believable enough to sustain Dickens’ fable if you believe it on both ends. Depp’s performance — an advent calendar of empty affectations without a soul to anchor them, every shot full of face and bereft of feeling — makes that exceedingly difficult. His offscreen unsavoriness certainly doesn’t help, but there’s a more immediate problem when the lights go down, one that makes him a unique case among Hollywood’s tainted array of mega-star actors: He seems to have become very bad at acting. Whatever my feelings about Depp as a human being, the truth is that I didn’t buy him as a glowering monster any more than I bought him as a beaming man who’s grown “better than his word.”

An unengaging Ebenezer is a tough break for a movie called “Ebenezer,” and screenwriter Nathaniel Halpern’s fidelity to the source material doesn’t exactly leave West with a wealth of opportunities to compensate for such fatal miscasting. West’s take on the holiday classic is faithful to the core — no Muppets, no ghosts of girlfriends past, no uncanny mo-capped Jim Carrey. As you might expect from the director of indie genre standouts like “Pearl” and “The House of the Devil,” West’s big idea is to scare the Dickens out of us by turning up the volume on this story’s implicit scariness. Sometimes literally, as this PG-13 carol offers a small handful of gentle jump-scares.

“Ebenezer” isn’t a horror movie in the strictest sense, but West does what he can to play up the fear that eventually terrifies Scrooge into giving a shit about his fellow man. Most — or all — of those flourishes are purely cosmetic in nature, and hellbent on sucking every glimmer of life out of Victorian England. Scrooge’s office has never looked more haunted, as Checco Varese’s grimdark cinematography and Eve Stewart’s Yharnam-esque production design combine to create a London that’s in dire need of Christmas cheer (the vibe should go a long way with tweenage audiences eager for a bit of spice with their holiday viewing, though I suspect the whole thing is too staid and oppressive to become any kind of perennial favorite).

And since West would sooner die than pass up a chance for death, this version of the story treats us to a musty prologue where we actually get to see Ebenezer’s business partner bite the dust with his mouth wide open (Marley is played by Ian McKellen in what currently stands as the most “remember ‘The Christophers?’” performance of the year). From there, the action skips forward to Christmas Eve 1843, whence Ebenezer is inflicting his usual “Bah, humbug!” routine on poor Bob Cratchit (Rupert Grint), the underpaid clerk he resents for taking the next day off (HR being a decidedly 20th-century invention). But the fates have plans of their own for the bitter-cold businessman, who promptly pisses himself when the ghost of old Marley bursts into his miserable bedchamber later that night.

Reaction shots ensue, as Depp curdles his face into a series of the most exaggerated expressions since the death of silent cinema, every one of them betraying his character’s frigidness. This Ebenezer takes an active pleasure in being cruel, which not only makes him more detestable (which is fine), but also endows him with an innate capacity for joy that makes the rest of the movie feel like it’s walking in circles (which is less fine). Given that Depp’s performance is only as wide as his lips and as deep as his pockets, it seems wasteful that we should have to walk through the hollows of Ebenezer’s past, present, and future in order to fix him — it would be easier and equally meaningful to just push the corners of his mouth into a smile.

Of course, that would deprive us of the “holy shit, that’s Andrea Riseborough” fun of the “To Leslie” star’s Ghost of Christmas Past, a white-eyed ghoul who looks like a spirit from “The Conjuring” who popped up for a sudden jolt and then forgot to leave the frame. She’s the most amusing part of a familiar tour through the sadness of Ebenezer’s childhood, where he was bullied by the other kids and kept apart from his beloved older sister. Tramell Tillman is equally compelling as the boisterous Ghost of Christmas Present, though his bizarre character design — a round-bellied man whose face appears to be rotting to pieces in real-time — turns out to be reverse-engineered from an unnerving reveal that both honors Dickens’ text and also underlines West’s limited conviction to rejuvenate it with the visceral immediacy of a horror film (his commitment to the bit falls well short of the Robert Eggers-level follow-through that conceit demands).

Given the emphasis the director puts on the film’s genre spin, it’s ironic and surprising that “Ebenezer” is at its best when it focuses on the most basic human elements of its story, if only because the supporting characters offer such a welcome contrast to whatever Depp is doing. Sam Claflin and Daisy Ridley don’t have a whole lot to do as Ebenezer’s kind-hearted nephew Fred and his wife Clara (respectively), but the film takes pains to stress how sad it is that Scrooge is Fred’s last connection to his dead mother, and it’s touching to see how much it would mean for him to have a cordial relationship with the old miser.

It is considerably less touching to see Ebenezer arrive at a mutual feeling after palling around with the film’s Nazgûl-coded Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come (Robert Strange, cloaked in CGI), who forces the misanthrope to face the emptiness of his own miserable existence. “The flame of humanity still flickers within you,” someone tells Scrooge, but the slapstick pageantry of Depp’s performance sabotages the movie by keeping that flame at a low simmer from the start. I didn’t believe the fire had ever gone out any more than I believed that it was eventually rekindled, as this Ebenezer Scrooge is far too elastic and self-amused to convincingly suggest that he’s experiencing a permanent change of heart. He can’t even sustain a facial expression for more than a few seconds before he starts mugging around in search of another one.

There will, of course, be those who insist that I only panned “Ebenezer” because Johnny Depp is in it, and I suppose they’re at least half-right about that, if not quite for the reason they assume. The truth is that it would be a lot more interesting and true to the spirit of Dickens’ classic if I liked this movie in spite of Depp rather than disliking it because of him, as I can’t help but share the author’s opinion that everyone is theoretically capable of redemption, be it measure by measure or miraculously complete.

Alas, the actor’s “comeback” performance is just yet another thing that he ought to be sorry for.

Paramount Pictures will release “Ebenezer” in theaters on Friday, November 13.

#3526. Mickey’s Next Lincoln Lawyer Season 5 Case Gets New Tease

New details have been revealed about The Lincoln Lawyer season 5 that tease what fans can expect when the legal drama bids farewell next year.

The series is based on Michael Connelly's bestselling novels about defense attorney Mickey Haller, played by Manuel Garcia-Rulfo in the small-screen adaptation. Several months ago, it was announced that The Lincoln Lawyer would end after the upcoming fifth season, which will reportedly be released on Netflix in March 2027.

With at least four months to go until The Lincoln Lawyer returns, What's On Netflix has now revealed the titles for all 10 episodes in season 5: "Artemisia," "Roots," "Table 12," "Sucker Punch," "Chemistry Problem," "Do or Die," "Footprints," "Overtime" and "Resurrection Walk."

Aside from episodes 5 and 6, which are confirmed to be "Sucker Punch" and "Chemistry Problem," respectively, none of the other titles have publicly been assigned to any specific episodes yet, which means there are still a lot of unknowns.

Showrunners Ted Humphrey and Dailyn Rodriguez wrote the premiere and finale, with Matthew J. Lieberman (episodes 2, 6 and 9), Katy Erin (episode 3), Matthew Cruz (episode 4), Isabella A. Rodriguez (episode 5), Dailyn Rodriguez (episode 6, co-written with Lieberman), Lisa Bao (episode 7), Jake H. Berstein (episode 8) and Audrey Lipsmire (episode 9, co-written with Lieberman) also writing scripts.

Sign in to claim your place on the leaderboard!

Sign in to claim your place on the leaderboard!

The final season will cover the events of Connelly's 2023 novel Resurrection Walk and continue from where The Lincoln Lawyer season 4 finale left off, with Mickey finding out that he has a half-sister named Emi Finch, played by Cobie Smulders. She shows up seemingly out of the blue and requests that he help her with a wrongful conviction case.

Smulders was only a guest star when she showed up in the finale, but she has been promoted to series regular status for season 5, with Neflix currently developing a potential spinoff for her character.

Some of the newly revealed titles give vague hints about the storylines that will be featured in those episodes of The Lincoln Lawyer season 5. For example, "Artemisia" is Emi's full first name. "Article 1, Section 9" refers to the habeas corpus clause in the United States Constitution that Mickey employs at one point in the book.

And "Resurrection Walk" is the name of Connelly's book, a trend that's continuing from previous seasons when some episode titles were named after The Brass Verdict, The Fifth Witness, The Gods of Guilt and The Law of Innocence.

Garcia-Rulfo and Smulders' co-stars on The Lincoln Lawyer are Neve Campbell, Becki Newton, Jazz Raycole and Angus Sampson. Joining them for the final season are Diane Guerrero, Richard Cabral, Teresa Maria, Patty Guggenheim, Steve Howey, Iker Garcia, Corbin Bernsen, Chris Diamantopoulos, Amy Aquino, Angela Trimbur, Elpidia, Nate Corddry, Tricia Helfer and Keir O'Donnell.

Filming ended back in July, and now the countdown is on for Mickey's story on The Lincoln Lawyer to reach its conclusion.

This legal drama follows Mickey Haller, a Los Angeles defense attorney known for operating from his Lincoln Town Car, as he revives his career after an accident by taking on a high-profile murder case.

#3525. 'Ocarina of Time' for Switch 2 Might Already Have a Weird Glitch

Thursday is a big day for Zelda fans. That's when the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time officially launches on Switch 2, marking the first major linear (i.e., non-open-world) 3D Zelda game since the 2016 Twilight Princess remake on Wii U. I, for one, have been waiting for this day for years. I loved the N64 original and the 3DS remake, so to have the chance to play a modern take on the definitive Zelda is so exciting—that is, if it actually runs as it should.

I stumbled upon this interesting post on X from Austin John Plays, a YouTuber with a host of Zelda coverage. According to Austin John Plays, Ocarina of Time already ships with a weird glitch that won't necessarily break your experience, but which may slow it down for a while, and perhaps even confuse players into thinking something is wrong with their game or their console.

As his post explains, if you're playing the physical copy of Ocarina of Time, and it's the first game you've ever played on your Switch 2—maybe you got one of those fancy new Zelda anniversary consoles and want to break it in properly?—you may run into glaring performance issues: The game may freeze, your controller may stop working, and the FPS may drop to single digits.

Luckily, Austin John Plays says the fix is easy: just wait. Eventually, your game will boot back to the title screen. When it does, don't try to play right away. Instead, close the game, restart your Switch 2, then try relaunching Ocarina of Time. Austin John Plays advises you may need to repeat this process two or three times, but after that, you shouldn't continue to run into issues. I wouldn't be surprised if Nintendo releases a patch right away for this glitch if it turns out to be as widespread as this post implies.

However, seeing as the game doesn't come out until tomorrow, there's something you can do to prevent it. Austin John Plays thinks the bug only impacts Switch 2 consoles that haven't run other games before. If you've had your console a while, you're likely set. But if you just bought the 40th anniversary Zelda edition of the Switch 2, you might not have had a chance to run a game on it yet. As such, download a game from the e-shop—even a free demo—just to get the system running. Hopefully, that will be enough to circumvent the glitch, and prevent issues when Ocarina of Time launches tomorrow.

#3524. Ebenezer Review: Johnny Depp Neither Helps Nor Hurts This Passionless Retelling

Charles Dickens' 1843 novella "A Christmas Carol" is one of the greatest stories ever written. It's a tale that is both very much of its time as well as timeless, speaking to systemic issues of cold-hearted greed and inequality as well as the ability to change one's ways for the better. It's a malleable text that can be calibrated for all ages, just as it can be told with everything from a lighthearted touch to a more dour and sinister horror-centric one.

This versatility has led it to become one of the most commonly adapted stories of all time. To put it mildly, we are not lacking for versions of Dickens' "Christmas Carol." That doesn't mean further adaptations shouldn't be made, but rather that the artists behind them should have a unique take on the material; like Shakespeare, it's well known enough to not have to play completely straight.

Yet playing it straight seems to be the entire ethos for "Ebenezer," the new adaptation from director Ti West and starring Johnny Depp as Scrooge. If a "Christmas Carol" adaptation isn't taking a big swerve with either a singing Will Ferrell or Muppets, for example, the general assumption is that some renowned actor will give their take on Scrooge, as luminaries like Alastair Sim, Albert Finney, and George C. Scott have done. That seems to be what West and company are assuming with Depp in the role, and it's likely why the rest of the film around him isn't taking too many big swings. Yet it leaves "Ebenezer" feeling a little too plain on the one hand, and potentially unsavory where Depp's personal status is considered. It's a movie that seems to exist on Depp's shoulders for better or worse, a choice that leaves it being technically competent but ultimately confused.

If you already know "A Christmas Carol," then "Ebenezer" will not hold many surprises for you. Ti West and screenwriter Nathaniel Halpern treat Charles Dickens' novella in much the same way the Royal Shakespeare Company might treat "Hamlet," which is to say that they retain the bulk of Dickens' dialogue and structure (the film is even separated into five staves, as in the novella) while coloring outside the lines ever so often. After an original opening sequence detailing the literal end of the partnership between Marley (Ian McKellen) and Ebenezer Scrooge (Johnny Depp), the film chronicles the usual beats of the tale, from establishing Scrooge's miserly, calloused attitude to the gradual thawing of his soul via his haunting by three Christmas ghosts.

Although Paramount Pictures' ghastly marketing campaign promised that "Ebenezer" would present a Scrooge we'd never seen before and go places other adaptations hadn't dared, the true extent of any changes or embellishments to the Dickens tale lies in the way that certain very small supporting characters who purport to either be in service of the needy or in need themselves are revealed to be greedy con artists.

The choice does add a nice little layer of moral complexity to what is typically a straightforward story, yet West and company don't do all that much with it in the end. Given his extensive indie horror background, West does lend the proceedings a welcome macabre aesthetic. This is certainly the spookiest "Christmas Carol" since Robert Zemeckis' bizarre 2006 version. The three ghosts are especially ghastly and eerie, and the whole film has a Victorian London by way of '70s British films feel to it, like if Ronald Neame's "Scrooge" was mashed up with West's "The Innkeepers."

While much of "Ebenezer" is solid and skillfully crafted, it's all clearly in service of the character and the performer at its center. To say that Johnny Depp brings some baggage to the role is to make an understatement, for even setting aside the considerable issue of his offscreen life, his onscreen persona would be its own monolith to reckon with. Especially in this material, as it blatantly conjures up his past successes with director Tim Burton.

What made the Depp/Burton duo special was how the director was able to draw out some truly bizarre character choices from the actor while making sure the film around him fit the outrageous, heightened tone of the performance. Here in "Ebenezer," Depp appears to be shooting more for respectable prestige than crowd-pleasing outrageousness. He's not trying to pull a Jack Sparrow, in other words, and instead is letting the prosthetic makeup do much of the transformation for him.

With the exception of a small moment here and there, Depp's Scrooge is largely solid yet unremarkable. Which begs the question: why bother in the first place? It seems like the entirety of "Ebenezer" was arranged to allow Depp to chew scenery and showboat around, which the actor perversely refuses to do. It's possible that Depp now considers such an approach something he's no longer interested in, and it's not like he hasn't given grounded performances before, like his turn as John Dillinger in "Public Enemies," for example. Depp's performance as Scrooge simply doesn't feel fully realized. It's fine on paper, and even has flashes of depth, yet it ultimately is more calibrated than inspired.

I have a deep affection for "A Christmas Carol," and generally find something to like in all of its many adaptations. In this way, "Ebenezer" is no different. Ti West, Nathaniel Halpern, Depp and the rest haven't twisted the story beyond recognition, nor have they sullied it. Yet in playing things so generally safe, "Ebenezer" becomes a muted film.

West throws in a flourish here and there, like the great work with the three ghost characters or a moment where Scrooge is abducted through his bed that deliberately recalls Depp's cinematic debut in "A Nightmare on Elm Street." There's even an extended denouement to the tale which stands in contrast to most versions of "A Christmas Carol," where instead of rushing through Scrooge's change of heart, the film takes its time as the man makes his reparations.

Yet even that choice feels calculated in a meta sense to better present Johnny Depp, Movie Star, back to the public after his cancellation. After all, this story is famously one about a loathsome man who learns contrition and seeks to make amends, and while the film itself never breaks the fourth wall with this idea, it comes damn close. Even with that held back, it feels like "Ebenezer" is more a proving ground than impassioned adaptation, with West demonstrating he can do more than just indie horror, and Depp showing more of his restraint as a performer. What will happen to Depp the person is not for me to say, but he's going to have to work harder and take more risks than "Ebenezer" if he wants to give his screen career a second chance.

"Ebenezer" opens in theaters on November 13, 2026.

#3522. Daniel Craig's Most Disappointing Bond Film Quietly Exits Streaming This Month

Craig’s time as 007 may be over, but there’s still time to revisit one of his most explosive adventures

Daniel Craig's time as James Bond may be over, but his legacy as the iconic British spy is still being felt across Hollywood. After five films and 15 years in the role, Craig helped usher in a grittier era for the long-running franchise, delivering some of 007's most memorable big-screen adventures along the way.

Now, the search for his successor is heating up. No replacement has been officially announced, but fans could find out who will inherit the famous tuxedo before the end of the year. While audiences wait for the next chapter of the franchise, there's an opportunity to revisit one of Craig's Bond adventures — unfortunately, it's leaving streaming soon and time is running out to watch it again.

Released in 2008, Quantum of Solace picks up shortly after the events of Casino Royale, with James Bond still dealing with the death of Vesper Lynd, the woman he fell in love with during his previous mission.

Determined to uncover the truth behind her betrayal and death, Bond sets out to track down the people responsible. His investigation leads him to Dominic Greene, a ruthless businessman secretly working with a mysterious organization known as Quantum. Greene is plotting to seize control of a valuable natural resource, putting Bond on a collision course with a dangerous conspiracy.

Craig returns as 007, with Olga Kurylenko (Black Widow) joining the cast as Camille Montes, a woman with her own reasons for seeking revenge against Greene. Mathieu Amalric (The Grand Budapest Hotel) plays the film's main antagonist, while Judi Dench returns as M.

Quantum of Solace is an important entry in Craig's Bond era, but its critical reception was somewhat divided. The film currently holds a 63% critics score on Rotten Tomatoes, alongside a 58% audience score. Most reviews praised its intense action sequences and Craig's performance, although some felt it has a weaker story than Casino Royale.

Still, with plenty of explosive action and another compelling performance from Craig, Quantum of Solace is worth revisiting for anyone looking to celebrate his time as 007.

#3520. 10 Shows Like 'Phony' You Should Watch Next

He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

What if you knew your mom wasn't really your mom, but no one believed you? That's the improbable but entertaining premise of Hulu's Phony, which stars Sam Nivola as a teenager who wakes up from a car accident and quickly comes to believe that his mother (Friday Night Lights' Connie Britton) is an imposter. Of course, no one believes him. I'm not sure I believe him, but it'll be pretty boring if it turns out that he just had a really bad concussion the whole time.

It's a coming-of-age drama and a surreal mystery with hints of comedy, and though it borrows elements from other shows, it stands apart for the skill with which it blends everything together. While you wait to see how the story plays out, here are 10 more twisted mysteries to stream now.

A twisty-turny (and well-reviewed) bit of fake identity folderol, Apple Cider Vinegar stars Kaitlyn Dever as Belle Gibson, a real-life Australian cancer survivor (except not really!) With a cheeky sense of humor and a willingness to distort reality, the show follows the wellness influencer as she fakes multiple cancer diagnoses in order to better market her alternative, MAHA-esque app and remedies to the unwitting. As her livelihood comes under threat, her lies grow more elaborate. Stream Apple Cider Vinegar on Netflix.

Alia Shawkat stars here as Dory Sief, an aimless millennial who decides, after seeing a missing-person poster for a college acquaintance, that she's going to make it her purpose to track her down—with the extremely begrudging support of her friends. But neither Chantal nor her disappearance are anything like what Dory expects. The show shifts focus from season to season. Initially a darkly comic take on a Nancy Drew-style mystery, it later finds the gang desperate to cover up a mostly unintentional murder, and getting in deeper each season. It's a funny, smart, and weird and shares talent with Phony in the form of writer/producer Anthony King, who serves as co-showrunner on the new series. Stream Search Party on Netflix.

This one's largely about adults, so it skips the coming-of-age angle central to Phony, but it has a quirky mystery, gaslighting, and a protagonist whose sanity is questioned by just about everyone all the same. This fun and very loose adaptation of the 1989 Tom Hanks film finds Keke Palmer's Samira and Jack Whitehall's Rob moving back to his impossibly safe and tidy hometown. Their house happens to be across the street from a dilapidated Victorian eyesore that may or may not have been the location of a murder a couple of decades before—a murder of a girl who made the mistake of trying to get away. As Samira adjusts to new motherhood and life on the cul-de-sac, she learns that even the nicest of her neighbors have secrets, and comes to suspect that her husband knows more about the missing girl than he's letting on. Stream The 'Burbs on Peacock.

When pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate, working her way into the missing girl's social circle, and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

Based on a Harlan Coben novel, Fool Me Once is a bit more of a political thriller than a coming-of-age thing, but we're still in "what the hell is up with my family?" territory: Michelle Keegan plays Maya Stern, a former special ops pilot dealing with the murder of her husband, whom she then impossibly catches playing with their daughter on a nanny cam. The resulting mystery ties into the earlier death of her sister and leads to a web of conspiracy involving her husband's family and a shady pharmaceutical company. Stream Fool Me Once on Netflix.

A vibe match more than anything else, this dark and twisty mystery with a slightly surreal sense of humor also features a single mom who is definitely not what she appears to be. Kim Mo-mi (Lee Han-byeol, initially), the Mask Girl of the title, is a uniquely complicated woman; she always wanted to be a K-Pop idol, but it was always made clear to her that she's not nearly pretty enough for that kind of stardom. So, in order to fill that void, she's got a side hustle. On top of her boring office job, she puts on a blonde wig and a mask to perform as a camgirl for anonymous men. It's a means to express herself creatively and sexually with a level of control—until a mistake causes her to lose that control, a co-worker discovers her secret life, and desperation leads to murder. The show shifts perspectives continually, feeling most like Phony when it focuses on Mo-mi's daughter. Stream Mask Girl on Netflix.

Flipping things around a bit, albeit in a similar "am I just being paranoid?" vein, The Girlfriend deals with a mom who may or may not be freaking out for no reason. Starring Robin Wright as Laura Sanderson, a wealthy art gallery owner in London whose son (Laurie Davidson) brings home a new, working-class girlfriend, Cherry Laine (Olivia Cooke)—immediately strikes Laura as not-our-kind. But is there more to it? Can someone with the name "Cherry Laine" truly be trusted? There's definitely something off, and we're kept guessing as to whether or not this is the story of a dangerous con artist or an overbearing mom—or maybe a little of each. Stream The Girlfriend on Prime Video.

Coming from Irish playwright and Derry Girls creator Lisa McGee, this show eschews the relatively subtle dark comedy of Phony for something much more gloriously surreal. Three high school friends from Belfast reunite after learning that an estranged bestie has died unexpectedly—except that maybe she didn't; a mixed blessing given that they all have secrets that they were hoping would be buried with the maybe departed. Now they're off to investigate the mystery of the murder(?), which turns into a hunt for the friend that they only thought they knew, while inadvertently revealing plenty of secrets of their own. The tone is all over the place in a way that somehow works, with flashes of sincerity balancing out the comedy. Stream How to Get to Heaven From Belfast on Netflix.

Shin Hye-sun offers up a phenomenal performance as Sarah Kim (well: sort of), a wealthy businesswoman who is discovered, at the series' opening, under a sewer grate. The police detective charged to investigate quickly finds inconsistencies in the woman's identity, and after interviewing Sarah's friend and business associate, comes to feel that neither woman is exactly (or anything, like she seems. Though it takes itself more seriously than Phony, it's still an addictively twisty mystery built around a constructed identity. Stream The Art of Sarah on Netflix.

There's a lot going on in this steamy, telenovela-esque drama. Camila Román (Carolina Miranda) finally meets Fernando Castell (Rodolfo Salas), a Tinder match, in Las Vegas, and things get very hot very quickly—he's everything he seemed to be and then some. If anything, she's the sketchy one: a dancer, not a nurse as she said, and with a possessive ex following her around. Still, it's all going great until she decides to surprise Fernando after he flies back to Colombia (which: never do that), and gets a totally different dude when she asks for him at his work. And that's just the beginning! Stream Fake Profile on Netflix.

#3519. James Gunn And Peter Safran's DC Studios Exit Was Driven In Part By Cost-Cutting (Report)

It's a bewildering state of affairs over at Warner Bros./DC. After seemingly being welcomed into the newly-formed Skydance (the name of the recently-merged Warner Bros. and Paramount), James Gunn and Peter Safran suddenly stepped down as DC Studios co-heads in a move that came as a shock to pretty much everybody outside of Skydance CEO David Ellison and his colleagues. Now, a report claims the pair's ousting was all part of an attempt to save money, which, considering recent developments, certainly seems plausible.

According to IndieWire, Gunn and Safran's exit was partly "about cost-cutting" as Skydance prepares to tackle its $80 billion debt and deliver the $6 billion in yearly savings over the next three years that Ellison has promised. As the outlet put it, "Skydance has also been stunned by the financial picture of Warner Bros.' film unit," which has struggled to deliver many hits in 2026. We already knew that Skydance had inherited massive flops from the Warner deal (including Tom Cruise's "Digger" and "The Bride!"), but an insider has now told IndieWire that the estimated losses stand at almost $1 billion.

According to the report, this played into Gunn and Safran's dismissal, especially since they oversaw one of the most egregious box office failures of 2026 in "Supergirl." (The Milly Alcock-led movie made just $126.5 million at the box office on a whopping $170 million to $186 million budget.) What's more, sources have informed Page Six that "Supergirl" ultimately lost $135 million. So, while the film's performance was always going to impact whether or not Ellison elected to keep Gunn and Safran in their posts, IndieWire's report has indicated that the cost-saving measures were even more integral to his decision than we previously realized.

After the "Superman" sequel "Man of Tomorrow" debuts in 2027, David Ellison will reportedly dismantle James Gunn's DC Universe, resetting DC's cinematic franchise once again. It's a less than ideal development amid the ongoing superhero fatigue that has already seen the genre fall out of favor with mass audiences. For Ellison, however, it seems the real motivating factor is the same thing as always: money.

What makes Gunn and Peter Safran's exit particularly surprising is that Ellison initially seemed to want to keep them at Skydance. In early October 2026, The Hollywood Reporter cited insiders as claiming the DC Studios co-heads met with Ellison and were asked to stay and "keep doing what you're doing." According to Page Six, however, plans were already in the works to replace the pair with the newly-appointed Jeremy Latcham. One source told the outlet, "It was a little bit strange to have it be so publicly stated that [Gunn and Safran] were safe, and during that time, the [Latcham] process had already been kicked off. They were saying one thing, and then they were actively doing another thing."

But as IndieWire points out, not only was Skydance inheriting multiple flops from Warner Bros. generally, Gunn and Safran's deal was "unusually generous." We already knew the pair were reporting directly to ex-Warner CEO David Ellison, who was seemingly content to leave them to it. But these two were also making a tidy profit of their own, with Safran simultaneously heading up his own The Safran Company and Gunn earning big pay days for producing "Supergirl" and "Clayface," and writing and directing both "Superman" and "Man of Tomorrow." According to IndieWire's insiders, Gunn was making as much as $10 million per DC movie.

David Ellison's post-James Gunn and Peter Safran plans make the cost-cutting explanation even more obvious. Jeremy Latcham, who becomes the president and chief creative officer of DC Studios on December 1, 2026, will now report to Skydance studio heads Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein instead of directly to Ellison. What's more, one thing we do know about Latcham is that he has a more mainstream sensibility that Gunn's prediction for lesser-known, more off-beat DC properties. What does that mean in Ellison's eyes? A better chance at earning a decent profit when compared with Gunn's plans to give Batman's two most popular Robins their own movie and churn out Mister Miracle animated shows.

Meanwhile, DC Studios hasn't exactly been the biggest money maker under Gunn and Safran. The Man of Steel is one of DC's marquee characters, yet Gunn's "Superman" made $618.7 million in 2025. That's not bad, but for one of DC's most popular characters, it's a little underwhelming (as was the movie). Elsewhere, things have been similarly underwhelming. "Supergirl" was a box office disaster, and the most recent DC release, "Clayface" has done okay, making $111.7 million on a $40 million budget. Bearing in mind this is DC, one of the jewels in the Warner Bros. crown, you can imagine Ellison taking a look at these figures with the weight of his financial commitments and simply deciding to cut Gunn and Safran loose.

For now, Gunn will stick around to oversee the release of 2027's "Man of Tomorrow." According to a source who spoke to Page Six, however, this is only because of Directors Guild of America rules that meant he "could not be removed." If these reports are accurate, Ellison looks to be more intent upon cutting costs than we realized.

#3518. ‘American Doctor’ and ‘You Can See Everything’ Lead 2027 Cinema Eye Honors Film Nominations

The Cinema Eye Honors have revealed nominations for the 20th annual awards ceremony. Leading the pack are Poh Si Teng’s “American Doctor” and Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s “You Can See Everything” with seven nominations each.

The A24 Elizabeth Holmes movie also made Cinema Eye Honors history as the first film to be nominated for Nonfiction Feature, Direction, Editing, Production, Cinematography, and Original Score — along with the Audience Choice Prize.

Other films that fared well in nominations for the ceremony honoring outstanding artistic achievement in nonfiction and documentary films and series, which is often a bellwether for the Best Documentary Feature Oscar race, are Sara Dosa’s “Time and Water,” which scored six nominations, and recent Neon acquisition “NAZA,” which earned five nominations. Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, directors of the latter film, won at the 2025 Cinema Eye Honors for their previous film “No Other Land,” which won the Oscar for Best Documentary Feature. Related Stories What Makes a Good Oscar Campaign? Just Ask Sony Classics’ Michael Barker and Tom Bernard ‘Ebenezer’ Review: Johnny Depp Is Absolutely Insufferable in a Dull and Dreary Christmas Carol

For individual recognition, “American Doctor” filmmaker Poh Si Teng has the most nominations this year, with five. “You Can See Everything” directors Fielder and Oppenheim received four apiece. Meanwhile, documentarian Jimmy Chin, who earned three nominations for “Everest: The Other Side,” which he co-directed with Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi, moves into third on the all-time nominations list with 14 total nods.

Among distributors, HBO, National Geographic and Netflix tied with the most nominations, with each receiving 12 nods across all categories. Neon followed with nine nominations, while A24 and Watermelon Pictures both had seven.

After a first round of voting that saw nonfiction fans worldwide cast tens of thousands of votes for their favorite films, the Audience Choice nominees were announced. The last eight winners of the Best Documentary Feature Oscar— “Mr. Nobody Against Putin,” “No Other Land,” “20 Days in Mariupol,” “Navalny,” “Summer of Soul,” “My Octopus Teacher,” “American Factory,” and “Free Solo”— were all first contenders for the Audience Choice Prize. Second-round voting to determine this year’s winner will take place in December.

In addition to the previously announced Unforgettables Honorees, Broadcast nominees, and the Shorts List, Cinema Eye announced that Steve James’ documentary masterpiece, “Hoop Dreams,” will receive this year’s Legacy Award, presented to a classic nonfiction film that continues to inspire today’s working filmmakers.

This season, Cinema Eye will return to the Times Center in New York City, the home of its second and third editions, for its 20th Awards Ceremony on Monday, January 11, 2027. Cinema Eye Week, which includes events and activities for Cinema Eye nominees and honorees, kicks off in New York on Friday, January 8.

Wednesday, December 2: Shorts List Screenings, DCTV, New York

Saturday, December 5: Shorts List Screenings, Vidiots, Los Angeles

Monday, December 14: Shorts Nominees Announced and Final Audience Choice Voting Opens

Friday, January 8, 2026: Cinema Eye Week/end begins in New York City

Monday, January 11, 2026: 20th Annual Cinema Eye Honors Awards Ceremony

See the full list of this year’s Cinema Eye Honors announcements and nominees below.

Note: This is the second year that the named nominees in the Nonfiction Feature category will include the entire creative team – the directors, producers, editors, cinematographers, composers, sound designers, visual designers, and significant on-screen participants.
