#3517. Firefox's New 'Mini Window' Feature Is a Game Changer for Productivity

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

For many of us, web browsing involves juggling dozens of tabs at once, and it's easy for important pages to get lost in the chaos. Now, Firefox has introduced something I think could help us multi-taskers: a "Mini Window." As highlighted by ZDNET's Jack Wallen, this new Firefox feature works like picture-in-picture overlays for videos—only here, that PiP displays a website.

"[Mini Window] lets you move a tab, or a selected section of a page, into a compact window that stays on top of your other windows while you browse," runs Mozilla's official blurb. "It's useful when you're multitasking and need to keep a few sources of information in view at once: Reference docs, a chat, a video call, a form you're filling out." As such, Mini Window doesn't necessarily replace running tabs side-by-side; rather, you can prioritize one tab in a full-size window, while keeping another page in view at all times.

This is a feature that's still in its early stages, and right now you can only get it in the "Nightly" version of Firefox, a very early beta version of the browser. Mozilla says it will push the feature to the full version of the browser later this month.

If you want to try this out as soon as possible, first install Firefox Nightly on your Mac or PC. Once up and running, you can launch Mini Window by right-clicking on a tab header and choosing Move Tab > Move to Mini Window. The tab shrinks and drops down to the lower right corner by default, staying on top of all other windows (not just Firefox). You can then scroll through the page and follow links as normal in the Mini Window—any links set to open in a new tab (manually or automatically) will launch in the main Firefox view, not the window overlay.

By dragging the title bar around, you can put your Mini Window anywhere you want on screen, and you can change its size by dragging the edges of the window too—so it doesn't necessarily have to be all that "mini." Firefox hides all buttons by default—including forward, backward, and refresh buttons, together with the address bar and buttons for closing the window or putting it back as a normal tab—though they appear when you hover over the Mini Window.

I'm finding the feature most useful when writing up articles where I need to refer to something else already on the web (so almost all of them), but there are a host of ways this can be used. It's particularly handy on a small laptop, where you don't necessarily have the screen space to put two tabs side by side, or when running a lower-priority window (like checking a social media site while reading an important document). No doubt, Firefox will continue to refine and improve the feature as it makes its way to the stable version of the browser, and it feels like something other browsers (looking at you, Google Chrome) might adopt as well in the near future. Eventually, using Mini Windows might become as common as opening up a long row of tabs.

#3516. 'Avatar: Seven Havens’ Season 2 Release Date Announcement Includes Some Shocking Good News

Book 2: Discovery will feature a big reunion and more answers about Korra

Book 2: Discovery will feature a big reunion and more answers about Korra

Avatar: Seven Havens spent its entire first season in the Haven of Ellora, but as the show's title makes clear, that's just one of many Havens spread across this post-apocalyptic landscape. Paramount Plus announced Thursday that Book 2: Discovery premieres surprisingly soon, while also confirming that Avatar Pavi’s (Saheli Khan) journey to repair the broken world is about to pick up speed. The announcement, which also confirms Avatar: Seven Havens Book 3 will come soon after Book 2, includes a synopsis that answers some of our most pressing questions following the season 1 finale: Is this now Pavi’s story? What will happen to Nisha (Aishu Devan)? Where will the plot take them and when will they reunite? Already, we’re getting answers to these and other questions.

Spoilers follow for Avatar: Seven Havens season 1.

Like Book 1: Survival, the next season of Seven Havens consists of 13 episodes released over four consecutive Fridays:

In Book 2, entitled ‘Discovery’, Pavi continues her chakra journey to the Floating Isles and learns more about what happened to Korra. Meanwhile, Nisha discovers vital information about the mysterious spirit energy Pavi released from Ellora. The girls are brought together in New Ba Sing Se, along with all their unresolved issues.

Throughout Book 1, Ellora was plagued by the Anomaly, a sort of spiritual affliction associated with fear that manifested as a diamond-shaped entity made of red energy. After a huge concentration of that energy exploded near Ellora, it created a large dome that threatened to consume the entire Haven. Only by unblocking her own root chakra was Pavi able to redirect the energy through her body and into the sky, where it manifested as an aurora. Based on a vision she received right after, another Haven called the Floating Isles needs her help. So at the end of Book 1, Pavi sets out into the Harshlands with Jae (Major Curda) at her side.

While inside the Anomaly dome, however, Pavi had learned the truth about her and Nisha’s past: Their parents had tried to surrender Nisha to the White Lotus, fearing her powers. In a fit of despair, Nisha emitted a jolt of red lightning that caused a rockside to seemingly crush her parents and sever Pavi’s leg. The twins then have a fight, and Pavi decides to leave Nisha behind. That accounts for the aforementioned “unresolved issues.”

My best guess about the “mysterious spirit energy Pavi released” has a lot to do with the state of the world. Bender birth rates are on the decline, spirits are virtually nonexistent, and the land itself is in a sorry state of decay. It would appear that spiritual energy worldwide has ceased flowing properly. Which is why the series has put so much emphasis on chakras. If the flow of energy in the world has stagnated into gross pockets of stale liquid like the red pool seen underneath Ellora, then transforming it back into its natural state could be precisely the mission that the Avatar(s) must accomplish to fix the world.

Pavi learning more about what happened to Korra in Book 2 is a welcome detail that feels like a must. One of Book 1’s more compelling sub-plots involves a flashback that the twins experience of Korra seemingly destroying Republic City. Everybody blames her for the Cataclysm, but there must be a deeper explanation there. What really happened to Avatar Korra?

The official description for Book 2 confirms, like I theorized, that the next stop on the Avatar’s journey after the Floating Isles is New Ba Sing Se. Pavi’s visions draw a clear connection between saving the Seven Havens and unblocking her own seven chakras. Ellora is the red earth chakra associated with survival and blocked by fear. Since the Floating Isles is associated with the color orange, we know it’s the second chakra which focuses on pleasure and is blocked by guilt.

In the Seven Havens world map shown during the show’s opening credits, the Haven associated with the yellow chakra is located in the northeast corner of what used to be the Earth Kingdom, which is exactly where Ba Sing Se was located until the Cataclysm. The third chakra is associated with willpower and is blocked by shame. That makes New Ba Sing Se a fitting place for the twins to reunite and grapple with “all their unresolved issues.” Think of the shame Nisha feels for what she did to their family. Think of the shame Pavi probably feels for abandoning Nisha after everything they’ve both gone through. And think of the shame they both feel for being the dual reincarnation of Avatar Korra, the person everyone thinks destroyed the world.

Letting go of all this shame seems like a natural place for Book 2 to go, which also means we’re probably going to get some cleaner answers about what actually caused the Cataclysm and what Korra’s real role was in it all.

To hear that Nisha has a parallel role that intersects with her sister again in Book 2 is a relief. Plenty of fans have voiced concerns about Seven Havens becoming “the Pavi show.” The finale positioned Pavi as the Avatar setting out to fix the world, while Nisha simply stayed behind and was praised as the hero of Ellora. For them to reunite seems like a wise decision.

Book 1 also established a practical reason for Nisha to travel. When members of the White Lotus tested her bending powers, they said that she needed to train in other Havens to sharpen her skills. And when Nisha exposed herself as the Avatar to fight Agam (Sakina Jaffrey) during the summit, Agam made a point to say that Nisha only knows Elloran bending styles. Each Haven seemingly has its own bending techniques, which could position New Ba Sing Se as a training destination that puts her on a collision course with Pavi, rather than somewhere she visits specifically to find her sister. Although, whatever information Nisha uncovers about the energy Pavi released could be so important that she has to find Pavi to tell her.

Paramount Plus hasn’t announced a premiere date or title for Book 3, but the streamer did confirm that it will also consist of 13 episodes and be released later in 2027. Book 4 will conclude the series, with release details still to come.

The accelerated release schedule means we may see substantially more of this world before the end of next year. If Book 2 covers the Floating Isles and New Ba Sing Se, four Havens remain for the final two seasons.

Following the chakra sequence, the next two would be green and blue: the heart chakra, which deals with love and is blocked by grief, and the sound chakra, which deals with truth and is blocked by lies. Feather Mountain and Akasha are possible matches, though their respective colors remain unconfirmed. Beyond those lie the light chakra, concerned with insight and blocked by illusion, and the final thought or crown chakra, associated with cosmic energy and blocked by earthly attachment. The light chakra appears to be located in or near the ruins of the old Fire Nation, and Republic Forest is almost certainly the final stop.

That gives the remaining story a framework, but it doesn’t dictate who visits each location or when. The twins could continue together after New Ba Sing Se or go their separate ways to help the remaining Havens separately. Saving Ellora felt like a big deal that took an entire season, but we’re about to step into a much bigger world in May when Book 2 begins.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3515. The Lord Of The Rings: The Rings Of Power Season 3: The Secret Fire Explained

You cannot pass! The dark fire will not avail you, flame of spoilers for "The Rings of Power" Season 3, Episode 3, "The Secret Fire."

"The Rings of Power" Season 3 does a lot of things right, especially when Sauron is on screen attempting to make a shiny piece of jewelry to master all other pieces of jewelry — all while being haunted by the ghost of Celebrimbor. Indeed, the show shines most when it focuses on the bad guys, like introducing the stunning-looking Nazgnagôl or Adam Young's orc with shifting loyalties and a penchant for poetry.

One thing that is different this season is the lack of mystery identities. We now know very well who Sauron is, we know that The Stranger is actually Gandalf, we finally learn this season who the Dark Wizard is, and we even know why Theo is still in this story. It's as if "The Rings of Power" creators J. D. Payne and Patrick McKay got tired of the waiting around and decided to have god himself come down and explain things directly at the audience.

Well, that is actually exactly what happens in Episode 3, because Gandalf (Daniel Weyman) has an actual burning bush moment and talks to the actual god of J. R. R. Tolkien's Legendarium to learn about the Secret Fire, and his purpose in the story.

In the episode, Tom Bombadil (Rory Kinnear) sends Gandalf on a quest to chase a rabbit. This leads Gandalf to an altar where the rabbit combusts into a flame that speaks to the wizard and explains he is the almighty, whose Secret Fire burns inside every creature on Middle-earth.

Even though "The Rings of Power" is set in a world of magic rings, dragons, dwarves and elves, we have not really seen a lot of thel supernatural — despite it being relatively common in Middle-earth. The world of J. R. R. Tolkien is one of angels and elves that get resurrected, a world that literally goes from flat to round when the creator of all existence gets angry at men and sinks an entire continent to the bottom of the sea.

This is the most overt example of supernatural fantasy we've got in "The Rings of Power" so far, as Gandalf hears a strange voice (Allan Corduner) coming from a manifestation of a flame. The flame gives Gandalf (after calling him by his original Quenya name Olórin) a cosmic vision as the voice reveals itself to be the one who "built the heavens and the stars," that which burns within all living things. As the voice says, "all of Middle-earth is cradled within my flame."

That is the Secret Fire, which is alluded to by Gandalf in the original "Lord of the Rings" trilogy. The Secret Fire, or Flame Imperishable, is Gandalf's higher calling, essentially the power of Tolkien's equivalent of God. Named Erū Ilúvatar, this being is the creator of the whole world, and his Secret Fire is what gives life to the universe. That fire is inside all living beings, and is the thing Morgoth craved most, because he was unable to create life without it, the reason he was driven to the shadow. In Tolkien's world, the Secret Fire is the equivalent of the Holy Spirit in Abrahamic religions, the manifestation of the almighty within all beings.

It is quite funny that "The Rings of Power" has arguably its biggest exposition dump of Season 3 come directly from god, who reveals to Gandalf the entire history of the Istari and reveals the identity of the Dark Wizard. After 2 seasons of audiences trying to work out the identity of the Dark Wizard and his purpose, along drops god from the heavens and just outright explains that he is actually a Blue Wizard and gives audiences the whole backstory in a single scene.

Of course, as shocking as Erū Ilúvatar appearing in "The Rings of Power" is, it makes sense for the show to introduce him now. That's because he has a big role to play in Season 4 and the fall of Númenor. Still, the idea that this show has now officially involved higher beings in the conflict against Sauron is a deep cut concept that separates this from other fantasy shows.

In Tolkien's text, the Valar (essentially the gods of Olympus under Erū Ilúvatar's Zeus) don't get directly involved in the wars of Middle-earth (at least not since Elrond's father convinced the Valar to physically aid in the fight against Morgoth), but their influence and power is felt all throughout the Second Age of Middle-earth and the war against Sauron. "The Rings of Power" leaning more into the supernatural fantasy of Tolkien is one way of making this already quite expansive world even more interesting and complex.

#3514. 6 Reasons The Rings Of Power Season 3 Has A Record-Setting Tomatometer Score

Prime Video's The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power has struggled to win over audiences since its debut, despite its ambitious approach to bringing J.R.R. Tolkien's Second Age of Middle-earth to television. With an enormous budget, impressive visuals, and an expansive cast of characters, the fantasy series has consistently delivered awe-inspiring spectacle. However, its storytelling decisions have proven far more divisive, and season 3 is continuing that trend.

As the series moves closer to Sauron's rise to power, it is navigating some of its most consequential storylines yet. Unfortunately, the increased stakes haven't necessarily translated into stronger storytelling or a more enthusiastic critical reception. Instead, season 3 has established an unfortunate Rotten Tomatoes record, raising questions about why the fantasy series continues to struggle despite its enormous potential.

The Rings of Power's record-setting Tomatometer score of a middling 80% reflects several criticisms that have followed the series since its premiere, alongside new concerns about season 3's creative direction. From controversial character relationships to disconnected narratives, the latest installment demonstrates that even Middle-earth's most ambitious television adaptation isn't immune to familiar storytelling problems.

The dwarves of Khazad-dûm have consistently provided some of The Rings of Power's strongest character relationships, particularly through Durin IV and Disa. Their marriage has been a grounding force amid the political conflicts and supernatural threats facing Middle-earth. Unfortunately, season 3 complicates that relationship with unnecessary drama that detracts from the more consequential events unfolding around them.

The introduction of Durin's estranged brother, Thrain, creates another power struggle within the kingdom. However, his complicated romantic history with Disa introduces an entirely different conflict, threatening the stability of her and Durin's marriage. Rather than building on these characters' established strengths, the series leans into a familiar love-triangle dynamic that feels out of place.

After a slight shuffle in its release schedule for season 2, Prime Video's The Rings of Power is doing things very differently for season 3.

With the dwarves already dealing with the dangerous influence of the Rings and the future of their kingdom, introducing marital tension seems particularly unnecessary. While family conflicts have always been central to Khazad-dûm's storyline, season 3 sacrifices some of the emotional authenticity that previously made Durin and Disa so compelling.

One of the most persistent criticisms of The Rings of Power has been its pacing, with the series frequently struggling to balance its character-driven storytelling against the larger conflicts unfolding throughout Middle-earth. Season 3 attempts to address this issue by increasing the action and bringing Sauron's growing influence to the forefront. However, the results aren't entirely successful.

The latest installment delivers more battles and confrontations, creating a greater sense of urgency than previous seasons. Nevertheless, these exciting sequences are regularly interrupted by slower developments involving the various kingdoms and characters. The political maneuvering in Númenor, in particular, continues to slow the narrative despite the increasingly significant stakes.

Although the series deserves credit for making its action sequences more ambitious, spectacle alone cannot resolve its pacing problems. With so many characters requiring attention, The Rings of Power struggles to maintain consistent momentum between its biggest moments. Consequently, season 3 occasionally feels like two different shows competing for the audience's attention.

Any adaptation of J.R.R. Tolkien's Middle-earth inevitably faces comparisons to Peter Jackson's acclaimed The Lord of the Rings trilogy. Unfortunately, The Rings of Power has struggled with those expectations since its premiere, and season 3's movement toward more recognizable elements of Tolkien's mythology makes the comparisons increasingly unavoidable.

The introduction of familiar characters and the continued development of Sauron bring the series closer to the Middle-earth audiences recognize from Peter Jackson's films. However, these connections also highlight the differences between the two adaptations. While Jackson successfully balanced enormous battles and complicated mythology with deeply personal character journeys, The Rings of Power has been less consistent in achieving that balance.

Additionally, the prequel's determination to explain the origins of familiar characters, locations, and objects occasionally makes its storytelling feel more concerned with establishing connections than creating something distinctive. Despite the show's impressive visuals and enormous production budget, it still faces the challenge of establishing an identity independent of Jackson's legacy.

The Rings of Power entered television with enormous expectations, but its reception was complicated long before audiences watched its premiere. From The Rings of Power's controversial casting decisions to concerns about deviations from Tolkien's established mythology, the Prime Video series became a frequent subject of debate among fans. Unfortunately, those disagreements have continued throughout its three seasons.

The show's creative liberties have been particularly divisive, especially among viewers who expected a more faithful interpretation of Tolkien's Second Age. Although adaptations inevitably require changes, The Rings of Power has introduced original characters, altered established timelines, and reimagined familiar relationships. These decisions have made it difficult for the series to satisfy every segment of its audience.

After a two-year hiatus between seasons, Prime Video has unveiled the release schedule for The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power season 3.

However, fan backlash doesn't directly determine the show's Rotten Tomatoes Tomatometer, which reflects professional critics' reviews. Instead, the ongoing controversy provides important context for the series' reception. After three seasons, The Rings of Power is still attempting to overcome criticisms that have shaped conversations about the adaptation since its announcement.

One of The Rings of Power's most controversial creative decisions has been its depiction of the relationship between Galadriel and Sauron. Beginning with their interactions when Sauron disguised himself as Halbrand, the series established an emotional connection that some viewers interpreted as romantic. Rather than moving away from that dynamic, season 3 makes it an even more prominent part of the narrative.

The introduction of Galadriel's long-lost husband, Celeborn, creates additional complications. His return should provide an opportunity to explore Galadriel's personal history and the emotional consequences of their prolonged separation. However, Sauron's continuing fixation on Galadriel also places their relationship within a potentially romantic triangle, despite his role as Middle-earth's central villain.

For viewers who appreciate the complicated dynamic, this creates additional dramatic possibilities. Nevertheless, others may find the emphasis on romantic tension distracting from the larger conflict between good and evil. By continuing to explore this controversial connection, season 3 risks alienating viewers who already questioned the show's interpretation of these iconic characters.

Despite its attempts to streamline the storytelling, The Rings of Power season 3 still struggles to connect its numerous narratives. The series covers an enormous geographical area, but not every storyline feels equally relevant to the larger conflict against Sauron. Consequently, some developments feel disconnected from the central plot rather than advancing it.

Gandalf's adventures in Rhûn are a particularly notable example. Although his confrontation with the Dark Wizard expands the mythology, the storyline largely operates independently of the events involving Sauron and the other major characters. This separation makes it difficult to understand how Gandalf's journey contributes to the season's overarching narrative.

#3513. These Signature Sony Headphones Are Under $200 Ahead of Black Friday

The Sony WH-1000XM6 headphones are the most recent entry in Sony's 1000X series, which has been around since 2016. They're the best over-ear headphones in terms of audio quality currently on the market—but not everyone can (or needs to) drop nearly half a grand on headphones.

The WH-1000XM5 are a generation older and were at the top of their class until they were supplanted by the XM6. On the plus side, by virtue of being older, they're currently discounted to $198 (down from the original $399.99) during Amazon's early Black Friday sale. That 50% off brings it down to the lowest price they've ever reached, according to price-tracking tools, a good deal for premium headphones that still sound incredible, even in 2026.

I have been a loyal customer of the 1000X line for many years; they're my go-to headphones for most activities. The WH-1000XM5 received an "outstanding" review from PCMag for their top-notch audio quality and exceptional audio when using the best-in-class active noise cancellation. The headphones are also well-designed to be comfortable for long listening sessions. The ear controls use tapping and swiping, which isn't my favorite, but it's what all modern headphones are moving toward. There's a companion app that lets you adjust your EQ settings to your liking, including what the swiping and tapping functions do.

These headphones also have a stereo 3.5mm connection, which is perfect for those who want to use a cable and not worry about battery life. And speaking of battery life, Sony says you can expect about 30 hours, but it will vary depending on your use of ANC. They are compatible with AAC, LDAC, and SBC codecs and have multipoint connection, meaning you can pair them with more than one device at the same time.

Personally, I think the value for the money you get with the XM5 for $198 is better than paying full price for the XM6. If you're looking to get ahead of the Black Friday chaos and secure an amazing deal on great headphones, this is it.

#3512. Marvel Officially Confirms Whether RDJ's Doctor Doom Is A Tony Stark Variant

When Marvel Studios announced Robert Downey Jr. would play Doctor Doom in "Avengers: Doomsday" fans used one word to describe it: desperate. But anticipation for RDJ's return has only grown as "Doomsday" has drawn nearer. Still, significant confusion remains. After all, Downey Jr.'s best-known role is that of Tony Stark/Iron Man in the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Now, he's back in that same franchise as a supervillain? It's all a bit confounding, really, and while Marvel Studios head Kevin Feige has just tried to clear it all up, he's also somehow made things even more confusing.

Speaking to Empire, Feige was asked whether RDJ is playing a Tony Stark variant in "Doomsday" or an entirely different character. The Marvel Studios boss seemed to indicate the latter is true. "Is Steve Rogers a Johnny Storm variant?" he said in reference to Chris Evans having played both characters at different points throughout Marvel's cinematic history. "People wondered, 'Is Doom just a variant of another character? Is this just a shortcut to bringing back another character?' The answer is no. He's Victor Von Doom."

Evans played Johnny Storm in a an entirely different cinematic universe, specifically portraying the Fantastic Four member in the 20th Century Fox Marvel movies. He then played Steve Rogers/Captain America in the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Downey Jr., however, played Tony Stark in the MCU and is now back as Victor Von Doom in that same universe. Sure, the multiverse has made all of this more nebulous. We saw Evans' Johnny Storm in "Deadpool & Wolverine," which means both he and Evans' Steve Rogers could, conceivably, appear together in the MCU. But it would surely feel like a letdown to bring back the most popular and important actor in MCU history as a villain and let that be that.

Doctor Doom was once Iron Man in the comics, and in 2010's "What If? Iron Man: Demon in an Armor" an amnesiac Tony Stark became the supervillain. But Kevin Feige has seemingly confirmed the Victor Von Doom of "Avengers: Doomsday" is like neither of these examples.

According to the Marvel Studios head, Robert Downey Jr. is playing an entirely separate character to Tony Stark, likely thanks to the multiversal incursions that threaten to collapse the universe in "Doomsday." What we'll essentially see, then, is a character named Victor Von Doom who hails from an entirely different timeline to the main MCU (likely the one that gave us 2025's "Fantastic Four: First Steps"), has no connection to Tony Stark, and just happens to look like the former Iron Man. I feel confident in saying that this only raises more questions. Is there another Tony Stark in Doom's timeline? Is there really no connection at all between RDJ's villain and the Iron Man of the MCU?

Regardless, "Doomsday" directors Joe and Anthony Russo promised Empire that this Doctor Doom will be a truly scary villain, with Joe saying he's "a Gothic character" and "a very powerful character with some very dark magic" who's "not above selling his soul to get what he wants. He's worth being scared of." Interestingly, the co-director added that RDJ's Doom is a "father who's a victim of trauma" and that he has "lost a child." The only parallel there between Downey Jr.'s Tony Stark and his Doom is that the former was once particularly shaken by losing Tom Holland's Spider-Man to Thanos' snap in 'Avengers: Infinity War." Otherwise, he's never lost a child, which is further proof that this is a different character and not a Tony Stark variant.

According to Joe Russo, those who've seen early screenings of "Avengers: Doomsday" have said "it's a very scary movie" due to Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom being "so profoundly damaged." Clearly, the loss of his child is what drives this particular incarnation of Doom — which puts some of the "Avengers: Doomsday" trailer footage in context. In the trailer, we hear Vanessa Kirby's Sue Storm/Invisible Woman saying, "Victor [...] used to be different. He used to be kind, he used to be caring. And then, everything he loved was taken from him." This is obviously in reference to the loss of his child. In that same trailer, Doom accuses all the heroes of having lived "stolen lives," suggesting that something they did in previous MCU installments might have triggered the event that led to his child's death.

Unfortunately, while Downey Jr. did talk to Empire, he didn't shed much light on the Tony Stark variant question. Instead he talked about Michael Douglas at the end of "Falling Down," saying "He goes, 'I'm the bad guy?' I had that realization a couple of days into shooting 'Doomsday,' because all the heroes are over there, and I'm the problem." The actor recalled having "leaned in" to being the villain and having a "glorious time." That's lovely Rob, but are you Iron Man or not? Otherwise, he described Doom as being on a "scorched earth" mission, adding "Whatever you think he may be entertaining, I would ten times it, and you'll probably be closer to the ballpark."

Did Marvel really bring back RDJ without intending to at least hint at Tony Stark's possible return? It seems unbelievable. For now, we'll have to wait until "Doomsday" hits theaters on December 18, 2026 to find out.

#3510. Five Hacks Every Una Watch User Should Know

The Una watch is pretty much made to be hackable, with its interchangeable parts and open development environment. But it’s also pretty barebones at launch, without many features available yet. However, here are five things I’ve discovered I can do with it—and I hope to expand this list quite a bit as the device and its community mature.

Because the Una watch has a regular USB-C port, you don’t need to remember any specific cable, dongle, or adapter to charge it. I knew that, but it didn’t occur to me until recently that I didn’t need a computer or a wall outlet to plug into the other end. I was able to take a USB-C to USB-C cable—the same kind I might carry around to charge my phone—and plug one end into my watch and the other into my phone. It charged!

(You can also charge some other devices from a phone, including an Apple Watch, but you’d need to carry around that specific adapter, which is why nobody bothers.)

The Una watch doesn’t have any built-in sleep tracking, but a few community-built apps aim to provide it. The Slumber app, for example, will let you know how long you slept and compare your most recent bedtime with when you usually get to bed. There are no sleep stages (honestly: refreshing, since watches are rarely good at this anyway), and the analysis is done on the watch itself.

But if what you’re really hoping for is a recovery score or an overnight HRV reading, the HabitLab app combines that with habit tracking. Every evening, the watch will buzz and ask you to check off which habits or factors played into your day: Alcohol and late meals are among the options, and the watch will automatically detect morning or evening workouts to add them to the list. In the morning, the watch asks you how you slept, and then it gives you a score based on your resting heart rate, HRV, and your subjective rating.

The app is supposed to be able to put together trends and insights from this data, but I haven’t managed to get it to do this. Maybe it’s waiting for more data (I’ve been using it a little over a week), or maybe it’s just buggy.

By contrast, the barcode app worked even better than I expected it to. It’s meant for a parkrun barcode; each participant in the free weekly 5K has a number that you can use to check your results online. But it works just as well for other barcodes.

I installed the Barcode app and entered the number for my library card. Perhaps because of the watch’s MIP screen, I found this barcode scanned more reliably than any barcodes I’ve previously tried to use on a watch. The library scanner picked it up just fine on the first try, and a phone-based scanner also had no problem with it. You can store up to six barcodes, so I’ve also entered a few others, like my grocery discount card.

The app supports QR codes as well as regular barcodes, and to enter a QR code, you just type in a shortened URL. (It needs to be 22 characters or less.) This means that the Barcode app is also a QR code creator, a nifty feature indeed.

Seeing how soon the sun sets is a bit of a downer as we leave daylight saving time and get into the dark winter months, but it’s also helpful in planning. The Sun & Moon Face puts a graphic on your wrist that shows how far along the sun is in its trajectory across the sky for the day. When evening is approaching, you’ll see just how little time you have left.

The app grabs your GPS location once a day, which means that for the first few hours I wore it, the sunrise and sunset times were incorrectly listed as 6 a.m. and 6 p.m. But as long as you aren’t flying to a drastically new location every day, the app does the job just fine. As a bonus, it changes the color of the screen’s sky to show daylight, nighttime, or sunrise/sunset colors.

If you want to hack this hackable watch, you might as well take the plunge and try to build something yourself. Instructions are here to download the development tools for Windows, Mac, or Linux, and there are tutorials for different features you might want to use and implement. There are also about a dozen example apps you can build on, including activity trackers, watch faces, and glances. I'm not much of a coder myself, but this is the friendliest setup I've seen for someone to get into building their own apps for a watch.

#3509. Sony's Bringing Back Spider-Man $2.5 Billion Hit With New Footage

Sony's $2.5 billion superhero hit isn't done dominating movie theaters yet

As Marvel Studios' release of Avengers Endgame: Encore proves, blockbuster movies can still dominate the box office, even after a multibillion dollar run. Sony is planning a rerelease of Spider-Man: Brand New Day to bring web-head-heads back to movie theaters — and like Endgame: Encore, the studio is adding new footage of Spider-Man's latest flick as an incentive.

Thanks to AMC Theatres, we now know what that rerelease will be called: Spider-Man: (Brand New) Brand New Day.

According to the AMC Theatres listing, Spider-Man: (Brand New) Brand New Day will be seven minutes long, with a run time of 2 hours 32 minutes. It's unclear how much of that will be new or restored footage, but it will be longer than Brand New Day's original theatrical run.

Spider-Man: (Brand New) Brand New Day is expected to arrive in movie theaters on Dec. 4.

According to a previous report from Deadline, the new footage will include at least one cut cameo from Spider-Man: Brand New Day that connects to the larger Marvel Cinematic Universe.

Deadline reports that Sony's planned theatrical rerelease of Spider-Man: Brand New Day will feature extra footage that includes an appearance from Rosario Dawson's character Claire Temple, aka Night Nurse. Dawson played Temple in multiple Netflix Marvel shows: Daredevil, Jessica Jones, Luke Cage, Iron Fist, and The Defenders. The Night Nurse had her own Marvel comic series in the early '70s, in which she tended to the medical needs of New York City's vigilante crime fighters (though that version of the character was named Linda Carter).

Dawson has said in interviews that she filmed a scene that was cut from the theatrical release of Spider-Man: Brand New Day. Deadline's report implies Sony has more than just a Claire Temple cameo in its pocket, saying there will be "more surprises in the extra footage."

If accurate, this wouldn't be the first time Sony has rereleased one of its Tom Holland-starring Spider-Man movies in theaters. The studio released an extended cut of Spider-Man: Far From Home and a "More Fun Stuff Version" of Spider-Man: No Way Home, the latter of which featured deleted scenes.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day's rerelease will no doubt help goose the film's box office haul, which currently stands at $2.52 billion, according to Box Office Mojo. Brand New Day is the highest-grossing movie at the domestic box office to date, with $959 million after two months in theaters. It's also the third-highest-grossing movie worldwide, behind Avengers: Endgame and the original Avatar. It's unlikely the rerelease would put Brand New Day on top; it's still $419 million behind Avengers: Endgame.

#3508. 20 Strongest One Piece Characters

One Piece's world and map aren't the only things that have broadened their scope over the last few decades. Luffy has continued to grow stronger and stronger with every new arc, which in turn means every new opponent he faces continues to do the same as well. As such, One Piece's power scaling has come a very long way since the humble East Blue.

From fighting an evil clown terrorizing a small town to taking down a centuries-old demon secretly ruling the world, One Piece's story and stakes have escalated to sky-high levels in very classic shonen fashion. And, as a result, One Piece now boasts numerous powerful characters, both enemies and allies alike. There are many, like Joyboy, who could be the strongest beings in the entire series, but One Piece has yet to reveal their full skill set properly. Luckily, there are countless others with tangible feats and demonstrated power and skill that immediately distinguish them as One Piece's strongest.

The current Fleet Admiral of the Navy, Sakazuki, is as twisted as he is powerful. His devil fruit gives him the scary power of becoming lava. Although he was no match for an angry Whitebeard, he dealt serious damage to him and contributed to his death.

Akainu's endurance is off the charts, as he battled Aokiji for ten days straight on Punk Hazard and came out on top. His body is extremely strong, withstanding two consecutive full-power punches imbued with both haki and devil fruit powers from Whitebeard and still getting up to fight. Given that his devil fruit power is heat-based, Akainu might also be Luffy's ultimate enemy, with his magma able to seriously wound the Straw Hat captain no matter how far he stretches.

Known as One Piece's strongest swordsman, Mihawk is a lone wolf who managed to become a Warlord despite having no crew. Many journey far and wide to challenge him, including Zoro, and they've all lost. He doesn't have devil fruit powers, as his sword skills and haki are more than enough to defend himself.

With one slash of his huge cross-shaped sword, Mihawk managed to cut a huge iceberg in half and destroy a huge ship. With his incredible agility, observant eyes that gave him the nickname Hawk-eye, and his mastery of haki, he came to be known as Shanks' rival, who is an Emperor of the Sea. Currently, Mihawk, Crocodile, and Buggy are leading the Cross Guild, and though the latter two members are powerful in their own right, there's no doubt that it's Mihawk who is the real muscle of this powerful pirate team.

King "The Conflagration," real name Alber, is one of the All-Stars of the Beast Pirates and Kaido’s second-in-command. Kaido freed King from imprisonment when they were both being experimented on at Punk Hazard, and ever since then, King has been Kaido’s most loyal confidant and the one who most supported Kaido’s quest to become the Pirate King.

One Piece has a surprisingly fiendish rogues gallery, but the worst of its worst have reached nightmarish proportions in strength.

King’s mastery of the Dragon-Dragon Fruit, Model: Pteranodon, gives him a lot of versatility with his attacks, but the biggest source of King’s strength comes from his being a Lunarian, a secret race of winged people with powerful fire abilities and immense speed and durability. Zoro only barely defeated King in their fight, and the fact that King’s Lunarian lineage factor was used as the basis for the powerful Seraphim only further cements his status as an incredibly powerful fighter.

Sanji is the chef of the Straw Hat Pirates and the last person to join the crew before they entered the Grand Line. Before coming to work at the Baratie, Sanji was the outcast of the Vinsmoke family, a notorious group of warmongering mercenaries from the North Blue, and it wasn't until the Whole Cake Island arc that Sanji was forced to confront them with help from Luffy.

Sanji fights using powerful kicks further strengthened by Armament Haki and, most recently, his cybernetic enhancements courtesy of his father, which even let him set his legs on fire to further increase his power and set his opponents ablaze. Sanji's biggest and most recent feat of strength is defeating Queen, one of the strongest members of the Beast Pirates, and there was no better way of solidifying his place within the "Monster Trio" of the Straw Hat Pirates.

Along with Luffy, Zoro has considerably increased his skills and power after setting out to sea only a few years ago in One Piece's timeline. Before he met his future captain in Shells Town, Zoro was already one of the most renowned and feared swordsmen in the entire East Blue. Still, as Mihawk demonstrated to him during the Baratie Arc, he still had a way to go before he'd earn the title of the World's Greatest Swordsman.

Zoro has a habit of pulling off unbelievable feats of strength, like cutting through solid steel and cleaving the Enies Lobby tower in two, and that was before he endured intense training during One Piece's time skip. During his time in Dressrosa and Wano, Zoro cut apart the mountain-sized Pica and deflected Kaido and Big Mom's combo attack, Ocean Sovereignty, which might be the most vigorous attack in the series yet.

Fans would be devastated if Zoro's rematch against Mihawk did not happen because it would show Zoro undoubtedly surpassing his previous feats yet again. And on Elbaf, Zoro is set to surpass his limits once again by finally mastering Conqueror's Haki in his fight against the Holy Knights.

The Holy Knights are One Piece's newest group of antagonists who have only just made their debut in the Elbaf Arc. This legion, which directly presides over the World Nobles, also possesses a contract with Imu in the form of the Depths Covenant. While they may not enjoy the immortality that the Five Elders do as part of the Abyssal Covenant, the Holy Knights of God are still blessed with advanced regeneration that makes them quite tiresome opponents for those unfamiliar with infusing their attacks with Conqueror's Haki.

In fact, the Holy Knights are pretty much unbeatable without Conqueror's Haki. In addition to this, the Holy Knights also possess fearsome devil fruit abilities, be it Gunko's Arrow-Arrow powers, St. Sommers' piercing thorns, or St. Killingham's broken ability to materialize nightmares and dreams. Even those without a devil fruit, like Shamrock, possess powerful devil fruit-infused weapons. The Holy Knights' abilities can also be buffed by Imu's Omen, which also grants them access to their family's weapon.

After nearly fourteen years of being missing in action and fans constantly asking about his whereabouts, Scopper Gaban, Roger's left-hand man, finally made his modern-day debut on Elbaf. Much like Rayleigh, Gaban completely lives up to his reputation as the "Mountain Eater" anda former member of the Roger Pirates with his overwhelming strength.

Gaban has mastered all three forms of haki, with his Observation Haki in particular being so advanced that he was able to sense the Straw Hats approaching Elbaf even when they were still miles away from the shore. Even though he may not be in his prime anymore, Gaban was still able to go up against Imu and the Holy Knights, wielding his twin axes in a most fearsome manner.

As Roger's first mate, Rayleigh's strength is all but given. Even though he may not possess a devil fruit like many of the other strong characters in One Piece, Rayleigh more than makes up for it with his powerful haki. Having taught Luffy everything he knows about haki, Rayleigh himself is a master of all three types of haki, which is quite a rare occurrence in One Piece.

One Piece has revealed a myriad of Devil Fruits thus far, but these 30 are stronger than the rest by a pretty wide margin.

Rayleigh's Armament Haki, in particular, is incredibly powerful and was able to block an attack by Kizaru with relative ease at Marineford. His advanced Observation Haki can instantly perceive every living thing across an entire island with no effort. Rayleigh still retains a lot of physical strength and vigor, as seen from his ability to swim across the Calm Belt and fight Sea Kings with his bare hands. However, he is not immune to the effects of age and even suggests that he no longer has the strength to defeat newer-generation powerhouses like Blackbeard.

Garp is a Vice Admiral but could've easily been a Fleet Admiral if he hadn't refused the multiple offers to be promoted. He frequently fought Gold D. Roger and the latter even said that they almost killed each other many times. Together with Sengoku, they were at the forefront of the fight against the pirates in their younger years. He earned the respect of Roger and even raised his son Ace together with Luffy at Roger's request.

A master of haki and the strength of a superhuman, Garp is one of the strongest, and barely anybody could go toe-to-toe with him in his prime. Though devil fruits might give out some of One Piece's flashiest powers, Garp and others like him prove that the mysterious fruits aren't the only way or the best way to truly obtain strength. He dramatically proved this point when he arrived at Blackbeard's base to rescue Koby, making quite the entrance with one of One Piece's strongest attacks that the anime has adapted so far.

A member of the Worst Generation, Emperor of the Sea and a Warlord, Blackbeard did the impossible by wielding two devil fruits at once. His thirst for power and strength is incredible — killing his own crew member, capturing Ace, and stealing Whitebeard's powers in a plan that finished off the strongest Emperor of the Sea. His pursuit of strength propelled him to monstrous levels.

With One Piece nearing its end, Teach will play a key role as one of One Piece's final villains, as Luffy's brother and adoptive father were killed by him. Blackbeard has been set up as Luffy's ideological opposite in many ways, with the villain using piracy as an excuse to further his own selfish goals, as opposed to Luffy, who is constantly freeing the oppressed. With Blackbeard's ability to wield two devil fruits, it will truly be a blowout when he and Luffy finally get their long-awaited true fight.

#3507. Saoirse Ronan Has Wanted to Direct Since She Was a Kid, and Her Exquisite First Short ‘Paper Plane’ Proves She’s Got the Goods

Like all great directors, Saoirse Ronan has the multitasking thing down pat. Earlier this week, IndieWire exclusively spoke with Ronan as she was walking around London during a particularly “crazy busy” time in her life (yes, we asked about Sam Mendes’ Beatles films, and Ronan could only smile and note that she couldn’t share a thing about them at this moment). Headphones on, jacket collar up, Ronan was getting her steps in while also talking about something she’s wanted to do for a very long time: direct a film.

Earlier this month, Ronan’s “Paper Plane” won Best Narrative Short at the Austin Film Festival after debuting at Venice earlier in the season. Any win is nice, but a win at an Oscar-qualifying festival like Austin comes with an added sweetener: The film is instantly eligible for Oscar consideration for the 2027 ceremony. Jumping behind the camera is something Ronan has wanted to do for years, and her first offering (which she also wrote) is exquisite. Related Stories ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Has 10 Credited Writers, Including Hugh Jackman and Ryan Reynolds Brad Pitt to Star in ‘Connector’ from ‘Sound of Metal’ Director Darius Marder for Apple

The 15-minute short film stars rising young actress Martha Malone as Fay, alongside Clare Dunne as Mam and Tim Creed as Dad. When we first meet Fay, she’s launched a silent protest, announcing to her mother (via a titular paper plane message) that she will not return to their home until her father, who we instantly understand is a toxic presence, leaves for good. As Fay and her trusty dog sit it out in a grassy lot across the street from the family home, Ronan’s film unfolds with grace and honesty, ending on a heart-stopping note.

Ronan also gathered an impressive roster behind the camera, including producer Shirin Eren, who previously produced Ronan’s “The Outrun,” IFTA-winning editor Nathan Nugent, and Kate McCullough, all of whom she describes in sparkling terms. You can get a taste of the film’s tone, visual style, and wonderful performances in an exclusive clip below.

Ahead, Ronan goes deep on her process, why she felt the need to make the jump to directing now (thanks to her “Little Women” co-star Eliza Scanlen), emulating her favorite collaborators like Greta Gerwig and Joe Wright, the one thing about directing that really surprised her, and if she’s ready to make the jump to directing features.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

IndieWire: When we spoke in 2024 for “The Outrun,” you told me that you had wanted to direct since you were a child. Why was this the right project and the right moment?

Saoirse Ronan: I think it was a number of things. It was where I was at in my personal life. I was definitely starting to move into the next stage of adulthood. It felt like a shift was taking place for me internally. I was married, becoming a parent. Change was on the horizon.

And I think it felt, to be honest, if I don’t do it now, who knows when I’ll do it. I also wonder how many mothers in particular feel that way before they go into that next stage of their life where they’re like, “Actually, this is all quite unknown, and I don’t know if I don’t do it now, will it be another 10 years before I can find the time or the space within myself to do something like that that’s for me?” So it really gave me a lot of motivation being in that place personally.

It’s something that I’ve always wanted to do. I was always drawn toward directing, even from before I became an actor. And I’ve been so hugely influenced by the directors I’ve worked with since the age of 10. I guess I was ready to put that into action, and it was always going to be something that involved a young person and a mother, probably. It just felt very serendipitous that it happened when it did. So felt like everything was aligning at that point.

You also wrote this script. What was your writing process like? What surprised you about that?

Maybe it’s different with journalism, although I’m sure it must be incredibly difficult in other ways, but writing’s just really hard. And I knew it would be, but to conjure up something out of nothing supposedly is mind-boggling. I guess I didn’t realize how much of it is about process. As the Italians say, piano, piano, little by little, you take a step forward, and you take two steps back. I’d never been in that position creatively and professionally where it was all on me, so to find the discipline to do that, sit down, and to go, “OK, well, it’s not going to happen if I don’t make it happen,” was a new challenge for me.

I was so lucky to have Shirin Eren, my producer and my partner, Jack [Lowden], and lots of close friends who had already taken that step. Brilliant actor Eliza Scanlen, who’s already done three shorts, and she’s so much younger than I am, has actually been a huge inspiration to me. And I just thought, well, Jesus, if Eliza’s doing it, I have no excuse.

What I’ve learned is, when it comes to doing a feature, I’d definitely love to work with a writer, because I’m not one, and I think there’s a lot I have to learn. This was incredibly personal, so it was coming from such a pure place that it had to come from me, and it had to be written by me. But I certainly am excited by the challenge of working with someone who actually does it for a living and to learn about how to structure something and add art and things like that.

In the film’s press notes, it says that this is “a love letter to your younger self.” What was the most important thing that had to be in there for you, in terms of the script or the visuals or the casting?

There were two things that were very important to me. One was, tonally, I kept circling back to the magical realism route. I wanted it only ever to feel like we were seeing this through a child’s eyes, and in the way that a child makes sense out of the nonsensical and the seemingly impossible and the incredibly difficult thing to fathom and to swallow and to digest and to overcome. Creativity and imagination always plays a part for a child and just making sense out of anything in the world from day dot, from the moment that they’re here. I didn’t want it to feel like a fantasy, but I wanted it to feel like it was heightened in some way, hence the addition of the paper planes, which was something I used to do with my mom.

I used to send her little paper planes when she’d send me to my room with a little note saying, “I’m really sorry that I did this. Please don’t hate me. Please don’t send me back,” or whatever. And I’d peek around the corner of whatever room she was in, I’d throw it at her, and then I’d run back to my room knowing logically she’d know it was me, but tricking myself into believing that she’d believed that this had seemingly come out of nowhere.

It was also very important to me that the father role was never vilified. I didn’t want this to be a piece that was overly black and white and critical when it comes to the situation. I didn’t want to just point the blame at one character. Although there’s clearly something very toxic and dark within the home that’s happening, and it’s ultimately being created by one member of the family for the most part, there’s a reason why this person unfortunately feels the need within themselves to create that toxicity.

I never wanted it to feel like there was any hatred or anger toward that character. It needed to very much be focused on the love of these two girls. Becoming a mother, I really felt with myself that you don’t ever stop being a child. You can say that we become more sophisticated, but I actually don’t know how much we do. And I think to have a character that’s an older female, an older person, and someone who’s younger, but who essentially both remind each other of their inner child, I wanted to bring that out too.

You’ve worked with so many incredible filmmakers over the course of your career. Was there any filmmaker you really wanted to emulate in terms of how you ran your set?

Oh gosh, how I ran my set! It’s a combination of a few people. I think back in the day, the way Joe Wright ran his set was fantastic. The way he was on the ground with his crew, the clarity that he had at the top of the day, the structure he had when it came to planning, I’ve always responded really well to that. I think I was really influenced by that from working with him so early on. The fact that he and Peter Jackson as well always played music live on set, I’ve always felt like that’s a really helpful way to remind cast and crew that, yes, there’s emotional truth in this, but for me, I want to make movies, I want to make films. They’re not documentaries, so there needs to be this heightened quality to it. I feel like having music on set can remind people of that and just get everyone on the same rhythm.

I think the way Greta [Gerwig] is just Greta and John Crowley, the way they are as directors with their actors, I haven’t marched with anyone greater than those two. They bring out something that I haven’t experienced with anyone else, really, and I’ll always strive to be a tenth to what they are as a director. One thing that Greta said is that you need to think of yourself as the most supportive audience member for your actors. She always makes you feel so loved and interesting and wanted, and so I wanted the actors to feel that way.

And to be honest, weirdly, out of every kind of hat that I had to wear as director, directing the actors was the thing that made me the most nervous. Everything else, I was all right, but it felt really natural. But to actually be in the driving seat with other actors and to guide them, I was really, really nervous about that and constantly feeling like, God, I can’t let them down. I can’t steer them wrong. I always want them to feel safe, and they can do whatever they want to do.

Was that the most surprising thing for you?

Yes, that really did surprise me. I wasn’t expecting that, but actually when I think about it and when I think about the kind of actor that I am, it does make sense, because I’m not one of those actors ever that’s like, “Don’t worry, I’ll take control of the room.” Maybe I’ve started to do that more as I’ve gotten older, but we all know plenty of actors that will start giving other actors notes, which is never helpful. Well, sometimes it is actually, maybe that’s not true, but I haven’t been that kind of actor. So that definitely took me by surprise just how self-conscious I was initially. But I think they were happy. The girls said that they felt good, so that’s all I can ask for really.

In our interview for “The Outrun,” we talked about process, and your process is so internal and personal. It’s about being in the moment. You’re not Method. You don’t get caught up in stuff, so I did wonder how that would translate to directing.

It was funny actually because that seemed to translate well. I think because of the way I work, it’s so much about working with the crew and enjoying the atmosphere on set, and it feels so natural for me to be there, so I felt really confident doing that. I’ve been on so many sets where I’ve looked at directors or producers who don’t quite know how to talk to their crew, don’t quite know what the crew needs, and how to wrangle the truth, how to make them feel appreciated and motivated. I feel like I know how to do that. I’ve been on so many sets and grown up with it, and more than anyone else, I spend time with the crew, and I hear what irks them, what their complaints are, what drives them forward, what they appreciate from a director, from a leader.

So I knew what to do in that sense, I think, I hope. I loved working with my first AD. I loved working on the schedule with her. I loved being able to work so in-depth with a production designer. Actors never get to do that kind of stuff. I don’t think being a director is necessarily the hardest job out of every crew member. I think that the skill of being a director is to surround yourself with really, really, really brilliant people who know what they’re doing and to have good taste.

Watch an exclusive clip from “Paper Plane” below.

It sounds like it was pretty joyous for you to assemble your crew.

I think what every director will tell you, which I now know, is that making a short film is fucking really hard and frustrating, because crew need to go and work on a film that will actually pay the money and will keep them employed for two, three months, and a short film is not going to do that.

So actually being able to get the crew that you want can be really, really difficult, but it does mean that the people who do come on board are there because they really want to be. It’s not because they’re getting paid. It’s not because it’s necessarily going to further their career or anything like that. It’s just, they’re doing it because they want it, because they love what they do, and they want to get their energy in the story. They were there because they wanted to invest themselves in the story, and they also wanted to support me, which was just so lovely.

You’re someone who started acting at a young age, so I find it very interesting and compelling that you centered your film around a young star. How did you make sure Martha felt safe and comfortable and supported?

I knew that on day one, Martha was going to be super nervous. She was 14, 15 at the time, and she’d done a few things, but I think whenever any of us have our first day on set, no matter how experienced we are, we’re always scared. I just wanted her to know that I was too, that I was nervous as well, and that we were going to be nervous together, and it was OK, and we were going to take care of each other.

I have the utmost respect for young performers, and I think that when you find ones that are disciplined as well as being talented, you just need to make them feel like they’re never pressured, they’re supported, but they’re being pushed. You’re not necessarily wrapping them in cotton wool, but you want them to feel loved. I wanted her and Claire to feel loved and wanted because they were, and that ultimately I would have to guide us because somebody does, but that there was a contribution they were going to be able to make as performers that I couldn’t, and I valued that.

You mentioned if you make a feature, you want to work with another writer. The inevitable question: Do you want to direct a feature?

Yeah, I do. I do want to do a feature, and I think part of the reason why I was making shorts is because I wanted to see if I could, and if I could, then what was my style, and what did I respond to, and what did I need to work on, and what were my strengths, so that I didn’t use everyone as my training ground on a feature film.

Again, I’ve been on the other side of that as well, where you’ve got someone in the driving seat, and you’re like, “Uh-oh.” I didn’t want to put anyone else in that position. I didn’t want to put myself in that position. I loved it so much, and I do have a lot to learn. I really want to keep going with it. So I would love to do a feature. I have a rough idea of what I want to do, but I know now that that can be the starting point and that it will become what it’s meant to become.

#3506. These Bose QuietComfort Headphones Are $160 Off Ahead of Black Friday

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Bose’s second-generation QuietComfort Headphones in Dewdrop Mint, Eucalyptus Green, and Hazelnut Taupe are down to $199 from $359 ahead of Black Friday, saving you $160 and bringing them to their lowest price yet, according to price trackers. Weighing around 8.1 ounces, they’re among the lightest premium noise-canceling headphones, with generously padded earcups and a cushioned headband that spreads pressure without gripping too tightly, making them comfortable to wear for extended periods. They’re also easy to pack for travel, as the earcups fold and swivel for storage in the included hard-shell carrying case. The removable earpads are another welcome touch, since you can replace them as they wear down without having to retire the entire pair.

Comfort aside, noise cancellation is another area where these headphones deliver, doing a particularly good job of reducing lower-frequency rumble and background chatter, though some higher-pitched voices can still come through, notes this PCMag review. As for their sound profile, it leans warm and bass-forward, with deep lows that suit bass-heavy genres, while the companion app adds Bose Immersive Audio for spatial sound and lets you create customized listening profiles—the three-band EQ is fairly basic, though, so anyone who likes fine-tuning their sound may find the adjustment options limiting.

Connectivity, too, brings some useful upgrades over the previous generation, including Bluetooth 5.4, multipoint pairing for two devices, Google Fast Pair, and lossless audio over USB-C. That same USB-C port lets you charge the headphones while you listen, and the included USB-C-to-3.5mm cable covers standard headphone jacks, including the ones on in-flight entertainment systems. That said, battery life is less impressive, topping out at 24 hours with ANC enabled, although a 15-minute charge adds around 2.5 hours of playback. Wireless audio is also limited to the standard AAC and SBC codecs, with no support for the higher-quality aptX Adaptive—a feature available on Bose’s QuietComfort Ultra Headphones.

#3505. ‘Calvin and Hobbes’ Has the Perfect Christmas Message for Anyone Who Hates the Holidays

The holidays can either be a heavenly experience or Hell on earth, depending on your point of view. If you're in the former camp, you probably love meeting up with family for Thanksgiving and Christmas or seeing decorations line stores as well as your own house. If you're the latter, you find yourself counting the days until the New Year's Ball drops. Movies centered on the holidays is no different; Miracle on 34th Street is a heartwarming tale about the power of belief, while National Lampoon's Christmas Vacation perfectly captures the stress of being around one's family during the holidays. It's Calvin and Hobbes that perfectly captures the malaise around holidays with a single strip.

That strip, which made its debut in 1993, takes the form of a rather humorous poem that Calvin receives from Santa Claus. In this poem, Claus tells an overjoyed Calvin that he's repealing his rules about who's "naughty" and who's "nice", encouraging the spiky-haired youth to embrace his naughtier tendencies. However, that's when the strip ends with a twist: it was all part of a dream, leading Calvin to lament, "I hate being good (or trying to fake it)/Six days until Christmas! I don't think I'll make it." While Calvin and Hobbes was no stranger to depicting the holidays, this strip nails the unspoken pressure that the holiday season puts on kids.

Everyone's heard the song "Santa Claus is Coming to Town," which paints Kris Kringle as an all-seeing force that knows when children are are naughty or nice. While this is more or less meant to get kids to behave, it underlines the pressure that's being put on them at an early age. People are human; sometimes you'll say or do something you don't mean, but it doesn't mean you have wicked intentions at heart. There's also the fact that in an age of constant online surveillance, Santa's observations come off as less benevolent and more creepy (no matter how many movies try to explain it.)

Calvin and Hobbes' Santa strip hits hard for this exact reason, especially when you take Calvin's characterization into consideration. Part of the draw of the series is Calvin's boundless imagination, as his flights of fancy lend themselves well to the comic medium but also get him into trouble. For a kid who loves Christmas as much as he does, it must be tough to try and restrain himself. Therefore, the idea of Santa flipping the script so that "naughty" kids triumph would sound like a legit Christmas miracle to him. It's rather fitting, as Calvin and Hobbes creator Bill Watterson seems to excel when he places the titular duo in a wintery setting.

Four of the largest communities on the planet, and four completely different reasons to belong to one. Here is yours, what it would give you, and the argument you would be having within a week.

You belong to the fandom that is really about comfort. Hogwarts works on people because it is a place rather than a plot, and the pull is not the wizard war so much as the corridors, the food, the weather and the sense that somebody is expecting you.

You belong to the deepest fandom on this list, the one where somebody has always read further than you and is quietly delighted to say so. Middle-earth rewards patience more than any other world in popular culture.

You belong to the loudest and largest tent of the four, the one where three generations are all watching the same thing and none of them agree about any of it. That disagreement is not a flaw in this fandom, it is the main activity.

You belong to the thinking fandom, the one that turns up for the argument rather than the explosion. Trek has always been a series of ethical problems in space, and the people who love it love being asked what they would have done.

A decade of Calvin and Hobbes strips reveals that some of the best ones are set around Christmastime or a wintery setting, and that's thanks to the way that Bill Watterson approaches the holidays. Instead of the usual heartwarming stories, Calvin and Hobbes fans could see Calvin annoying his parents by waking up early on Christmas morning, or him and Hobbes dealing with an army of grotesque mutant snowmen. They could also expect the strip's signature introspection and wit to be deployed, especially in one moment where Calvin's dad criticizes a televised Christmas special for being about "cola, fast food, and beer." Watterson expressed similar thoughts in the documentary Dear Mr. Watterson, where he spoke on the fact that he never chose to merchandise Calvin and Hobbes.

"My strip is about private realities, the magic of imagination, and the specialness of a certain friendship. Who would believe in the innocence of a little kid and his stuffed tiger if their popularity was used to sell over priced kick knacks nobody needs?"

The holidays can be extremely stressful, putting unneeded pressure on people to be around their families or to act a certain way. Calvin and Hobbes highlighted why this pressure is a bad thing, and is a balm to anyone who prefers saying "bah, humbug!" to "happy holidays."

Developed by Relic Entertainment, Company of Heroes 3 is a real-time strategy game that takes players to the Mediterranean theater of World War II. Released in February 2023, it features two single-player campaigns alongside competitive multiplayer and cooperative modes.

Players can command different military factions, manage resources, construct bases, and lead infantry and armored units into battle. Its two campaigns take place across North Africa and Italy, with the Italian campaign featuring a dynamic map that gives players more freedom to approach the conflict. Known for pushing himself to psychological and physical limits for his work, Leonardo DiCaprio is considered one of the greatest actors of his generation. From blockbusters that blend artistic ambitions with emotional vulnerability to gritty indie films, the actor is celebrated for his range and versatility.

Even before Titanic made him a household name, DiCaprio had already proved his chops as a young actor in films like What's Eating Gilbert Grape, which earned him his first Oscar nomination. After Titanic, he pivoted to taking on more mature roles instead of playing similar heartthrobs and forged a career-defining partnership with Martin Scorsese.

Similar to DiCaprio, Tom Hanks is considered one of the greatest actors of all time, but the Forrest Gump actor took a very different route to building his career. Hanks got his start in community theater and television comedies and transitioned to playing everyman heroes and historical figures.

Instead of pursuing a dramatic pivot, the actor built long-term working relationships with mainstream directors like Steven Spielberg, Robert Zemeckis, and Ron Howard. He also took on commercial projects, such as voicing Sheriff Woody in Disney and Pixar's Toy Story franchise.

Despite having very different careers, their paths once crossed in Spielberg's 2002 biographical crime comedy, Catch Me If You Can, inspired by a true story. Fans can now watch the movie for free in the comfort of their home.

Based on the semi-autobiography of real-life con artist Frank Abagnale Jr., Catch Me If You Can takes some creative liberties and sees DiCaprio as the titular con man trying to escape consequences in a cat-and-mouse chase with Hanks's FBI agent Carl Hanratty.

In addition to two of the biggest names in the movie scene, the crime comedy's star-studded cast also features Christopher Walken as Frank Abagnale, Jennifer Garner as Cheryl Ann, Ellen Pompeo as Marci, and Elizabeth Banks as Lucy.

On November 1, Catch Me If You Can joined Tubi as part of the platform's movie lineup, which allows fans to stream it for free. In addition to Tubi, the 2002 crime comedy is also free with ads on YouTube and included in Paramount+, Peacock, and MGM+ subscriptions.

From Jurassic Park to Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade, Spielberg's most entertaining movies usually combine high-stakes stories with humor and a breathless pace. Frank Abagnale Jr.'s story, on its own, already has the marks of what would make a highly entertaining movie. Spielberg pushed it even further by adding a personal touch.

The Jaws director was particularly invested in Frank Abagnale Jr.'s story, having lived a similar chapter in life following his parents' divorce. He explained it to Back Film in an interview: "I thought it was one of the most amazing stories I'd ever heard... some of this pictures is important to me because it deals with what Frank and I both share, which is broken homes." He once spent a summer dressing up as an executive in on the Universal Studios lot so that he could study filmmaking up close.

#3502. This TP-Link Wi-Fi 7 Travel Router Is 27% Off for This Early Black Friday Deal

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

A novel solution for connecting to the internet on the go, the TP-Link Roam 7 travel router is now down to $87.99 from $119.99 in an early Black Friday deal—marking its lowest price to date, according to price trackers. This is not a full-size home router but, as the name suggests, a compact travel companion that measures roughly the size of a paperback book, with foldable antennas so it slips easily into a bag.

More about convenience than chasing top speeds, you can use the Roam 7 as a standard router, connect it to public wifi to create a private network, or share your phone's internet through USB tethering. It also supports Ethernet input and USB modems, along with range extender and wireless client modes. That flexibility is particularly useful when you’re juggling a laptop, phone, and maybe a tablet and would prefer not to sign each one into a shaky network separately. Setup is straightforward through the TP-Link Tether app: scan a QR code, choose your connection type, and you’re online in a few minutes.

Once it’s running, the hardware covers the basics, with a 2.5 Gbps port for a wired connection like a hotel’s Ethernet jack, a 1 Gbps port for a wired device, and a USB 3.0 port for a storage drive or phone tethering. And since it draws power over USB-C (5V/3A), a basic power bank can keep it going through a long layover or a camping trip. As handy as it is on the road, though, it’s not meant to replace a full-size home router—even with its 5 GHz band and Wi-Fi 7 support—which will generally offer better coverage and more consistent speeds. Real-world performance also depends heavily on your connection and setup. USB tethering, for example, can feel slower than using your phone directly. It also leaves out features like automatic band steering, so you may end up managing networks yourself. Still, if you travel often or need a portable network hub for multiple devices, you’ll find it holds up pretty well.
