#3501. ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Has 10 Credited Writers, Including Hugh Jackman and Ryan Reynolds

It appears that Marvel has assembled a team of earth’s mightiest screenwriters to shape its most epic blockbuster yet.

The Writer’s Guild of America has added the full list of writers who worked on “Avengers: Doomsday” to its directory, and comic book movie fans are already scanning it for clues about the film‘s contents. For one thing, the credits erase all doubts that Deadpool and Wolverine will appear in the film, as both Ryan Reynolds and Hugh Jackman are listed as providing additional literary material for the film. Reynolds was a writer on 2024’s Deadpool & Wolverine,” but this is actually Jackman’s first official writing credit listed in the WGA directory. Related Stories Brad Pitt to Star in ‘Connector’ from ‘Sound of Metal’ Director Darius Marder for Apple ‘American Doctor’ and ‘You Can See Everything’ Lead 2027 Cinema Eye Honors Film Nominations

When the credits finally roll at the end of the gargantuan superhero team-up, audience members will see that the screenplay was written by Marvel veterans Stephen McFeely and Michael Waldron. But the Guild’s database also lists writers who did behind-the-scenes work on the script. A whopping eight writers received that “additional literary material” credit: Reynolds, Jackman, Eric Pearson, Chris McKenna, Erik Sommers, Jeff Loveness, Andrew Lanham, and Destin Daniel Cretton.

The large list of writers is understandable when you consider how many characters “Doomsday” has to cover. In addition to catching audiences up with everyone who survived “Avengers: Endgame” (and in all likelihood, some people who didn’t thanks to the endless power of multiverses), the film also has to introduce Robert Downey Jr.’s Dr. Doom as the MCU’s new villain, integrate the characters from “Thunderbolts*” and “The Fantastic Four: First Steps,” and introduce the new X-Men that the studio hopes will become its next juggernaut superhero property. Many of the credited writers on “Doomsday” have recently written or directed those characters’ standalone films.

The writing credits also speak to the uniquely chaotic production process that the film employed. Joe and Anthony Russo, who returned to direct their first Marvel movie since “Endgame,” have publicly admitted to starting production without a finished script. Joe Russo recently told the Associated Press that they “always view the script as a living organism” that evolves throughout the shooting process. It’s unsurprising that such long shoot with a changing script and a revolving door of A-list actor schedules required the services of double digit writers along the way.

Disney will release “Avengers: Doomsday” in theaters on Friday, December 18.

#3500. ‘The Good Daughter’ Showrunner Explains What the Finale’s Biggest Twists Mean for Sam and Charlie

Editor's note: The following contains spoilers for The Good Daughter.

With the six-episode Peacock series The Good Daughter, author Karin Slaughter knew she had to be the one to adapt her 2017 novel and take the reins as showrunner. Having spent so much time developing the sister bond between Charlotte and Samantha, figuring out how tragedy would shatter their family dynamic before piecing it back together, and unraveling all the twists and turns on their way to newfound hope, she felt responsible for getting it right. What resulted is a suspenseful thriller rooted in a deeply emotional story about a single night of violence that rippled through so many lives, altering them forever.

Collider recently got the opportunity to chat with Slaughter about her experience putting so much of herself into bringing The Good Daughter to the screen. During the interview, she discussed wanting to capture the heart of the story and characters with the adaptation, watching Rose Byrne and Meghann Fahy bring estranged sisters Sam and Charlie together after 20 years, the energy Brendan Gleeson brought to the set while playing their father, revealing all those layers of secrets, figuring out exactly how much to show of the heaviest moments, and the importance of leaving these sisters in a better place. She also talked about how she feels about the ABC series adaptation of Will Trent, which will return with Season 5 in 2027.

COLLIDER: There’s definitely no better way to stay true to the source material and ensure that what you want the show to be is what it becomes then to be the showrunner, writer, and co-executive producer of the adaptation of the story you wrote. Was that something that was always very important for you to do, especially for this story?

KARIN SLAUGHTER: Yeah, 100%. I’ve had stuff adapted before, and I love it. I thought they did a great job with Pieces of Her. Will Trent is still going strong. I think they’re doing an amazing job with that. But with this, I thought, “If you’re going to do it, then you need to really commit to doing it.” Writing all the scripts, being on set for 71 days, learning all the ropes, and figuring out how to make things work was really part of the endeavor for me. I’m very much a control freak. I like to think of myself as a benevolent dictator. Just being really hands-on gave me the ability to make sure that the scripts matched the book and the show matched the scripts.

When you adapt a book from 2017 into a TV series in 2026, do you want to change things or create any new or different surprises for viewers who will have read the book and come to this with that knowledge?

SLAUGHTER: Yes and no. The most common complaint is, “The show changes things and it’s not like the book.” So, what was most important to me is that I capture the heart of these characters. Anybody who’s read the book will immediately recognize the characters. They haven’t changed in any demonstrable way. But you do have to figure out how to have this plot work in six episodes and to have something at the end of every episode that leads you into the next one, so by necessity, things have to change. With the book, I get 500 manuscript pages to tell you how people are thinking. But with a script, I have to express that through dialogue. So, it’s necessary to change things, but what I wanted to hold onto was the spirit of the book so that there was some cohesion.

You have so many layers to the reveals at the end of this story. Did you want to throw anything in to just completely surprise people who had read the book?

SLAUGHTER: The thing about writing a show is that it’s so collaborative. What I think of when I’m writing in my head is so different from readers think about because they’re bringing their own experience and their own lives into the reading of the story. Then you take that and you create a script, and you give it to someone who is your set designer that’s going to find these remarkable locations you’ve never thought about, or you’re going to give these lines to someone like Rose Byrne or Meghann Fahy or Brendan Gleason and watch them put a different interpretation on it because they are incredible artists and they find their own way into a character.

It was really interesting watching Rose because of the fact that she’s just Rose Byrne. She brought this warmth to Sam that you don’t really have in the book. It was really incredible to watch how she balanced that tightrope of keeping true to the character, but also adding her own spin. When I write a book, it’s my name on the book and it’s my final say. If I want a thousand people or one person in a chapter, that’s what’s going to happen. But as an executive producer, I start making these calls of, “Okay, if we had three people instead of five people, then we could save money so that we could put more into this effects shot.” I had to think about budgeting and the logistics of things in such a different way, and that was a real challenge and it was exciting to figure out those different puzzle pieces.

I loved Brendan Gleeson in this and can’t imagine anybody else playing Rusty.

SLAUGHTER: He really interrogated the script. We had these very in-depth conversations about what Rusty was thinking. I would watch Brendan take those conversations or bits of information and you could see it in his face. For every muscle I have in my face, he’s got 20 more, and can control them all. We did some changes to make them look younger and some de-aging to make him look younger in some of the scenes. It was just remarkable in post thinking, “Wow, if we take away this one line from his face, it changes his entire performance.” We had to be so careful about how we edited him to make sure that performance came through because he gave us gold. Our jaws were on the floor watching him turn into Rusty.

This is a flawed but loving family. You can tell that they love each other, even when there are times that they just can’t be around each other. These sisters are estranged because of what happened, but before that, this was a tight family. What did you love most about watching that brought to life and seeing what Rose and Meghann did together?

SLAUGHTER: It’s interesting because we showed our young actors, Drew [Cheek] and Audrey [Grace Marshall], who play the younger versions of them, their footage so that they could pick up on mannerisms and reflect that relationship as kids. They were teenagers in the show when this tragic thing happens, and the thing about memory is that it’s told through consensus. So, the fact that they don’t talk about what happened, that they are estranged, and they’re putting the pieces together of that day so that they have a clearer picture of what actually happened, is where some of the tension comes from in the narrative. We talk a lot about plot having tension, but there’s a lot of emotional tension in this, and Rose and Meghann just instinctively got that.

This is a hyper-articulate family that talks all the time, but they never say what they need to say. Their words are their shields against each other and they’re always trying to top each other and they’re always going for the joke. They’re the sorts of people you wouldn’t want to get into an argument with, especially because Charlie has this surgical precision with her speaking, and they just stepped right into that. We first started filming with the girls and Meghann and Harper [Steele], so we had almost a month of just us gals on set. A lot of our heads of department were women, our director was a woman, and our cinematographer was a woman. There was a lot of lady energy.

And then, we were a little nervous because here comes Brendan, and we didn’t know what he would be like or if he would change the vibe. But everybody loved him. The Rusty you see on screen that you love is Brendan. Brendan is such a raconteur. He’s got eternal stamina. We would cut at three in the morning and he’d be like, “Who wants tacos?” And we’d be like, “We’re going to sleep.” And then, Rose came and she had to fit into all that. We were anxious and wondered, “Is she going to be like, ‘I only want white roses in my trailer’?” But she was so down to earth and such a lovely person and so well-prepared.

Rose comes from a big family, so she understands sibling dynamics. She just clicked with Meghann. There was so much chemistry. That scene when they first see each other in the hospital was one of the first scenes that we filmed of them together and they really captured that familiarity wrapped in discomfort in such an electric way. Steph [Green], the director, and I were standing at the monitors watching it like, “How did we get so lucky? They’re just so great together.”

There’s something so interesting about their dynamic because Charlie recognized that Sam needed the story of what happened to them to be a certain way, so she’s just lived it that way, even though it wasn’t true.

SLAUGHTER: They both think they’re protecting each other. Sam thinks she’s protecting Charlie when she’s trying to get her to move to New York and trying to create this life for her, away from the bad stuff that happened. And Charlie has this secret. I think that’s very common in families. You don’t really ever break that mold completely, of who you were as a child inside your family. Some families remember the version of you they had the most control over, and that’s definitely true, as far as Sam and Charlie. Sam just thinks of Charlie as this person she needs to take care of and is her responsibility, and she’s messy and all these other things, which is not necessarily true. On the flip side of that, Charlie thinks of Sam as this hyper-competent, always in control, always in charge, straight down the line, but when we meet her, she’s actually grieving. She’s lost the love of her life. Her life is spinning a little out of control. There’s a reason why, after all this time, she came home.

Mark your calendars for this must-watch mystery.

It takes until close to the end of the season before we learn the details of what really happened to Sam and Charlie in the woods. How did you decide the best way to handle all of that? When it came to what you would tell us and what you would show us, did you know exactly what you wanted that to be? You were also working with young actors doing very heavy material, so how was all of that shaped?

SLAUGHTER: It started with conversations. When we were talking to directors, one thing that I really liked about Steph was that she was very forward-thinking about how we would protect these young girls. She’s a mother. I’m not a mother, but I felt the same way. We saw very eye-to-eye on making sure these girls were protected. We used body doubles. We were very clear with the parents about what was going on. The kids knew what was going on. They knew the story. We weren’t hiding anything from them. Every day, when we would have something difficult, we would go over the rule that if they were uncomfortable, they’d get to stop. I brought puzzles to the set, so they could work on putting together puzzles in between takes. We just held them so precious in our hearts because we wanted to protect them and make sure that they were okay at all times. We made sure we had their teacher, the intimacy coordinator, and a mental health person, not just for the girls, but for everybody.

The actors who played the bad guys, those were heavy roles to do, especially because they loved the girls as much as we did. We just wanted to make sure everybody was okay. From a writing standpoint, I thought it was very important to hint but not show. When I was thinking about how I wanted this to go, I really envisioned where Charlie would go in her mind that felt safe, and that was Sam. That was being the person Sam wanted her to be. Charlie hated running on the track. She always screwed it up. She was not going to be like Sam, that person driven to win.

And so, she goes to this moment where Sam accepts her and sees who she is, and they’re running together. I think that amplifies how horrible the estrangement has been for her because that safe person is gone right, through some fault of her own. There’s complicity on both sides. But also, I was very mindful of a phrase that you hear in trauma recovery, and that’s, “Speak from the scar and not the wound.” They needed time for that wound to heal a little bit, so that they could both look at it and talk about it without the pain being too all-encompassing that they couldn’t go on.

I actually thought it was really very moving that Rusty never judged or questioned his daughter when she told him what happened to her. Charlie tells him what happened and he just listens and puts the agency in her hands, telling her that it’s up to her if she ever wants to talk about it. Was his reaction very important to you?

SLAUGHTER: A thousand percent. As someone who’s written a lot of books, the violence is not as important as what happens after. That’s where the hope comes from. There are two important lines, but the first one that Rusty has is, ‘Whatever you did to survive is exactly what you should have done.” That’s something that we need to tell all survivors. It’s the only crime where we’re like, “Well, what did you do?” No one says, “Why did you get murdered?” And then, he says to Sam, “A father loves his daughter the way she needs to be loved.” Those two lines go hand in hand. His reaction is so important because he’s the most important man in Charlie’s life. The fact that he’s a good man and he listens to and supports her is why she ends up with someone like Ben, who’s a good man that listens to and supports her.

It’s this moment that bonds them together. I put in so much work, in the book and on screen. I had so many meaningful conversations with Brendan because, not that he had this, but there’s a very masculine desire to go out and punish those guys. But Rusty is a defense attorney, and he’s represented men who have been accused of rape, so he knows what happens on the stand. We have this idea of justice and doing the right thing and reporting. But when they do report, we say, “Well, why did you take so long?” He knows what the system can do to a person who has experienced that, so he comes to that conversation with that understanding. His only goal is, “What can I do for my daughter to help her in this moment?”

We learn about Mason’s involvement after we know Charlie’s truth. What was it like to see how all of that played out between him and the sisters?

SLAUGHTER: From a structural standpoint, it’s meant to be very cathartic. This happened to them as children, but now they’re adults with adult understanding and adult language, and they can articulate to this person exactly what this act did to them. Jake [McDorman] was remarkable that day. He was remarkable every day. He’s such a nice guy. But that performance he gave and the turn he makes with, “I was a victim too, I saved you," come on! You’re the hero of this story? Really?! What Rose and Meghann did, I got goosebumps watching it. We were in Locust Grove in South Georgia in August and it was 9000 degrees. I don’t know how they were able to move. We were all like snails because we were so hot and we were covered in mosquitos, but they just brought it. Also, Michael [Dorman] was amazing.

I know from my work as a novel writer that you can write a mediocre novel and people will be like, “This is mediocre.” But if you write a novel that has an amazing opening and the ending is crap, people will hate you. So, I said to Steph, “We need to focus as much, if not more, on the end as we do on the beginning. People have to go away feeling like justice was done.” You get that with that cathartic scene. You also get it with Kelly because it feels fair, what happens. You get this sense that Sam has gotten to this moment where she can breathe again. She’s fulfilled her mother’s sense of fairness, and she’s resolved this with Rusty. And Charlie gets the sense that this chapter of her life that she’s kept open and that’s been bleeding for so long, she can finally close that and move on.

After everything that happens between Mason and Sam and Charlie, I loved that Sam decided to use that recording with him admitting to having taken the weapon and that you brought that back into the story.

SLAUGHTER: When I first started talking about adapting this, I said, “It has to make sense.” I hate when I see a thriller and you get to the end and you think, “What just happened? None of this make sense.” I kept clue sheets. I had them for the actors. I had them for Steph. And then, when we went to post, which took as long as shooting, I gave the editors the clue sheet. Sometimes they would be like, “Oh, crap, now we see why we can’t truncate this in Episode 1 because it pays off in Episode 5.” It’s the showrunner’s job to hold onto all those narrative threads through every step of the process. It’s a lot of work, but it’s much more satisfying.

All six episodes of 'The Good Daughter' are now streaming.

With the unraveling of the shooting, we learn that it was Judith that was there alongside Kelly. Was Judith’s fate always inevitable? Was there no other way for that to turn out?

SLAUGHTER: Yeah. The thing about Judith is that I wanted to write someone who was religious. A lot of times, religion plays as shorthand for a bad guy, but she’s really conflicted. She lives by her values, and in the end, dies by her values. Her fatal flaw is that she knows she did a bad thing, but she doesn’t think the bad thing is what happened to Douglas. She thinks the bad thing is what happened to [the child]. She apologizes to Charlie by saying, “I would have done it some other time if I’d known you were going to be there.” It had to make sense. That’s why Paula Malcomson was my first and only choice. She’s so good in this. You believe her as all these different sides of her. She’s this woman who thought she had gotten a cool guy, with the coach at the school. What a love story. But he turns out to be an evil prick. She took care of Charlie. She was really good to Charlie. She was a good teacher. She tried to be good in the church. She did everything she was supposed to do, and none of it worked out. I wanted to make her believable and complicated, but also someone who lived by their values.

When you initially wrote this story, did it feel good to leave these sisters in a better place after everything that they were put through?

SLAUGHTER: Yeah, absolutely. The most important thing in my writing is to make sure I leave people with hope. I very carefully balance that dark and light. That’s why you have a lot of humor after something bad happens. People need to feel like, “Okay, this is going to work out.” It gives us something we don’t really get in real life, which is a sense that justice has been done and the good people get up and go on with their lives.

Now that it’s moving into its fifth season in 2027, how have you felt about Will Trent? Characters have come and gone, and fans are still asking if they’re every going to see Sara Linton. What has it been like to see how that show has continued over the seasons?

SLAUGHTER: I love it. I love it as a viewer. I get the scripts. I’m an executive producer. I occasionally give a light note. They’re doing a great job. Looking at the last four seasons and what I’ve seen of Season 5 that’s already done and the scripts that are in line for the rest of the season, they’re just doing an amazing job. It’s so clever, it’s interesting, it’s fun. I love Ramón Rodríguez as Will. Everybody loves Betty. She’s the real star. I just think they’re doing a tremendous job. To be able to do something like that, year after year, is quite an accomplishment. But to do it really well is a gift.

Is it funny to you to hear how often people ask about Sara Linton?

SLAUGHTER: They ask constantly, and I cannot answer you. But don’t worry.

The Good Daughter is available to stream on Peacock.

#3499. There's a New Way to Automatically Back Up Your Android Photos for Free

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you're an Android user looking for a way to save your photos and videos without maxing out your cloud storage space, your device may soon be able to back up automatically to your PC. As spotted by Android Authority, Google included automatic backups from Android to Windows via Quick Share in its release notes for Google Play services v26.43.

Quick Share is a wireless file-sharing feature for Android that allows users to send photos, videos, and documents to nearby devices, including Windows computers and iPhones with AirDrop. The new automatic backup feature, which is likely to roll out gradually, uses Quick Share's functionality to transfer copies of photos and videos on your phone to your PC when nearby.

Since these backups happen locally, you don't need to rely solely on cloud storage in your Google account, nor do you need to remember to initiate transfers of photos and videos between devices. Plus, this is all free and doesn't require a separate cloud service subscription. While you can back up your media to Google Photos, as of earlier this year, more data from your Android backups count toward your Google Account storage cap unless you exclude specific types. Alternatively, you can also cobble together a decent amount of cloud storage from other providers at no extra cost, but automatic backups between Android and Windows minimize the likelihood that you'll forget to save data, and your PC provides plenty of space for free.

Once the feature is available on your device, you'll be able to initiate backups in the Quick Share for Windows app. Your Android and Windows devices must be in close proximity and signed into the same Google Account. You can toggle Automatic backups on and change the settings for what gets backed up and to where. The transfers will then occur wirelessly in the background.

As Android Authority reports, early hints at this feature suggested that Samsung phones and PCs would be excluded from automatic backups, but the release notes don't specify any further details.

#3498. Fall Festival Movies Sold: ‘Woman Unknown,’ May el-Toukhy’s Golden Lion Winner, Sells to Cohen Media Group

What will the buyers be snapping up at the fall festivals? With this year’s Toronto International Film Festival already touting a high number of premieres for movies that originally bowed at Cannes or Sundance, there’s fewer world premiere sales titles that aren’t already with distributors than we’re used to. Still, the festival (with its very first market in place), plus Telluride, Venice, and New York are loaded with options, and there’s always the potential for another historic breakout like last year’s “Obsession.”

We’ll be tracking all the sales as they come in here, so check back frequently.

Distributor: Cohen Media GroupDirector: May el-ToukhyFestival: Venice CompetitionBuzz: Venice’s top prize winner of the Golden Lion has found a U.S. deal, this one made out of AFM with Cohen Media Group. Not only did el-Toukhy (“Queen of Hearts,” “The Crown”) movie win the Golden Lion this year, star Mathilde Arcel also won the Volpi Cup for Best Actress. The Danish film, also Denmark’s official Oscar selection, is a period drama set after World War II about a former housekeeper now set to be married to the household’s wealthy patriarch. But as she plans an extravagant dinner party to celebrate the occasion, hidden aspects of her past begin to resurface. Namely, it has to do with Danish witch hunts of those associated with Nazis after the war, and our positive review called it an “angry, despairing film” with a “Haneke-level bleakness in its assessment of human nature.” Cohen Media Group also recently bought an Isabelle Huppert comedy called “All About Corinne” that played at TIFF and premiered at Locarno. Related Stories ‘American Doctor’ and ‘You Can See Everything’ Lead 2027 Cinema Eye Honors Film Nominations What Makes a Good Oscar Campaign? Just Ask Sony Classics’ Michael Barker and Tom Bernard

Distributor: Sony Pictures ClassicsDirector: Niki ByrneFestival: TIFF Special PresentationsBuzz: Sony Pictures Classics have acquired all rights in the United States, Benelux, Switzerland, Italy, Scandinavia, Spain, United Kingdom, Eastern Europe (excluding Poland), Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, Israel and Asia (excluding Singapore) to “The Julia Set,” written and directed by Niki Byrne. The film had its world premiere at this year’s Toronto International Film Festival and follows a gifted young math prodigy (“One Battle After Another” breakout Chase Infiniti) who is “recruited into an elite prep course culminating in the most punishing exam in mathematics, while at the same time falling into a romantic relationship with her charismatic teaching assistant, Pascal (Christopher Briney).”

Distributor: Strand ReleasingDirector: Hanaël El YousfiFestival: TIFF DiscoveryBuzz: This directorial debut follows two friends, one Muslim and one Jewish, spending a carefree summer in Marseille, only to see the expectations and tensions between their traditional families start to get in the way of their friendship and leads them to take hold of their own destinies. El Yousfi both wrote and directed the feature, co-writing it with Raphaël Chevènement and Mia Grace Brown. It had its international premiere at TIFF, but it actually had a small bow at a French festival called the Angoulême Francophone Film Festival, where it won an Audience Award and a Special Prize for its cast. “The Daughters of Abraham” first opens in France on December 30. But Strand, a Culver City-based distributor behind recent releases like Mexico’s Oscar submission “On the Road,” “In a Whisper,” and the 4K restoration of Gregg Araki’s “Mysterious Skin,” will release it in North America in 2027.

Distributor: Black BearDirector: Nahnatchka KhanFestival: TIFF MarketBuzz: This market title is a rom-com starring an indelible trio of Greta Lee, Rebecca Ferguson, and Carrie Coon, and it wrapped production in September. Read more about the film here.

Distributor: 1-2 SpecialDirector: Jacqueline LentzouFestival: Venice OrizzontiBuzz: This Greek coming-of-age story won filmmaker Jacqueline Lentzou the Best Director prize in the Horizons section of the Venice Film Festival, but 1-2 Special picked it up after its North American premiere at NYFF and head of additional screenings at BFI London Film Festival, the Chicago International Film Festival, and the Busan International Film Festival. Blending what the release describes as both the “cosmic and the mundane,” the film follows a 15-year-old girl who meets a new classmate named Phaedra but also begins to notice signs and symbols from a dream world surfacing around her, ultimately leading her to an ethereal transformation. This is Lentzou’s second feature after 2021’s “Moon, 66 Questions.” 1-2 Special is planning a theatrical release for 2027.

Distributor: Sony PicturesDirector: Roshan SethiFestival: TIFF CentrepieceBuzz: This action-thriller starring Michelle Yeoh as a surgeon who is abducted and forced to operate on a mysterious patient is a bit of a departure for Sethi. Sethi’s previous film was the charming rom-com “A Nice Indian Boy,” and he’s also the co-creator of the medical drama “The Resident.” But reviews for the film were solid, and it’s not typical for the majors to buy festival titles, but Sony is already dating it for release on April 2, 2027.

Distributor: Universal Pictures and Blumhouse Atomic MonsterDirector: Joshua GiulianoFestival: TIFF Midnight MadnessBuzz: IndieWire first broke the news about the film originally set up at the Independent Film Company and Shudder being picked up by Universal and Blumhouse Atomic Monster for a deal that could surpass $10 million as the companies hope to find the next “Obsession,” just as they did last year. Read more here.

Distributor: HBO Documentary FilmsDirector: Rebecca HunttFestival: TIFF DocsBuzz: “Rapinoe” about US Women’s National Soccer star Megan Rapinoe was the opening night documentary at TIFF. Rapinoe was in attendance at the premiere screening of director Rebecca Huntt’s (“Beba”) film, which grapples more with Rapinoe’s progressive politics, such as her kneeling in solidarity with Colin Kaepernick, and her coming out story, than it does on the stories from her soccer career about how she led the US Women’s team to two World Cup titles, an Olympics Gold, and the Ballon d’Or. HBO Documentary Films has North American TV and streaming rights to the film. THR first reported the news.

Distributor: Roadside Attractions and VerticalDirector: Lauren Miller RogenFestival: TIFF Gala PresentationBuzz: Lauren Miller Rogen directs her husband Seth Rogen alongside Anna Kendrick and Kate Berlant in this comedy about parenthood and prospective parenthood. It follows a childless couple who begin debating the merits of having kids when their divorced friend and her child move in with them. The cast is stacked, including Issa Rae, Dan Stevens, Zach Cherry, Ed Helms, Ashley Park, Sharon Stone, and David Strathairn in supporting parts.

“Babies” is described as heartfelt and poignant in what is shaping up to be a strong year for Seth Rogen. The movie launched sales at TIFF nearly a year to the date prior to its Roy Thomson Hall premiere. The distributors are planning for a release in early 2027.

Distributor: Focus FeaturesDirector: Simon StoneFestival: Telluride and TIFFBuzz: Andrew Scott is said to be fantastic in this performance based on the true story of “Chariots of Fire” and “Gandhi” star and thespian Ian Charleson, who died of AIDS at the age of 40 but managed to raise awareness for the epidemic after his death. Focus has already dated the film for late November, the same time slot it gave “Hamnet” last year.

Distributor: NetflixDirector: Danny BoyleFestival: Venice CompetitionBuzz: The opening night film for this year’s Biennale, “Ink” is the story of the birth of The Sun tabloid in the ’60s and the collaboration between editor Larry Lamb (Jack O’Connell) and Rupert Murdoch (Guy Pearce) that made it the notorious publication it is today. Netflix didn’t acquire worldwide rights to the film, so it could easily be something it sees as both commercial and an awards play.

#3497. Star Trek’s Ultimate Prequel Officially Changed Canon Forever

Star Trek: Strange New Worlds became the franchise's ultimate prequel in season 4, with Captain Christopher Pike (Anson Mount) and the USS Enterprise becoming the catalyst of human history. Directed by Chris Fisher and written by Akiva Goldsman and Henry Alonso Myers, Strange New Worlds season 4's premiere, "Valles Marineris," was the first and arguably the biggest of the season's 'big swings.'

For 25 years, prequels have largely dominated the Star Trek franchise. From 1966 to 2001, the saga of Star Trek was forward-moving. Star Trek: The Original Series started in the 23rd century, and Star Trek: The Next Generation began the canon's massive expansion in the 24th century. That ended with Star Trek: Enterprise, which launched in 2001 as Star Trek's first prequel series.

J.J. Abrams' Star Trek movies were a prequel trilogy set in the alternate Kelvin timeline. Star Trek's Paramount+ streaming era began with Star Trek: Discovery, which was also a prequel in its first two seasons. Star Trek: Picard, Star Trek: Lower Decks, and Star Trek: Prodigy finally moved the 24th century forward into the 25th, but Star Trek: Strange New Worlds went back to the 23rd century again.

Star Trek: Starfleet Academy is now the franchise's farthest point in the 32nd century, until Star Trek: Short Treks' "Calypso," which is set a thousand years later. Among Star Trek's four major prequel sagas, however, Strange New Worlds went back further and became more instrumental than any of them.

Star Trek: Strange New Worlds season 4's premiere turned the series into Star Trek's ultimate prequel. In "Valles Marineris," the Starship Enterprise time-traveled 65 million years into Earth's past. This led to two game-changing revelations: Mars had a space-faring society, and the Red Planet was at war with the fifth planet in the solar system occupied by an insect species called the Dol'drm.

Star Trek: Strange New Worlds' fifth and final season only has 6 episodes to answer a lot of questions left behind by season 4.

"Valles Marineris" kept the bombshells coming, as the Martian Commander Cassell (Saffron Burrows) came aboard the Enterprise and stole a warp cell to make a doomsday weapon against the Dol'Drms. Instead of stopping the Martians, Pike allowed their genocide when he realized there was no fifth planet in Earth's solar system. Thus, the destroyed Dol'Drm planet became the Main Asteroid Belt between Earth and Mars, and a remnant became the Chicxulub impact meteor that wiped out Earth's dinosaurs 65 million years ago.

In turn, the Martians abandoned their doomed homeworld, which became barren of life. Meanwhile, Commander Una Chin-Riley (Rebecca Romijn), an Illyrian, becomes the second known alien to visit Cretaceous-era Earth, following a crashed Dol'Drm ship that Una, Lieutenant La'an Noonien-Singh (Christina Chong), and Lieutenant Erica Ortegas (Melissa Navia) discovered.

Most importantly, Captain Pike's choice not to prevent the Dol'Drms' genocide directly led to humans replacing dinosaurs as Earth's dominant species. Star Trek: Strange New Worlds not only sent the USS Enterprise to Earth's prehistoric past but made Pike and his crew responsible for all of human history to come. What more can Star Trek ask of a prequel?

Star Trek: Voyager fans who watched Star Trek: Strange New Worlds season 4's premiere understandably wondered about the Voth. "Distant Origin," the 23rd episode of Star Trek: Voyager season 3, revealed that the Voth, a reptilian-humanoid species in the Delta Quadrant, were descended from Earth's hadrosaurs.

Over the last 65 million years, knowledge of the Voth's origins was lost and replaced by religious doctrine.

According to Voth paleontologist Professor Forra Gegen's (Henry Woronicz) 'Distant Origin Theory,' the Voth evolved on Earth and somehow survived the meteor that wiped out the dinosaurs. The Voth then developed space travel capabilities and left Earth, eventually arriving in the Delta Quadrant. Over the last 65 million years, knowledge of the Voth's origins was lost and replaced by religious doctrine.

Star Trek: Strange New Worlds' Starfleet Officers may have visited Cretaceous era Earth, but they only explored a tiny amount of ground. The Voth were likely on another land mass elsewhere on Earth, and may or may not have had the technology to detect the spaceflight-capable Martians, Dol'Drms, or the USS Enterprise. Even if they did, the Voth lost that knowledge in the succeeding 65 million years.

Star Trek: Strange New Worlds is streaming on Paramount+

#3496. Windows Laptops Just Closed a Major Gap With the MacBook Neo

To say the MacBook Neo disrupted the laptop market would be an understatement. When the Neo dropped, former Apple CEO Tim Cook said Apple had its best-ever launch week for first-time Mac customers, and the company is reportedly planning on doubling the MacBook's sales for 2027. It's not hard to see why the MacBook Neo is such a hit: Apple is offering the essential Mac experience at a fantastic price point. You no longer need to spend $1,000 or more for a MacBook, so long as you're okay making some sacrifices to get there—which, it seems, many customers are.

While the MacBook Neo has been a boon for Apple and Apple fans alike, I can only imagine the stress it brought to PC manufacturers—especially those with budget or midrange machines. Windows PCs have long won the price war against Apple. While MacBooks have their passionate customers, buyers looking for the best value have had to weigh expensive Apple laptops against many far cheaper options from companies like Dell, HP, ASUS, and Lenovo. But with the Neo, suddenly a MacBook was competing in this space, and well.

Part of the issue for PC manufacturers was Apple's control over its own ecosystem. Unlike most PC makers, which only produce the hardware for each machine, Apple makes both the hardware and the software for its MacBook lineup. As such, the company has the advantage of optimizing that hardware. It can design macOS to run more efficiently on weaker hardware, in a way that companies like Dell or ASUS can't. You might be comparing the MacBook Neo against a Windows laptop with similar specs, or even better specs, but because Microsoft makes Windows, not the laptop manufacturer, it's possible the Neo ends up with the better overall experience. While that might still be the case, Microsoft may have just closed that gap in a meaningful way.

This week, Microsoft announced key upgrades to memory-management efficiency, particularly for machines with 8GB of RAM. This is the amount of memory the MacBook Neo has, as well as many budget and midrange Windows laptops. That's not much memory for 2026, regardless of platform, but Apple seems to have squeezed a lot out of it for the Neo. Now, Microsoft may have just done the same for PCs, as Windows is reportedly 20% more responsive, with 40% faster multitasking.

In its blog post, Microsoft highlighted improvements that users with 8 GB of RAM can expect from Windows going forward. First, Microsoft says it focused on better utilizing the RAM your machine already has. The company compares its memory management to a desk: Anything on the "desk" is stored in RAM; anything in your "drawer" is stored in your drive. As you use your PC, Windows used to move more of your apps and tabs to your drawer to free up more RAM for other things, meaning you'd need to reload those items whenever you returned to them. Going forward, the company says that Windows can keep up to 2GB more of your active data in RAM instead of moving it to slower storage elsewhere. That means apps and tabs should refresh less frequently when you leave and return to them.

Microsoft also says that small actions should be faster across the board. When you open the Start menu, search across your PC, right-click, open Settings, launch the Snipping Tool, and open File Explorer, those actions may be up to 20% faster than they were in January. Microsoft Edge may open up to 33% faster, while Teams can enable Efficiency Mode by default on 8 GB machines, which means it can launch up to 20% faster too. Microsoft put together an interesting stress test to compare multitasking performance between today and January. It opened 20 tabs in Edge, a 4K video, large Word, PowerPoint, and Excel files, then Outlook and File Explorer, all without closing any windows. That experience was 40% faster following this latest update.

Microsoft says it also improved the memory efficiency in its apps: The company claims it reduced committed-memory growth by up to 900 MB, and saved up to 360 MB in RAM across Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and Outlook. That extends to third-party apps as well: Microsoft says that WhatsApp has double-digit memory improvement now. Widgets also only load when you open the app, which saves 200 MB of RAM when the app is closed, while Edge tabs go inactive after 15 minutes instead of two hours.

Microsoft isn't making these upgrades in a vacuum. Hardware costs, particularly for RAM, have skyrocketed in the age of AI. Microsoft knows that people are likely going to hold onto existing hardware for longer than they usually do, or that they'll opt for less-expensive configurations, including, perhaps, machines with 8 GB of RAM.

PCMag's Chris Hoffman was adamant before this latest Windows update that buyers should steer clear of PCs with 8 GB of RAM. Now, he's pulling back a bit. In his testing, Hoffman noticed improvements when multitasking on an 8 GB PC when compared to similar tests from months ago. He could run multiple Chrome tabs, a Microsoft Word window, and Spotify without bogging down the computer much. Hoffman isn't a lightweight user, so he still wouldn't personally choose an 8 GB machine, but he admits, "If I were an average PC buyer looking for a reasonable desktop experience and could save hundreds of dollars by opting for 8GB of RAM, I might be happy with the performance."

To that point, I think this new Windows update makes 8 GB PCs competitive, especially against the MacBook Neo. We'll still need direct comparisons to know how well this new Windows experience holds up across the board, but these updates are promising. Users with 8 GB machines just got a free, valuable update overnight; new customers can opt for a more affordable PC without feeling like performance will take a nosedive just because they opened one too many Edge tabs.

As Hoffman says, 8 GB of RAM is not ideal for any user looking for serious multitasking or professional workflows, regardless of whether they choose a Mac or PC. But for the average computer customer looking for a solid machine without breaking the bank, I no longer see the Neo as necessarily the default choice. After all, Apple has slowly raised its price, too, from $599 to $699. If you're platform-agnostic, or even prefer Windows to macOS, these updates from Microsoft are quite promising. If you're in the market, check out PCMag's excellent list of budget laptop recommendations.

#3495. ‘The Good Daughter’ Review: Rose Byrne Sizzles in Peacock’s Brutal Trauma-Drama About Crime-Solving Sisters

Peacock‘s latest limited series “The Good Daughter” adds to the streamer’s solid run of women-led thrillers, though it’s best to interpret that label loosely. When stretched to include biographical mysteries, the streak dates back to 2022 with Nancy Oliver’s limited series “Angelyne,” showrun by Allison Miller and starring Emmy Rossum as the enigmatic ’80s era L.A. personality known only by her mononym (until some man decided that’s not good enough).

Then came a slight pivot into pulpy book adaptations with “Apples Never Fall” (2024) an adaptation of Lianne “Big Little Lies” Moriarty’s novel of the same name that was showrun by Melanie Marnich and centered around a wealthy family’s missing mom, played by Annette Bening. Not only did “Apples Never Fall” make the perfect amuse-bouche for Peacock’s next whodunit — “All Her Fault” (2025) the Emmy-nominated yet deeply unserious Sarah Snook showcase — it also teed up Jake Lacy, Hollywood’s leading expert in the field of “entitled douchebags,” for a meta-fun Keyser Söze moment as the devil hiding in plain sight (while his wife took on all of their family’s emotional and physical labor). Related Stories ‘American Doctor’ and ‘You Can See Everything’ Lead 2027 Cinema Eye Honors Film Nominations ‘Ebenezer’ Review: Johnny Depp Is Absolutely Insufferable in a Dull and Dreary Christmas Carol

Two less successful entries, by viewership anyway, were this year’s jaunty critical favorite “Ponies,” from co-creator and director Susanna Fogel, which starred Emilia Clarke and Haley Lu Richardson as the CIA’s first female spies operating within the Soviet Union; and the jaundiced “Long Bright River” (2025), a limited series co-created by Liz Moore (who wrote the novel on which it was based) and Nikki Toscano (who served as showrunner), starring Amanda Seyfried as the only cop in a bad/pale part of Philly who cares about neighborhood sex workers and opioid addicts getting killed (one of whom may turn out to be her missing sister).

All of these shows share common tropes, despite disparate tones, topics, and objectives — not the least of which are their glorious feminist underpinnings. Within each of these thrillers lurk so many shady husbands, brothers, bosses, and dads. The patriarchy looms large enough to get name-checked, and the leading ladies are all fighting an uphill battle just to be seen, heard, and understood. “All Her Fault” was so attuned to the ways men routinely let down their families Vulture hailed it as a “misandrist masterpiece.”

But “Long Bright River” carries the most direct parallels with “The Good Daughter,” both by design and on accident. They’re both gritty and dark. They both follow leads whose careers connect back to their personal demons, and they both track working-class women fighting for their impoverished communities (and against the shitty men who run them). Where “All Her Fault” and “Apples Never Fall” could be carelessly devoured as melodramatic amusements, “Long Bright River” and “The Good Daughter” are too brutal and self-serious to constitute anyone’s idea of a “fun” binge, even if there is a morbid bit of fun to be found in the latter’s performances, dialogue, and many, many character quirks.

“The Good Daughter” is set in the fictional town of Pikesville, GA, where Charlie (Meghann Fahy) works as a public defender, adjacent to her sole-surviving parent, town pariah, and private defense attorney, Rusty Quinn (Brendan Gleeson). Her mother, lovingly referred to as Gamma (Olivia Williams), didn’t live long enough to be a grandma; she was murdered in front of her daughters when they were just kids, and the resulting assaults left Charlie’s sister Sam (Rose Byrne) with a lifelong motor speech disorder called dysarthria, as well as impaired vision and a notable limp.

Sam is also a lawyer, but she specializes in patent law (to avoid the anxiety that comes with criminal cases) and moved to New York as soon as she was old enough to get out of Georgia. She only returns to Pikeville when Rusty, for the first time, calls to say her sister needs help. Why now? Well, the list of Charlie’s hardships is nearly as long as her sister’s, but Rusty — who tends to speak in Flannery O’Connor quotes — is likely referring to the most recent trauma: a school shooting she witnessed that left the principal and a 13-year-old student dead.

Once Sam is back in town, the two sisters start mounting a defense for their dad’s client: the school shooter, Kelly Wilson (Shayna Benardo), an 18-year-old student with an intellectual disability. The maniacal powers that be are eager to kill her — first at the scene of a shooting, where a teacher (played by Jake McDorman) saves her from the trigger-happy cops, and then in court, where a self-righteous district attorney argues for the death penalty, competency laws be damned.

They’re all under the Coins’ thumb, a powerful family (with connections throughout the local government) who turned the township against Rusty and his family long ago. Everyone believes Charlie and Sam lied about who killed their mother, and they resent Rusty for defending so many “obviously” guilty parties. The only folks willing to help the Quinns are Rusty’s best friend and legal aide, Lenore (Harper Steele), and Charlie’s husband and assistant district attorney, Ben (Michael Dorman). Otherwise, they’re on their own, standing up for Kelly, standing up to the Coins, and standing against Bad Men™️.

Adapted by Karin Slaughter (from her own book) and directed entirely by Steph Green (“Duster,” “Dare Me”), “The Good Daughter” holds back too many revelations for the finale, creating an exposition-heavy ending that covers its bases but functions like an endless list of answers. It’s not as powerful as it needs to be in order to justify its upsetting subject matter, and it’s trauma-drama plotting skews into overkill well before it’s done doling out distress.

And yet, I have to say, much of it works. Credit goes to the cast, particularly Byrne and Gleeson, for internalizing their showy character quirks to such a degree that Sam’s limp, vision impairment, and sporadic stutter — yes, also a stutter! — never feel like her defining traits. The same goes for Rusty’s folksy banter, poetry quotes, and even his red-nose routine, in which the professional attorney pops on a clown nose whenever he feels the moment calls for a little levity. Such a strange, impractical choice, deployed as often as it is here, could spoil a curious character who’s always viewed from his children’s removed perspective. Maybe he’s unbelievable, maybe he’s too cute for the rest of the story, maybe he’s simply too silly. But Gleeson gathers it all up to form a heartbroken widower who just wants to give his traumatized children the light they need in an ever-darkening world.

Fresh bursts of creative Southern witticisms are similarly rewarding, like hearing Gleeson say, “Never kick a fresh turd on a hot day” or Byrne tell a patronizing windbag “to shit in both hands and start clapping.” The series ultimately rests on Sam and Charlie’s relationship, and their relationship is strong. Their dialogue, particularly when poking fun at one another, rings true, and there’s a buddy-cop dynamic to their investigation that demands to be extended into an ongoing series.

Not this series, mind you. Peacock should limit this limited series to its established, er, limits. But I know a streamer where Byrne and Fahy could pitch another thriller centered around two crusading women looking to crack a case, save their souls, and destroy the patriarchy in one fell swoop.

Just maybe base the next one on a slightly easier read.

“The Good Daughter” premieres Thursday, November 12 on Peacock. All six episodes will be released at once.

#3494. 5 Most-Watched Movies To Stream This Weekend (Nov 13-15)

Feel free to connect with him or check out his work. He's everywhere — Upwork, YouTube, Spotify, SoundCloud, Collider, LinkedIn, Instagram.

An animated nightmare with button-eyed parents, a Roman gladiator fighting for survival, and a Polynesian princess answering the ocean's call have something unexpected in common: Americans are watching it all these days. An animated nightmare with button-eyed parents and a Roman gladiator — they’re watching them both in enormous numbers. Throw in a devastating hurricane and a kidnapping thriller, and the latest streaming rankings cover just about every mood imaginable.

Choosing what to watch this weekend has become a surprisingly interesting problem. According to Nielsen's latest U.S. streaming movie rankings, covering October 19–25, 2026, these five movies collectively generated more than 1.5 billion minutes of viewing. The chart measures total viewing time on television screens in the United States, with familiar favorites competing against recent releases. Here are the five most-watched movies, their streaming homes, and the reasons they are attracting so much attention.

Eleven-year-old Coraline Jones (Dakota Fanning) discovers a mysterious doorway inside her family's new home, leading to an alternate world where everything initially seems better. Her parents are more attentive, the food is delicious, and her neighbors are considerably more entertaining. Unfortunately, the Other Mother (Teri Hatcher) has black buttons for eyes and increasingly disturbing expectations. Coraline turns a child's frustration with ordinary family life into an extraordinarily imaginative nightmare.

Henry Selick's stop-motion animation remains astonishing, particularly the contrast between Coraline's gloomy home and the elaborate wonders awaiting beyond the little door. But the Other Mother's affection becomes genuinely frightening once its conditions emerge. The film is adapted from Neil Gaiman's novel and possesses the rare ability to delight children while making adults profoundly uncomfortable. Its 198 million viewing minutes also demonstrate the remarkable staying power of a classic fantasy movie released more than seventeen years ago.

A dream promotion turns into a nightmare when Wirpul (Benny Emmanuel) takes command of a yacht off the coast of Acapulco, Mexico. His estranged half-brother Candi (Kristyan Ferrer) joins him for the job, despite their strained relationship. Then Hurricane Otis intensifies with terrifying speed, trapping the brothers aboard a vessel facing a Category 5 storm. Surviving Hurricane Otis dramatizes events surrounding the devastating 2023 hurricane.

The movie is directed by Jorge Michel Grau and builds the tension around the brothers' difficult relationship and the impossible decisions forced upon them. Their wealthy employer's yacht represents an opportunity for financial security, yet protecting it becomes increasingly dangerous as the storm approaches. The contrast between economic necessity and personal survival gives the disaster considerable weight. It was just released on Netflix on October 23, but the Mexican drama attracted 203 million viewing minutes during its opening reporting window, securing fourth place.

A politician's carefully cultivated image becomes dangerously fragile when his family is targeted by kidnappers. Animals stars Ben Affleck as Mark Kimball, a Los Angeles mayoral candidate whose young son is abducted, leaving him and his wife Abigail (Kerry Washington) scrambling to gather the ransom. Their desperate efforts expose troubling questions about wealth, ambition, and the lengths people will go to protect their families. The crisis also threatens to destroy everything Mark has worked to achieve politically.

Affleck directs and co-writes this dark thriller movie, surrounding its central couple with a cast that includes Gillian Anderson and Steven Yeun. The kidnapping creates an uncomfortable collision between public responsibility and private desperation, with Mark's political ambitions complicating decisions that could determine his son's fate. Animals was released on Netflix on October 9, and it has attracted attention despite a divided critical response. Its 292 million viewing minutes were enough to place it third on Nielsen's latest movie chart.

More than two decades after Ridley Scott brought ancient Rome to spectacular life, Gladiator II returns audiences to the Colosseum for another story of revenge and political betrayal. Lucius (Paul Mescal) has built a life far from the imperial capital, but a Roman invasion destroys his peaceful existence and forces him into slavery. As he becomes a gladiator, he attracts the attention of the calculating Macrinus (Denzel Washington), whose ambitions threaten to reshape Rome's future.

Washington's theatrical performance gives the film a particularly entertaining antagonist, while Scott delivers extravagant arena battles, including a confrontation involving a flooded Colosseum and sharks. General Acacius (Pedro Pascal) and Lucilla (Connie Nielsen) add competing loyalties to a story already overflowing with political intrigue. The sequel's return to streaming prominence demonstrates the continued appetite for historical spectacle, with 299 million minutes watched across its listed streaming platforms. It narrowly finished ahead of Animals to claim second place.

Disney's live-action Moana is currently enjoying the top of Nielsen's streaming movie rankings. Moana (Catherine Lagaʻaia), in this live-action remake, is played by Catherine Lagaʻaia. She is the adventurous daughter of Chief Tui, a young woman who feels an irresistible connection to the ocean despite her father's insistence that she remain on the island of Motunui. When darkness threatens her community, Moana ventures beyond the reef and seeks the help of Maui (Dwayne Johnson), a powerful demigod whose legendary accomplishments are matched by his enormous ego.

The movie is directed by Thomas Kail; the 2026 adaptation revisits the beloved 2016 animated adventure with live-action performances, sweeping island landscapes, and familiar songs. Johnson reprises his role as Maui, while Lagaʻaia brings a new interpretation of the determined heroine to the screen. The story's celebration of courage, family, and cultural identity continues to offer considerable appeal to audiences seeking an accessible family adventure. With 579 million minutes watched, Moana comfortably outperforms every other movie on the chart, generating nearly twice the viewing time of second-place Gladiator II.

#3493. Miles Teller Opens Up About ‘Paper Tiger,’ Adam Driver, and Losing His Home Before Filming James Gray’s Movie

[Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. Neon will release “Paper Tiger” in theaters on Friday, November 6.]

An actor who started at 22, Miles Teller earned rave reviews out of the gate for his debut performance in “Rabbit Hole,” when he was signed swiftly by CAA, followed by “Whiplash” and “The Spectacular Now.” He has worked steadily ever since, with everything from auteur fare like “Whiplash” and studio franchises such as “Divergent” and “The Fantastic Four” to his name. Holding his own opposite Tom Cruise in the blockbuster “Top Gun: Maverick” pushed him into the limelight, but he was still playing Rooster, the son of radar intercept officer Nick “Goose” Bradshaw (Anthony Edwards). Related Stories Fall Festival Movies Sold: ‘Woman Unknown,’ May el-Toukhy’s Golden Lion Winner, Sells to Cohen Media Group Saoirse Ronan Has Wanted to Direct Since She Was a Kid, and Her Exquisite First Short ‘Paper Plane’ Proves She’s Got the Goods

His latest role in James Gray’s “Paper Tiger,” which earned raves at Cannes, sees Teller play a real grown-up, Irwin Pearl, a Queens engineer and family man opposite Scarlett Johansson as his wife Hester, and Adam Driver as Gary, his older brother, a former cop. No longer the onscreen son of a leading man, Teller is now firmly in father roles. Irwin is slowly building a solid business when his brother offers a quicker route to success. Alas, the naive Irwin goes for the idea and, during an unscheduled night reconnaissance, blunders with the Russian mafia, seeing things he should not see.

I sat down with Teller at the Carlton Hotel in Cannes after the movie wowed in its world premiere. He was seeing it for the first time. We do not count fake standing ovations at IndieWire, but I was there and can vouch that it played well. The dynamic between Driver and Teller is powerful, with Johansson holding her own in the middle. Even though the movie did not land a Cannes prize, it will play the fall festivals and enter awards contention.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

Anne Thompson: You’ve played the Cannes game before.

Miles Teller: I’m one of those actors [where] it’s pretty hard to watch yourself. I always have a hard time. I was here with Nic [Winding] Refn for this limited series that we did [“Too Old to Die Young”]; that was my first time at Cannes. I’ve done Cannes with “Maverick.” It’s truly an overload of the senses.

You’ve never given this kind of performance before.

Hopefully, your taste evolves as you get older. It struck me that on my first film, “Rabbit Hole,” I was playing the wide-eyed teenager, and we filmed the majority of that movie in a house in Queens. And now I’m playing the part of the parent.

That was your breakout. You revealed some strong emotions related to your own car accident. I’m so sorry you lost your home in the Palisades Fire.

When I met James for this movie, our house had just burned down. And I had just lost my grandfather. We were renting a place in Santa Barbara, and then I got the call saying James wanted to meet me for this. That infused this story and performance with a lot of love as well, because of that feeling of home that Keleigh [Sperry] and I had lost. I’d lost it with my grandfather, but then also just the physical place where you can have people come gather, where you have memories attached. We did not have that, so that probably came through.

Do you believe that you have to grow up a bit before you can find your way in Hollywood?

If you want to have a long career, the audience, hopefully, that you attract in your early 20s, as they get older, and they start having kids or not having kids, but just getting more life experience under the belt, you want to reflect that in your choices as well. And James makes movies for adults, he deals with characters. I’ve loved every one of his films, and I’ve always felt like he gets incredible performances, so I was excited to play a man at this point.

Every actor is going to get to a place where you know it’s tough because you do something that has some success to it, and then people want you to keep doing that same thing, whether that’s from the studio side or you keep getting scripts that are that same kind of thing.

When I started out with “Rabbit Hole,” and then I wanted to audition for comedy, they’re like, “he’s not funny.” And then you do comedies, and you want to be going back to drama, and they’re like, “Willard from ‘Footloose,’ what are you talking about?”

I remember “Bleed for This.” [He gets up to close the shutters to block the noise for my audio, and pours me some water.] That was a point where I was 27, and I said, “OK, I want to step up and play, not the funny friend. Playing Vinny Patz, as a five-time world champion boxer, very much a man’s man, absolutely, that was something. But it always comes down to a director, oftentimes taking what I feel is a chance on me, casting me in a role that I haven’t necessarily shown those abilities before, but believing that I could do that.

You had to carry the TV series “The Offer,” in which you play Al Ruddy, who produced “The Godfather,” running interference between Francis Ford Coppola, Robert Evans at Paramount, and the mafia. That must have been tough.

I was intimidated by portraying Al, to be honest with you, not just his bravado and accomplishments, but it felt like I was playing somebody who had more life experience than I had at that point, and there was a certain maturity to that. I enjoyed that Al, being a man of action, if he takes a step back, he’s taking two steps forward. Typically, there’s five or six different producers doing all these things: that was all Al.

In “Paper Tiger,” there’s one scene between you and Adam Driver where you get into a fight. Your face was shaking with anger.

I know. I saw that. Yeah, there was a twitch going on there. At least in my own life, your family can get to you in a way that nobody else can. Those feelings are so deeply rooted and established from childhood, so I guess in that moment, and neither one is fully aware of the ramifications of the Russians, this deal going bad, and how it’s affecting that person in their life. In that particular scene you’re letting out. It’s not just about what they’re talking about right there. It’s an entire lifetime of misgivings — he’s going to let him have it. When that’s happened to me in my personal life, you feel so bad afterwards. It’s a horrible feeling when you’re not talking to a sibling or your parents, and often it’s hard to make amends.

How did James Gray base this film on his own father’s experience?

With his father, that was the biggest regret. He took it to his deathbed, the fact that he brought this [danger] into his home, and his family became collateral damage for his business ambition. [In the movie] the venture that he went into, to go into business with his brother, he makes a mistake that was very naive. I think it’s easy to forgive this mistake. When I read this script, I had a ton of empathy for this family in this situation, and then also what Hester is going through.

Did you have any models for your character in this movie? Your own father was an engineer.

No, he was a project controls manager, but worked nuclear. The men that I grew up around, my father and my grandfather, were strong men, but very sensitive, and were dependable, reliable. My grandfather was married to my grandmother for 60-something years. I never saw her open a door for herself. I never saw her carry her own bag. He was a Marine, but he also was well-versed in world history, and he was a sweet man who was never afraid to show that side of him, but he also would stand up for himself, or his wife, or his kids, whatever it is. He took a lot of pride in that.

I found it refreshing, even comforting, to watch a movie about a kind, loving family man who’s good at his job, who’s competent. He’s a good dad. You haven’t shown that side to such a degree.

I felt immensely for this father and husband. It was clear he loves his kids, and he’s trying to lead by example, and to show them that success in life is not based on the car you drive. He wants to show them that you can build something on your own merit, and if you work hard and treat people right, that you can earn it.

Those values are no longer as respected as they once were. So, if you were to look back at your career, you did some studio work, like the “Divergent” series. Have you made a course correction? That comes with maturity, too, when an actor recognizes what they want to do rather than doing what people tell them to.

Early on, I didn’t want to feel like I was repeating what I had just done. I didn’t want people to be able to expect what I was going to do next. I always want to defend young actors in their careers, because people say, “Oh, why did you make that choice? Why did they make that choice?” You’re just hoping to get a role, and it’s less than 10 percent of people in SAG who pay their bills off acting alone. We all want to work on the best material with the best directors and the best actors. There’s an ebb and flow. I used to be more critical of work other people were doing, because you get thrown into this rat race when you’re first starting out.

Who were you competing with? Who was in your class?

It was me, and Michael B. [Jordan] and [Robert] Pattinson and Shia [LaBeouf] and [Zac] Efron was big, “The Hunger Games” stuff was blowing up. As I’ve gotten older, I appreciate and have respect for longevity, if you can hang around. I always wanted to contribute. When I was going to the Lee Strasberg Institute at NYU, and looked on the wall, there’s all these incredible actors that went through there. I hold acting and actors in such high regard, whether it’s theater or film or TV.

You seem to be delivering performances at such a level that you keep getting more work. The work itself is selling you. You had to counteract some bad press. Did that hurt you in terms of getting roles?

That was so mishandled. The reason why I have not done profiles is because I said, “Wow, if I’m not doing this interview on camera, this person can misquote things or put things out of order or say things that didn’t happen.” It felt like such a violation of what actually transpired. I told my team, “Guys, I don’t think I’m doing this again, because I’m reading this and this doesn’t sound like me to me. This is not life, so why would I ever want to be a part of something where they can just put that in?” So it’s unfortunate that being a good person, that doesn’t sell. People want to click on the negativity. If you go to bed and put your head on your pillow and how you treat people truly, that’s what matters. That [2015] interview was like 12 years ago.

Some people still remember. Well, casting directors know who you are and what you can do.

The actors, the directors, the crew, the producers, you can’t hide who you are when you’re on set.

Legal questions surround the Michael Jackson estate and his lawyer, John Branca, who you play in “Michael,” which has grossed $707 million worldwide. What’s going on with the sequel?

They had to rework the third act of the last movie. As far as the sequel goes, I know they’re working on it. I haven’t had any direct discussions, other than the team is excited to complete that story.

#3492. Sony Wants to Give You Up to $400 for Your PS5

Companies usually want you to buy something from them. They might cut prices to make their products more enticing, or introduce perks and upgrades to make stagnant prices (or even price hikes) more appealing. But rarely do I see companies encourage customers to sell their products.

Such is the case with Sony and its PlayStation console. This week, the company began reaching out to some customers with an odd prompt: Rather than buy a new PS5 or PS5 Pro, you can sell your existing PS5 console for up to $400. There are stipulations there, of course: Your console needs to be in good working order, and, apparently, come with two controllers—even though Sony only includes one in the box. The price could also fluctuate depending on your console model, storage capacity, and included accessories. But, still, the company says it'll help you net up to $400 for your existing PS5.

It's a bizarre deal, especially when you consider who you're trading your console to. Sony isn't necessarily accepting trade-ins itself. Instead, it's partnering with BackMarket. The thing is, you can trade in your PS5 directly through BackMarket and get a better value than Sony is offering through its direct link. When I try to trade in my standard PS5 with one controller, BackMarket offers $435, $35 more than Sony's highest offer. If I add a second controller to that deal, BackMarket bumps up the total to $455.

You might also be wondering why Sony would do this. Not only is it weird for a company to encourage you to sell one of its products, but the PS5 is about to have a big moment. Grand Theft Auto VI is finally about to launch, and it'll likely be one of the biggest video game launches, if not the biggest video game launch, of all time. Why, then, would Sony encourage users to jump ship?

While Sony doesn't say, the answer likely has to do with how expensive it is to pick up a PS5 right now. Even though the console launched back in 2020, units are few and far between, jacking the price up to unreasonable levels. Sony raised international prices due to tariffs last year, but the current shortage is more probably tied to the ongoing memory crisis that's putting a strain on all tech, including game consoles. A new PS5 on Amazon will easily cost you over $800. If you want to find a PS5 Pro, don't be surprised to find it well over $1,000. Sony likely wants players who aren't using their consoles to sell them, so that active players (who will also buy games like GTA VI) will pick them up. It's not just Sony, either: Microsoft has been offering similar deals to inactive Xbox gamers this year.

If Sony reached out to you directly, you can take advantage of the deal without issue—just click the link in the email. But if you never received such an offer, you still have options. For one, that BackMarket deal is live for anyone. That links takes you to the deal for the standard PS5, but you can also head to this link to enter the info for your specific PS5 model. GameStop, of course, will happily take your PS5 off your hands, but it doesn't seem as generous as BackMarket. Right now, it seems you can get up to $275 in store credit, or $192.50 in cash for a standard PS5.

#3491. Dragon Ball Super: Beerus Episode 6 Release Date & Time

Time is officially up for Goku's divine transformation, but Beerus is nowhere near finished with him. Episode #5 of Dragon Ball Super: Beerus ended with Goku's fiery red Super Saiyan God aura flickering out, dropping him right back into his regular golden Super Saiyan form in the middle of their fight. What dragged on for four whole episodes in the original 2015 Dragon Ball Super broadcast (episodes #10 through #13) has now been condensed into a single, hard-hitting episode, taking the battle from the ocean floor straight into Earth's ozone layer without wasting a minute.

Gone are the stiff frames, dragged-out beam struggles, and uneven animation that plagued the 2015 release. Toei Animation has clearly put serious work into making this remake feel like the version fans should have gotten all those years ago. Under chief animation director Tadayoshi Yamamuro and episode #5 director Ayaka Noro, early Super has never looked this sharp.

Now, with Goku preparing to trade final blows with Beerus without even realizing his god timer has expired, Dragon Ball Super: Beerus episode#6 is set to bring the opening six-episode God of Destruction arc to an explosive finish, clearing the way for the next saga and the return of one of the franchise's most iconic villains, Frieza.

Meanwhile, the English dub finally kicked off on Crunchyroll on November 12 after a month-long wait, bringing back Sean Schemmel (Goku), Christopher R. Sabat (Vegeta), Jason Douglas (Beerus), and Ian Sinclair (Whis). With new dubbed episodes arriving every Thursday, episode 6's English dub is scheduled for December 17.

With the God of Destruction arc wrapping up, the remake is already preparing to bring back one of Dragon Ball's most iconic villains. Episode #7 kicks off the six-episode Golden Frieza arc on November 22, bringing back the tyrant who was sliced apart and vaporized by Future Trunks. This time, Frieza actually spends four months training after being revived by the Frieza Force remnants Sorbet and Tagoma, eventually unlocking his Golden Frieza form.

But Frieza isn't the only one getting a new transformation. Vegeta joins Goku on Beerus's planet after bribing Whis with Bulma's instant ramen, and both Saiyans begin training to master God ki. This leads to Super Saiyan Blue, while the arc finally gives Vegeta a much bigger share of the spotlight. Considering how rough the original 2015 Resurrection 'F' TV arc looked, Toei's revamped animation and tighter pacing should make this rematch worth watching.

If Toei Animation can maintain this level of animation and pacing, the future of Dragon Ball Super: The Galactic Patrol is looking pretty bright. The sequel was officially announced at January 2026's Dragon Ball Genkidamatsuri 40th-anniversary event, confirming that the long-awaited Galactic Patrol Prisoner saga is finally getting an anime adaptation.

There's still no official release date or year, though Toei's financial schedules point toward a possible late 2027 or 2028 launch. With Dragon Ball Super: Beerus expected to finish its 19-episode run in early 2027, that could be the perfect time for Toei to share a proper release window and full trailer.

Dragon Ball Super's anime is returning to tell its next major story arc, so get ready with us ahead of its release!

The original Dragon Ball Super ended its television run in 2018, right after Goku's battle against Jiren introduced Ultra Instinct to the world. That silver-haired transformation became an instant fan favourite, but Goku still couldn't use it at will, even after Dragon Ball Super: Broly. The Galactic Patrol Prisoner saga finally takes that story further. Goku and Vegeta join the galaxy's peacekeepers to hunt down Moro, the magic-wielding Planet-Eater, while Goku trains under elite Galactic Patrolman Merus, who is secretly an Angel-in-training. For fans waiting to see Goku truly master Ultra Instinct, there's a lot to look forward to.
