#3489. No, We Aren’t All Eating 'Too Much' Protein

If you’ll permit me a rant—I promise to make it fact-filled and interesting—I am sick of the articles that seem to pop up every few months claiming that we are all eating “too much” protein. They convey an inaccurate picture of how the body uses protein, and they demonize perfectly healthy meals that happen to be high in protein. It’s time to set the record straight.

It is true that most of us eat more than the RDA (recommended daily allowance) of protein, but that's a good thing—the RDA is meant as a minimum. It's true that protein-boosted foods are trendy, and that they're not necessarily great dietary choices in the big picture. It's also true that you can eat a healthy diet with little to no meat, but meat is not synonymous with protein. Let's look at what we actually know about the role of protein in a healthy diet, and how to tell if you're eating too much or too little.

As a refresher, protein is one of the three calorie-containing macronutrients (fats, carbs, protein) that make up most of the food we eat. Proteins are made of amino acids, and these amino acids are required for the growth, repair, and functioning of our bodies.

We can get protein from a variety of sources. Meats are particularly protein-dense; a chicken breast contains about 35 grams of protein. Other animal products, like milk and eggs, are also rich in protein. Plant-based foods tend to have less protein than animal products, but it’s not hard to meet or exceed protein requirements even on a vegan diet. Beans, grains, and soy products like tofu contain significant amounts of protein, for example.

If you’d like a cheat sheet on how much protein you’re supposed to eat based on your activity level, you can find one here. And that’s a good place to start dissecting this “too much protein” myth, because before we can declare an amount of protein to be “too much,” we need to understand how much is “enough.”

The government communicates targets for different nutrients to encourage us all to eat a healthy, balanced diet. These targets are the basis for the “% daily value” labels on the back of packaged foods, and for the nutrient makeup of school lunches. The RDA, or recommended daily allowance, is defined as “the average daily dietary intake level that is sufficient to meet the nutrient requirement of nearly all (97 to 98 percent) healthy individuals in a group.”

In other words, if 100% of us were to eat the RDA of protein, at least 97% of us would be getting enough protein—we'd be meeting the minimum to be healthy. That's right, this number is a minimum to avoid malnutrition, not a maximum, and not a recommendation for optimal health.

By the way, if you're wondering how that number is determined? For protein, it is based on nitrogen balance. Humans break down proteins, as part of our body’s daily function, and we excrete nitrogen as a result. If you eat enough protein (which contains nitrogen), the amount of nitrogen you excrete will be the same as, or more than, the amount you eat. In other words, if you aren’t breaking your own body proteins down (in excess of what you eat), then whatever you’re eating must be, in some sense, enough.

In this way of thinking, the RDA is the minimum to stay healthy. More is fine; less would mean that you may not be getting enough. For some nutrients, there is also an UL, or upper limit, telling you that more than a certain amount is too much. Upper limits are calculated for vitamins and minerals; there is no upper limit defined for protein.

Therefore, there is no official definition for “too much” protein. If somebody eats more than the RDA, they’re not eating too much; they’re just eating more than the minimum. You’re supposed to eat more than the minimum.

The RDA for protein is set at 46 grams per day for a 125-pound woman, and at 56 grams per day for a 154-pound man. (The USDA chose those as their examples.) That’s based on an RDA of 0.8 grams of protein per kilogram bodyweight, which works out to 0.36 grams per pound. So a 200-pound person would need 72 grams of protein per day.

This USDA report found that most adult men average roughly 90 to 100 grams of protein per day, although men aged 70 and up only get about 80 grams of protein per day. Women tend to average around 70 grams per day, with those aged 70 and up averaging 62 grams.

Above the RDA? Yes. Too much? I don’t see any way of arguing that. And before you say that we’re getting almost double the recommendation, let's check the math. Those RDA numbers are for 125- and 154-pound people. On the other hand, the averages for what we eat are based on actual people, not ideals. The average American man is 200 pounds, and the average American woman is 171 pounds. So, to compare the numbers:

The average woman is 171 pounds, so her RDA would be 62 grams per day. (Women, on average, eat 70 grams of protein per day.)

The average man is 200 pounds, so his RDA would be 72 grams per day. (Men, on average, eat 90 to 100 grams of protein per day.)

Again, there’s no need to stick to the minimum; going 8 grams over, or even 28 grams over, is fine. It’s probably better to go over than to just scrape by, and many of us arguably don’t get enough. Let me explain.

Let’s start with older adults. Not only does protein intake tend to decrease with age, older adults are vulnerable to issues that stem from a loss of muscle mass. People tend to lose 3-5% of their muscle mass per decade starting at age 30, but strength training and protein intake can support maintaining our muscle, and thus likely prevent or reduce that decline.

The Dietary Guidelines include a note that “About 50 percent of women and 30 percent of men 71 and older fall short of protein foods recommendations.” Meanwhile, a study found that older adults who don’t meet the recommendations are “more likely to be limited when stooping, crouching, or kneeling, standing or sitting for long periods, walking up 10 steps, preparing meals, and walking for a quarter mile.”

So even if it’s true that the average adult gets more protein than recommended, there are clearly a lot of elderly folks who don’t. These are the same people who have more issues functioning in everyday life. This may be a chicken-and-egg situation—was the functional decline a cause or an effect of the change in their diet?—but this sure does not seem to be a group of people who should be eating less protein.

There’s another large group of people who benefit from more, not less, protein: people who are pregnant or lactating. Instead of 0.36 grams of protein per pound of body weight (62 grams for a 171-pound person), the RDA for people who are pregnant or lactating is 0.5 grams/pound (so, 86 grams of protein per day).

When you’re pregnant, you also have higher caloric needs, so the increased total amount of food makes it easier to get the higher protein amount. Still, it makes more sense to spend your energy on making sure you’re getting enough protein, rather than worrying about getting too much.

You knew we were heading in this direction (I say between reps of barbell squats, wiping protein shake off my lips): People who exercise should get more protein than just the RDA.

While the fear-mongering “too much protein” articles sometimes mention that bodybuilders or elite athletes need their protein, they tend to hand-wave this away as a special concern that doesn’t apply to normal people. But I think it’s worth a closer look—and honestly, this situation applies to a lot more people than just a few athletes.

Officially, there isn’t an RDA for athletes; people who exercise can stave off malnutrition with the same 0.36 grams per pound as everyone else. But that doesn’t mean that the RDA is the best target to aim for.

The International Association of Athletics Federations, which governs track and field competitions, recommends that most athletes who are maintaining or gaining weight eat 0.59 to 0.77 grams of protein per pound of bodyweight per day. That’s 101 to 131 grams for the average 171-pound woman, and 118 to 154 grams for a 200-pound man.

A group of organizations, including the American College of Sports Medicine, largely agrees, recommending a range from 0.54 to 0.9 grams per pound for all athletes whose weight is stable or gaining. That includes people who do endurance training like distance running, as well as strength athletes whose exercise involves mainly lifting weights. Those ranges would go as high as 153 grams for our 171-pound woman, and 180 grams for our 200-pound man.

You don’t need to be an Olympian to consider yourself an “athlete” in this sense. If you’re training for a half marathon, you’re doing plenty of distance running, and should fuel accordingly. And if you’re “just” lifting weights in the gym, but taking it seriously enough that you’re training regularly and working hard, you should consider eating in these ranges as well.

Dieting to lose weight is not only a popular American pastime, it’s also arguably good for at least some people's health. If you’ve been on a diet recently, or if you’re planning to go on one, you aren’t a person who should settle for the RDA either.

Research shows that protein intake (and strength training—they go together!) is important to maintain muscle mass when we’re losing weight. After all, you’re aiming for fat loss, not trying to get your muscles to waste away. Muscle loss is especially a concern with weight-loss drugs like Ozempic, but any dieter should be aware of this issue.

For example, this study found that diets ranging from 0.48 to 0.72 grams of protein per kg of body weight (that’s 82 to 123 grams for our 171-pound woman, 96 to 144 for our 200-pound man) resulted in less weight regain after the diet, and helped people to maintain muscle mass and feel more full while they were dieting.

And if you’re losing weight and exercising? The IAAF recommends that athletes who are “undertaking high-quality weight loss” need at least 0.72 grams per pound of bodyweight, and possibly as much as 1.09 grams per pound. That would be 186 grams for a 171-pound athlete, or 218 grams for a 200-pound athlete. Most people won’t need to go that high, and it’s unclear whether athletes need to go that high. But I’m including these numbers so you see how high the ranges actually go.

Ultimately, weight loss is widely understood to be more effective and have healthier results with higher protein intakes rather than lower ones. When people focus on just eating less, without thinking about what their diet actually consists of, it’s easy to forget about protein. But the evidence suggests that you should increase protein when you’re decreasing overall calories.

The idea that protein causes weight gain is a common talking point in those articles about “too much” protein, and it’s sort of true—but it also doesn’t mean what you think it means.

When you eat more food than your body needs, your body can store it as fat. That’s true no matter what the excess is made of—protein, carbs, fat, or even alcohol. The protein you eat gets used for many different things in your body. You can build it into muscle tissue, use it for growth and repair of different kinds of cells, and so on. You can also use it for energy—basically, burning it for the calories.

So if you were eating a perfectly balanced diet, and then decided to add an extra 100 grams of protein per day, then sure, a lot of that protein would be used for energy, and since we’d have excess energy, it would get stored as fat.

But if you ate more protein, but that protein replaced other foods in your diet, then there would be no excess calories to store. Nobody is saying you should chug a couple of protein shakes on top of your regular diet. They’re saying (I’m saying) that you should plan your meals and snacks to include more protein.

For example, if your regular lunch is a turkey-and-cheese sandwich with a side of chips, you could improve the protein content of your diet by adding more turkey to the sandwich and replacing the chips with an apple. Same total calories, but more protein. As long as your total calories for the day aren’t in excess of your needs, the “extra” protein won’t get stored as fat.

In general, high protein diets don’t have any serious health consequences. There’s a major exception, though: in some medical conditions, you may be told to limit your protein intake to protect your health.

For example, people with chronic kidney disease are often advised to use the RDA (0.36 grams per pound of body weight) as a maximum rather than a minimum. Your kidneys play a role in processing protein for excretion, so a lowered protein intake reduces the amount of work that a damaged kidney has to do. That said, once a person with chronic kidney disease begins dialysis, they may be advised to increase their protein intake for better health now that their body has help to handle the higher levels.

People with certain other disorders, like phenylketonuria and homocystinuria, may also be advised to eat a low-protein diet. Obviously, if you have one of these conditions, you should be getting your dietary advice from your medical team (ask for a referral to a dietitian!) rather than from general articles on the internet.

Besides those known medical issues, the occasional findings about eating “too much” protein tend to fit into the “X is good for you/X is bad for you” ricochet news cycle. They’re not holistic assessments of protein in general on health in general, but rather specific research questions that are still being figured out.

For example, this 2017 study found that a high-protein (and high-fiber) diet seemed to slightly worsen one measure of insulin resistance, but it also improved metabolic health and body composition. The researchers concluded that the subjects’ body chemistry was probably just responding appropriately to the changed nutrient content of their diet. A few years later, a study of high-BMI women with insulin resistance saw improvements to their insulin resistance on a high-protein diet.

Or to take another example, a study in 2024 found a link between high-protein diets and atherosclerosis. But if you look at what the researchers were actually studying, they were looking at how leucine (one amino acid found in protein) affects the mTOR biochemical pathway in certain types of white blood cells. By the way, that mTOR pathway is involved in a lot more body processes than atherosclerosis, and does a lot of good things too.

So are these results interesting, and worth further study? Definitely. Worth changing protein recommendations? Only if this effect turns out (1) to actually lead to worse health outcomes, and (2) to outweigh the known benefits of higher protein. The body of evidence doesn’t yet support lowering protein recommendations, nor adding an upper limit.

So if protein is good for us, and most of us can’t really get “too much,” why are so many people arguing that we’re overdoing it? I think part of the reason is just misunderstanding (the writers don’t tend to have a background in nutrition and especially not in sports nutrition), but more often, I think they’re talking about a different issue entirely.

Often the “too much protein” stuff is just a way of talking about the environmental effects of meat consumption or dairy farming. People making this argument are trying to pry the double cheeseburgers out of our hands and reassure us that we’ll be okay. I don’t think an attack on protein is an appropriate way to make that point, since plant-based proteins exist and are a fine alternative. But I understand where they’re coming from.

Ultimately, if you’re trying to make the argument that we’re eating “too much” protein for our health, you really can’t do that without some evidence that we’re eating so much protein that it’s harming our health on a widespread level. And that evidence just doesn’t exist.

#3488. Every DCU Movie and TV Show, Ranked

In the immortal words of Dwayne Johnson: the hierarchy of power in the DC Universe is about to change. As Skydance acquired Warner Brothers, James Gunn and Peter Safran are being replaced by former Marvel executive Jeremy Latcham, marking the beginning of the final chapter in the short DC Universe launched by the duo. Several projects like Swamp Thing and The Brave and the Bold are now in limbo or facing possible cancellation.

For now, we'll look at all the titles released under the new DC Universe. The Suicide Squad and Blue Beetle are excluded because they were technically released during the DCEU era despite being canon, while The Batman and the Joker movies exist in the Elseworlds realm. There are still titles yet to be released, like the Superman sequel Man of Tomorrow and a new series The People vs Gorilla Grodd, but they will certainly rank among the top 10.

Unlike her cousin, Kara Zor-El (Milly Alcock) is struggling to find her own place in Supergirl. Constantly partying and moving, she finally has a mission when the ruthless Krem of the Yellow Hills (Matthias Schoenaerts) endangers Krypto's life. With a young orphan named Ruthye (Eve Ridley) tagging along to seek revenge against Krem, Kara has to find the cure for Krypto before time runs out.

Drawing from a beloved miniseries, Supergirl: Woman of Tomorrow, the film has a lot of material to explore. Milly Alcock herself is amazing and refreshing as the titular Supergirl. However, the film struggles to adapt the storyline, and the changes made for the film break the story's nuance. The film also has a bland antagonist in Krem, despite being played by a reliable actor. The film is way too overpacked but never really gels together. We haven't even mentioned Jason Momoa's Lobo or the now-notorious final battle needle drop. Reflected in its middling reviews and box office, Supergirl marks DCU's first and perhaps the only setback.

In Creature Commandos, Amanda Waller (voiced by Viola Davis) manages to find an even weirder group to carry out her mission. Now, she assembles a team of imprisoned monsters, including the Bride (Indira Varma), Doctor Phosphorus (Alan Tudyk), Nina Mazursky (Zoe Chao), G.I. Robot and Weasel (both Sean Gunn). Led by General Rick Flag Sr. (Frank Grillo), the squad is sent to Pokolistan to protect Princess Ilana (Maria Bakalova) from a potential assassination attempt.

Creature Commandos is an unconventional start to a cinematic universe. However, it reflects James Gunn's sensibilities very well. The series is filled with his trademark combination of irreverent humor, violence, and great character development. Through the individual backstories, this group of misfits becomes more interesting as the series progresses. Nevertheless, the main story is often shadowed by the much more entertaining flashbacks. It is a fun series to watch for die-hard fans but never becomes a must-see show for those who are uninitiated with deeper DC lore. A second season is set to be released in 2027.

Clayface follows Matt Hagen (Tom Rhys Harries), a promising Hollywood actor whose life and career are destroyed after sleeping with the girlfriend of a ruthless crime boss, Markos Szabo (David Dencik). With his face horribly disfigured, Hagen seeks an experimental procedure conducted by Dr. Caitlyn Corr (Naomi Ackie) using supercharged nanites. Thanks to the nanites, his face is back to normal, but the procedure has devastating side effects.

Clayface was not part of James Gunn and Peter Safran's original plan, but it still fits the overall Gods and Monsters theme. It is also another unconventional entry in a nascent cinematic universe. However, with a strong story spearheaded by modern horror master Mike Flanagan, the film is a unique entry to the comic book genre. It is a body-horror tale, filled with shocking, horrific moments. Tom Rhys Harries is a compelling lead, and he is joined by a strong supporting cast. The film would benefit from a stronger villain, but Hagen's journey and the film's exploration of vanity and perfection are engaging enough. It is a shame that audiences might never see this Clayface face off against Batman.

Four franchises, four completely different ways of getting underneath your skin. This is the one built out of your particular fear, why it works so well on you, and what it would leave behind.

Your nightmare does not wait outside the door. It waits for you to close your eyes, which you are going to have to do eventually, because nobody has ever won that particular argument.

Your nightmare is not really the doll. It is the face of the person you tell, and the way they decide, very kindly, that you have imagined all of it.

Your nightmare has your number, knows your name, and has almost certainly been inside your house before. The worst part is that you already know them.

Your nightmare is not really about you. It is about the people asleep down the hall, and the feeling that whatever is here is not interested in leaving.

Despite saving the world, Christopher Smith (John Cena), better known as Peacemaker, is still not considered a hero by his superhero peers. With the rest of his gang busy with their own problems, he stumbles upon an alternate universe through his father's (Robert Patrick) pocket dimension. Here, he finds himself praised as a hero. But everything in this universe seemed too perfect to be true.

With a tweaked Season 1 finale scene, the second season of Peacemaker is firmly in the new DC Universe. The series and John Cena have developed the character so much that he evolved from being somewhat of a villain into one of the most compelling figures in this universe. Arguably the most versatile wrestler-turned-actor working today, Cena juggles the sincerity and the ridiculousness of the character perfectly. The alternate universe storyline brings a lot of entertainment and fun, including a cameo from the fan favorite Joel Kinnaman's Rick Flagg. The whole story about him and his father as well as his team is emotional and touching as well. With a well-rounded cast that brings exciting action and absurd humor, the latest (and maybe final) season of Peacemaker becomes one of the essential comic book shows to watch.

Superman follows the Man of Steel, played by David Corenswet, who lives in a world full of metahumans. Superman finds himself facing public scrutiny after intervening in an international conflict involving warring nations of Boravia and Jarhanpur. Lex Luthor (Nicholas Hoult) further undermines him by releasing a damning message from his Kryptonian parents and attacking him with his superpowered henchmen.

James Gunn’s Superman is an incredibly refreshing take on the world's most famous superhero and comic book adaptations in general. Gunn brings an abundance of characters into this film but is still able to make Superman the focus. It also adds quirky creatures and technology like the pocket universe, which makes the whole film feel more like a comic book came to life. Clark Kent and Lois Lane's (Rachel Brosnahan) relationship is electric and important to both characters. Meanwhile, Nicholas Hoult delivers an excellent Lex Luthor, portraying him as an intelligent but insecure individual. The film's best quality is its infectious, hopeful message, deeply ingrained in Superman's belief. It's a sneakily effective film that serves as a strong foundation for this new cinematic universe.

Lanterns introduces John Stewart (Aaron Pierre), a Green Lantern hopeful who is paired with the experienced and cocky Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) as his mentor. They travel to the small and very peaceful town of Rushville, Nebraska to investigate a murder that Jordan believes to be linked to an alien. Greeted by the town's Sheriff (Kelly Macdonald), Stewart and Jordan both sense that there is something more dangerous in town.

Lanterns is easily the most impressive entry in the DCU. It has a considerably longer runtime that helps both Lanterns' character development but it also has a grounded approach that makes them shine even more. Aaron Pierre and Kyle Chandler deliver great performances as men with opposite personalities who constantly clash yet have deep respect for each other. There is a highlight episode where the series tells the upbringing of John Stewart, which has never been explored in the comics before. Throughout its 8-episode run, it manages to enthrall fans and win new viewers. Lanterns is not just DCU's best production, but it is definitely one of the best superhero series ever made.

#3487. Five Race-Day Smartwatch Hacks Every Marathon Runner Should Know

I love my Garmin Forerunner 970, but the fact is, most runners don't need all the features it has to offer. In fact, for most road races, you can get by with whatever smartwatch you already own—as long as you know how to use it. If you've got a marathon or half-marathon coming up, these five tricks will only take a few minutes to set up, and they can save you from one of many of the small-but-avoidable disasters that can derail a good race.

Nothing spikes pre-race anxiety like standing in a corral of hundreds of people watching your watch fail to latch onto a signal. Tall buildings, crowded starts, and a sea of other devices make the first minute of GPS unreliable, which can leave your opening mileage pace wildly off.

The fix is simple: start the GPS search early. Step outside, into the open, as soon as you've dropped your bag, and select your run activity at least 10 to 15 minutes before the starting gun. If your watch supports multi-band or dual-frequency GPS, turn it on in the activity settings, since it's noticeably better in dense downtown starts. Then, don't press start until the gun goes off (or you cross the line, if you want chip-accurate pacing).

Bonus tip: If you're in a start corral with a long wait, you can lock the signal and then pause the activity screen. Just remember to hit start when you actually take off.

Multiple data screens are great for training, but overwhelming during a race. Too many numbers invite overthinking, and seeing the "wrong" number at mile two can lead you into a very stressful mile ten.

My recommendation is to build a dedicated race screen with three to four fields at most:

Lap pace or average lap pace (not instant pace, which jumps around constantly with GPS)

Distance or lap distance, so you know where you are relative to the mile markers

Heart rate, especially in the early miles when adrenaline tempts you to go out too fast

Elapsed time, for splits against your goal

Keep it clean and stripped down, and avoid the temptation to add cadence, power, vertical oscillation, and everything else. You can always review those stats during your cool-down.

A text from your boss at mile 14 is nobody's idea of a good time. Before race day, switch your watch to Do Not Disturb or Airplane mode, or turn on a dedicated activity mode that blocks notifications. This also saves battery, which matters if your marathon is going to take you four-plus hours.

After blocking the outside world, you can set race-specific alerts, like a high heart-rate alert to keep you honest in the first half. I also know runners who set a recurring time or distance alert for fueling—say, every 30 to 40 minutes, or every 5 miles—so remembering to down a gel or a sports drink doesn't depend on your fading brain.

Here's one thing I learn the hard way, every time: Your watch will almost always say you've run farther than the race course says you have. Race courses are measured along the shortest possible route, but along the way, you'll weave around people, take wide turns, and generally add extra distance. I've run marathons where my watch reads closer to 26.6 miles (nearly an extra half mile), so my "on pace" watch is actually behind my chip time.

The hack: Ignore the watch's auto-lap and press the lap button manually at each mile marker (or at every kilometer marker, if that's what the course uses). This gives you pace data aligned to the official course, not the satellite's best guess. It also gives you a quick mental check against your plan. If you've set up your watch for it, display average lap pace, then glance at it a few hundred meters after each marker to see how you're tracking. And don't panic if your watch beeps for a mile before you pass the marker—trust the course and your lap presses, and do your best to ignore the mismatched distance adding up.

Rain, sweat, high-fives, and a hasty cup grab at an aid station can all trigger accidental taps on a touchscreen watch. Few things are worse than discovering at mile 18 that you accidentally paused, ended, or switched screens on your activity. So before the race, turn on your watch's screen lock, so a stray touch doesn't do anything.

If your watch has a configurable wake gesture, consider turning it off to save battery, and set the backlight to a short timeout. While we're talking watch-wearing protocol, remember to wear it snugly, one finger-width above your wrist bone, for a better heart-rate reading as you sweat. Finally, if your watch has one, use the post-race auto-save reminder. (Otherwise, do your best to hit stop after you cross the finish line.)

Again, you don't need the most premium running-specific watch ahead of race day. If you have time, test these hacks on a long run, so that you're not wasting any precious mental energy during the big day.

#3486. Naruto's 4 New Episodes: Everything We Know So Far

Vanessa Piña has been writing as a journalist for over two years. As a senior writer, she focuses on timely coverage of the latest anime releases and popular comic franchises.

While the Naruto franchise has provided fans with a significant amount of content, setting aside the Boruto anime, it has been nearly a decade since the last release featuring a brand-new adventure centered on Naruto Uzumaki. Although the possibility of receiving new anime episodes once seemed remote, Masashi Kishimoto’s story is returning to the screen in the form of a limited series, giving fans plenty to get excited about.

Originally announced as part of the 20th-anniversary celebration of Naruto's anime adaptation in 2023, the project faced a difficult path and significant delays, leading fans to believe it had been canceled entirely. Fortunately, new information has been revealed regarding the four-episode Naruto anime special, confirming that the project is well underway. From where it fits into the franchise's timeline and which characters will appear, to what to expect from the story and the release date, here's everything known about Naruto's major anime comeback.

In a post on the official Naruto website in March 2023, four new anime episodes of Naruto were revealed to be in the works. On August 29, 2023, less than a week before the first episode was supposed to begin airing, Naruto's anime return was postponed. The sudden decision by the production committee was made in order to "create a work that meets everyone's expectations."

The post on X from the official Naruto account was made with an apology to fans, stating, "We have made the decision to postpone the broadcast due to the further improvement of the quality of this work." At the time, the Naruto anime special wasn't officially canceled; however, in the years that followed, there were no further updates from Studio Pierrot, which created a great deal of uncertainty among fans about whether the project would ever be released. Fortunately, this changed at New York Comic Con 2026, where more details about the anime special were finally revealed.

After three years without any updates, a major announcement regarding the Naruto anime special was made on October 10, 2026, during the franchise’s panel at New York Comic Con. Instead of a conventional anniversary project, Studio Pierrot is preparing a four-episode limited series titled Naruto x Ninku, confirming a crossover with Koji Kiriyama’s legendary anime franchise.

Ninku is not only one of the major ninja-themed manga ever published in Shonen Jump, but it's also a work that Masashi Kishimoto has acknowledged as a major influence on Naruto. In a message shared with fans, Kishimoto expressed his joy about the crossover, revealing that he was the one who proposed the project.

"I created NARUTO because I personally wanted to see the continuation of NINKU. I think many of you have already noticed, but NARUTO was immensely influenced by NINKU. Without NINKU, NARUTO would not exist.

Simply put, Fusuke is Naruto’s secret mentor.

Eventually, I began dreaming of bringing this master-and-student relationship out of the shadows, and into an actual storyline.

Kiriyama Sensei, who is as much a mentor to me as Fusuke is to Naruto, graciously agreed to my selfish request.

By meeting with me in person and with his extensive cooperation, he helped make my long-standing dream a reality." - Masashi Kishimoto

The Ninku anime, which aired between 1995 and 1996, was also produced by Studio Pierrot. While this might have made it easier for the studio to handle this crossover at the request of the creator of Naruto, the creative process and logistics could have taken longer than anticipated, which would explain why the anime special was postponed. Furthermore, Naruto x Ninku is being developed by Pierrot Films, a sub-studio that wasn't established until February 2024.

Although the plot details for the new Naruto episodes were initially a mystery, it was known that the special would be set during the period when Naruto Uzumaki and Team 7 were genin, with official art showing Sasuke Uchiha, Sakura Haruno, and Kakashi Hatake. However, now as a crossover bringing together two classic ninja franchises, Team 7 will cross paths with Fusuke and his friends, Aicho, Toji, Hiroyuki, and Rihoko. Along with the announcement, a teaser was presented in which characters from both series can be seen meeting. The official Naruto website also revealed the synopsis for the limited series.

Team 7 members Naruto, Sasuke, and Sakura are given a mission by Kakashi. Since Kakashi cannot participate himself, Naruto is appointed acting leader.

As a result of this decision, Naruto is fully motivated to make the mission a success. However, on the way, Team 7 finds themselves lost in another world. What appears before the bewildered trio is a boy with a face resembling a frog's, named Fusuke. What awaits them in this strange new world?

The crossover is directed by Noriyuki Abe, who worked with both franchises in the past, and the creators of Naruto and Ninku helped oversee the story, while Pierrot Films is handling the production. They were also responsible for Bleach: Thousand-Year Blood War, a project that marked a significant leap in the studio's animation quality, so fans can look forward to plenty of ninja action. The official Naruto website features visual material related to the crossover, as well as detailed summaries of each series and its characters, which helps to fuel fans' interest in the new series.

There's currently no release date for when the Naruto x Ninku episodes will air. This crossover is part of "Project Rasengan", appearing on the series' roadmap for upcoming releases between 2027 and 2029. Although it lacks a specific date, unlike the Naruto Card Game, which is scheduled for a global launch in June 2027, its placement on the roadmap suggests that this special could be released during the first half of 2027.

Luckily, fans won't have to wait too long for further updates since the release date for Naruto x Ninku is expected to be confirmed during the Naruto panel at Jump Festa 2027. The panel will take place on Saturday, December 19, 2026.

The Naruto crossover anime special will drop the iconic young Team 7 into a new world that Western audiences are unfamiliar with but owe a lot to.

In recent years, Studio Pierrot has had a rather packed schedule, with several major projects either in production or recently released. But perhaps the biggest obstacle to the return of Naruto's anime thus far has been Bleach: Thousand-Year Blood War, a series in which Studio Pierrot invested a significant amount of time and personnel to ensure a high-end adaptation. However, now that Bleach's anime has concluded, the studio’s most prominent series is Black Clover, which is also nearing its end. Given the popularity of Naruto, it is highly likely that fans will see its anime return soon.

Despite the Ninku crossover not being what fans had expected, they probably have more reasons to be hopeful than not. Project Rasengan made it clear that this special is just the first step in the plans for the franchise, so fans can look forward to more anime content, including the continuation of Boruto's anime.

Naruto is not some wildcard whose appeal or fanbase is unclear. The series represents one of the largest anime/manga franchises in the world. Naruto is the sixth best-selling manga of all time. If for no other reason, Naruto's popularity makes the anime's return feel bigger than ever. Signs are pointing toward good things in the future for fans of the biggest ninja anime in the world, both in terms of the manga and the animated format. A case in point is that Kishimoto is launching a new Naruto sequel in manga form, which could potentially be adapted into an anime.

Another great story that new Naruto anime projects could cover is the short manga revolving around Naruto's mom and dad titled Naruto: The Whorl Within The Spiral. After winning the Naruto worldwide popularity poll, the Fourth Hokage and father of Naruto, Minato Namikaze, received his own short story written and even illustrated by series author Masashi Kishimoto. Minato's manga definitively proved that the Naruto series still has great stories to tell, and it would be a fantastic project to adapt into anime.

The original anime adaptation of Naruto premiered in October 2002 and ran for 220 episodes. The follow-up series, Naruto: Shippuden, aired shortly after the original series ended in February 2007 and ran until March 2017. While the series generally followed the plot of Kishimoto's original manga, there were a number of anime-only Naruto stories called filler by fans.

The creator of Naruto is working on an entirely new sequel manga that is teasing the exploration of the franchise's biggest blank spot.

During their run, Naruto and Naruto: Shippuden grew to become international hits and beloved pillars of anime fandom. The story of a young Naruto bootstrapping his way to success is a story that appeals to a wide range of people and cultures. The diversity and complexity of the Narutoverse also make it easy for fans to see themselves in many of its characters. With Boruto: Two Blue Vortex bringing new life to the sequel series and Naruto's anime set to return, it's never been a better time to be a fan of Masashi Kishimoto's ninja world.

#3484. We Officially Ranked Every James Bond Actor

James Bond is one of cinema’s great characters, and one that will never fall out of fashion. Although other franchises have attempted to invent or expand upon new continuities, the Bond series has adapted to the times by reframing its story to fit the cultural, social, and political trends of the era. Bond is unabashed entertainment representing pure heroism, but he’s drawn from a darker character imagined by Ian Fleming as a ruthless assassin who wears his license to kill as a badge of honor. Each actor to take on the role has had to contend with the pressures of being a smoldering hero, a fantasy of charisma, a loyal patriot, and a womanizing charmer, resulting in very different performances over time.

The speculation as to who could be the next Bond always illuminates conversation, as it's more than just a role that can be recycled in the vein of Batman, Spider-Man, or even more classical characters like Robin Hood or King Arthur. The Bond films screen for the Royal Family and become historical artifacts that attract attention and analysis for years on end, making it all the more important to make the right choice in selecting the person to play him. Denis Villeneuve is currently underway on casting the next actor to take on the role, meaning that either Robert Pattinson, Nicholas Hoult, Josh O’Connor, Callum Turner, or Jack Lowden will have massive shoes to fill. Each Bond actor has value in one way or another, but time has painted a fairly evident hierarchy.

It’s often forgotten that there were two Casino Royale adaptations before the 2006 film that launched the most recent iteration of the series. The first was a television episode of an anthology show from the ‘50s, but the first cinematic version was in a feature length parody film released by Warner Bros. as one of two non-EON entries in the series. Although it’s a spoof that gathers an entire cast to play different versions of Bond, the main star is David Niven, who had ironically enough been Fleming’s first choice during the casting of Dr. No.

Niven is a charismatic actor who can deliver the one-liners needed to play a slick version of Bond, but he’s trapped within an insufferable parody film that wasn’t all that funny in 1967, and has aged even worse today. Bond becomes a caricature and Niven is encouraged to be a stickler for British protocol in a manner that doesn’t fit with the edgier persona that Fleming had created. It is nonetheless interesting to consider what Niven could have done with the role had he been given the chance to make a “proper” Bond film; the best idea of what his 007 would have looked like is in the World War II classic The Guns of Navarone, where he plays a sharp British commando whose bravery and intelligence feel quite Bond-ian.

On Her Majesty’s Secret Service is one of the best Bond films ever made, and it would contend Skyfall and Goldfinger to be the top pick if it weren’t for a mediocre performance by George Lazenby. Lazenby does a decent enough job, all things considered; he has virtually no acting experience before being cast, and attracted a fair amount of backlash for doing something different with the character. On Her Majesty’s Secret Service plays Bond as being a more wholesome, romantic character with a wry sense of whimsy, and Lazenby both gives a charming performance without ever feeling totally believable as a secret agent.

Lazenby lacked the physical prowess needed to be an action hero and can come off as rather stiff in some of the dialogue exchanges, although to be fair there’s no telling what more he could have done with the part had he agreed to star in Diamonds Are Forever. That Lazenby refused to return is partially due to the pressure he was facing from EON and the fan backlash, but it also might simply be because he never felt completely comfortable in the part. While he’s not necessarily a great Bond, the chemistry Lazenby has with Diana Rigg makes for one of cinema’s greatest love stories.

Roger Moore is a divisive Bond who is widely misunderstood by some contemporary Bond viewers who don’t understand that his version of the character was intentionally campy and completely in-on-the-joke. Moore was an older version of Bond who developed a more bemused perspective on the potentially world-ending scenarios he often found himself in, and the fact that his emotions rarely rise above mild concern is part of the charm of his films. With that being said, each Bond can only be judged by the totality of their time as the character, and Moore’s output in the role was quite mixed.

Live and Let Die is a fantastic debut that showed Moore could be suave and swanky in a way that was different from Connery, as he felt both decidedly modern and classically gentlemanly. The Spy Who Loved Me is a similarly great film that offers Moore the chance to show the most range because it unlocks a darker side of the character; a moment where he reveals a shocking secret to Barbara Bach’s Agent XXX is among the greatest moments of acting in the franchise’s entire history. Yet, Moore often felt secondary to the spectacle in some of the sillier installments, and even admitted by the end of his run that he was far too old to be playing the character.

Timothy Dalton is perhaps the hardest Bond to judge, even more so than Lazenby, because his run as the character was cut short prematurely. While On Her Majesty’s Secret Service felt like a complete statement about Bond as a character, Dalton had only really started to encompass the role by the time that his two entries in the series were up. The Living Daylights is a good movie, but the script was clearly styled in Moore’s sensibilities and didn’t totally unlock the more mature take that Dalton had. License to Kill was a swing in the completely different direction that turned Bond into a vengeance-seeking vigilante, and it’s not until the end of the film that he returns to MI6 to become a more classical version of the character.

Dalton is nonetheless one of the few Bond actors to show an actual interest in Fleming’s books and clearly knew the text well enough to purposefully distinguish himself from his cinematic predecessors.

Pierce Brosnan is in a similar place to Moore in his run as Bond being somewhat uneven, but the difference is that he was locked into his performance the entire time. Brosnan’s debut in Goldeneye didn’t just save the franchise as a whole, but split the difference in terms of what every film since should aim for; it retained all the classical elements of the series, but felt hip and modern, showing self-awareness without being too cheeky. Brosnan was believable as a killer and a master of spycraft, but he was also the most handsome and charming actor to play Bond as a romantic foil.

Brosnan’s strength in Bond is made clear by how much he elevates his films, as he was able to successfully bring a darker component to The World Is Not Enough in spite of a ridiculous script with some truly terrible lines. Although Brosnan has admitted to being disappointed that he did not get to make a fifth film, Amazon and MGM would make a lot of fans happy if they brought him back for a one-off legacy sequel.

Sean Connery is one of the greatest movie stars of all-time and is responsible for defining what Bond became. There is no question that he is the reason that the character remains a popular culture titan and not an obscure character from Cold War-era spy novels, as Connery created a larger-than-life hero who still had one foot planted in reality. Connery had the dexterity as an actor to lean into the Hitchcockian elements of From Russia With Love or the spectacular audacity of Goldfinger, but he was so naturally compelling that he turned more routine Bond adventures like Thunderball and You Only Live Twice into great entertainment.

Connery found something very unique within Bond that cut through some of the character’s inherent contradictions. He’s an unabashed servant of the crown who doesn’t feel prickly, a womanizer who isn’t toxic, and a killer who can still deliver a one-liner. Bond is more than just an action hero, and Connery is still who most people think of when they imagine the character.

Daniel Craig is responsible for revamping Bond for the modern age and turning him into a truly complex character while also delivering the most authentic interpretation of what Fleming imagined him to be. Casino Royale wasn’t just the technically impressive and gritty installment in the series, but a truly harrowing drama that saw Craig making a vulnerable character stooped in tragedy. Skyfall placed Craig’s Bond in a place where he had to advocate for his own existence, arguing on behalf of the franchise itself, and it was so convincing that it became the highest-grossing entry in the series to date with over $1 billion.

Craig retained the dry sensibilities of Connery while showing the intensity of Dalton, and also took Brosnan’s tips of doing extensive training to ensure that his stunts would look real. One of the reasons the next era of the franchise faces so much pressure is the intimidation of following Craig.

The Roborock Qrevo Edge 2 robot vacuum and mop is down to $799.99 from $1,299.99 in an early Black Friday deal, saving you $500 and bringing it to its lowest price to date, according to price trackers. Much of its appeal comes from a slim 3.1-inch profile that lets it reach under beds, sofas, and other low furniture where taller robot vacuums often can’t fit. It manages this with a feature Roborock calls RetractSense, which checks the clearance as the robot approaches a tight gap and lowers the laser navigation tower into the body, leaving a camera with a 100-degree field of view to guide it underneath.

Beyond its low profile, the Qrevo Edge 2 pairs 25,000Pa of suction with a split DuoDivide main brush that guides hair toward the suction opening, so long strands and pet fur are less likely to end up wound around the roller. Edges get extra attention too, since its FlexiArm Arc side brush reaches out into corners while its mop module swivels to get closer to walls, with the two mop pads spinning at 200 RPM as they work. It also adjusts its cleaning based on whether it encounters dry or wet dirt, boosting suction for dust and lifting its main brush over spills. For all that adaptability on the floor, getting between rooms can be trickier—the robot lacks an adjustable chassis to lift itself over obstacles, so it can struggle with thresholds higher than 0.8 inches.

Once a cleaning run wraps up, most of the upkeep happens at the dock, which washes and dries the mop pads and empties dust into a bag rated for up to 65 days. That said, its onboard water tank is relatively small at 2.3 fluid ounces, potentially requiring extra trips to the dock during larger mopping jobs. There's also no dedicated cleaning solution tank, meaning you'll have to add approved cleaning additives manually to the fresh water. The rest of the fine-tuning happens in the Roborock app, where you can set cleaning schedules, adjust suction power and water flow, and choose how the robot handles carpets.

#3482. One LEGO Harry Potter Set's Upcoming Retirement Comes With A Major Twist

A popular LEGO Harry Potter set is leaving shelves for good, but it also comes with a major twist.

LEGO's Harry Potter collection has been a major part of the company since its debut in 2001, coinciding with the release of Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone. Over the past 25 years, the line has expanded a lot. The collection consists of hundreds of building sets inspired by the Wizarding World.

LEGO collectors have an opportunity to pick up a retiring Harry Potter set at a significantly reduced price ahead of the holidays. The LEGO Harry Potter Book Nook: Hogwarts Express, which was first released in 2025, is currently being offered for $50 on Amazon and at Walmart, lowering its original price of $99.99 by 50%. The discount comes as the popular set approaches the end of its run, making the deal more appealing and allowing fans to pick up the set before it is discontinued.

LEGO recently announced that the Book Nook: Hogwarts Express set is nearing the end of its run, listing it as "Retiring Soon" on its website. The set is also completely sold out on the company's site. However, it is still available on Amazon and at Walmart, for the time being. Considering how quickly the set sold out on its original platform, collectors shouldn't waste any time picking it up at other retailers.

The promotion arrives ahead of Black Friday this year and coincides with Walmart's first round of holiday deals. With $49.99 knocked off the price, the Book Nook: Hogwarts Express is likely one of the best LEGO Harry Potter discounts. However, it is important to keep in mind that prices and deals can change.

The LEGO Harry Potter Book Nook: Hogwarts Express recreates one of the film franchise's most iconic locations, Platform 9¾ at London's King's Cross station. The 832-piece set features the famous red train on the platform. It captures the scene when Harry begins his journey to Hogwarts with his owl, Hedwig. It also includes a mini figure of Ron Weasley and his rat Scabbers.

Unlike traditional LEGO train sets, this model was created specifically to be a bookshelf display. Its design allows collectors to arrange it in several different ways, including being able to close it like a book, which makes it easier to place in smaller spaces. When closed, it can actually be placed between books on a shelf, which is very fitting as the train station is beyond the barrier between two platforms.

With such a wide range of sets spanning from individual Hogwarts classrooms to major locations outside of the castle, LEGO Harry Potter continues to be an integral part of LEGO's brand. Its wide variety of products has helped the collection remain relevant and popular over two decades after its launch.

Bose has issued a recall of more than 670,000 lithium-ion battery packs used in the company's S1 Pro and S1 Pro+ Bluetooth speaker systems due to overheating issues.

According to a Consumer Product Safety Commission announcement, Bose has received reports of the battery packs overheating to the point of melting, producing smoke or catching fire. Fortunately, no injuries have been reported.

The recall specifically affects battery packs that include any one of the following six digits in the serial numbers: 083723, 078352, 084105, 078591, 078592, 084106, or 086409. You can find the 17-digit number on the label printed on the bottom of the pack.

These packs were sold both with the S1 Pro and S1 Pro+ speakers as well as accessories, for between $100 and $160 from December 2017 through July 2026. The speaker systems cost $700.

In total, 634,759 were sold in the US, with an additional 35,400 in Canada.

If you have the S1 Pro or S1 Pro+ Portable Bluetooth Speaker Systems, Bose requests that you stop using the battery packs immediately and remove them from the speakers. You can still use the speakers connected to AC power.

If you have an uninstalled battery pack, you just need to find the serial number and send it to Bose.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Bose is asking owners to register and provide the serial number at http://www.bose.com/support/s1-battery-recall. The company is providing a free replacement battery pack.

You'll need to dispose of the battery safely, which means do not just throw the battery pack in the trash or in used battery recycling boxes at retail or home improvement stores. Lithium-ion batteries must be disposed of differently from other batteries because of the greater risk of fire.

You'll need to look up your local municipality's household hazardous waste collection center. You should contact the center because not everyone accepts lithium-ion batteries. They will generally be able to point you in the right direction.

The 75-inch Hisense U6SF Pro has dropped to $747.97 from $1,399.99 ahead of Amazon’s Black Friday sale—bringing it to its lowest price to date, according to price trackers. The rest of the U6 Pro lineup is discounted as well, so you can pick up the same TV in sizes from 55 inches to a massive 100 inches, for anyone with the room for something closer to a home-theater-sized screen. Whichever size you choose, you’ll get free delivery to the room of choice—a service that normally costs $19.99. As for the TV itself, it’s a 2026 model that sits below the U7SG (also on sale for $1,297.99, from $1,999.99) in Hisense's lineup as the brand's entry point into Mini LED, pairing a 4K panel and local dimming with a matte, anti-reflective coating meant to cut down on glare, notes this PCMag review.

For a budget set, the U6 Pro gets a lot right when it comes to picture quality—its high peak brightness helps it hold up during a sunny afternoon in a living room with big windows, so a daytime football game or cooking show won’t look washed out, while its excellent contrast and effective local dimming keep dark scenes looking deep when you settle in for a movie at night. It also does a good job cleaning up lower-quality content, which is useful for older cable broadcasts or compressed YouTube videos—and its Fire TV interface makes it easy to jump between those kinds of content and the major streaming services without needing a separate streaming device.

The U6 Pro also brings plenty to the table for gaming, with HDMI 2.1, VRR, ALLM, and a 144Hz refresh rate that PC gamers can push to 240Hz at a lower 1080p resolution. That said, the panel’s slow response time and poor motion performance can reportedly make fast-moving scenes look noticeably blurry. Viewing angles are limited too, with the picture losing quality fairly quickly when you move off-center—and its built-in speakers aren’t particularly impressive either, so a soundbar could be worth budgeting for.

#3479. Apple now sells ‘innovative’ game controller play pad and 20+ more accessories

Apple has updated its third-party accessories lineup ahead of the holidays. The refreshed lineup includes products for gaming, iPhone filmmaking, charging, and more. Among the most interesting additions is an “innovative” game controller that works with iPhone, iPad, Apple TV, Apple Vision Pro, and more.

The GAMR Active Game Controller retails for $199.95 at Apple. Apple describes it as an “innovative, pressure-sensitive game controller play pad” that lets players control compatible games by stepping and moving across nine responsive zones.

Those zones map to directional controls and the A, B, X, and Y buttons of a traditional controller. GAMR connects over Bluetooth to iPhone, iPad, Apple TV, Mac, and Apple Vision Pro, with support for compatible Apple Arcade and App Store games. There’s also a free GAMR app with original games.

Apple lists up to eight to ten hours of battery life, and the pad rolls up for storage between gaming sessions. Think a dance mat-style approach to playing games across Apple’s devices.

Another notable addition is the ShiftCam ProRig Filmmaker Kit, which sells for $169.95 in Titanium Silver.

The kit puts an open frame around your iPhone, with repositionable handles for shooting in landscape or portrait. A Bluetooth shutter lets you capture shots from the grip, while two cold shoe mounts and six quarter-inch mounting points provide room for lights, microphones, tripods, and other accessories.

ShiftCam also includes an adapter for compatible filters and lenses, a carrying pouch, and interchangeable bumpers for iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 17 Pro Max, iPhone 18 Pro, and iPhone 18 Pro Max.

For something smaller and more affordable, Apple now sells the ShiftCam SnapPocket Light 2 Magnetic LED Ring Light for $39.95.

The pocket-sized light attaches to a MagSafe-compatible iPhone or case and flips 180 degrees to illuminate either you or your subject. It offers five brightness levels and five color temperature settings ranging from warm to cool, with a built-in battery that recharges over USB-C. ShiftCam also includes a magnetic ring sticker for attaching it to an iPad or MacBook.

The light is also included in the $159.95 ShiftCam SnapTravel Kit Pro 2, alongside a camera grip with a 5,000mAh battery and Qi2 charging, a selfie stick that converts into a tripod, and a travel pouch.

Elsewhere, Apple’s latest accessory selection includes two Belkin power banks. The $99.95 UltraCharge Pro 20K features an integrated USB-C cable with up to 70W output and two additional USB-C ports. The $49.95 BoostCharge Slim Magnetic Power Bank 5K with Stand offers 15W Qi2 wireless charging, 20W wired charging, and a built-in kickstand.

There’s also the $49.95 MOFT Snap Field MagSafe Wallet Stand, which holds up to eight cards and unfolds into a stand for your iPhone. You can also find it on Amazon.

Cases and bags round out the selection, including Tech21 FlexFolio and mophie Knit folios for iPad Air and iPad Pro, a Tech21 EvoShell for MacBook Neo, Rains sleeves, and Herschel sleeves, bags, and organizers.

#3478. HBO's 'Big Little Lies' Is Officially Returning, but Its Biggest Mistake Remains

The debut of Big Little Lies was one of the most important moments in the contemporary history of HBO because of how significantly the miniseries expanded the possibilities of the medium. Not only was it a high-profile, expensive show that featured major A-list stars and Academy Award winners, but it adapted a bestselling novel in order to take advantage of the cultural zeitgeist; this was something that traditionally would have been done with a film only a few years prior, but Big Little Lies had managed to do it on the small screen and become “event television,” despite not being a spectacle-based genre show. Big Little Lies was a phenomenon that hasn’t been replicated, as evidenced by a Season 2 that faced several major issues. Although the notion of the cast reuniting for another outing is hard not to be excited about, it does present some serious questions about what the show’s intentionality has become.

Big Little Lies is based on the novel of the same name by Liane Moriarty, and was adapted by television legend David E. Kelley. The series examines a closely-knit community of wealthy parents in Monterey, California, in which many of the women have put on public-facing personas that mask the challenges that are going on in their domestic setting. The first season is centered around the death of Perry White (Alexander Skarsgård), who had been abusing his wife Celeste (Nicole Kidman) and putting their children in danger. Although Celeste and her friends Madeline Mackenzie (Reese Witherspoon), Jane Chapman (Shailene Woodley), Bonnie Carlson (Zoë Kravitz), and Renata Klein (Laura Dern) are able to get away with their involvement, the trauma of the event causes fissures within each of their personal relationships. Big Little Lies struggled when it went on its own path beyond the source material, and it’s unclear if Season 3 will be able to rectify any of these narrative constraints.

It’s not completely unusual for a miniseries to be expanded into a recurring drama show if the appeal is strong, but adding on to a self-contained story that was wrapped up in a novel can be self-defeating because it is altering an ending that had already been satisfying. Although the ending of Season 1 of Big Little Lies isn’t necessarily rousing because of everything that the characters went through, it did provide some sense of closure by showing that their healing process had begun, even if it never could be truly completed. The issue with Season 2 is that committing to showing this gradual recovery from painful circumstances is not as inherently interesting on a dramatic level, and it led to a season in which the new issues many of the characters dealt with felt very soapy. Seeing Celeste and Jane cope with their collective trauma at the hands of Perry, and how it affected both of their children, was undeniably powerful, but Renata’s financial issues and Madeline’s familial conflict weren’t nearly as compelling.

Season 2 also suffered from a behind-the-scenes struggle, as the show was not able to let a new creative voice take the story in a new direction, resulting in a season that was at odds with itself. The brilliant British filmmaker Andrea Arnold had been hired to showrun Season 2, but her vision was significantly altered and resulted in creative differences that made it a shadow of what she had intended; it certainly was not a good look for HBO to do so much meddling in the vision of a female artist for a show that had such strong feminist themes. While the logical choice would have been to bring back director Jean-Marc Vallée, who handled Season 1 with the utmost respect and grace, his tragic death in 2021 meant that HBO is forced to find another showrunner who has yet to be announced. Given what Arnold went through in Season 2, it’s hard to imagine that a lot of top-line talent would be willing to immediately sign up.

Season 3 is reportedly set to be based on Big Little Truths, a sequel to the original novel that Moriarty published this year. The issue is that the sequel novel includes events that contradict those of Season 2 of Big Little Lies, meaning that adaptive choices will need to be fairly significant if the third season wants to follow the book. Although having an outline does give Season 3 more of a template than its predecessor, it is not automatically a guarantee of quality; subsequent adaptations of other Moriarty novels, such as Nine Perfect Strangers and Apples Never Fall, were not nearly as well-received, suggesting that the first season of Big Little Lies was an anomaly in which everything seemed to go just right. It was a big deal initially to see so many major actresses on television at once, but it is less exciting in an era in which star-studded television has become more normalized.

The more critical question that Big Little Lies faces in its future is that it is not clear what the season is trying to say. Although the first season was certainly entertaining and had some conventional television moments, it felt like an appropriate reaction to a hostile cultural moment for women that examined the complications of justice. The season’s goal was to find a way to set these characters on a better path, and continuing to focus on their misfortune and misery sends mixed messages. Big Little Lies had the chance to be a perfect miniseries, but every subsequent season puts it at risk of undermining its own legacy.

#3477. ChatGPT's New GIF Generator Is Fun, but Won't Replace Us Humans (Yet)

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

When it comes to generating AI images, both Gemini and ChatGPT do a passable job. In most cases, the results will look AI-generated, but they likely won’t have glaring spelling issues or missing limbs. Now, OpenAI is trying something new, introducing GIF support for ChatGPT. It's the company's first "moving images" feature since OpenAI shut down Sora, and while you can generate hyper-realistic videos in Gemini, this new ChatGPT feature is trying to fill in the gap, in a small way.

OpenAI is pitching the new feature as an animation tool, not exactly as a way to create looping videos—though that’s how I ended up using it. You give ChatGPT a prompt, as detailed as you can make it, and the chatbot produces a GIF in just a few seconds. You can start with your own drawings or images, too. ChatGPT uses sketches as the base for animations, though it can turn any still image into animated GIFs. Like other AI editing tools, you can edit it if ChatGPT didn't quite get it right: You can ask ChatGPT to make the GIF longer or shorter, remove certain objects, change the style, slow down transitions, among other edits.

AI art can be quite sterile, but I was surprised by how adding motion and animation to the mix makes generating images a lot more fun. Unlike traditional GIFs, which usually pull from existing video clips, you can turn anything you want into a GIF, which is especially cool if you're using your own art. In my testing, I found this to be the most rewarding part. It’s not always possible to one-shot a GIF with a single prompt. But after a few rounds of edits, I ended up creating some GIFs that I actually wanted to share in my WhatsApp groups.

That being said, I think human-made GIFs are still the gold standard here. For example, I asked ChatGPT to generate a video of someone brewing a pour-over, with a gooseneck kettle, showing the coffee blooming process. It did okay, but it’s nothing like actually making a pour-over. The kettle doesn’t move in circles, the water doesn’t rise evenly, there are no bubbles, and the steam is all over the place.

Compare that to the GIF below, which comes from a royalty-free video. Even though it’s a compressed, low-quality, and noisy GIF, it still shows the movement of the pour, the water rising, and even the bubbles. The details captured by a real video just aren’t there in ChatGPT GIFs. If that’s what you’re expecting, you will be disappointed. But I don't think that's the point of this feature anyway.

I found that ChatGPT excels when you’re making something fun, and you don’t look into the details too much. It pulled off a loop of a cat playing with a ball, and it was great at making a festive GIF for Diwali. It even made a GIF based on a photo. I asked it to create a fun promotional GIF for my JBL Bluetooth speakers, and it did the job quite well. At first, the transitions were too jarring, and the movement just made no sense. After some editing, though, I got it to a decent place.

Still, the main issue with ChatGPT GIFs is that complex movement and transitions aren’t nailed down. A hand shifts position weirdly between frames, and colors and objects appear out of nowhere. But if you can get over these issues, you can make some fun, lighthearted GIFs and memes to share with your friends on Instagram or WhatsApp.

#3472. Why John Lennon Is Responsible for Wings’ Biggest Hit

On April 9, 1970, the entire world sat down to read one slip of paper. By the time they reached the end of the press release, if they could still see through tear-blurred eyes, one conclusion was drawn: Paul McCartney was leaving The Beatles.

In hindsight, it's not really that surprising McCartney felt called to split from the pack. The "Fab Four" had a less than ideal relationship with each other, specifically the band's two workhorse songwriters, John Lennon and Paul McCartney. If you find yourself looking up the term "creative differences" in a dictionary, there's a non-zero chance there's a picture of Lennon and McCartney hurling insults at each other like grenades during a writing session. But it was this conflicting nature that led to McCartney's most popular post-Beatles song, and one that even Lennon had to give him props for.

During the sessions for 1968's The White Album, tensions rose so high that Ringo Starr — synonymous with the mantra "peace and love" — had to take a two-week sabbatical from the studio. But while Starr was merely just caught in the crossfire, it was John Lennon and Paul McCartney on the frontlines against each other.

Both sides let this boil over into the press. In that very same press release announcing his departure from The Beatles, McCartney included a "self interview" detailing his next steps in his solo career, as well as promotional copies of his solo debut album, McCartney. John Lennon made it known that he didn't care for his former bandmates' actions, almost as much as he hated his songs, saying McCartney would "drag his feet," when discussing business with him and referring to him as an "egomaniac," in a 1971 interview with Rolling Stone.

It's impossible to deny that both of the frontmen wielded a golden pen, but they were also a rare case of utter opposite sides of the songwriting spectrum. Lennon always tried to force the audience to see the world through his eyes, attributing his reality to the world in the anti-establishment "Imagine," or "Instant Karma!," a threat-shaped single aimed at his harshest music critic. McCartney, on the other hand, was a vessel of pure unadulterated creativity, someone who was just gnawing at the chain to keep making more and more music. While he was undoubtedly productive, he was often seen as oafish in comparison to his writing partner, lacking true purpose in his songs. He even admitted in his 1977 autobiography that he made up the lyrics to "Jet" with no real meaning in mind, although he has claimed the song to be about a pregnant dog, a pony and meeting his wife Linda's father for the first time.

Both of their reputations followed them out of The Beatles, but while Lennon was lauded by critics as a revolutionary, McCartney was pushed to the side, and just dismissed as another pop star that had nothing real to say. The media would continue to push the narrative that Paul McCartney was just a pretty face with no good stories to tell. But even someone as charming as Sir Paul McCartney has their breaking point. Rolling Stone dubbed his 1971 project Ram, "so inconsequential and so monumentally irrelevant," that you couldn't even focus enough on the songs to decide whether you hated them or not. America's self-appointed "only Rock 'n Roll magazine," Creem, called him "stereotypical and vapid," after Wings' showing on ABC-TV.

And the final straw came, of course, from an all too familiar source.

"There were accusations in the mid-1970's — including one from John [Lennon] — that I was just writing 'silly love songs'," McCartney said in a 2021 autobiography, The Lyrics: 1956 to the Present.

Most songwriters would've found themselves intimidated by the pressures of falling into a typecast. But thankfully, Paul McCartney is not most songwriters. McCartney took the very words that had been belittling him, and gave them an entirely different meaning. In March 1976, Paul McCartney and Wings released the first single for their Speed of Sound album: "Silly Love Songs."

McCartney's musical prowess had never been in question — the instrumental for the track has the signature brightness of a Wings song, spearheaded by a classically captivating McCartney bassline. But after being dragged through the dirt for years about his lyrics having no substance, every line in the song is packed with purpose.

From the opening lines (Some people want to fill the world with silly love songs / But I look around me and I see it isn't so) to the bridge refrain, (How can I tell you about my loved one?) the entire track feels less like a lead single from one of the biggest pop stars on the planet, and more of a strongly worded entry into McCartney's personal diary. It's so expertly written and still filled with McCartney's tongue-in-cheek sense of humor: just repeating "I love you" as a chorus comes across as a wry wink to those trying to pigeon-hole him.

On his birthday, let's review Paul McCartney's incredibly prolific career.

The term "instant classic" gets thrown around a lot, but there was no debate that Paul McCartney had almost immediately changed public perception of himself and Wings. For five weeks, no one could get away from the number one song on the U.S. Billboard Hot 100, and it was eventually awarded the number one pop song of the year at the end of 1976. It caused many of the publications and music writers to eat their previous words, and admit McCartney's songwriting prowess. However, the biggest praise came from the same person that had coined the song's title, and his harshest critic.

Even John Lennon was enamored with the song. His personal photographer, Bob Gruen, said that Lennon took the song personally, seeing it as a direct confession of love to him from his former writing partner. There are many theories that the song even lit a fire under Lennon to write "(Just Like) Starting Over," his own version of a sappy song designed for radio play.

After the stress of being one of The Beatles, it was evident that Paul McCartney just wanted to find his love of music again with his solo work and Wings. And in trying to just have fun, too many people forgot about the powerhouse penmanship behind hits like "Yesterday" and "Hey Jude." "Silly Love Songs" was a statement by McCartney, an attempt to brush off some of the chips on his shoulder and remind those very critics that he still has the fastball.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.
