#3471. 10 Shows Like 'Cyberpunk: Edgerunners' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following the dramatic conclusion of Cyberpunk: Edgerunners way back in 2022, the show has returned for a new season set in the megalopolis of Night City with a standalone story and a new cast of characters (by necessity).

Though the aesthetic and themes of cyberpunk have their roots in American science fiction of the 1970s and '80s, anime and manga of the '90s and beyond embraced the form and took it to entirely new places—so much so that a Japanese/Polish co-production of an adaptation of a video game from a Polish designer has taken its cues from a couple of decades' worth of great anime and cerebral sci-fi. Which is to say, if you're looking for more heady sci-fi series, these 10 are a good place to start.

An iconic, effortlessly cool genre classic, Cowboy Bebop is one of the undisputed GOATs of anime, blending western, noir, and crime genres and setting the resultant mash to a killer soundtrack of old-school jazz (which serves much the same purpose as Cyberpunk's propulsive electronic grooves). The title's "cowboys" are bounty hunters in a near-future in which humans have been forced to colonize the solar system after Earth became uninhabitable. Different settings, but both shows offer up ragtag crews with highly dubious fates. Former hitman Spike Spiegel leads his crew on one nearly disastrous mission after another, their standalone adventures all building to a thoroughly memorable climax. Stream Cowboy Bebop on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

This one's set in 22nd-century Japan, with a slick Blade Runner-esque aesthetic and a setup reminiscent of Minority Report. Here, technology exists to measure intentions, so crimes can be stopped before they’ve occurred, at which point the “criminals” are placed into psychological treatment (à la A Clockwork Orange)—or subject to summary execution because their threat potential is too high. That ability to predict behavior bleeds over into every aspect of life: careers and even relationships are determined in large part by the same systems that sniff out criminal intent. Obviously, this is all perfectly fine, and there’s no potential for abuse or miscalculation whatsoever...though there are a couple of warning signs. The first involves a new Enforcer who becomes a potential murderer himself when he miscalculates the extent of a criminal’s potential to do wrong, and, even more significantly, the existence of a criminal mastermind who is somehow invisible to the tech, even as his criminal actions grow more and more elaborate. Stream Psycho-Pass on Prime Video and Crunchyroll.

Created by Tim Miller and with director David Fincher as an executive producer, this animated anthology series is a grab bag of wildly diverse offerings: Each episode is produced by a different international studio, with the only link between them being one of the three words in the show's title. One episode deals with robotic gladiator fights in dystopian London, another finds us under the threat of sentient yogurt, yet another finds an ambitious cat learning to make use of a family's robot helper. Its format dictates that no two episodes are going to have the same premise, but it shares with Cyberpunk an edgy sensibility and stories set in an apocalyptic future, albeit with a dark sense of humor—its four seasons offer up a mix of tech, sex, violence, and gorgeous animation. Stream Love, Death & Robots on Netflix.

One of several completely standalone spinoffs of the wildly influential 1995 film (itself based on the beloved manga series), Stand Alone Complex requires no prior knowledge. The style is largely the draw, as the series luxuriates in its fictional Nihama City setting, a world unto itself in a future Japan in which cybernetic people hack directly into the internet. Our sympathies are more with the authorities—in this case, Public Security Section 9, a cybercrime and antiterrorism police unit—than the cyber criminals, but the show approaches some of the same themes as Edgerunners with legit punk style. Stream Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex on Tubi and The Criterion Channel.

In this adaptation of the Richard K. Morgan cyberpunk classic of the same name, Joel Kinnaman and Anthony Mackie (yes, both of them) star as Takeshi "Tak" Kovacs. In this future megacity setting, human consciousness can be transferred between bodies. The tech is widely available, but only the wealthy can afford the backups and protections that make it a form of virtual immortality. Kovacs is a former soldier turned mercenary, revived from a backup after 200 years by Laurens Bancroft (James Purefoy), one of the wealthiest men alive. His motives for bringing the man back are shrouded in mystery, but he's giving Tak a chance to solve a very cold case: his own murder. Stream Altered Carbon on Netflix.

Another popular (and Emmy-winning) game adaptation, Arcane is based on League of Legends, a top-down actioner involving online opponents shooting lasers across a map. It doesn't sound like fodder for a show this impressive, but here we are. The League of Legends lore forms the backdrop for the show, but the pull is in the narrative involving two sisters caught up in the growing conflict between a utopian city and its oppressed underclass, without whom it couldn’t exist. The painted animation style is truly something special—not a stylistic match for Cyberpunk, but the two shows both go far above and beyond to create striking visual worlds. Stream Arcane on Netflix.

Vash the Stampede is a hunted outcast with a dark history that slowly comes to light over the course of the series. He’s got a reputation as a human wrecking ball, bringing destruction wherever he goes, and seemingly just for fun—but in reality he’s far more respectful of life than his pursuers. Still, cities evacuate at the mere possibility of his arrival, and a huge bounty sits on his head (no matter that the bounty hunters do far more damage than Vash). He and his friends—actually a couple of insurance agents—find themselves in a series of misadventures on the planet Gunsmoke, building to a final showdown that caps the series with finality. Visually, it’s probably one of the defining ‘90s shōnen-style action series, with elegantly choreographed gunfights that never get old. Tonally similar, Trigun also shares with Cyberpunk 2 the work of legendary composer Tsuneo Imahori, his music being crucial to both shows. Stream Trigun on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

Another from animation studio Trigger, Darling in the Franxx leans heavily into the mecha sub-genre, set in a post-apocalypse where children are bred and indoctrinated into piloting the title's massive Franxx to defend the remnants of humanity. Adults are pretty much immortal, so the kids simply don't have any other utility. Two of these teens begin to develop romantic feelings for each other, potentially complicating their usefulness to society and leading to an explosive, bittersweet finale. Stream Darling in the Franxx on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

What starts out as a relatively straightforward action show about space bounty hunters (the title's “Killjoys”) develops surprising depth over the course of its five seasons. As officially sanctioned Killjoys, the trio at the show’s heart (Hannah John-Kamen, Aaron Ashmore, and Luke Macfarlane) are bound to remain politically neutral at any cost. Initially, that’s a way to get them right into the heat of a fight, but as they develop ties of friendship and family in an exploited community, they come to understand the high cost of unchecked wealth and greed, and the ways in which neutrality always benefits the oppressors. The show’s creators make exceptionally good use of a limited budget and offer up some impressive queer rep along the way, a rarity in pop sci-fi. Stream Killjoys on Tubi or buy it from Prime Video and Apple TV.

Another great cyberpunk metropolis: here it's Kansai, an increasingly lawless city run by elite criminals known as Akudama. An ordinary girl, quite inadvertently, becomes caught up in a major planned heist and is forced to fake credentials as a master swindler in order to stay alive. Like Cyberpunk, the show tackles anti-authoritarian themes among a diverse crew of outsiders. Stream Akudama Drive on Cunrchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

#3469. D.C. Shooter Killed At Least One Person and Himself, Identified as ER Doctor

The man who shot several people in D.C. killed one person and later himself has been identified as an emergency room doctor ... who was locked in a dispute with his homeowners' association.

The shooter, Dr. Matt Lambert, opened fire Thursday morning in the VIDA Fitness gym next door to his building, where he killed 1 person and injured 4 others.

He reportedly then went upstairs and barricaded himself inside his 7th-floor apartment before killing himself.

Lambert had sued Metropole Condominium Association last year, claiming he had black mold in his million-dollar apartment that he believes was caused by repairs to the building.

According to the New York Post, an X account called OfMiceandMold -- reportedly connected to Lambert -- had been documenting his ongoing battle with the HOA.

The account shared a chilling post Thursday where he wrote ... "My manifesto is an engineering report" and included screenshots of the document.

Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.

D.C. officials say they're investigating the ongoing battle with the HOA as a possible motive for the deadly shooting.

Ward 2 Council Member Brooke Pinto told NYP that information seems to suggest Lambert had been targeting someone in the gym he' "been in active litigation with over a condo issue."

She said ... "It’s just so sad and so senseless to kill someone over a dispute that should be worked out reasonably."

According to WUSA 9, police spent an hour trying to get Lambert to surrender peacefully before he turned the gun on himself.

#3467. Apple launches $50 ‘intelligence usage packs’ for select AI features

Apple has said it will eventually charge for expanded usage of select AI features. Now the first ‘intelligence usage packs’ have arrived tied to Apple Creator Studio apps. Here are the details.

It’s common for AI services to offer limited free access then sell a paid subscription if you need more. Until now though, all Apple Intelligence features have been available free on Apple devices. The company has said that won’t be the case forever, however.

And now, Apple has officially launched its first take on charging for AI features via the new Logic Pro update—with more coming soon.

With Logic Pro’s latest update, if you select Logic Pro from the menu bar, then ‘Intelligence Features’ and ‘Show Usage,’ there’s an option to ‘Buy More Usage.’

The only option is a $49.99 one-time purchase of an ‘intelligence usage pack.’

Unlike most other AI offerings, which depend on subscriptions, Apple is (at least initially) selling expanded AI access through these $50 one-time purchases. Per Apple’s website:

Right now the only app that lets you buy additional AI usage is Logic Pro, but when the rest of the already-announced Apple Creator Studio updates debut this month, usage packs are expected to be available in Final Cut Pro, Pixelmator Pro, and the iWork suite as well.

Another squid tentacle gorging on our bank accounts. They are going to need some compelling ai features that don't hallucinate to ever get me to sign on.

For now, these usage packs are limited to Creator Studio apps. But we’ll likely see a similar model arrive for expanded access to other server-based AI features like Siri AI, Image Playground, Photos editing tools, and more in the future.

Full terms and conditions for AI usage packs are available here.

Hargitay told Variety the milestone has been emotional ... recalling a celebratory dinner with the cast and crew where creator Dick Wolf toasted the show's historic run.

With paychecks like that, it's no mystery why she's still on the case.

#3465. 8 Most Perfect Sitcoms of the Last 30 Years, Ranked

The sitcom genre is rife with some of TV's most unforgettable and entertaining watches, and over the last 30 years, viewers have been well-fed with an incredible variety of comedic masterpieces that have introduced iconic characters, redefined television humor, and delivered countless memorable moments that continue to keep audiences fantastically captivated even decades later. While the list is quite long, only a select few sitcoms have managed to stand out as perfect examples of the genre.

TV series like HBO's Veep, which turns the world of American politics into a nonstop series of embarrassing moments, and the long-standing audience favorite, The Office, which transforms the ordinary environment of a paper company into laugh-out-loud funny workplace comedy, are just two sitcoms that prove that over the last 30 years the genre has delivered brilliantly written and endlessly entertaining gems. Compiled on this list are such gems, sitcoms that effortlessly stand among TV's comedic masterpieces of the last thirty years.

This underrated sitcom is an entertaining combination of youthful energy and heartfelt parenting moments, giving it a special charm that allows the show to remain incredibly enjoyable even decades later. The Black sitcom One on One follows a single father, Flex Washington (Flex Alexander), whose comfortable bachelor life comes to an end when his teenage daughter moves in with him.

One on One is an early 2000s sitcom that captures the complicated but entertaining relationship between father and daughter pretty well. It's a show that is often outshined by bigger hits like Martin, Family Matters, and The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air, but it does deserve its flowers for offering audiences real humor and genuine warmth with a fun, familiar comedic premise. One on One even avoids relying on exaggerated situations just for comedy, instead finding humor in recognizable struggles between fathers and their daughters. It's an underrated gem that definitely stands as a worthy contender among some of the most entertaining sitcoms of the past three decades.

Archer stands as an outstanding animated sitcom of the last 30 years because it effortlessly blends ridiculous workplace comedy with the glamorous world of espionage. The series centers on elite spy Sterling Archer (H. Jon Benjamin), whose competence with fieldcraft and weapons is offset by recklessness, narcissism, and a catastrophic relationship with his mother and boss, Malory Archer (Jessica Walter).

Archer is a pretty underrated series—one worthy of the praise it's received. Its earlier seasons have achieved extraordinary verbal precision, offering viewers brilliantly timed jokes, razor-sharp dialogue, and an almost effortless ability to turn even the most ridiculous situations into pure comedic gold. What makes Archer especially impressive is how seamlessly its absurd humor works alongside its unforgettable characters, their constant bickering, and dysfunctional relationships, making it a great pick for this list of well-crafted sitcoms of the last three decades.

This HBO comedy is one of the most ruthless and verbally inventive shows ever made. Veep focuses on the vice president, Selina Meyer (Julia Louis-Dreyfus), whose desperate attempts to gain influence frequently result in mortifying disasters as she gradually realizes proximity to power can be more humiliating than possessing no power at all.

Veep is an exceptionally well-written series with vicious humor that has been dubbed one of TV's sharpest political comedies. In fact, the show is quite frequently praised as one of the clearest demonstrations of verbal comic engineering. From insults that are not just detachable one-liners but instead cleverly woven into the political rivalries and characters' relationships, to perfectly timed interruptions, rapid-fire exchanges, and laugh-out-loud uncomfortable conversations, Veep transforms almost every interaction into an opportunity for brilliant comedy. The outstanding show, with its clever writing, fantastic attention to comedic timing, and character-driven humor, makes it a perfectly crafted sitcom of the last 30 years.

Derry Girls is an underrated Netflix sitcom that deserves far more attention than it's received since its debut. Set in 1990s Derry during the Troubles, the series follows the self-dramatizing teenager Erin Quinn (Saoirse-Monica Jackson) and her friends, the anxious Clare Devlin (Nicola Coughlan), fearless Michelle Mallon (Jamie-Lee O’Donnell), cousin Orla McCool (Louisa Harland) and Michelle’s English cousin James Maguire (Dylan Llewellyn), as they navigate family expectations, school, friendship, and constant embarrassment.

Derry Girls absolutely refuses to make historical violence the sole subject of its story, yet somehow the series never allows viewers to forget that it's happening. The show is actually an extremely clever series that wields a combination of dark humor, raw writing, and a Northern Irish setting. Derry Girls is a truly rare gem that delivers jokes with confidence and speed—a genuinely overlooked sitcom featuring brilliantly performed comedy and a recognizable cultural setting, making it one of TV's most memorable shows in its genre over the last three decades.

Four Netflix characters, four completely different ways of showing up for somebody. This is the one who fits how you actually do friendship, and what having them in your life would be like.

You do not do friendship at half volume, and neither does he. What you want is somebody who says yes to the plan before you have finished describing the plan.

You are the friend who makes things happen, and so is she. Together you would be mildly exhausting to everyone around you and completely delighted with yourselves.

You have no patience for pleasant lies, and she has no ability to tell them. What looks like coldness from the outside is the most reliable friendship on this list.

You look after whoever is having the worst day. So does he. It is the least strategic way to move through the world and the best possible quality in a friend.

This recently made sitcom is a fantastic reboot of the 1987 hit series, and it has definitely begun to make its mark. The Netflix 2026 sequel, A Different World, centers on the daughter of the beloved characters, Dwayne Wayne (Kadeem Hardison) and Whitley Gilbert (Jasmine Guy), Deborah Wayne (Maleah Joi Moon), as she begins her own journey at Hillman College.

A Different World is an enticing mesh of contemporary student experiences and nostalgic connections. It's already very well-loved as a standout modern sitcom, praised for its lovable cast and relatable scenes. Rather than simply relying on familiar faces, the show instead uses its original legacy as the foundation for meaningful conversations and new comedic situations, offering something unique to this new batch of viewers tuning in. A Different World may be stemming from a truly beloved sitcom of the past, but it still manages to carve out its own place among the best of the best sitcoms.

Tittering on the thin line between sitcom and fun-filled drama, The Good Place brilliantly balances hilarious comedy with thought-provoking questions about life, morality, what it truly means to be a good person, and heartfelt storytelling. The series focuses on Eleanor Shellstrop (Kristen Bell), who dies and wakes up in the presumed "Good Place," only to quickly realize that she has been confused with a morally superior person and must learn from new friends how to be an actually good individual.

The Good Place somehow transforms moral philosophy into useful sitcom plotting rather than simply using it as decoration. With virtue ethics, utilitarianism, and deontology acting as a strong source for character conflict, while also providing truly hilarious situations, surprisingly emotional moments, and meaningful personal growth, the series is impressively entertaining. Of the last three decades, The Good Place defiantly claims a spot among some of the greatest sitcoms ever made.

The Office is a cherished and enduring sitcom whose characters gradually become far more than the subjects of workplace jokes. The series centers around the manager of the Scranton branch of Dunder Mifflin, Michael Scott (Steve Carell), who has a desperate need to be loved, and usually forces his employees into performances, meetings, and "team-building" exercises that often expose his insecurity more than his so-called leadership.

The Office is honestly one of the most beloved sitcoms to ever make it onto screens. Its standing as the “perfect sitcom,” is less about absolute flawlessness throughout its entirety and more about how it totally redefined mainstream, heartfelt comedy. Few American sitcoms have even come close to influencing modern comedy as significantly as The Office. The mockumentary definitely had a hand in establishing the comedic formula that continues to influence TV today, making it a great pick for this list of sitcoms.

This series is completely overlooked as a brilliant sitcom—one so well written that it turns personal grief, self-destructive behavior, and romantic confusion into a cleverly funny and heartachingly emotional experience that feels both deeply personal and hilariously entertaining. Fleabag follows a woman who is only known as Fleabag (Phoebe Waller-Bridge), a sharp, sexually impulsive Londoner, carrying grief that viewers initially only understand in fragments.

Fleabag is one of those rare finds that is capable of completely blowing away its audience with its depth. It is not only an emotional watch, but also a fantastically hilarious one. Almost every well-crafted joke reveals something about the characters, which often tends to catch viewers off guard, as it also hides much deeper emotions. Fleabag may be an incredibly short series, but one that is definitely deserving of tons of praise—an unconventional sitcom that is a masterful combination of honesty, originality, and comedic brilliance, which places it among TV's finest of its generation.

#3464. Five Smartwatch Heart Rate Zone Hacks Every Runner Should Know

If you've spent any time in or around running culture over the last few years, you've undoubtedly encountered someone preaching the gospel of Zone 2 cardio. Legend has it that easy, conversational effort cardio—also known as cardio that takes your heart rate into "Zone 2"—is the secret to unlocking everything from a bigger aerobic engine to faster race times and even a longer life.

To train by heart rate, you aim to keep your heart rate in the "zone" that gives you the desired workout. The catch is that Zone 2 is easy to get wrong, especially since no one can agree on what it actually means.  Your smartwatch can show you your heart rate, but many recreational runners will still drift into a “gray zone” that's too fast to be truly easy, and too slow to give them a real workout. If you're struggling to hit Zone 2 consistently, there are a few smartwatch hacks that can help.

Pace can be a distraction during easy runs, especially considering all the different variables that affect your effort, like hills, humidity, and general fatigue. A 9:30 mile might be Zone 2 on a flat, cool day and Zone 4 on a hot, hilly one.

Dig into your watch's activity settings (on Garmin, it's Activity > Data Screens; on Apple Watch, the Workout app's metrics layout; on Coros, Polar, and Suunto, similar menus) and put live heart rate zone front and center, ideally as a zone number or colored gauge rather than just a raw bpm figure (though this assumes these zones are accurate—more on that below).

Create an alert when your heart rate goes above or below a target range, delivered as a vibration pattern, a beep, or both. Set the alert for the upper boundary of Zone 2, and you've essentially hired a mini coach who taps you on the wrist whenever you get overzealous. Whenever you hear or feel that buzz, you’ll know you need to ease into a slower jog until your heart rate settles.

Instead of free-running and checking your numbers afterward, build structured workouts that carry the targets for you. In Garmin Connect, TrainingPeaks, Apple's Custom Workout feature, Coros Training Hub, or similar platforms, you can create sessions like "10-minute warm-up in Zone 1, 40 minutes in Zone 2, 5-minute cooldown" and sync them straight to your watch.

During the run, your watch displays the current step, the target range, and whether you're above, below, or in the pocket. Many will automatically advance between intervals and alert you when it's time to shift gears.

Heart rate-based intervals, like 4 x 4 minutes in Zone 4 with Zone 1 recovery, where you don't have to do mental math or check the clock.

Progressive long runs that start in Zone 2 and finish in Zone 3.

Hill repeats, where pace is meaningless but effort matters.

Most watches calculate default zones using a generic formula like 220 minus your age, which can be off by 10 to 20 beats for any given individual. If your zones are wrong, your Zone 2 training isn't Zone 2 training.

Here’s how to fix your watch’s heart rate zones:

Find your true max heart rate. The informal way is to just notice what number you see on your watch when you can no longer speak comfortably; the more formal way is this treadmill test. You can also look through your recent hard efforts, like races, hill repeats, or all-out intervals, and see the highest sustained heart rate you've recorded.

Use lactate threshold heart rate instead. Many watches can estimate this automatically after a few hard efforts, and zones built from threshold tend to be more personalized than ones built from max.

Customize the boundaries. Dive into the heart rate zone settings and input your own numbers. Some runners prefer the "MAF" method (180 minus age, with adjustments) for aerobic base building, and most watches let you set that as a custom range.

Recheck every few months. Fitness changes, and so do your zones.

A screen crowded with cadence, vertical oscillation, ground contact time, running power, and lap pace is a recipe for second-guessing.

Create a dedicated Zone 2 data screen with just two or three fields: current heart rate zone, elapsed time, and maybe distance. Turn off auto-scroll so it doesn't flip to a screen full of numbers you don't need. If your watch supports multiple activity profiles, make a separate "Easy Run" profile with this stripped-down layout and keep a different profile for tempo days and races.

A chest strap (or a forearm or upper-arm optical band) is generally more accurate and responsive than the wrist-based sensor on your watch. For heart rate training, where a few beats can mean the difference between Zone 2 and Zone 3, I recommend buying one. This COOSPO heart rate monitor is one of my favorites, and it's only $31.99.

The bottom line: Your smartwatch can make heart rate training far easier, but only if you set it up to support you rather than overwhelm you.

#3462. Tyra Banks Dishes on Beef with Law Roach After 'Project Runway' Blowup

Tyra Banks isn't letting her recent dust-up with Law Roach on "Project Runway" affect her mood ... instead, she's smiling her way through a convo about it -- and taking credit for Law's impressive career.

We caught up with the model and TV personality Thursday ... and we had to ask her about getting into an argument during Season 22 of the hit show, which aired over the summer.

If you haven't seen the war of words ... the two disagreed over which look was better during a paper towel challenge -- and Tyra accused Law of talking over the other judges.

Tyra says the two haven't spoken since the argument ... but she adds a phone call isn't necessary -- because she knows this is just the way Law is.

She says the world used to see Law as just a designer ... but she knew he'd be a star early on -- since she says he tends to speak in soundbites. She also notes she gave Law his first chance on TV.

Tyra says she's now experiencing the treatment firsthand ... and claims she's actually enjoying it -- laughing off the whole situation.

To be clear, Law has shot down rumors of a feud recently ... though he did say anyone can end up in his crosshairs.

Basically, Tyra's claiming credit for Law ... and we can't imagine the powerful stylist is going to appreciate that much.

The main catch with both devices is the ongoing subscription cost: Live viewing, two-way talk, and basic real-time notifications all work without a subscription, but reviewing saved footage requires a paid plan, starting at $4.99 per month or $49.99 annually for one device; coverage for multiple devices at one location starts at $9.99 monthly or $99.99 annually.

At these prices, the Ring Indoor Cam 2K is perfect for occasional live check-ins, while the Ring Battery Doorbell 2K is better suited to monitoring your front entrance. Buying both makes sense if you already have a Ring plan that covers extra devices.

The Amazon delivery driver who *attempted* a jump on a dirt bike outside Sean Strickland's home says he lost his job after the failed stunt ... adding insult to injury.

The driver, Gordon Da Don, chopped it up with Babcock on Thursday -- just days after a video posted by the UFC's middleweight champ went viral -- and broke down the crazy scene.

Waiting for your permission to load the Instagram Media.

"I was basically at the end of my route. I had five more stops left. I was pulling into this neighborhood, and I saw a dirt bike, and I seen somebody on it, and it happened to be Sean Strickland," Gordon explained.

"I used to ride dirt bikes all the time. I had a dirt bike when I was a little kid. Me and my brothers still go ride the ATVs up there in North Las Vegas. So I was like, 'Yeah, why not.' And then I seen they had a ramp, I never did a ramp before, but I was like, 'Mays well jump the ramp.'"

A short time later, Gordon was flying through the air, and he immediately understood he was in trouble.

#3457. Marvel’s ‘WandaVision’ Trilogy Ended Without Its Original Creator Giving ‘VisionQuest’ a Single Note

2026 has been an exciting year for Marvel fans, and it all started with the release of Wonder Man back in January. Marvel has continued this run of success with new Disney+ entries such as second seasons of Daredevil: Born Again and X-Men '97, but the franchise really picked up steam late in July with the launch of Spider-Man: Brand New Day. The movie grossed over $2.5 billion at the box office and is now one of the highest-grossing feature films of all time. Everything in the last few years for Marvel has been leading to the behemoth event film, Avengers: Doomsday, which is slated for release in theaters on December 18, the same day as Dune: Part Three. The final project before Doomsday was VisionQuest, the series starring Paul Bettany that's now streaming in its entirety on Disney+.

VisionQuest is viewed as the third installment in a trilogy that started with WandaVision back in 2021 and continued with Agatha All Along in 2024. Both of the first two shows were written and created by Jac Schaeffer, who has also been tasked with writing the new Stargate series in the works at Prime Video. However, Marvel enlisted Star Trek icon Terry Matalas to serve as the lead writer and showrunner for VisionQuest, a decision that clearly paid off after the show was a hit with both critics and audiences.

Collider's Maggie Lovitt recently sat down for an episode of Collider's Behind the Scenes series with Matalas to speak about the season finale of VisionQuest, and she asked if he had any conversations with Schaeffer about how to tie up the WandaVision trilogy, or if she had any advice to impart on finishing this story. His answer might shock you:

“No, not at all. I called her early on, right when I got the job, because I wanted to just tell her what an honor it was to do this. I love WandaVision. I saw every episode twice when it came out. I would pop it back on. And the first thing she said is, ‘I don’t want to talk about anything creative. You have your blank canvas here.’ And I thought that that was really generous, you know? She certainly could have [said], ‘Be mindful of X, Y, and Z,’ and she didn’t. She wanted us to go do our own thing. And so, that was that. We had exactly that, a blank canvas.”

Throughout the first season of VisionQuest, fans certainly enjoyed the performances from Paul Bettany and James Spader, who was back playing Ultron for the first time since Avengers: Age of Ultron in 2015. However, there were questions from the first episode about whether Elizabeth Olsen would return as Scarlet Witch after she was last seen at the end of Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness with a mountain being dropped on her. It wasn't until the post-credits scene that Doctor Doom (played by Robert Downey Jr) showed up and revived Wanda to use her power. The Scarlet Witch is expected to play a major role in Avengers: Doomsday, which opens in theaters on December 18.

Check out all episodes of VisionQuest on Disney+ and stay tuned to Collider for more MCU updates and coverage. You can watch Matalas' full episode of Collider Behind the Scenes above.

#3456. Apple Won't Make a Small Phone so This Company Is Stepping In

Big smartphones have long been the norm. It seems many, if not most, of us prefer our smartphones to be akin to tiny tablets. Even Apple's smallest iPhone isn't that small, with a 6.1-inch display. (Compare that to the 5.4-inch iPhone mini it used to sell.) But just because a lot of us like it that way doesn't mean all of us do.

Despite what companies like Apple would lead you to believe, there are plenty of people out there who want their smartphones to be smaller. For some, the iPhone mini was perfect, featuring a design that most could use comfortably with one hand. While the sales might not have been steady enough for Apple to continue producing the mini line, anecdotally, I know quite a few people who would happily keep using iPhones this small, if only Apple would make more of them. Perhaps you know people like this too; maybe you're one of them.

While the rumor mill does not suggest that Apple plans to make a new iPhone mini, that doesn't mean the dream of the tiny smartphone is dead. Enter "Enough Phone," a new device with a humble goal: to create a "small, modern smartphone that's enough."

Enough Phone really does seem small. The company says its upcoming device is 133mm by 64mm, and less than 12mm thick. That's the equivalent of 5.24 inches by 2.52 inches, and less than 0.47 inches thick. It's remarkably similar to the iPhone 13 mini, at 5.18 by 2.53 inches, and 0.3 inches thick. While the Enough Phone might be a tad larger overall, and perhaps noticeably thicker, it's still reminiscent of that "mini" footprint.

The Enough Phone's 5.3-inch display isn't particularly modern, however. While we don't know the display type, we do know that it has a resolution of 1520 x 720, which may look less sharp to anyone coming from the 2340 x 1080 resolution of the iPhone 13 mini. I'd wager that most people interested in a device like this aren't looking for an ultra-sharp OLED display anyway, but it's worth noting here.

As for the Enough Phone's other specs, the company says it plans to pack in a 2.4GHz MediaTek Dimensity 7500 chip with 8GB of RAM, 128GB of built-in storage, though you can expand that with a microSD card (something you don't see on many smartphones these days). The current plan is to ship with a single 50MP Sony IMX766 rear camera, and a 32MP selfie cam, which would be amongst the highest-resolution front-facing cameras on any smartphone. It supports 5G, Wi-Fi 6, and eSIM, with the option to use a physical SIM as well.

Enough is also aiming to make its smartphone more repairable than the competition. While smartphone OEMs have made slight improvements to repairability in recent years, few phones are made to be opened up by the user, and their components replaced. While Enough Phone isn't fully modular, it is designed with easy-to-open screws, and comes with a fully replaceable 3,500 mAh battery. Combined with promised software support through 2032, Enough says this device "should last you into the next decade."

Now, all of these specs are targets, as the phone is currently in the prototype stage. Enough says that final details may change "slightly" during testing. I would at least hope that the dimensions, particularly the screen size, remain the same by launch. What will likely stay the same, however, are the ringtones: Enough says they hired composer Brian Squillance of LAANDS to produce the jingles for its phone, which is a neat touch.

Unfortunately for Apple fans, however, Enough Phone isn't an iPhone. That said, it doesn't have to be an Android phone, either. While you can buy the phone with Android 17 installed, you can also choose to run OdysseyOS, a minimalist "de-Googled" operating system made by SLEKE. Enough says OdysseyOS is meant for "intentional phone use," which might appeal to anyone looking for a phone that's "dumb" as well as small.

Of course, neither operating system is iOS. Unfortunately for Apple users, the only true iPhone options here are to continue using an old iPhone mini, which Apple does still support, or to opt for an iPhone 17e, the smallest iPhone the company currently makes. It's pretty easy to find a used and refurbished iPhone 13 mini for reasonable price; but while they can still run the latest version of iOS, you won't be able to take advantage of all of Apple's newest features. Plus, while there's no telling how long Apple plans to support the 13 line for, it won't support it forever—by iOS 28 or iOS 29, your phone might lose support entirely.

If the promise of a modern mini smartphone entices you, you can back the Enough Phone on Kickstarter today. While the company's $399 "Super Early Bird" reward is already sold out, as of this article, the "Early Bird" reward is still up. That reward costs $449, and includes a glass screen protector pre-installed, a protective case, a USB-C cable, a USB-C to 3.5mm headphone adapter, a hex screwdriver, and green "Founders' Edition" backplate screws. Enough says that the retail price for its phone will be $599 after the campaign, so you can save $150 by backing the phone today—if you're serious about small phones. The Enough Phone is slated for a May 2027 launch.

Karin Slaughter adapts her own novel in this six-episode Peacock series

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Although she has a long way to go before reaching Harlan Coben status, novelist Karin Slaughter creates similarly addictive yet disposable crime thrillers, full of sudden twists and complicated backstory.

I get a similar feeling from watching TV adaptations of both authors’ books, eager to tune in for the next episode but a bit let down when all of the secrets are revealed. That was my response to the first TV series based on a Slaughter novel, the 2022 Netflix hit “Pieces of Her,” and it’s the same for the new Slaughter series, "The Good Daughter."

There’s more emotional depth to Slaughter’s stories than Coben’s, and “The Good Daughter” is anchored by two strong performances from Meghann Fahy and Rose Byrne as estranged sisters Charlie and Sam Quinn. The six-episode Peacock original series, adapted by Slaughter herself from her 2017 novel, is more briskly paced than “Pieces of Her,” although it still gets bogged down in lengthy stretches of exposition.

It deals with some heavy themes, but always in a pulpy, airport-novel kind of way, making it an easy binge despite the dark subject matter.

Set in the fictional Georgia town of Pikeville, “The Good Daughter” shifts between past and present as it tells the connected stories of two terrible incidents involving Charlie and Sam (played as children by Drew Cheek and Audrey Grace Marshall). Their father Rusty (Brendan Gleeson) is a steadfast local defense attorney who frequently incurs the wrath of the corrupt legal system run by the powerful Coin family.

When he angers the wrong people, the Quinns’ house gets burned down, and then they’re attacked by two gunmen in their new home while Rusty is out. The assailants kill Charlie and Sam’s mother, Gamma (Olivia Williams), and the two young girls barely get away.

Decades later, Charlie still lives in Pikeville, working as a defense lawyer alongside her father and separated from her husband Ben (Michael Dorman), an assistant district attorney. She finds herself in the wrong place at the wrong time when she witnesses the aftermath of a shooting at the local high school, and soon she’s deeply involved in defending the shooter, a scared and possibly mentally disabled young woman named Kelly Wilson (Shayna Benardo). After he’s incapacitated, Rusty calls in Sam for help, and she arrives from New York City, where she’s been working as a patent lawyer.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

That’s just some of the set-up for this overstuffed story, which can get a bit unwieldy as it moves back and forth across time periods and works out all of the intricate, overlapping relationships among the characters.

Of course, everyone in town is hiding something, and that includes the Quinns, who have to reveal their own long-buried secrets while searching for the truth about what actually happened at the high school, where the principal and one student were shot dead.

In the hands of lesser actors, “The Good Daughter” could have come across as low-rent exploitation, but Fahy and Byrne find the honesty and vulnerability in their characters, and the show succeeds as a story about sisters learning to trust and care for each other again.

As the present-day story begins, Charlie and Sam haven’t seen each other in 10 years, and Sam initially intends to spend only a day in town to help Rusty get back on his feet. But the more they’re together, the more they renew their connection, while also pushing each other’s buttons.

Fahy and Byrne have convincing sisterly chemistry, and it’s easy to believe that these people care deeply for one another and also carry deep resentment. The family dynamic is ultimately more engaging than the mystery of the school shooting, and the resolutions of the past and present storylines aren’t tied together as closely as might be expected.

Both Charlie and Sam are holding onto issues from the day their mother was murdered, and those revelations are cathartic, while the solution to the present-day mystery just feels like wrapping up loose ends.

Once the pieces start to fall into place, it’s not difficult to see where the story is going, and the final episode offers a string of long explanations that clear up every little question. Like the many Coben shows, “The Good Daughter” is both complicated and superficial, and it’s unlikely to linger in viewers’ minds for long.

That doesn’t mean it isn’t worth the time, though, especially for Coben fans or anyone who enjoyed seeing Fahy in fellow beach-read adaptations “The Perfect Couple” and “Sirens.” I was never hesitant to press play on the next episode, but I also found it easy to walk away at the end.

“The Good Daughter” premieres Nov. 12 on Peacock

Tolkien is never going to be an easy job, particularly when you're dealing with a story that spans thousands of years, introduces entire civilizations, and features enough characters to populate several television shows. That's the challenge The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power has faced since its debut, with the Prime Video fantasy epic juggling storylines involving Elves, Dwarves, Númenóreans, Harfoots, and the increasingly troublesome Sauron. While the series has certainly never lacked ambition, keeping all those moving parts together hasn't always been straightforward. And now, one of the people responsible for bringing Middle-earth to television has acknowledged that the show may have been asking a little too much of its audience.

Speaking exclusively with Collider's Maggie Lovitt for an episode of our Behind the Scenes series, The Rings of Power co-showrunner Patrick McKay admitted that the first two seasons occasionally tried to juggle too many storylines, revealing that Season 3 has been deliberately designed to bring the narrative into sharper focus. Rather than continuing to expand the show's enormous collection of characters and subplots, McKay and fellow showrunner J.D. Payne have made Sauron's creation of the One Ring the central event around which everything else revolves. He told Collider:

"You would think that would be one of the real challenges of this show, but actually, the challenge is trying to keep it small. J.D., my co-showrunner, and I have imaginations that we don't know how to stop. They are these waterfalls of ideas, and really we're constantly trying to focus them and make sure we're not asking too much of an audience. I think there were times in prior seasons that, just being our own harshest critics, we realized looking back we were juggling too many balls.

We were asking the audience to juggle too many balls. We're so close to it; it makes perfect sense to us. But one of the things this season we really tried to do is focus it. This is the season where Sauron makes the One Ring. Everything should tie into that. And if it doesn't, even if it delights us, maybe that's not the time for that story."

It's a wild admission to make, but it's one that makes a lot of sense, because the One Ring is, well, the One Ring. And it should be the focus of a show called The Rings of Power. The decision to focus the third season around the One Ring also reflects the show's broader approach to adapting Tolkien's Second Age, which contains major historical events separated by enormous stretches of time.

"We looked at the text, we looked at the history of this particular era of the mythology, and there were these series of events that to us felt like they could lead one right into the next, right into the next, and build momentum with an audience the way that a serialized show should," explained McKay. "And then really the work that we do is taking those fixed points, whether it's the forging of the One Ring — that's a big moment this season — or it's Pharazôn bringing a massive Númenórean army to Middle-earth — that's a big moment this season — and there's others. And then it's about, 'How do we make those feel like earned emotional turns in a story rather than fixed historical events, if that makes sense?'" He went on to say:

"We want to bring audiences to it who maybe aren't anticipating those moments or don't know that they're going to come. If you're a Tolkien superfan and a lover of the books and a scholar of the lore, in theory, there's all kinds of things in every episode that you're responding to and picking out that we're dangling there, whether it's an Easter egg or a huge historical moment, like you're saying. But also, for my mother, who's never really gotten Lord of the Rings, it's not her thing, it should play like a novel does, where it's an emotional experience even if it wasn't in Middle-earth."

The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 is streaming on Prime Video. #3447. Yella Beezy Asked Judge to Block 3-Way Jail Call About Mo3's Murder From Being Used As Evidence

Before Yella Beezy was found guilty of hiring a hitman to kill Mo3 ... he asked a judge to block a three-way jail call involving the man who gunned down Mo3 from being used as evidence in his trial unless prosecutors specifically asked the judge outside of the jury's presence and got permission to admit it first ... TMZ has learned.

In court docs, obtained by TMZ, Beezy's legal team had argued that the call that happened just hours after the shooting -- which included Kewon White, who was allegedly paid $40,000 by Beezy to kill Mo3 -- was inadmissible hearsay.

They also claimed the other two callers -- Dallas County Jail inmate Darius Fields and Nyreon Beasley -- were not alleged to be co-conspirators of the Nov. 2020 killing.

According to the filing, Fields told Beasley during the call that he heard that Beezy -- real name Markies Conway -- "put 50 on that n****," referencing the bounty on Mo3's life.

Beezy says when White was merged into the call, and Fields brought up the rumor again, White laughed and responded ... "That b**** is hell. That n**** just don't know."

Since Fields and Beasley were not co-conspirators, Beezy's lawyers insisted the fact they repeated street rumors amounted to hearsay that could not be admitted in the case.

They also argued a conspiracy ends once its objective is achieved ... and conversations about a conspiracy are only admissible after the fact if they are related to covering it up.

While White is a co-conspirator, Beezy's legal team says that he didn't try to recruit anyone during the call or make any efforts in the chat to try to conceal the murder ... and he didn't admit to killing Mo3 or receiving money from Beezy.

The judge agreed to Beezy's motion, but Beezy and White were both found guilty of murder and sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole.

High-end Garmin vs. flagship Apple Watch: Which will win?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I walked exactly 6,025 steps (manually counted) with the Apple Watch Series 12 on my left wrist and the Garmin Venu X1 on my right wrist to find out which is the more accurate fitness tracker.

I also logged my walk using the Strava app on my iPhone 16 Plus as a control for pace, distance, and climb. Read on to find out which of these two top-tier smartwatches came out on top, along with five takeaways from the workout data.

But first, how does the Apple Watch Series 12 stack up against the Garmin Venu X1 in terms of specs, features, and price? Apple's latest flagship starts at $399 for the small (42mm) non-cellular model.

The Garmin Venu X1 is a more premium device, with a starting price of $699, which technically makes it more of a direct competitor to the Apple Watch Ultra 4 than the Series 12.

Even so, both models sport bright, well-saturated displays, slim, sleek all-metal cases, and state-of-the-art heart rate trackers, multi-band GPS antennas, and barometric altimeters.

This is to say, when it comes to logging a basic walking workout, both the Apple Watch Series 12 and Garmin Venu X1 should be more than well-equipped to record my efforts with best-in-class precision. But is that actually the case? Check out the data for yourself below.

The Garmin Venu X1 packs nearly all of Garmin's best training features into a super-sleek all-metal case equipped with a stunning AMOLED touchscreen.

The Apple Watch Series 12 features the brand's latest heart rate sensor, support for lots of new holistic metrics and trend reports, a bright display, a comfortable case, and access to the world's largest smartwatch app store.

With step count being our primary grading metric, the Garmin Venu X1 decisively beats the Apple Watch Series 12. For any walk tests of this distance, I consider a step count tally within 100 steps of the actual count to be excellent and within a reasonable margin for error.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The Garmin Venu X1 meets the mark, overcounting by a forgivable 51 steps. The Apple Watch 12, on the other hand, overcounted by a much more notable 391 steps, a result that ultimately surprised me.

After all, in recent walk tests with the Apple Watch 12 vs. the Fitbit Edge and again vs. the Garmin Forerunner 170, the Series 12's step count total was pretty much right on the money.

For what it's worth, Strava's step count total of 6,032 was the closest of the bunch.

Apple and Garmin noted similar uphill effort, within five feet of each other, during my ~55-minute walk. However, these tallies appear to be somewhat inflated, assuming, of course, Strava's elevation data is correct, which seems likely, though not certain.

I say this because in past testing, the Garmin Venu X1 has proven time and again to be an incredibly reliable elevation tracker. The Apple Watch 12, on the flip side, does occasionally exaggerate uphill efforts.

Strava logged a little more distance than both the Apple Watch and Garmin — by about a tenth of a mile — and a quicker elapsed pace. And while Garmin's average elapsed pace is the slowest of the bunch, the Venu X1's moving pace metric is nearly identical to Strava's.

Garmin logged an average moving pace of 16 mins 18 secs per mile, not too far off from Strava's 16 mins 11 secs pace. Note: Apple doesn't log moving pace.

Despite some notable discrepancies in step count, climb, and pace, both the Apple Watch Series 12 and Garmin Venu X1 logged the exact same average and maximum heart rate for my walk.

I can't help but wonder if the outcome has anything to do with both watches being worn on stretchy, nylon straps secured with Velcro. I find this strap style fits more securely and comfortably than the dreadful silicone pin-and-buckle alternatives. Better fit = better heart rate data.

Finally, the Venu X1 used 1% more battery than the Series 12 to log my nearly one-hour walk. And even though Apple's climb and elapsed-pace metrics are a little closer to the control, the Garmin Venu X1 wins this head-to-head comparison with a closer total step count, distance, and moving-pace metrics.

Up next, I plan to test the Garmin Venu X1 against the Apple Watch Ultra 4 to see if it can pull off a repeat win. Until then, which smartwatches would you like me to test head-to-head next? And between the Garmin Venu X1 and Apple Watch 12, which do you prefer? Let me know below.

I’ve been on a Pelican kick this fall. The Pelican Protector Magnetic Money Clip Wallet is really helpful is you want something rugged, but also supports holding cash.

MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

Most magnetic wallets are a simple card sleeve and nothing else. If you carry a few $5 bills for tips, cash-only places, etc., you end up folding them around a card and hoping they don’t slip out. The Pelican Protector Magnetic Money Clip Wallet has a stainless steel money clip on the outside of the wallet, so the cash rides on the back, where you can access it without pulling your credit cards out. It’s the same hard-shell construction as the rest of Pelican’s lineup, with the same MagSafe magnets.

The wallet holds up to five cards, which is just about perfect for my use cases. That covers my Driver’s license, debit card, and a few credit cards. Two things to know going in with this wallet. Five cards plus a clip of cash makes for a thick back on your phone, so this isn’t a very slim wallet. If you’re replacing a money clip, you are basically combining the two into one.

If you never carry much cash, the original Pelican wallet is the better pick. If you do want to carry a bunch of cash, the Pelican Protector Magnetic Money Clip Wallet is an awesome pickup.

#3444. Three Ways to Avoid CAPTCHA Prompts When Using a VPN

VPNs make it harder to track your online activity across websites, but it also makes them suspicious about your origins. When you borrow an IP address that hundreds of other people are also using for any number of reasons, you’re much more likely to get repeat verification requests from online firewalls.

CAPTCHAs are simple puzzles that websites use to filter out bots and spam. They’re supposed to be easy for people but hard for robots, such as simple object recognition tasks or audio-visual challenges. However, they can still disrupt your browsing experience if they happen too frequently.

Most modern CAPTCHA providers, like Google's reCAPTCHA v3 or Cloudflare Turnstile, start working long before they give you a puzzle to solve. It usually starts with a risk score that studies your IP address, browser and device signals, or recent online activity.

If the CAPTCHA provider can’t confidently identify your request as human based on those signals, it requests that you complete a puzzle before deciding if the request should be blocked. That means when you get repeat CAPTCHA requests, there’s something affecting your browser’s risk score. For example, popular VPN servers spread the same IP address across any number of users, which can easily make a website mistake you for a bot farm. If you change your IP address frequently by switching servers often, that might look suspicious too.

Luckily, there are ways to deal with frequent CAPTCHA requests using tools and services available with your browser and VPN. Cloudflare has already cut its CAPTCHA requests by 91% using its Managed Challenge platform. Apple has also been shipping token-based verification on devices since iOS 16 and macOS Ventura. In June 2026, Cloudflare even announced a joint effort called the Private Access Control Tokens (PACT) standard with Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Shopify.

While there’s no direct off switch for CAPTCHAs, you can use different fixes to improve your browser’s trust signals when using the internet. That way, you’re less likely to be hounded by verification requests.

The easiest fix for repeat CAPTCHAs is to stop connecting to whichever server your VPN app picks automatically. Proton recommends choosing servers with lower traffic load. In fact, its apps display load as a percentage to help you avoid the most crowded options. I'd also skip big traffic hubs like New York or London, since that's where most traffic originates from. Servers in smaller cities located nearby are often just as fast but never as populated.

You should also avoid changing IP addresses too frequently, which can look suspicious on its own. Pick a server that seems to behave well, then continue using it for at least one session. Also remember you’re more likely to get premium server options if you’re on a paid VPN plan. Major platforms like ExpressVPN, Surfshark, Proton, and Nord are particularly likely to have a larger server collection to pick from.

Costs nothing more than your current subscription

Hopping between servers often can backfire

Private Access Tokens (PAT) let you verify the authenticity of your request using your device rather than an IP address. Apple calls it Automatic Verification, where an Apple server validates your device and Apple Account to assign you an anonymous token.

To enable Automatic Verification on an iPhone or iPad, go to Settings > [your name] > Sign-In & Security > Automatic Verification. On a Mac, open System Settings > [your name] > Sign-In & Security > Automatic Verification.

Unfortunately, there’s no equivalent feature for Windows, Android, and Linux users. That said, Cloudflare offers the Silk extension for Chrome, Firefox, and Edge that serves a similar function. A quick look at the ratings will tell you it’s not as effective, but Cloudflare’s upcoming cross-browser standard called PACT seems promising once it is released.

Doesn’t share personal details with websites

Chrome and Firefox extensions can be unreliable

If you pay a bit extra for a dedicated IP add-on, VPN providers can assign you a unique IP address that isn’t shared with anyone else. For example, NordVPN offers dedicated IPs in 30 countries for $2-5 a month and Surfshark charges $3.75 a month for it.

There are also dedicated providers like Private Internet Access, which charges $3.99 per month for a zero-trust setup so not even their employees know which IP address is assigned to you. On the other hand, Proton VPN offers dedicated IPs only to business plan users, so you’ll need to be on the Workspace Standard, Premium, or Enterprise plans to get one.

That said, there is a trade-off here too. NordVPN itself admits that a dedicated IP makes it easier to link online activity back to a single user. Also, many websites can still tell that the IP address originated from a VPN data center rather than a consumer’s device.

Get unique IP addresses with pristine reputation

Works across desktop, mobile, and even smart TVs

Also functions as an allowlisted address for work

Add-ons cost more on top of the VPN subscription

Offers less anonymity than shared VPN servers

Don't forget to mouse-proof these forgotten areas in your home

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I can usually cope well with most common household pests (spiders are a breeze) — but I absolutely draw the line at mice or any other rodent. And since the colder weather marks the onset of 'peak rodent season', I've made a point of mouse-proofing my home and gathering all the essential supplies to keep mice away.

Not only are these rodents notoriously hard to get rid of, but they can cause severe damage to your building's structure and property.

Yet in my bid to remove the obvious things that attract rats and mice to your home, it turns out I had completely missed several unexpected entry points.

According to pest experts, these particular entry points frequently go unnoticed — so let my surprise serve as your lesson: here's what you need to look for.

While I typically focus my mouse-proofing efforts on inspecting baseboards and ground-level entryways, I don’t ever think to look up. However, the roof is one of the most overlooked and surprising access points where mice can enter your home.

“The roofline is probably the most underestimated entry point,” states Ed Dolshun, Vice President of Business Development and Technical Director at Catchmaster.

“Homeowners instinctively look at ground level, but mice climb — walls, utility wires, tree branches — and enter from above. Roof rats are commonly found along piping, fences, and shrubbery, working their way up rather than in from the ground”.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

To prevent rats from entering through your exterior walls or roof, you need to seal off gaps with steel mesh or hardware cloth combined with sealant to block any holes.

What’s more, to keep mice from scaling your walls, make climbing as difficult as possible by trimming back high shrubs, overgrown tree branches, and other nearby vegetation.

Another forgotten place we often overlook is the small gaps under garage doors and sheds. “A gap as small as a quarter inch along the bottom seal is enough for a mouse to squeeze through,” says Dolshun. “Most people assume their garage door closes tight, though many don't”.

So how small could the gap be for a mouse to sneak its way in? “This is the detail that tends to surprise people most: a mouse needs a gap roughly the size of a dime to get in, and a rat needs only a quarter-sized opening,” adds Dolshun.

A mouse needs a gap roughly the size of a dime to get in, and a rat needs only a quarter-sized opening.

“And critically, if a rodent can fit its head through an opening, it can work the rest of its body through. That should change how you think about inspecting your home because you're not looking for obvious holes, but rather anything that small.”

Similarly, seal gaps and cracks around doors and windows with caulk or mesh wool.

Also, ensure that leaf piles and plant debris are regularly raked clear from entryways. Allowing these to accumulate creates an inviting, warm shelter where rodents can easily hide and dwell during the colder months.

So if you want to make your home completely mouse-proof, don’t miss these common overlooked areas — or else you may have to call in the pest experts in the long run.

#3438. Apple to open new Developer Center in Istanbul as part of broader Turkey investment

Apple today announced a long-term investment in Turkey, with seven new facilities focused on app development and manufacturing set to open in the country starting next year. Here are the details.

In a press release issued on its Turkish Newsroom (via MacRumors), Apple today announced a series of long-term investments in Turkey.

The announcement comes as former CEO and current executive chairman Tim Cook visits the country, as he’s been sharing on X.

Merhaba Istanbul! What a stunning view from the Grand Bazaar this morning alongside talented creator Cem Başak. Thrilled to visit this remarkable country! pic.twitter.com/c4daBBXe1l

The company’s investment in Turkey will be three-pronged, with the opening of five new Apple Developer Academies, one Apple Developer Center, and one Apple Manufacturing Academy.

Apple says it will open five new developer academies across Turkey over the next three years, with the first opening in Istanbul in 2027, alongside its new developer center. The Apple Manufacturing Academy, meanwhile, is set to open in Ankara in 2028.

Here’s Cook commenting on today’s announcement (translation ours):

“Apple has been serving our customers and communities in Turkey for 35 years. With this new commitment, we are proud to support the next generation of innovative entrepreneurs in the years ahead. […] Turkey’s developer community is developing apps used around the world. Meanwhile, small and medium-sized businesses stand out as organizations creating opportunities throughout the country. This investment provides developers and businesses with access to the training and resources they need to take their brightest ideas even further, as well as to Apple experts.”

Apple explained that its developer academies will offer “free, intensive nine-month programs focused on coding, design, marketing, project management, and artificial intelligence technologies,” while the developer center “will provide developers, entrepreneurs, and start-ups with a hands-on learning experience by providing access to the latest tools, technologies, and resources, as well as Apple experts and events.”

As for its manufacturing academy in Ankara, which will mark the company’s first Apple Manufacturing Academy outside the US, it will “provide free training and consultancy to small and medium-sized businesses, students and innovative entrepreneurs.”

Led by Apple experts, the curriculum will help participants adopt AI and intelligent manufacturing techniques through courses on machine learning technology, predictive maintenance, advanced automation, and robotics, as well as interactive workshops on lean operations and production efficiency.

#3433. I Played Wendy's RPG, and It's Actually Worth It for the Free Food

November is a huge month for video games. Nintendo dropped its remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Switch 2 last week, and the long-awaited Grand Theft Auto VI is right around the corner. But the game we've been waiting for most of all also launched this month: WendyQuest, the free RPG from Wendy's. (No, this is not a joke.)

Despite the absurdity of a hamburger chain making a full video game (complete with Wendy's-themed puns), the thing is, this game is pretty solid—even if it is a promotion at the end of the day. WendyQuest's main purpose is to offer customers coupons they can use toward purchases in real life, though it's a bit of a commitment. It took me just under an hour of gameplay before I earned my first coupon, and Wendy's says it takes roughly 15 hours to beat. All that to say, this is a pretty unique marketing campaign.

I was surprised booting up WendyQuest on my iPhone. This doesn't necessarily feel like a thrown-together product. On the flip side, the production quality is quite high. The music is solid and very much traditionally RPG; there are even three save slots, in case you plan to return to this RPG again and again.

There's even a story, albeit cheesy (no pun intended): As the game explains, the "Four Great Spirits of Flavor" created Savoria, "a food-rich paradise." All was well until Mech Corp, led by the evil Dr. MechBorg, built robots to take over Savoria. The plot is far from compelling, and the writing can be a little over the top, but hey, I'll give them credit: They thought through a full story here.

You play as Wendy, the "representation of true culinary excellence and taste as dictated by the four ancient spirits of flavor." Wendy (or The Wendy, as some call her) is tasked with saving the world, traveling between villages and picking up new characters along the way. The game world even has "real" Wendy's locations you can visit. These act like inns and shops in other RPGs, giving you a chance to heal while also buying equipment.

Like other RPGs, WendyQuest uses turn-based combat. You have to charge up your attacks, but stop before they hit 100%, or you'll miss. (It took me a while to master the timing.) I'm pretty impressed with how challenging some of these battles can be, though you are quickly given the option of an amulet that gives you a huge leg-up in combat. You don't have to take it, but it makes fights easier if you're only in it for the coupons. That, combined with the spatulas the game encourages you to buy, lets you mow down enemies. You can also utilize your companions here: "Frygor," for example, can either attack enemies with a barrage of fries, or use those fries to build a shield to protect you.

While there are tons of enemies to fight, the key baddies are the "mechs." There are five in total, and after you defeat each, you get a coupon. Spoiler alert: The first mech drops the "Fry Stone," which nets you a coupon for a free order of medium fries—though you need to buy something in tandem, as well as use the Wendy's app. While I stopped my gaming here for this article, the other four coupons are:

Free biscuit or croissant (I didn't even know Wendy's sold biscuits and croissants)

Again, it's wild that WendyQuest has a 10+ hour campaign, with over 1,000 lines of dialogue to boot. I'm not sure this is a game I'm going to see through to the end, but I'll admit, it's a fun marketing approach from Wendy's. Sure, they could have run a promotion in the Wendy's app to give people coupons, but instead, they built an entire RPG. I respect it. You can download the game for iOS, Android, or Steam.

Google's most powerful model yet allows users to do more than ever

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Google has officially launched Gemini 4 Carbon, its most powerful AI model yet, and some of its most interesting capabilities go far beyond what most users have previously done with a chatbot.

The new model is designed to take on complicated projects that require planning, problem-solving and several steps to complete. That could mean building an interactive website, making sense of hundreds of pages of documents or analyzing information that would take hours to sort through manually.

Still, it's worth knowing what Google's latest model can do. Here are five practical ways to put Gemini 4 Carbon to work, along with prompts to get started.

Getting a handle on your finances usually means digging through statements, adding up expenses and figuring out where your money is going. Even with a spreadsheet, it's time-consuming.

Gemini 4 Carbon is designed to analyze dense documents and spreadsheets while keeping track of information across multiple sources. That makes it worth trying for tasks such as comparing monthly expenses, spotting recurring subscriptions and identifying spending patterns.

You could upload sample financial data and ask Carbon to group your expenses into categories, calculate totals and suggest where you might be able to save. Of course, you'll want to be sure to verify the totals yourself. AI can still make calculation errors, and it's best to avoid uploading sensitive account information.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

Try this prompt: Analyze these three months of household expenses. Categorize every transaction, identify recurring subscriptions and show me where my spending has increased. Create a monthly budget with realistic savings goals and explain which expenses I should review first. Double-check your calculations before presenting the results.

This might be one of the most exciting uses for Carbon, especially if you've ever had an idea for a website but didn't know where to begin.

Google says that Carbon can work through complex coding tasks, design interfaces and check its own work for errors. The company also provides a dedicated AI Studio environment for building full-stack web apps and 3D experiences.

For example, you could ask it to build a family vacation planner that organizes your itinerary, tracks your budget and keeps everyone on the same page.

Instead of spending hours learning to code, you can describe what you want and have Carbon generate a starting point. You can then ask for changes to the layout, additional features or fixes when something doesn't work. For this one, use Google AI Studio's app-building environment, where Carbon can help create and verify a working app.Try this prompt: Build an interactive family vacation planner with a five-day itinerary, packing checklist, budget tracker and countdown to departure. Make it colorful, easy to use on a phone and simple enough for kids to understand. Include editable activities and check that all buttons and calculations work.

Most AI chatbots can explain a math problem or summarize a science lesson. Carbon is designed to go further when a question requires multiple stages of reasoning.

Google says the model has improved capabilities in scientific reasoning, including working through complex problems, exploring different approaches and checking results.

For students, that could mean turning a confusing textbook chapter into a personalized study guide or getting a detailed explanation of a problem rather than simply receiving the answer.It's important to remember that more reasoning doesn't guarantee a correct answer. But Carbon's ability to work through complicated problems could make it useful when a quick explanation isn't enough.

Parents could also use Carbon to create practice questions tailored to their child's grade level. I recently did that to help my middle schooler prepare for a science test. The interactive experience actually made studying fun since it was gamified.

Try this prompt: I'm studying Newton's laws of motion and struggling to understand the difference between force, mass and acceleration. Explain the concepts using everyday examples a seventh grader would understand. Then create five practice questions, starting easy and getting harder. Include the answers separately and explain each solution step by step.

We've all encountered documents that seem to go on forever, whether it's an insurance policy, a research report or the terms of a new service. Knowing what's important and what we can skip is almost impossible when faced with several pages of documentation.

Carbon supports a context window of up to 1 million tokens, allowing it to process large amounts of information within a single request. It can also work with images, audio and video alongside text.

Google says Carbon has improved at grounding responses in source material, particularly when analyzing complicated PDFs, spreadsheets and presentations.

For everyday users, the appeal is straightforward. Instead of spending hours hunting for important details, you can ask Carbon to find the information that matters and explain it in plain English. The ability to trace answers back to their sources is particularly useful here, although you'll still want to check important details against the original documents.

Try this prompt: Compare these two insurance policies and identify the biggest differences in coverage, deductibles, exclusions and out-of-pocket costs. Create a side-by-side comparison table, cite the relevant pages and flag anything that isn't clearly explained. Don't make assumptions about missing information.

You don't have to be a game developer to come up with an idea for a fun game. With Carbon, you can try turning that idea into something interactive.

Google has highlighted the model's ability to work on complex coding projects, including 3D scenes and interactive applications. Carbon can generate code, investigate problems and make revisions as it works toward a finished result.

That opens the door to creating simple browser games, interactive learning activities or even personalized games for kids.Google AI Studio's app-building environment is the best place to start with a project like this. A more ambitious game may still need multiple rounds of adjustments, but you can experiment without writing every line of code yourself.

Try this prompt: Create a colorful browser game where a cartoon cat collects fish while avoiding obstacles. Include three difficulty levels, a score counter, sound effects and a restart button. Make the controls simple enough for a six-year-old to use. Test the game and fix any problems you find.

Gemini 4 Carbon spends more time reasoning and verifying its work, so it's worth noting that it can be slower and use more tokens than Gemini 4 Argon. For writing an email, planning dinner or asking a straightforward question, Argon may be the more practical choice.

For complex projects, though, Carbon offers something more interesting. It gives users a way to take an idea that might otherwise require specialized software, technical knowledge or hours of manual work and see how far AI can get them.
